raw_text: For Kriti, a Gurugram-based marketing professional, Thursday's workday came to an abrupt halt even before it began, as Microsoft services went down globally. With her company relying heavily on Outlook for official sign-offs, the outage stalled its approval pipeline, forcing employees to turn to alternative communication channels and negotiate deadline extensions to keep work moving. “With Outlook inaccessible since morning, external communication has been stalled, delaying roughly half a day’s worth of urgent approvals and project rollouts,” she said. Kriti's experience reflects a wider disruption across enterprises and individuals in India and globally. Microsoft Outlook/Office 365 is used at companies such as Infosys, Wipro, Lupin, CitiusTech, CSS Corp, Indigo, along with banks such as State Bank of India, Equitas Small Finance Bank and others. What Caused The Outage The outage, which began late on November 12, crippled critical functions across Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and several other Microsoft 365 services in 74 countries, including India. By November 13, the disruption was still unresolved. Downdetector data showed Outlook complaints in the country peaking at 2,157 late night on Thursday, easing overnight, then climbing back to nearly 4,000 by 10 AM Friday before settling to over 2,500 by noon. Globally, the monitoring website has detected 1,40,000 complaints. To be sure, over 430 Mn people use Microsoft 365 apps according to the company’s website. The trouble traces back to roughly 11:30 PM IST (6 PM UTC) on Thursday, when a core process responsible for setting up secure connections on Microsoft's servers became overwhelmed. Microsoft said a number of servers began failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which pushed more load onto the machines left standing, a cascade that eventually hit Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, Copilot, Defender for Office 365, Windows 365 Cloud PCs, and even the admin tools IT teams needed to diagnose the mess, such as Intune. Microsoft has attributed this outage to infrastructure failure. By Friday afternoon (November 13), Microsoft was still offering no confirmed timeline for full recovery, describing progress only as "limited." The disruption even reached outside Microsoft's own walls: OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors, a small but telling sign of how deeply the Exchange and Graph APIs are now wired into the newer AI tool stack. India's Slice Of The Downtime For workplaces that rely on Outlook and Teams for daily operations, the outage translated into familiar disruptions: employees unable to access calendars, delayed client responses and teams switching to alternatives such as Slack, WhatsApp and phone calls to stay coordinated. The disruption also spilled over into customer-facing services. IndiGo, India's largest airline, said its email support services had been affected and that it might be unable to receive customer emails. Akasa Air reported delays in its email support services, advising passengers to contact its 24-hour Akasa Care Centre or reach out through social media for immediate assistance. Media reports also indicated disruptions at IT services companies, including Infosys and Cognizant. The impact extended to business operations beyond communication. HR tech startup Keka told customers that the outage had affected services such as offer letter generation, scheduling one-on-one meetings, and interview scheduling and rescheduling. Equitas Small Finance Bank, meanwhile, asked customers to use its customer service helpline instead of email to reach the bank. The outage is a reminder of how concentrated enterprise India's software stack has become. A large share of Indian offices run their calendars, email, files and meetings entirely inside the Microsoft 365 ecosystem, a convenience that turns into a single point of failure the moment Exchange Online wobbles. “Businesses have a disaster recovery plan for servers, networks and data. Very few have one for the inbox, and the inbox is where contracts, approvals and payments actually move. Today's Microsoft 365 outage shows email is a single point of failure that boards have never had to sign off,” said Amit Singh, practice head for managed services at WeP Solutions. It is also not an isolated event. Microsoft's service-health page has logged a string of outages through 2026 alone, touching Azure, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365 at various points in January, May, June, July, August and October, well before this week's episode. Each one has drawn fresh scrutiny of how much global and Indian enterprise IT now leans on a small number of hyperscale providers. That scrutiny is starting to translate into advice: analysts are increasingly telling Indian enterprises to treat multi-vendor redundancy as a backup email client, an alternate collaboration tool, contracts that do not assume round-the-clock uptime as a baseline requirement rather than a nice-to-have. “My larger concern is not that Microsoft had an outage; outages are inevitable. It is that enterprises have progressively concentrated email, identity, collaboration, security, and now AI into the same cloud ecosystem. We have reduced application complexity, but inadvertently increased dependency concentration,” said Ritwik Batabyal, CTO at Mastek, a Mumbai-based digital and cloud transformation. That is particularly relevant for India, where cloud adoption is accelerating rapidly. The answer is not an expensive multi-cloud copy of everything, but enterprises should identify their few “minimum viable business” capabilities—identity, critical communication, customer transactions and operational control—and ensure these can degrade gracefully or fail independently, he added. On a side note, Microsoft offers uptime credits to eligible Microsoft 365 customers if monthly service availability falls below its contractual commitment of 99.9%. Depending on the extent of downtime, customers may qualify for credits of 25%, 50% or 100% of the monthly fee for the affected service. However, these are credits are subject to few conditions and is applicable only when the customer purchases products sold through the Cloud Solution Provider programme. Microsoft’s Restructuring Microsoft's latest workforce restructuring has also raised questions about whether cost-cutting could have implications for the reliability of its cloud services. The company recently confirmed that around 60,000 employees, or 27% of its global workforce, including those in India, are eligible for a voluntary exit offer, following a separate round of 4,800 job cuts in July. The company employs around 23,000 people in India across various products and roles. However, there is no evidence so far linking the workforce reductions to the Microsoft 365 outage. Microsoft has not attributed the disruption to staffing constraints, and its investigation into the technical cause is ongoing. The larger question is whether aggressive cost optimisation, even as Microsoft ramps up investments in AI infrastructure, could create operational risks for services used by millions of businesses. Already the outage has stretched into its second day, and if it goes on, this could be a real bodyblow to Microsoft and could hand a big piece of the enterprise productivity software business to its rivals.

Bihar flags 1.09 lakh mule accounts holding Rs 72.53 crore linked to fraud cases
According to Bihar Police data for September and October 2026, Patna recorded 14,644 mule accounts, followed by Gaya Ji with 6,172, East Champaran with 4,414, Muzaffarpur with 4,244, Bhagalpur with 4,197 and Nalanda with 4,146.
Bihar Police identified 1.09 lakh mule accounts across all 38 districts of the state under its Cyber Prahar 5.0 campaign, according to a report by news agency Press Trust of India. Patna recorded the highest number of such accounts.
A mule account is a legitimate bank account used by criminals to receive, conceal and launder illegally obtained money. The campaign targeted networks of such accounts across Bihar.
According to Bihar Police data for September and October 2026, Patna recorded 14,644 mule accounts, followed by Gaya Ji with 6,172, East Champaran with 4,414, Muzaffarpur with 4,244, Bhagalpur with 4,197 and Nalanda with 4,146.
West Champaran reported 3,945 such accounts, Siwan 3,859, Rohtas 3,153, Bhojpur 3,144 and Purnea 2,813.
Sheohar recorded the lowest number in the state at 427, followed by Sheikhpura with 813, Lakhisarai with 1,009, Kaimur with 1,222 and Khagaria with 1,330.
The police report also flagged 7,728 accounts that appeared in two or more complaints registered on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. Patna topped this category with 1,111 accounts, followed by Gaya Ji with 437, Nalanda with 360, Bhagalpur with 314 and East Champaran with 278, PTI reported.
The disputed fraud amount linked to the cases across Bihar stood at Rs 72.53 crore. Patna accounted for the largest share at around Rs 13.81 crore, while Siwan accounted for Rs 3.83 crore, Muzaffarpur Rs 3.31 crore and Bhagalpur Rs 2.58 crore.
Separately, data from the portal showed that Bihar recorded 47,659 cybercrime complaints involving fraudulent transactions worth Rs 121.26 crore during the two months. Of this amount, Rs 36.94 crore was put on hold and Rs 8.04 crore was refunded to victims.
The state also registered 876 first information reports and arrested 159 people in connection with other cybercrime and social media-related complaints during the period, according to the report.
Overall, the campaign identified 1.09 lakh mule accounts across Bihar, including 7,728 linked to multiple cybercrime complaints, while Patna reported the highest number of accounts and the largest disputed fraud amount.

For the last few years, Indian commercial cinema has been witnessing an interesting trend. Many of its biggest heroes are angry, aggressive and often morally questionable. They break rules, indulge in extreme violence, deliver intimidating dialogues and take matters into their own hands. Filmmakers have increasingly presented such characters as larger-than-life entertainers, and audiences have often responded enthusiastically.
From KGF and Animal to several other action-packed blockbusters, the formula has proved commercially successful. The louder the hero, the bigger the action and the more ruthless his enemies, the more spectacular the cinematic experience is expected to be. However, amid this trend arrives Ramayana, featuring a leading man who represents almost the exact opposite.
Ranbir Kapoor's Lord Rama doesn't need to scream, intimidate others or constantly demonstrate his physical strength to establish his authority. He is calm, composed, dignified and guided by his principles. And interestingly, audiences have turned up in enormous numbers to watch him.
This raises a fascinating question: In their enthusiasm to create angry and aggressive protagonists, have Bollywood filmmakers underestimated the audience's appetite for traditional heroes?
Perhaps the most striking aspect of Ramayana is the casting of Ranbir Kapoor. His portrayal of Ranvijay in Animal (2023) was built around aggression, violence, obsession and emotional volatility. The character frequently expressed himself through anger and confrontation, and the film became one of the biggest commercial successes of his career.
Three years later, the same actor is playing Lord Rama, a character celebrated for his patience, righteousness, compassion and self-control.
The contrast could hardly be greater.
In Animal, Ranbir's character often seeks to establish his dominance through aggression. In Ramayana, his authority stems largely from his dignity and convictions. His strength is not defined merely by his ability to defeat an opponent, but also by his willingness to exercise restraint.
This is precisely what makes his performance interesting. Instead, he allows the character's inherent qualities to make an impact.
The angry young man is hardly a new phenomenon in Indian cinema. Amitabh Bachchan became a phenomenon in the 1970s by portraying characters who rebelled against injustice and an unfair system.
However, the modern commercial hero has often taken this aggression several steps further. He may be a gangster, a criminal, an outlaw or a deeply flawed individual. His methods can be ruthless, and his moral choices are not always defensible.
Yet, these characters have found tremendous acceptance among moviegoers.
Ramayana offers a useful counterpoint to that assumption.
One of the defining qualities associated with Lord Rama is his ability to maintain composure even when faced with difficult circumstances. He is not portrayed as someone who lacks strength or courage. On the contrary, he is an accomplished warrior. However, his power is accompanied by discipline, responsibility and a strong sense of duty.
This combination makes him fundamentally different from many contemporary screen heroes.
His decision to accept exile, his devotion to his family and his commitment to his principles are essential parts of his character. These moments may not feature spectacular action sequences, but they give the character emotional weight.
Ranbir's comparatively understated portrayal reinforces this contrast. His performance suggests that a hero does not need to be aggressive in every scene to command the audience's attention. In fact, when a character known for his restraint eventually takes a decisive stand, the moment can become even more powerful.
Does Ramayana's success mean audiences are tired of violent films? Not necessarily. It would be incorrect to conclude that the success of Ramayana signals the end of violent or morally grey protagonists. After all, audiences have enthusiastically supported such films, and there is little reason to believe that the genre will suddenly lose its popularity.
Moreover, Ramayana benefits from several advantages that cannot be attributed solely to its protagonist. It is based on one of India's most revered epics, features an ensemble of major stars, offers grand visual spectacle and has benefited from the festive release period.
Nevertheless, the film challenges the notion that aggression is essential for commercial success.
The audience that enjoyed Ranbir Kapoor's angry and unpredictable avatar in Animal has also shown enormous interest in watching him play a restrained and principled character in Ramayana. This suggests that viewers may be more open to different kinds of heroes than the industry's prevailing trends sometimes indicate.
For decades, Hindi cinema has celebrated characters who stand for honesty, kindness, sacrifice and justice. The hero didn't necessarily have to be morally complicated to be compelling. That doesn't mean every modern hero needs to become a model of virtue. Flawed characters are an essential part of cinema, and morally complex stories can be fascinating.
Ramayana serves as an important reminder that commercial cinema doesn't have to follow one formula. There is room for the angry rebel, the morally conflicted antihero and the principled traditional hero to coexist.

Guwahati: Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma will visit the site of the devastating road accident near Kaziranga on Saturday morning and meet the families affected by one of the worst road tragedies in the state. The latest reports said the death toll has risen to 26, while around 20 others sustained injuries. Several of those injured were rushed to hospitals, including the Jorhat Medical College and Hospital, for advanced treatment.
CM Assures All Possible Assistance To Affected Families
The Chief Minister said he would personally visit the accident site to ensure that the affected families receive every possible assistance.
“I will visit the accident site tomorrow morning to meet the affected families and ensure they receive every possible support, from medical care for the injured to relief for those who have lost loved ones. They are not alone in this difficult hour,” Sarma said in a post on X.
The Chief Minister said that the state government stands with the bereaved families and prayed for the victims of the tragedy.
Mini-Bus Collides With Container Truck Near Kaziranga
The horrific accident took place at Rongajan near Kaziranga National Park in Golaghat district on Friday when a passenger mini-bus collided head-on with a container truck on National Highway-715.
Many of the victims were reportedly students returning from their classes. Rediff The collision left the mini-bus badly mangled, prompting a massive rescue operation involving police, district administration officials and local residents.
Initial reports suggested that the passenger vehicle was travelling at a high speed before the collision.
Authorities To Conduct Detailed Enquiry
Authorities have said a detailed enquiry will be conducted to ascertain the exact circumstances surrounding the accident and examine whether traffic and other safety norms were violated.
Sarma had earlier expressed deep anguish over the tragedy and assured the best possible medical treatment for the injured.
His visit on Saturday is expected to focus on reviewing relief measures, meeting bereaved families and assessing the treatment being provided to those injured in the devastating accident.

A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.
Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.
After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.
On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.
The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks from 1969 to 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.
Security footage showed Bertulazzi dropping from a building into a public road as cars drove past.
A detective tracking the former member of the Red Brigades reportedly told La Nación that Bertulazzi rappelled down from the fifth floor using a harness.
“First, he removed his electronic ankle monitor and placed it in a tube filled with pork, along with a blood pressure monitor to maintain the temperature. He then climbed on to a roof and, using a rope, lowered himself five meters until he jumped onto a vacant lot behind the building where he lived, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street,” the detective said, according to the publication.
The footage, which indicated the time was 6.01am on 10 November, showed a possibly shaken Bertulazzi sitting down to rest for a few moments.
Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.
Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

As the nation’s air traffic ground to a halt Friday afternoon amid an FAA ground stop, Ari Emanuel had strong words for former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg.
The WME executive chairman posted on X, “No one’s hands are clean here. However, Mr. Secretary Buttigieg, you had four years in the job and infrastructure money, yet made zero progress modernizing the FAA. You left a failing system in place. THANKS!”
Buttigieg left his post at the end of the Biden administration. Current transportation secretary Sean Duffy addressed the public just after the flight stop was lifted on Friday evening, referencing his demands to Congress for modernization funds. “I can’t build things if I don’t have money,” Duffy said. “We should talk to our senators and members of Congress to say, ‘We don’t deserve this.’”
Duffy said making upgrades was necessary but admitted it may have introduced instability into the air control system. “By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said, adding, “I didn’t anticipate that we would have an outage like this.”
Emanuel’s tweet was quickly answered by more than 3,000 commenters questioning why he was blaming a previous administration. “Yeah let’s blame the guys from 2+ years ago when the FAA has been a burning dumpster fire since Duffy stepped into office,” said one commenter.
Others commented, “Did someone hack your account? Two years into a new administration and no specific evidence yet as to what failed. And your first go-to is blaming Buttigieg?”
Another commenter referenced Ari Emanuel’s brother Rahm Emanuel, who is seen to be angling for a 2023 presidential bid. “I know your goal here is to attack one of your brother’s presidential rivals, but I am certain it will backfire in the eyes of dem primary voters,” the commenter said.
Meanwhile, Buttigieg was stranded at Denver airport, and after watching the press conference from Duffy and Markwayne Mullin, Buttigieg told the New York Times, “You can just write down the comic book asterisk swearing characters,” Buttigieg said. “I have questions.”

Chennai breathes far cleaner air than Delhi. A study that followed 12,064 adults in the two cities put the typical yearly level of fine particles around Chennai homes between 2010 and 2016 at 40.2 micrograms per cubic metre, just above the national standard of 40, against 101.5 in Delhi. In both cities, the dirtier a person’s air, the likelier they were to develop type 2 diabetes.
The World Health Organization’s theme for World Diabetes Day, on November 14 this year, is early action. The sixth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6), carried out in 2023-24, found 17.8% of women and 20.9% of men aged 15 and above had high blood sugar or were on medicine for it, up from 13.5% and 15.6% per cent in NFHS-5, conducted in 2019-21. In Chennai district, nearly 3 in 10 women fall in the group.
That said, there are limitations to this data: NFHS teams prick a finger at whatever hour they visit, so people may or may not have eaten, and a reading above 140 milligrams per decilitre counts as high. One such reading cannot diagnose diabetes. However, what is most routinely blamed for the rising burden of diabetes in the country -- and it is rising -- are weight and diet. And while these are significant factors, dirty air is rarely blamed. Perhaps it’s time it is.
The outdoor evidence
Siddhartha Mandal of the Centre for Chronic Disease Control in New Delhi and his colleagues used satellite and weather data to estimate daily levels of fine particles, called PM2.5, near each participant’s home.
Over a median of almost five years, 743 people developed type 2 diabetes. Each extra 10 micrograms in a person’s yearly average accounted for a 22% higher risk, after the researchers allowed for age, socio-economic status, tobacco and alcohol use, diet and exercise. Studies in richer, cleaner countries have put the rise at 7 to 11%.
A 2024 global review of 46 studies also linked PM2.5 and the coarser PM10 to type 2 diabetes. Its authors point mainly to inflammation and oxidative stress (damage from reactive oxygen), which blunt the body’s response to insulin, the hormone that moves sugar into cells. The Global Burden of Disease project puts about a fifth of the healthy years lost worldwide to type 2 diabetes in 2019 down to PM2.5, about 14% from outdoor air and 6% from household smoke.
Smoke in the kitchen
Between 2018 and 2021, researchers from the Madras Diabetes Research Foundation tested adults in 30 villages of Cheyyur taluk in Chengalpattu district as part of a project called TREND.
All but 208 of the 13,877 adults lived in homes cooking on traditional fuels such as firewood or kerosene. Diabetes was more common among them, 14.2% against 12%, and more common still, 16.5%, in homes without a separate kitchen. Among women, traditional fuel use was linked with 80% higher odds of diabetes of diabetes, after the researchers allowed for age, weight, family history, education and income.
One round of testing, however, cannot prove what causes diabetes, and the group using clean fuel was small. Even so, a 2022 review of nine studies with 45,620 people found that those who cooked with solid fuels had 46% higher odds of diabetes. However, in homes that burned only biomass like wood or dung, the link was too weak to be certain.
Short of gas, short of data
The NFHS used to report cooking fuel and blood sugar from the same homes. Clean fuel, mostly LPG, reached 58.6% of homes in 2019-21, up from 43.8% in 2015-16, as the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana distributed connections. Even at that pace, about 3 homes in 10, mostly in villages, would still have cooked on fuels such as wood, dung and kerosene by 2023-24. The NFHS-6 fact sheets, released on May 29, leave this figure out. The Health Ministry has said this, and other missing statistics are being monitored through dedicated national surveys and administrative databases; however these other surveys do not take blood samples, leaving possible connections unable to be made.
Much of India’s LPG comes from abroad. About 90% of those imports pass through the Strait of Hormuz, which the West Asia war choked in early March, leading to shortfalls across the country. Poor homes, though, used little gas even before the war. The average Ujjwala household bought 4.71 cylinders in 2025-26, and about one in seven in Bihar bought none, the Petroleum Ministry told the Lok Sabha. The ministry has since cut subsidised refills from nine a year to four, about half of what a family cooking only on gas needs, as per figures cited by think tank, the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW).
Every return to the wood stove brings back smoke tied to diabetes, and even a month of dirtier air nudged up blood sugar in the Delhi and Chennai study, a worry for anyone already living with the disease. As long as India’s kitchens depend on imported gas, the next war or blockade can push them back to wood, and more people towards diabetes.
The Kerala puzzle
If dirty air alone drove the numbers, the least polluted States would sit at the bottom of the survey’s tables. A satellite study of 2024 pollution by independent research organisation, the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), put Kerala among the seven States and Union Territories with the cleanest air. Yet Kerala has the highest share of women with high blood sugar of any State or Union Territory, 28.9%, according to NFHS-6. Meghalaya, where CREA found every district above the national pollution standard outside the monsoon, has the lowest of any State, 7.1%. Kerala also has the oldest population of any State, and diabetes grows more common with age. This complicates the picture.
What could help, would be more data, and long-term studies that could tease apart the effects of air, with those of age, weight, diet and access to doctors, of the same people.
The NFHS, though, could provide answers sooner than any new study. The Health Ministry has said that a more detailed NFHS-6 national report will be released, though it is not clear if this will include cooking fuel numbers. If the report and household data include cooking fuel, researchers could compare blood sugar in homes using wood and gas, taking age and weight into account, and use data from before the shortage as a baseline. The Petroleum Ministry already tracks Ujjwala refills by State, and could publish this information monthly for every district.
It remains to be seen, however, if the data will materialise. Until then, India remains the country with the highest burden of diabetes, and one of the highest levels of air pollution.
(Dr Margubur Rahaman is a public health researcher at MAMTA Health Institute for Mother and Child, New Delhi. margubur48@gmail.com; Ankit Mishra is an ICSSR Doctoral Fellow at the Govind Ballabh Pant Social Science Institute, Prayagraj. ankitmishrakoraon@gmail.com)

Amazon has plans to build a vault of data on every product sold anywhere on the internet, even products Amazon doesn’t sell, and make the information available through its own site, according to Reuters. The project, called the “World Product Graph,” is meant to make it less likely that shoppers leave Amazon to do their product research on Reddit or Google, and make it more likely shoppers end up at Amazon even if they’re searching for a product sold elsewhere. The same goes for AI agents — if Amazon has the largest stockpile of shopping data, AI agents may rely on its index of products over others, so even people shopping with bots will end up on its pages.
Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
Listing the details of everything for sale everywhere is meant to make Amazon more useful than Reddit for people and AI agents.
Links to outside retailers’ products have already started popping up on Amazon through the “shop direct” feature it launched last year. The company also has its own AI shopping assistant, Alexa for Shopping, previously called Rufus. The World Product Graph project would also be aimed at fixing issues with the AI by providing it more data. According to Reuters, an internal Amazon document on the project says “Many Rufus answers are factually wrong or incomplete” and running users’ Amazon searches with the AI is expensive. Adding more data is reportedly supposed to make the system more accurate and able to use cheaper models.
Whether this actually ships is still up in the air. The internal document reportedly says the project “depends on discovering how brands organize their products on their own websites,” which could involve Amazon crawling other retailers’ sites. Reuters says it’s unclear “if or when this plan may be implemented,” but said the document on it included an October 1st, 2027 release date.
Amazon said in a statement to Reuters that “Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current plans.”

- You can get the Transponder Snail Sprite in Fortnite by defeating the Buggy boss, completing Wanted Posters, and searching chests.
- The Transponder Snail Sprite grants extra resources to you and your team on pickup.
- Level up the Transponder Snail Sprite by searching containers, getting eliminations, and extracting other Sprites in Fortnite
The Transponder Snail was added to Fortnite as part of the One Piece collab and is, without a doubt, the strangest-looking Sprite in Treasure Hunters. It resembles a snail, is blue in color, and has a yellow shell with a red line painted across it. If you want to learn more, including how to get the Transponder Snail Sprite in Fortnite, here’s everything we can tell you.
Fortnite Transponder Snail Sprite Locations and Where to Find It
Transponder Snail is of “Legendary” rarity, which makes it easier to obtain than the Sweet Dreams Sprite in Fortnite Treasure Hunters. You will still need to actively search for it, but it shouldn’t take too long, unlike searching for the Pirate Shop Token in Fortnite.
Here are a few ways to get the Transponder Snail Sprite in Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season:
- Defeat Buggy: The guaranteed and best way to get the Transponder Snail Sprite is to defeat the Buggy Boss in Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season. He can be found outside Buggy’s Beachfront POI. Eliminate him in combat, and the Sprite is yours.
- Wanted Posters: Complete Wanted Posters in Fortnite, and if you’re lucky, you can get the Transponder Snail.
- Lucky Locator: If you don’t want to do a boss fight to complete Wanted Posters, using the Lucky Locator Gizmo is the next best option.
- Vaults: Open Vaults and search rare Treasure Hunt Chests in Fortnite to improve the odds of finding the Transponder Snail Sprite.
Although it’s a rare find, the Transponder Snail is still easier to find than the Crused Plundarrgh Sprite in Fortnite. If you’re yet to find it, attend Captain’s Day this week to boost your chances or consider partaking in Fortnite Treasure Hours, which is when Sprite drop rates are increased.
Best Locations to Find Transponder Snail Sprite in Fortnite
We’ve already mentioned that the best place to get the Transponder Snail in Fortnite is at Buggy’s Beachfront, by defeating Buggy. However, if you prefer searching chests and completing Wanted Sprite Posters in Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season, there are more suitable locations for this task.
Here’s a map of other locations to get the Transponder Snail Sprite in Fortnite Treasure Hunters:
As seen on the map, since the Transponder Snail Sprite is part of the Fortnite One Piece collab, it’s best to search POIs that are related to the anime/manga. There’s no guarantee of finding it there since it’s based on RNG, much like the Pirate Shop Token’s drop rate in Fortnite, but it’s worth trying.
Fortnite Transponder Snail Sprite Powers Explained
The Transponder Sprite in Fortnite grants extra resources on pickup, with teammates who also have it equipped receiving some extra resources as well. This is a very unique power and sets it apart from every other Sprite in Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season, but there’s just one problem: The Transponder Snail is all but useless in Fortnite Zero Build.
You can level up the Transponder Snail in the usual way by searching containers and chests, getting eliminations, and extracting other Sprites, but you get no benefits in Zero Build. Unless you play regular Battle Royale, you are better off using Chester or the Wayfinder Sprite in Fortnite Treasure Hunters.
All Transponder Snail Sprite Variants in Fortnite
As of the Fortnite update 43.10, there is only one variant of the Transponder Snail Sprite in Treasure Hunters Mini Season. Given it’s part of a collab with One Piece, there’s likely not going to be another variant.

Navy chief urges Agniveers to aim for full-term service
Navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan urged the latest batch of Agniveers to work towards a permanent career under the revamped Agnipath scheme.
Navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan on Friday urged the service’s latest batch of Agniveers to aspire to a full career in the Indian Navy under the revamped Agnipath scheme unveiled last week, addressing newly inducted sailors at the INS Chilka training establishment in Odisha.
“I need to mention that during your training here at Chilka, there has been an important addition to the Agnipath scheme. You now have an additional opportunity to become a regular sailor and build a long and rewarding career in the Indian Navy,” said Swaminathan, who was the chief guest and reviewing officer at a passing-out parade involving more than 3,300 recruits, including 2,756 Agniveers.
This is the first batch of Agniveers to join the services under the revised Agnipath framework, which offers those not retained an extension of two years in service and another opportunity to qualify for regular service. The batch includes naval medical assistants and regular Naviks of the Coast Guard.
“I would encourage each one of you to pursue a full career in the service. The Navy can offer you the opportunity, but you must earn it through your performance, conduct, behaviour, commitment and competitiveness. So, work hard from day one, make the most of every facility and opportunity you get, and strive to be among the best,” the Navy chief said.
Swaminathan added that he expected the recruits to “master their profession, never stop learning, and live by a value system”.
Of the lakhs of young aspirants who applied, only about 1.5% made it through, he said. “You are among them. You have earned your place through a very competitive selection process. And you are joining the Navy at a particularly opportune time.”
The Navy chief said the battlespace had changed tremendously over the years, adding that satellites, drones, artificial intelligence, quantum technologies and autonomous systems were changing how the Navy fights at sea.
A life in the Navy is unlike any other, he said.
“It offers adventure and challenge. It also offers opportunities for professional growth and personal development that few other careers can match. There will be tough days, but there will also be many moments of achievement, happiness, satisfaction and quiet pride. Above all, you will have the honour and privilege of serving your country and making a difference.”
The next batches of Army and Indian Air Force Agniveers will pass out of their training establishments in December. The new Agnipath framework was cleared by the Cabinet and unveiled by Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani on November 4. The revamped scheme will apply exclusively to the 300,000 Agniveers currently in service. It is expected to undergo further changes for recruits inducted after December 31.
Subramani announced the Agnipath reboot weeks before the three services were set to release 75% of Agniveers from their first batch after four years of service, retaining only the 25% selected on merit for another 15 years under the scheme’s earlier provisions.
All existing Agniveers will become permanent after this two-year extended service, subject to meeting specific eligibility criteria and giving their individual consent. Around 18,300 Agniveers were set to be discharged between mid-November and December 31, forming three-fourths of the 24,400 recruits inducted into the Army, Air Force and Navy in the first round of recruitment.

The Federal Aviation Administration late Friday afternoon issued a nationwide "ground stop," affecting flights across the country.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said just after 4:15 pm. Eastern time that the nationwide flight traffic halt came "following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers."
"FAA technicians are investigating the issue," he said in a post on X. "We will provide immediate updates as we have them."
The agency said the stop was due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."
As of late Friday afternoon, delays were already piling up at airports across the country, according to the FAA's monitoring system: At Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, outside of New York City, the average delay was more than 45 minutes. It was the same at the Houston-Bush Intercontinental Airport — and even worse at Chicago O'Hare, where delays were 75 minutes and rising.
The FAA notice said that inbound international flights would be managed on a "case-by-case basis."
"The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all US airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," an FAA spokesperson told Business Insider. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates."
The last time a nationwide ground stop occurred was in January 2023, and it lasted only about 90 minutes. Before that, it was in 2001 on 9/11.
At least 7,000 flights have been delayed so far, per Flightradar24.

Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
- Published
A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.
William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.
Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.
He was located on Thursday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".
Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.
The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.
"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.
"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."
Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."
Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.
"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

Kenya Contains Ebola Outbreak as Last Patient Leaves Hospital
The milestone is further evidence that African countries have mostly succeeded in preventing community transmission and isolating the small number of cases that have come in from Congo.
Kenya began a countdown on Wednesday to declare the end of its Ebola outbreak.
The final patient who had tested positive for the virus was discharged from the hospital on Wednesday. And the Kenyan cabinet secretary for health, Aden Duale, said at a news conference that the last 11 people being monitored for Ebola symptoms had also been discharged after completing a 21-day quarantine period.
“For the first time since this outbreak began, Kenya has no patient under treatment and no contact in quarantine,” he said.
The milestone is further evidence that countries have succeeded in containing the small number of cases, most coming in from the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak continues to spread.
Since Kenya announced its first-ever Ebola case on Oct. 6, two people have died and nine have tested positive in the country. The initial case was a Kenyan man who returned from Congo and infected others before the virus was diagnosed and he was put in isolation. He died days later.
The Kenyan authorities say that all of those who subsequently became ill were in quarantine before they developed symptoms and became infectious. As a result, there have been no instances of what experts call community transmission, when a person passes on the virus outside a medical setting.
Kenya’s outbreak will be officially declared over on Dec. 23, or 42 days from when the last case was recorded, if there are no further positive Ebola tests, the health secretary said. In all, 135 people have been monitored for signs of the virus.
The current Ebola outbreak has killed more than 5,300 people since it was first declared a global health emergency by the World Health Organization in May. But so far, the fear that the epidemic might spread unchecked across Africa has not materialized.
Uganda has recorded 20 cases and three deaths, but the outbreak was declared over in the country by August. The authorities in Nigeria last month identified a case in the capital, Abuja.
Individuals with Ebola have since been medically evacuated to several European countries. Two Americans who worked for humanitarian organizations involved in the Ebola response have also tested positive. Both were treated outside of the United States and have recovered.
Several countries have instituted travel restrictions to prevent the spread of the virus. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention instituted a requirement in November that anyone traveling by air into the United States must sign a document confirming that they have not been in Congo in the past 21 days before boarding their flight.
Kenya has also announced new rules for its citizens returning from Congo, including 21 days of quarantine and monitoring, Mr. Duale said. He gave no details of whether the quarantine would take place at home or in a medical facility.
Matthew Mpoke Bigg is the East Africa bureau chief for The New York Times, based in Nairobi, Kenya.

Nations Championship - France 21-19 South Africa: Les Bleus put injuries behind them to hold on and stun Springboks in Paris
Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, Théo Attissogbe, Louis Bielle-Biarrey score first-half tries for sensational France, who then withstand enormous second-half pressure from South Africa to secure Nations Championship victory and move closer to securing top spot in northern hemisphere table
Last Updated: 13/11/26 11:06pm
France put a raft of injuries behind them to withstand huge pressure and defeat South Africa 21-19 in a stunning Nations Championship victory in Paris.
The win is only the second for Les Bleus over the Springboks in the last 11 contests, with the hosts playing sensationally in the first half and digging in to survive and get over the line in the second.
Back-three Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, Théo Attissogbe and Louis Bielle-Biarrey each scored tries in the opening half, with France belying the fact they had to play Antoine Dupont at 10 due to four fly-halves being out injured (Matthieu Jalibert, Romain Ntamack, Thomas Ramos, Antoine Hastoy).
All three tries were converted by Maxime Lucu, with France 21-7 ahead at the half-time break, but the second half proved entirely different.
France 21-19 South Africa - Score summary
France - Tries: Grandidier-Nkanang (15), Attissogbe (24), Bielle-Biarrey (32). Cons: Lucu (16,24,33).
South Africa - Tries: Wessels (30), Reinach (51), Marx (72). Cons: Feinberg-Mngomezulu (31,52).
Though South Africa were shown a 20-minute red card to back-row Cobus Wiese for an illegal ruck clear-out, France coughed up sin-bins to Lucu, Grandidier-Nkanang and Régis Montagne - the latter as a result of scrum penalties which kept flowing the visitors' way.
Scrum-half Cobus Reinach and hooker Malcom Marx scored tries in the second half for South Africa - adding to a first-half Jan-Hendrik Wessels effort - but Manie Libbok crucially missed the third conversion and the chance to draw level.
South Africa's wholesale front-row changes less than an hour before kick-off - swapping their starting front-row for their replacements - had little impact on France's fast start, with Dupont floating between fly-half and scrum-half from the off in a marvellous individual performance.
The match was considered a potential preview of the final at Twickenham in two weeks, but while France are closing in on representing the northern hemisphere - England and Ireland are now six points behind with two games to play - South Africa may not make it.
The Springboks will be overtaken atop the southern hemisphere standings and lose their No 1 world ranking if undefeated New Zealand beat Wales on Saturday in Cardiff, as expected.
On Friday, the Springboks closed to 21-14 with 30 minutes to go, revving up their power game for a grandstand finish.
France were bleeding penalties - nine in the scrum alone - but desperate scramble defence roused a packed Stade de France.
South Africa's Pieter-Steph du Toit was held up over the try-line late on, while Lucu - France's goalkicker with an 85 per cent success rate - ramped up the tension when he missed a straightforward penalty attempt that would have given France a 10-point lead.
Springboks hooker Marx inevitably scored from a rolling maul but Libbok, on for Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, botched the conversion attempt that would have levelled the score with eight minutes left.
The Boks had one last chance in the final minute, but Bielle-Biarrey stopped the charge and Dupont jumped on the loose ball, earning Lucu the chance to kick out and end a gripping Test match.
Dupont: We kept intensity up the whole match - 'That's huge for us'
France fly-half Antoine Dupont told ITV:
"I feel tired! They [South Africa] are really intense during the 80 minutes.
"It was so hard today with the yellow cards. We kept the intensity the whole game, and that's a huge thing for us today.
"We tried to adapt [Dupont at fly-half], we just had one day of training this week.
"I tried with Max [Lucu] to have the best combination possible. In attack and defence.
"With the energy of the entire team, it worked."
What's next?
For France, they next face Argentina in their third Nations Championship Test of the autumn at the Stade de France in Paris on Saturday, November 21 (8.10pm kick-off).
South Africa travel to face Ireland at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin for their next Test, also on Saturday November 21 (4.40pm kick-off).

Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology-Kanpur have identified a molecular pathway through which immune cells in the pancreas can rapidly suppress insulin release, opening up a potential new avenue for developing therapies to protect insulin production in people with obesity and Type-2 diabetes.
The findings, published in ‘Journal of Clinical Investigation’, show that immune cells called macrophages can switch off insulin secretion by neighbouring beta cells within minutes, rather than gradually damaging them through inflammation over months or years, according to a note issued by IIT-Kanpur on Thursday.
Simran Singh and Ashish Kumar led the study as co-first authors under the supervision of Sai Prasad Pydi, assistant professor, department of biological sciences and bioengineering, IIT-Kanpur.
“We discovered that immune cells that are present next to beta cells can switch off insulin release within minutes,” Pydi said.
The researchers found that the process involves sphingolipids, a class of fats released by macrophages, rather than the inflammatory proteins traditionally associated with obesity-related pancreatic damage.
The team traced the trigger to GPR18, a receptor on macrophages. Once activated, it prompts the immune cells to release sphingolipids, which are taken up by neighbouring beta cells through a surface transporter, and interfere with their insulin-producing machinery.
Using a precision genetic technique, the researchers found that activating this pathway reduced insulin secretion in mouse models, while switching it off improved insulin release. Blocking GPR18 or other steps in the pathway also restored insulin secretion.
The team, working with the Indiana Biosciences Research Institute in the US, confirmed that the same pathway was present and active in human pancreatic tissue.
Activating it in donated human tissue also suppressed insulin secretion, according to the communique.
While the study does not offer an immediate treatment for diabetes, the findings establish a potential target for developing drugs to preserve insulin production in people with obesity and Type-2 diabetes, it said.

Passenger van plunges into river in northern Pakistan, killing 11 people
Officials say a passenger van veered off a mountainous road and plunged into a river in northern Pakistan, killing 11 people and injuring three others
ISLAMABAD -- A passenger van veered off a mountainous road and plunged into a river in northern Pakistan, killing 11 people and injuring three others, rescue officials and police said Friday.
The crash happened in the Gilgit-Baltistan region Thursday night after the driver lost control of the vehicle, local police official Mohammad Afzal said.
Rescuers said a search and rescue operation continued into early Friday, and all 11 bodies and the three injured people had been taken to a nearby hospital. Regional Chief Minister Amjad Hussain in a statement expressed his deep sorrow and grief over the road accident and instructed authorities to ensure the best possible medical care for the injured.
Road accidents are common in Pakistan because of poor road conditions, inadequate enforcement of traffic laws and unsafe driving practices, particularly in mountainous areas. Last week, a bus collided with a truck in eastern Pakistan, killing 11 people and injuring 33 others.

Ex-NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang is set to testify before Congress this month
House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast said the hearing will take place before Thanksgiving.
Jensen Huang might have stepped down from his roles at the top of NVIDIA, but he won't be sliding out of the spotlight just yet. The company's former CEO and president is set to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving, according to House representatives.
House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast said Huang agreed to testify on Wednesday — hours before NVIDIA announced his resignation with immediate effect — after lawmakers threatened him with a subpoena. It appears the hearing will take place behind closed doors (which is unfortunate, because that's likely to be some spicy testimony). However, Mast expects it to be filmed and transcribed, according to Bloomberg. The House's Intelligence and China-focused committees will join the Foreign Affairs cohort for the hearing.
"Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but NVIDIA is a very important company to the United States of America," Mast said. "I don't want to see anything hurt in NVIDIA, but he has some very serious questions to answer."
NVIDIA has been in turmoil after it emerged over the weekend that the company was investigating Huang over an affair to which he admitted, allegedly with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the situation as well.
On Wednesday, it was reported that Huang had another affair, this time with Kimberly Powell, an NVIDIA executive who reported to him. The company's board met later that day to determine Huang's future. Colette Kress, NVIDIA's executive vice president and chief financial officer, is stepping in as interim CEO while the company seeks a permanent successor.
Meanwhile, the Department of Justice is reportedly investigating Alice Huang, the alleged spy, to determine whether entities associated with her were involved in attempts to smuggle Super Micro Computer products to China. The DoJ is also said to be taking the lead in an investigation into her former company, the Singapore-based Megaspeed International, over alleged smuggling of US-made chips into China in defiance of export restrictions. The company said it would cooperate with the probe.
Officials in Singapore opened an investigation into Alice Huang, Megaspeed and associated individuals last year. The Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement on Thursday that she was barred from re-entering the country after police determined she knowingly offered up inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed. However, they "concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated." The investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals is ongoing.

ఫాక్ట్: ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను మాఫీ చేస్తున్నట్లు జాతీయ లేదా రాష్ట్ర లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీలు ఎక్కడా ప్రకటించలేదు. అయితే, 2026లో కర్ణాటక, బీహార్, ఒడిశా వంటి పలు రాష్ట్రాలు పెండింగ్ చలాన్ల చెల్లింపులో రాయితీని కల్పించాయి. తెలంగాణ, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ రాష్ట్రాలు గతంలో ఇలాంటి రాయితీలు ఇచ్చినప్పటికీ, డిసెంబర్ 2026లో జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లో మాత్రం ఎలాంటి రాయితీని అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా ఈ విషయం గురించి జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించే నేషనల్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీ (NALSA) అధికారిక వెబ్సైట్ను పరిశీలించగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న దేశవ్యాప్తంగా పలు రాష్ట్రాలలో లోక్ అదాలత్లు నిర్వహిస్తున్నట్లు తెలిసింది. దీనిలో భాగంగా విచారణలో ఉన్న సివిల్, క్రిమినల్, చెక్బౌన్స్ కేసులు, కాంపౌండబుల్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్ కేసులు, మోటారు వాహన ప్రమాదాలు, కుటుంబ తగాదాలు మొదలైనవాటిని రాజీ మార్గం ద్వారా పరిష్కరించుకునే అవకాశాన్ని ఈ లోక్ అదాలత్లు కల్పిస్తాయి. అయితే, పెండింగ్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను 100% మాఫీ చేయనున్నట్లు ఇందులో ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు.
ఇదే విషయమై తెలంగాణ స్టేట్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీ (TSLSA) వర్గాలను సంప్రదించగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న తెలంగాణలో జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లకు మాఫీ/ డిస్కౌంట్ ఇస్తున్నట్లు తాము ఎక్కడా అధికారికంగా పేర్కొనలేదని స్పష్టం చేశారు.
అంతేకాకుండా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో తెలంగాణ వ్యాప్తంగా పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను రాయితీపై చెల్లించే అవకాశం కల్పించడం లేదని తెలంగాణ పోలీసులు కూడా మాకు ధృవీకరించారు. మార్చి 2026లో కూడా ఇటువంటి వార్తలే వచ్చినప్పుడు వారు దీన్ని ఖండించారు. మరోవైపు, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీని, పోలీసులను సంప్రదించగా వారి స్పందించలేదు. అయితే, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ పోలీసులు కూడా పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లపై రాయితీ కల్పించే విషయం గురించి ఎక్కడా అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు.
అయితే కర్ణాటక, ఒడిశా, బీహార్ వంటి పలు రాష్ట్రాల్లో 2026లో ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లకు రాయితీ కల్పిస్తూ సెటిల్మెంట్ చేసుకునేందుకు వీలుగా ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించిన సందర్భాలు ఉన్నాయి. గతంలో హైదరాబాద్ ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు కూడా ఇలాంటి లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించారు. 2016, 2017 సంవత్సరాల్లో హైదరాబాద్ ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు గోషామహల్లో లోక్ అదాలత్ నిర్వహించి, 50% రాయితీతో పెండింగ్ చలాన్లను చెల్లించే అవకాశం కల్పించారు. అయితే, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో తెలంగాణ, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ రాష్ట్రాల పోలీసులు లోక్ అదాలత్ ద్వారా ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లపై రాయితీని కల్పించే పథకాన్ని అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు.
చివరిగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరిగే జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లో పెండింగ్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లు 100% మాఫీ అవుతాయని సోషల్ మీడియాలో జరుగుతున్న ప్రచారంలో నిజం లేదు.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said today that Starshield has again been disabled on fast-moving drones in Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces, and that the US has provided “very little” information about the return of the restriction.
“We have detected speed restrictions on Starshield on our Ukrainian territory again, in the temporarily occupied parts of Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in a speech at the 9th European Political Community Summit in Ireland. “The speed limit is back at 161 kilometers per hour—that’s 100 miles per hour.”
Zelenskyy’s allegation is that Starshield—the military variant of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service—stops working on Ukrainian military drones when they travel above 161 kilometers per hour.
SpaceX today denied Zelenskyy’s allegation. “This is false. There has been no change,” SpaceX’s media relations department told Ars today when asked if SpaceX has any response to Zelenskyy’s statement that Starshield is being restricted again.
“This means more Russian strikes get through”
SpaceX has received multiple Pentagon contracts to give Ukraine access to the military-focused Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said last month that any decisions on Starshield restrictions are made by the US government. The Pentagon inspector general’s office has since declined a request from US senators to investigate who ordered the restrictions.
Ukraine officials reportedly said today that they believe the limit was reinstated to put pressure on Ukraine in the latest round of peace talks with Russia. Zelenskyy said in today’s speech that without satellite connectivity on its drones, Ukraine cannot intercept Russian drones that fly in from the occupied parts of Ukraine.

Is honesty always the best policy? When to speak up — or stay silent

Should you tell your partner how you really feel about their casserole? Offer a colleague feedback about their subpar interview performance? Let a stranger know she has toilet paper on her shoe?
Life Kit
How honest should you really be? Tips for sharing good and bad news
Sometimes the hardest part about talking to other people isn't finding the right words to say — but deciding if you should say anything at all, says social psychologist Vanessa Bohns.
"There are times when honesty is the best policy," she says. "On the other hand, honesty is not the best policy if whatever we say is going to be honest without any instrumental value."
Bohns is the author of Should I Say Something? The Science of What to Share—and What to Keep to Yourself, published in October. The book provides research-backed strategies to help you figure out when to share the truth or a personal opinion. It also offers advice on when to share good news, say sorry or be vulnerable.
There's a reason why giving difficult feedback or even loving criticism can feel like a dilemma. "It pains us to embarrass or hurt other people," Bohns says. So we don't tend to like doing it. In fact, there's a name for the phenomenon — the MUM effect, or minimizing unpleasant messages.
But with care and intention, it's possible to make informed choices about when to speak up or stay quiet, no matter how small or big the situation. Bohns shares three questions to ask yourself before sharing an opinion.
Is this information helpful?
When you decide to tell someone something, remember you're sharing two things: the message itself, and the fact that you are choosing to speak up at all, Bohns says.
People often spend far too much time worrying about the content of their messages, she says. "But the choice of saying something at all communicates so much. It says, 'I see you. I care about your suffering. I want to help you in some way.'"
So, before telling your boss/spouse/mother-in-law how you really feel about that new haircut, Bohn says to consider whether your feedback is actionable.
Honesty is only the best policy if your opinion is going to help someone "perform better or avoid embarrassment or learn something about themselves." If your feedback is mean-spirited, unrelated to the matter at hand or simply can't be enacted, you're probably better off holding your tongue.
For example, flat-out telling your roommate the cake she baked for your birthday tastes terrible? That's just mean. But if she bakes that same cake to enter into a baking competition? It would be mean not to offer her some feedback!
Would I want to hear this?
Just because you don't want to share the truth doesn't mean the person on the receiving end shouldn't or wouldn't want to hear what you have to say.
A 2022 survey, for example, found that people consistently underestimate others' desire for feedback. In the study, researchers put visible smudges of lipstick, chocolate or marker on their faces. Then, without acknowledging those smudges, they went out on the street asking random people to participate in a survey on a different topic.
Less than 3% of the survey participants spoke up, even though the smudges were something the researchers "clearly could have done something about and would have wanted to know," says Bohns.
So, if you choose to stay silent when your new co-worker keeps mispronouncing the name of the company CEO, for example, reflect on your own motivations. "Are you being kind, or are you avoiding your own discomfort?" writes Bohns in her book. Speaking up may help your colleague in this instance.
Do they want your feedback?
Has anyone ever given you advice about a topic you knew more about than they did? Or misjudged how much you knew based on how you looked?
When in doubt, don't assume you know what information the other person wants or needs from you. Pre-assessing how valuable the truth is to someone else, or their ability to handle it, can quickly make well-meaning feedback sound patronizing, writes Bohns in her book.
So just ask the other person if they want the feedback you have to share. "Give them the autonomy, then respect their decision, whatever it might be," she says.

China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.
The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.
Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”
China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.
Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.
Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.
Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.
“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.
“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”
It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.
After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.
The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.
China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.
Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.
That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.
India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.
The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.
No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting, which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has introduced a new scheme to expand UPI acceptance among small merchants. Under the new initiative, the payments body will offer incentives to banks for deploying QR codes and soundboxes to further drive transaction growth. The scheme will be funded through a portion of the merchant discount rate (MDR) earned by banks and other UPI ecosystem participants. In a circular dated November 11, NPCI announced the launch of the ‘UPI Vyapaar Saksham Scheme’, which aims to address the limited availability of digital payment acceptance infrastructure among small merchants, particularly in smaller cities and towns. The scheme will run for a period of three years from the implementation of UPI MDR, which is yet to be notified. The initiative will focus on merchants in Tier III to Tier VI cities, northeastern states, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. Small merchants covered under notified central government schemes, including PM SVANidhi and PM Vishwakarma, will also be eligible. NPCI defines small merchants as businesses with an annual turnover of up to ₹40 Lakh in the preceding financial year. The fund will be created from MDR collections rather than a separate government allocation. Each issuing bank, acquiring bank, payer payment service provider (PSP) and UPI application provider participating in UPI will contribute 5% of its MDR share to the fund. The contribution will exclude MDR earned from categories that are not eligible for the scheme. The fund will be divided into three components, with the largest allocation going towards increasing transaction volumes among existing merchants. Under the first component, which accounts for 30% of the fund, acquiring banks will receive ₹300 for every physical QR code and ₹750 for every soundbox deployed at an eligible new small merchant. To qualify, a merchant will have to record at least 25 eligible transactions in any two months of a quarter, with a minimum transaction value of ₹5,000 per month. For context, the scheme defines eligible transactions as successfully settled UPI payments of up to ₹2,000 at small merchants. It excludes transactions that are subsequently reversed, refunded or cancelled, as well as artificial transactions created by splitting payments to remain below the ₹2,000 threshold. The second component will receive 50% of the fund and reward acquiring banks for growing UPI transaction volumes among existing and newly onboarded small merchants. Banks will need to demonstrate at least 5% QoQ growth in eligible transaction volumes to qualify for incentives. They will receive 0.03% of the aggregate value of eligible transactions, with merchants in the targeted geographies receiving an additional 50% incentive. The remaining 20% will be allocated towards incremental growth in targeted geographies. Under this component, acquiring banks will receive an incentive of 0.2% of the incremental value of eligible transactions compared with the previous quarter, over and above the incentive under the second component. NPCI has also set out ambitious deployment targets. The scheme is expected to facilitate 6 Lakh to 1 Cr new physical QR code deployments and 5 Lakh to 10 Lakh new soundbox installations annually. It also aims to drive 30% to 50% annual growth in transaction volumes among existing small merchants. UPI's MDR Transition This comes as the Centre is all set to re-introduce MDR on select “high-value” UPI transactions after nearly six years of a zero-MDR regime. In September 2026, the government notified amendments to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, paving the way for MDR on select merchant transactions. Subsequently, NPCI introduced a framework under which person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000 would attract an MDR of 0.4%, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above. Transactions of up to ₹2,000 and peer-to-peer (P2P) payments have been kept outside the MDR framework. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh per month through UPI QR codes under the P2M-to-P2P merchant (P2PM) category were also exempted from MDR. The government said the move was intended to create a sustainable revenue stream for banks and payment companies while supporting the infrastructure required to operate UPI at scale. The MDR collected is distributed among ecosystem participants rather than retained by the government. The proposed MDR framework faced pushback from retailers, with a possible deferment of its rollout to January next year. Later, the imposition was pushed beyond Diwali. Four days after Diwali, NPCI is yet to come out with a date for the implementation for this. Whenever MDR comes into place, the new NPCI scheme would effectively channel a portion of the MDR revenue back into expanding UPI acceptance among this merchant segment. That said, NPCI will administer the fund, validate incentive claims and oversee settlements. Acquiring banks will submit claims quarterly, with NPCI required to process incentive payments within 30 days of claim submission, subject to validation. The scheme also mandates that acquiring banks report merchant locations, unique merchant identifiers and details of deployed QR codes and soundboxes to enable transaction-level monitoring. The underlying policy shift is significant: while the MDR framework creates a revenue stream for UPI ecosystem participants, the new scheme attempts to use a portion of that revenue to address the infrastructure gap that has kept digital payment acceptance concentrated among larger merchants and in urban markets.

The Union Home Ministry on Friday extended the ban on controversial preacher Zakir Naik's Islamic Research Foundation (IRF) for another five years, noting that it has been indulging in activities prejudicial to the security of the country and has the potential to disturb peace and communal harmony.
The ministry had invoked the powers conferred by Section 3 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, to declare the IRF an unlawful association, a decision upheld by the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Tribunal. The earlier ban was ending on November 14.
Centre Cites Threat To National Security
"The Central Government is of the opinion that the IRF and its members, particularly the founder and President of the IRF, Dr Zakir Abdul Karim Naik alias Dr Zakir Naik, has been encouraging and aiding its followers to promote or attempt to promote, on grounds of religion, disharmony or feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between different religious communities and groups which are prejudicial to the integrity and security of the country," it said.
Ministry Flags Naik's Speeches
The statements and speeches made by Naik are objectionable and subversive, and he has been promoting enmity and hatred amongst different religious groups and inspiring youths of a particular religion in India and abroad to commit terrorist acts, it said.
Naik made radical statements and speeches to millions of people worldwide through international satellite TV networks, the Internet, print and social media, it said.
Centre Warns Of Communal Disharmony
If the unlawful activities of the IRF are not curbed and controlled immediately, it will continue its subversive activities and re-organise its activists, who are still absconding, disrupt the secular fabric of the country by polluting the minds of the people by creating communal disharmony and propagate anti-national sentiments, it said.

A tiny, $900 wearable device being developed by an Indian billionaire entrepreneur and showcased by some of the country’s top sportspersons has sparked criticism from doctors who say its claims of tracking blood flow to the brain are exaggerated.
The Temple device is less than 1 inch (2.54 cm) wide and weighs under 2 grams (0.07 oz). It sticks to the side of the head between the forehead and the ear, or the temple area.
Promotional materials for the device, developed by Deepinder Goyal, say that its BrainFlow feature shows how well the brain is being supplied with blood in real time and its Entropy feature can detect how hard the body works to shed heat.
It can also measure thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive and emotional readings that help to transform how a person regulates their health, they say.
Priced at 85,000 rupees ($907), the device comes in six colours. India’s cricket captain Shubman Gill and Olympic medal-winning badminton player P.V. Sindhu have worn it.
Some well-known doctors in the country, however, are sceptical of the claims, saying the device’s capabilities are not backed by peer-reviewed research. In prime-time shows and on social media, they are calling for the device to come under the purview of medical regulators.
Prominent Indian hepatologist Cyriac Philips, known as “TheLiverDoc”, has been criticising the device on his X account with 328,000 followers, calling Temple “the biggest health scam”.
“People must be aware of wellness hacks such as wearables also, even though they are not marketed as health devices,” he told Reuters.
On one prime-time TV discussion, paediatrician and nephrologist Sanjeev Bagai called Temple a “gimmick”, saying it had “no formal approval or clearance”.
Goyal has hit back at the criticism from doctors, saying Temple is a “fitness tracker, and wellness device”, not a medical one.
Indian doctor Jason Philip wrote on X that assessing blood flow to the brain was not easy, and optical signals placed over the temple skin would only give data on the “superficial temporal artery” that supplies blood to the face and skin.
In a statement to Reuters, Temple said BrainFlow and Entropy were new metrics “with emerging science”, and that more research would follow, adding that some metrics would eventually need regulatory approval.
India’s health ministry did not respond to Reuters queries, and the government has so far not reacted to the public debate.
The debate on Temple comes as wearable makers overseas also face questions on when a fitness feature becomes a medical one.
Some Apple Watch features, such as hypertension notifications, have received US Food and Drug Administration clearance as software-based medical features. Last year, the US FDA warned Whoop, saying its wrist-worn fitness tracker’s blood-pressure feature looked like a medical one — a view the company disputes.
Goyal is best known for co-founding Eternal, which houses India’s biggest listed food-delivery company Zomato and has a market value of about $35 billion. The 43-year-old stepped down as chief executive of Eternal this year to focus on Temple.
Temple, which has professors from the University of Ottawa and Harvard on its advisory board, raised $54 million in February at a valuation of about $190 million.
Goyal said Temple has received orders from more than 62 countries since November 1.
On its website, Temple says it is also working on detecting conditions including snoring and jaw clenching.
