Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.

Surface Laptop Ultra review: The most powerful Surface yet, but it still lags behind Apple
It’s a beautiful flagship device for NVIDIA’s RTX Spark.
With a name like Surface Laptop Ultra, Microsoft's latest notebook better be impressive. It's one of the flagship devices for NVIDIA's new RTX Spark platform, making it the most powerful Surface device yet. It can be equipped with up to 128GB of unified memory, which is ideal for running local AI models. And in just about every other respect, from its super-bright 15-inch screen to its sleek case, the Surface Laptop Ultra screams quality. So sure, the name fits.
But with its high $2,599 starting price, which easily escalates if you want to go beyond its stock 24GB of RAM, the Surface Laptop Ultra is really only meant for the most demanding users. To be fair, though, the same is true of all the RTX Spark laptops, including the excellent ASUS ProArt P16 we recently reviewed. Even Apple is pushing the limits of laptop pricing with its new touchscreen MacBook Pros with PROLED screens, which start at $2.899.
Like some sort of cosmic capitalist joke, PC makers have inexplicably decided to release pricier computers, even though we're already suffering from AI-driven memory price hikes. I'm sure the Surface Laptop Ultra's high price won't stop AI enthusiasts who've been eagerly awaiting capable Windows systems from buying one, but most gamers and content creators would likely be better off saving $1,000 and buying a capable gaming laptop instead.
What's notable about the Surface Laptop Ultra?
Much like the standard Surface Laptop, the Ultra variant doesn't have any of the bells and whistles from Microsoft's convertible Surfaces. It just looks like a sleek, all-metal business laptop. Pop it open and you'll notice that its 15-inch screen has a tall 3:2 aspect ratio instead of the typical widescreen configuration. And if you peer along the bottom of the case, you'll see a slightly segmented base (reminiscent of the Surface Laptop Studio), which makes a bit of room for cooling vents and downward-firing speakers.
While there's a lot to admire about Microsoft's design prowess, the biggest selling point of the Surface Laptop Ultra is NVIDIA's RTX Spark chip. It's an Arm-based system-on-a-chip that can be equipped with up to 20 CPU cores and 6,144 GPU cores. Take note: You'll need to shell out $3,700 to get the most powerful RTX Spark hardware here, but at least that ships with 32GB of RAM. The base $2,600 Surface Laptop Ultra has 18 CPU cores and 5,120 GPU cores.
Taking a cue from Apple Silicon and Qualcomm's recent Snapdragon X chips, the RTX Spark also features unified memory, which is accessible to both the CPU and GPU. That gives it even more memory bandwidth than a typical Intel or AMD-based Windows PC, which have their RAM, CPU and dedicated GPUs spread out across their motherboards. By having direct access to tons of RAM, RTX Spark hardware can also house large AI models locally, which is a major reason why both Microsoft and NVIDIA are pitching it as a major evolution for PCs.
Thanks to its NVIDIA GPU cores, the RTX Spark chip also delivers gaming performance similar to an RTX 5070 laptop GPU. That makes it ideal for 1440p gaming, and you can probably also get decent performance in 4K and other higher resolutions thanks to NVIDIA's DLSS upscaling and frame generation. The Surface Laptop Ultra starts at a much higher price than most RTX 5070 gaming notebooks, though, so it's not something you'd want to buy for pure gaming.
The RTX Spark's Arm CPU is both a blessing and a curse: It technically can perform more efficiently than Intel and AMD's x86-64 chips, but it also requires emulating older Windows software and drivers. That opens the door to unforeseen bugs and issues, especially for niche apps and minimally-supported third-party drivers. While this was a major problem when Microsoft first started dabbling with Windows on Arm (think back to the original Surface with Windows RT or the Surface Pro X), the company's emulation for x86-64 software has dramatically improved. Kernel-level anti-cheat software for multiplayer games initially didn't work on the first Snapdragon X Windows systems, but both Microsoft and NVIDIA have worked on resolving that. Now, you can easily play Fortnite Arm-based Windows systems.
Microsoft initially touted the Surface Laptop Ultra's 15-inch screen as the brightest laptop display on the market, thanks to its eye-searing 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. Apple's new MacBook Pro with PROLED Display stole that thunder a bit, though: Its screen can reach the same brightness, and its OLED screen delivers deeper blacks and higher contrast. The Surface Laptop Ultra's mini-LED display is still plenty impressive though, especially while watching films in HDR with rich colors, or playing games that truly push its brightness and HDR capabilities.
The Surface Laptop Ultra also features a keyboard that's similar to the Surface Laptop's, which has always felt great to type on thanks to its deep key depth and satisfying feedback. Its large trackpad also supports newer haptic feedback in Windows — for example, you can feel a slight nudge as you move apps along the edges of the screen to lock them into place. We've seen similar haptic feedback in mice like Logitech's MX Master 4, and while it's not exactly groundbreaking, I find it to be a nifty addition to the aging Windows interface.
Strangely enough, one of the most interesting things about the Surface Laptop Ultra is its magnetic USB-C charging cable. It allows the notebook's charging cable to snap into place on one USB-C port, and similar to Apple's MagSafe cable, it also lets the cable easily slide out if someone trips on it. It's a useful replacement for the proprietary Surface charging connection, since it allows Microsoft to keep a standard USB-C port on the Laptop Ultra for charging, which will also work seamlessly with every other USB-C charging cable. The magnetic USB-C charging cable is Microsoft's invention, but the company says it could bring it to partner laptops if they're interested.
The Surface Laptop Pro's ports mostly match the MacBook Pro's, with three USB-C ports, HDMI, SD card slot and a headphone jack. But, crucially, there's also a USB Type-A connection for older devices. I could see that being very useful for some Windows creatives.
In-use: Living up to the name... mostly
The Surface Laptop is a beautiful beast. While every RTX Spark laptop will be similarly speedy, Microsoft has gone to great effort to make the Surface Laptop Ultra stand out from every other Windows notebook. Its aluminum case feels both as solid as a rock, and as smooth as a piece of fine jewelry. It also rejects fingerprints so it always looks pristine — something the ASUS ProArt P16 completely failed at. I wish the Surface Laptop Ultra was a bit lighter, though: At 4.4 pounds, it feels more like a brick than I'd expect for a premium notebook in 2026. Dell's XPS 16 weighs 3.65 pounds, and Apple's new 16-inch PROLED MacBook Pro comes in at 4 pounds.
In benchmarks, the RTX Spark chip excelled at multi-threaded tests, like Cinebench 2024, where it scored several hundred points higher than the ASUS ProArt PX13, which was powered by AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395 chip. NVIDIA still lags behind Apple, though. The new PROLED MacBook Pro, which was powered by an M5 Pro chip, scored 2,188 points in that same test, whereas the Surface Laptop Ultra came in at 1,553 points. Apple also has the lead in single-threaded performance: The M5 Pro scored 192 points to the Surface's 120. Apple's newer M6 chip in the 14-inch MacBook Pro does even better, reaching 210 points.
NVIDIA's big draw is that its chip can power Windows and Linux, while you'll need to become a macOS convert to use Apple's hardware. While doing so isn't tough these days, I've talked to AI researchers who rely on Windows apps to get their work done. Moving to a Mac would just be a pain for them.
The Surface Laptop Ultra scored 1,000 points lower than the ASUS ProArt P16 in the PCMark 10 Applications test, which is surprising since they're both using the same RTX Spark chip. It could be a difference in RAM: The Surface Laptop we tested had 32GB of RAM, while the ASUS was stuffed to the brim with 128GB. But in real-world usage, that extra RAM is only useful if you want to run large AI models on your system, it doesn't directly mean faster performance. And personally, I'll take Microsoft's refined build quality over slightly better benchmark speeds any day.
With 32GB of RAM, our review unit couldn't run the massive AI models that fit into the ASUS P16, but I was still able to get OpenClaw running with Qwen3.6 35B-A38. It was quick to fetch me updates on recent news, as well as transcribe audio from a podcast. I even had it generate an audio podcast from a written review — sacrilege for a podcaster, I know — and it managed to do so in a few minutes. I don't personally use agentic AI models, but with a bit more RAM, I could see the Surface Laptop Ultra being a fitting home for one.
Given its GPU prowess, I wasn't surprised to see the Surface Laptop Ultra reach 87 fps in Cyberpunk 2077 while playing in 1440p with maxed-out graphics settings, 4x frame generation and path tracing enabled. That would be my ideal way to play that game on a 15-inch screen. I could even hit 117 fps by pushing the frame generation to 6x, but that leads to occasional graphical weirdness. I was also able to crank up the graphics settings in Star Wars: Galactic Racer and Gears of War: E-Day while keeping a decently high frame rate.
While I would have liked to see more than a 120Hz refresh rate on the Surface Laptop Ultra, that's still fast enough to make most games look pretty smooth. (There's also the additional benefit of making scrolling around Windows look much smoother.) And I can't praise Microsoft's screen technology enough. At times, I preferred playing Gears of War on the Surface Laptop Ultra instead of my 32-inch 4K gaming monitor, simply because it looked so much brighter.
As for battery life, the Surface Laptop Ultra lasted for 13 hours and 25 minutes in the PCMark 10 battery benchmark. That's two and a half hours longer than the ASUS ProArt P16 and 90 minutes more than the XPS 16. During the workday, I used the system for around seven and a half hours before it conked out, handling a variety of video calls, writing and web browsing across dozens of tabs.
Should you buy the Surface Laptop Ultra?
If you're a diehard Windows user (yes, they exist) who's really into AI, and you want one of the most premium laptops around, the Surface Laptop Ultra is a solid choice. But just be aware that you'll have to pay out the nose to enjoy it. Our review unit, which was equipped with 32GB of RAM, 1TB of storage and the full-powered RTX Spark chip, sells for $3,700. Bumping up to 64GB of RAM would run you $4,300, and it jumps to $5,900 with 128GB of RAM. All of a sudden, the $2,600 base price doesn't seem so bad.
It's strange that the Surface Laptop Ultra maxes out at 2TB of storage, though. Other premium systems have offered up to 4TB for years, shouldn't the "Ultra" Surface device at least match that?
If you have deep pockets and want the most for your money, though, Apple's MacBook Pros are still a better choice when it comes to pure power. NVIDIA's first-gen RTX Spark chip just can't beat the M5 Pro, and it's certainly no match for even more capable M5 Max and Ultra chips. Sure, they'll cost a ton, but you can also get a 16-inch MacBook Pro PROLED that weighs just four pounds and is stuffed with 128GB of RAM. If you're already spending close to $10,000 on a laptop, why not get the best one possible?
Wrap-up
Microsoft has finally managed to make a powerful Surface device with modern hardware, something it failed to do with the previous Surface Book and Laptop Studio systems. The Surface Laptop Ultra's sheer refinement is a sign of just how far Microsoft has come. It sure is expensive, though. And even with its high price tag, it still lags behind Apple's hardware when it comes to raw performance.

Who is Colette Kress, NVIDIA's interim CEO?
Kress spent 25 years in various finance roles before joining NVIDIA in 2013
After 33 years as the chief executive officer of NVIDIA, Jensen Huang has resigned from the AI and gaming giant he founded. On Thursday morning, the company's board of director announced Colette Kress, NVIDIA's current executive vice president and chief financial officer, as Huang's temporary replacement.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," newly-minted NVIDIA board chair Harvey Jones said in a release announcing Thursday's news.
Kress is a relative unknown, but is taking lead of NVIDIA at tumultuous time in the company's history. Huang departure comes days after NVIDIA's board said it would investigate Huang after he admitted to having an affair with a former tech executive accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset. The New York Times later reported that Huang had also had an affair with an NVIDIA executive who reported to him. Before the revelations, the company did not have a succession plan in place. And for at least the immediate future, it's now on Kress to lead the company. Here's what we know about the executive.
Who is Kress?
Kress worked at three companies before joining NVIDIA. She first spent eight years in finance roles at Texas Instruments before joining Microsoft in 1997. In 2006, six years after Steve Ballmer took over as Microsoft's CEO, she became the chief financial officer of the company's Server and Tools division. She remained with the company until 2010, when she moved to Cisco. There, she was the senior vice president and chief financial officer of the company's Business Technology and Operations Finance unit.
To hear Kress tell it, Huang went out of his way to recruit her. Sometime before she joined NVIDIA in 2013, the CEO apparently sketched his vision for the company on a whiteboard. Per a 2023 interview, Huang wanted to transform NVIDIA into the dominant player in the nascent AI industry. Say what you will about Huang's personal life and judgement, the man was an AI visionary.
It would be almost another four years following Kress joining NVIDIA before a group of Google researchers published "Attention Is All You Need," the paper that introduced the world to transformer models, and nearly a decade before the release of ChatGPT. Kress partly credits her sons, who were only eight and 10 at the time, for buying Huang's pitch. Despite their young age, the two already knew of NVIDIA and its importance to gaming. In a 2024 Fortune interview, Kress said NVIDIA was the smallest company she had worked for when she joined in 2013.
At the start of her tenure, NVIDIA's revenue was $4.28 billion for the year. In fiscal 2026, the company recorded a record $215.9 billion in revenue.
What comes next?
When NVIDIA's board of directors announced Kress as Huang's temporary successor, it said it would consider both internal and external candidates to take on the role of CEO permanently, leaving the door open for her and other current NVIDIA employees to win the job. In any case, it's far too early to speculate who the company's board might interview for the job. But if you can forgive a writer a tired analogy, if Kress stays on as CEO, she is likely to be a Tim Cook-like figure, one that can stabilize the company and guide it toward continued growth.
"The Board, [executive staff] and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication," Kress wrote in her first email to NVIDIA employees after the transition was announced, according to CNBC.
Still, she has a very difficult job ahead of her. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress in a hearing that the House aims to hold before the Thanksgiving holiday. The chair of the House Foreign Affairs committee, Brian Mast of Florida, said he wasn't ruling out the possibility of "public hearings for other people or other things down road." You can bet NVIDIA is likely to face an intense amount of scrutiny in the coming weeks, particularly when Democrats take control of the House and Senate at the start of next year.

Quick Answer
If your Android phone’s battery drains too quickly, try enabling auto-brightness, using dark mode, limiting background apps, reducing screen timeout, and turning off unused features. These 15 practical tips can improve battery life and help maintain battery health.
I cannot function without my phone. It makes my experience better during my walks, jogs, and all other activities throughout the day. Unfortunately, I have to charge my phone multiple times a day or keep a power bank as a backup, just in case. The ease created by my Android phone is instantly undone by the quickly draining battery. Along with the phone, I should carry a cable, an adapter, and a power bank.
In that frustration, I started looking into why my Android phone battery was draining fast. I checked the battery usage data, identified what was causing the drain, and fixed those issues. Now, my battery lasts longer. These are the tips that helped me improve the battery life on my Android phone.
Table of Contents
Android Phone Battery Draining Fast? Try These 10 Tips
I used these tips to improve my Android phone’s battery life on a single charge. You can use the tips that work for you without sacrificing the functionality you need.
Enable Auto Brightness
Brightness affects how visible the display is, irrespective of the light in our surroundings. When we keep the brightness too high, it affects our eyes in the dark. In addition to that, the battery drains too quickly when powering the high brightness for your phone’s display.
If we keep the brightness low, it affects the visibility of our phone’s display during daytime when we are out in the open under the sun. To not affect the visibility and save the battery from draining quickly, we can enable Auto Brightness on our phone.
The auto-brightness feature on our phones adjusts the brightness of our display based on the light in our surroundings. For example, when you are outside where there is abundant sunlight, the auto-brightness feature increases the brightness to make visibility better for you. Similarly, it decreases the brightness when you are in a dark or dimmed environment.
To enable auto-brightness on your phone, open the Settings app and go to Display or Display & brightness settings. The jargon for options varies by manufacturer.
Find Brightness options and toggle the button beside Auto brightness to enable it. You will see the brightness of your screen increase or decrease as per your environment in real time.
Enable Dark Mode
Android phones with OLED or AMOLED displays consume more power for display. If it is set to light mode, a major chunk of battery life goes to power. Setting the screen to dark mode makes it easier on the battery. The battery does not need to power the entire display by switching off the black pixels.
You can enable dark mode in the display settings of your phone. Open the Settings app and find the display settings. Set the display mode to Dark mode.
Dark mode, at first, may look odd. Once you get accustomed to it, there is no going back.
Disable Always-On Display
Always-On Display consumes a significant amount of power from the battery. The display always shows time or notifications even when you are not using the phone actively.
You must disable the Always-On Display feature if you do not have any use for it. Open the Settings app on your Android phone and search for Always-On Display. It will show the option. Tap on it. Toggle the button beside Always-On Display to turn it off.
It may not reduce battery drain noticeably, but small things like these can help optimize battery life.
Set Screen Refresh Rate to Auto
The screen refresh rate feature on Android gives us a smoother display experience. Manufacturers flaunt the screen refresh rate while launching and advertising new smartphones. The higher the refresh rate of a screen is, the more battery it consumes. If you are not a gamer or do not use your phone for experiences that demand a higher refresh rate, you may set the Screen refresh rate to Auto.
Open the Settings app on your phone, search for refresh rate, and open the refresh rate options. Then, set the refresh rate to Auto or Auto-select. Instead of using a higher refresh rate that consumes more battery, your phone now optimizes the screen refresh rate based on the app or activity for a smoother experience. You may also set it to Standard or anything that offers a 60 Hz refresh rate to extend battery life.
If you are a gamer, Auto refresh rate would be the best option.
Decrease Screen Off Time
Screen off time is something we mostly overlook when looking to optimize battery on our phones. If the screen off time is set to a longer time, it consumes battery and aids in draining faster. Small things like these add up and drain the battery.
Open the Settings app on your phone and search for screen off. You can find the Screen off feature in Display settings. Tap on the Screen off or Auto Screen off options (based on your manufacturer) and select a shorter time.
Now, when you do not use the phone, the screen will be turned off as per the time you have selected. The shorter the time, the more you optimize the battery.
Disable Unnecessary Sounds and Vibrations
Sound and vibration for ringtones and notifications are okay. But touch vibrations, keyboard sounds, dial pad tones, lock sounds, and other such sounds or vibrations when we do something on our phone are not necessary. They stress the battery and make it drain faster.
Disabling those unnecessary sounds and vibrations enhances the battery life and saves you from charging the phone frequently.
Open the Settings app on your phone and go to Sound & vibration settings. Go to More sounds (on OxygenOS) or similar settings where you can enable or disable additional sounds, based on your manufacturer.
Then, disable the sounds that you feel are unnecessary by toggling the buttons beside them.
This can optimize battery life, and you can notice the difference within a few hours. Additionally, you can tweak the vibration intensity to optimize your battery further regarding sound and vibration settings.
Check for Apps That Use a Lot of Battery
Android provides detailed battery data where we can see which app is consuming more battery, how long each charge lasts, etc. Using the battery data, we can optimize the apps that consume a lot of battery or install alternatives that consume less battery.
We can access the battery data through the Battery settings. Open Settings and go to Battery settings on your device. Scroll down to the Battery usage by app section in the Battery settings and see which app is using more battery. Tap on the app that is consuming a lot of battery.
It opens the detailed view of battery consumption in the last 24 hours. You can also see options to control battery consumption for the particular app by restricting background activity, etc. Select Restrict background activity if you want to optimize battery and extend its life.
If you want the app to run in the background, you can set it to Smart mode if your manufacturer provides such an option. Repeat the process until you restrict all the power-hungry apps on your device. This significantly improves the life of your battery in each charge.
Turn On the Option to Enter Power Saving Mode Automatically
In the Battery settings, you will find Power saving settings or options. Go to Power saving settings and toggle the button beside Automatically enter Power saving mode. Then, set the battery percentage that should trigger the power saving mode on your device.
Your device will enter Power saving mode when it triggers the battery percentage you set, and it will last longer.
Disable WiFi, Mobile Data, Location, and Bluetooth When Not in Use
You might have noticed your phone battery drains quicker than normal when you pair Bluetooth devices or use location actively. It is better to turn them off when you do not use them.
Keeping WiFi, mobile data, location, and Bluetooth on, even without any usage, consumes a good amount of battery. When you are not actively using any of them, turning them off saves you some battery.
Turn Off Additional Features
There are many features that we rarely use, but consume a good amount of battery. They are live wallpapers, widgets that we do not use, opening web pages and leaving them running in the background, manufacturer apps that run automatically, etc.
Disabling or turning them off saves us a lot of battery. In addition to them, when we install a new app, it asks for notification permissions, location permissions, etc. Disabling notifications for unimportant apps also saves our battery from draining quickly.
These tips, when used together, will optimize your Android device’s battery and extend its life in each charge cycle. Even after doing all this, the battery may drain quickly due to deteriorated battery health. Let’s see how to check and optimize battery health on Android.
How to Optimize Battery Health on Android
The battery on our Android phone degrades with use, and the health drops from 100% to lower levels. The lower the health of your battery, the less power it stores. The capacity keeps on degrading. This is not limited to iPhones. Android phones also started showing battery health. It depends on your manufacturer.
To check the battery health on your Android, you can use third-party apps like Battery Guru or AccuBattery. You may use the app of your choice too, if your manufacturer does not provide an option to look at your battery’s health.
To expand the life and usability of our Android phone, we need to preserve the health of the battery. If not, we may have to replace the battery or the phone altogether. You can preserve the battery health on Android by following these simple tips.
Set a Custom Charging Limit
Android phones let us set a custom charging limit to preserve battery health and protect it from fast degradation of capacity. Manufacturers recommend setting the charging limit to 80- 90% and not beyond that. Charging our phone up to 100% every time is actually not recommended by manufacturers.
We always need to make sure our phone battery never falls below 10% or charges beyond 90%. You can set a custom charging limit in the Battery settings of your phone.
Open the Settings app on your phone and search for Battery health. Open the Battery health options. Toggle the button beside Custom charging limit. Then, set the limit as per the recommendations of the manufacturer.
These options may vary based on your phone manufacturer. The options remain the same, but the wording may change. Follow accordingly to set a custom charging limit.
After setting the custom charging limit, your phone will never charge beyond that percentage. If your manufacturer offers Smart Charging, Adaptive Charging, or Smart Charge options, you may even enable them to let them implement charging patterns based on your charging habits.
Use Chargers or Cables From Device Manufacturers
Charging phones with the available charger is bad for our device’s battery. We must get an adapter and cable made by the manufacturer to save the battery. If they are not available, we must ensure we get charging accessories that are compatible with our device from trusted brands.
Before getting a new charger for your phone, look at the specifications of your device and get the adapter and cable that support the power specified for your device.
Never Let Your Phone Overheat
Batteries degrade faster when they overheat or are exposed to heat. Do not expose your phone to direct sunlight or hot areas. Do not use your phone for heavy activities like gaming while it is charging.
Use Recommended Battery Settings
Phone manufacturers recommend certain settings to preserve battery health and extend its life. They can be found under the options provided in the Battery settings or the Battery optimization app provided by the manufacturer.
Follow those recommendations strictly to save your battery from degradation and faster draining.
Install Updates Regularly
It is not a wise choice to ignore installing pending updates. Android phones get monthly security updates and software updates regularly. We need to make sure they are installed automatically.
Fix a Fast-Draining Battery on Android
If you notice the battery of your Android phone is draining fast, you need to make sure there are no apps running in the background. Limit app activity in the background, update apps, turn off features that you do not use, install updates, and fix all the issues that are contributing to fast battery drain.

“In focusing attention on the mortality associated with Alzheimer disease, our goal is not to find a way to prolong the life of severely demented persons, but rather to call attention to our belief that senile as well as presenile forms of Alzheimer are a single disease, a disease whose etiology must be determined, whose course must be aborted, and ultimately a disease to be prevented.”

Nvidia Scandal Prompts Questions of What It Means to Be a Spy
U.S. intelligence agencies believe a woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang was a Chinese asset. But there is much more that they are still assessing about her role.
Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the center of the Nvidia spying scandal, was believed to be using her affair with Nvidia’s founder to help China get around U.S. efforts to restrict access to advanced A.I. chips, people who have read U.S. intelligence reporting said.
But there remains much that intelligence agencies are still assessing about Ms. Huang including when she began working with China’s top spy agency, whether her cooperation was willing or coerced, how much direction Beijing gave her, and how much she relayed to officials there, the people said.
Her relationship with Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday, gave her potential access to crucial information about the company’s technology, Mr. Huang’s strategic thinking and his knowledge of Washington’s debates about A.I. policy.
She also had a business interest in ensuring a flow of chips to her own company, one of a number in Southeast Asia that provided Chinese tech firms with the computing power needed to train advanced artificial intelligence models.
The aftershocks of the scandal continue to play out as President Trump prepares for a trip next week to Asia, where he is scheduled to meet with President Xi Jinping of China, who has made a top priority of catching the United States in the race for A.I. dominance.
The unknowns surrounding Ms. Huang have generated intense scrutiny of how Chinese intelligence operates, prompted questions of what it means to be a spy and given backers of Mr. Huang an opening to raise questions about the extent and nature of her role.

Hajra Begum rolls a potato in her hands, checking its skin for cuts, soft spots and signs of rot. After a day harvesting in her family’s field in Chorwan, a remote mountain village in Gurez, Indian-administered Kashmir, she is sorting the crop for winter storage. Some of the potatoes will feed her family through the cold months; others will be saved for planting in spring.
“It should be perfect for planting,” she says. “If you keep a bad potato, you will waste the whole next year.”
Begum, 40, is preparing to lower the potatoes into a khraw, a traditional underground storage pit lined with straw and sealed against the cold. For generations, khraws have kept potatoes, turnips and cabbages through Himalayan winters, when heavy snowfall cuts villages off from the Kashmir valley and temperatures fall below -20C (-4F) – cold enough to crack pipes and freeze diesel.
But the practice is slowly dying out. As roads have improved and young people have left for work and education, fewer families maintain the pits. Their decline threatens not only a traditional way of storing food but also the local potato varieties themselves and the knowledge of which ones store well, resist rot and produce reliable harvests.
“When I was young, almost every family had three or four pits,” Begum says. “Now, down in the main valley, they have abandoned the practice altogether. Only a handful of families still use them. The rest buy from the market or subsidised ones from the government.”
Begum learned from her mother how to tell potatoes that store well from those that rot or sprout too quickly. She is passing this on to her daughter, but is unsure whether the skill will survive into another generation.
Gurez is a high-altitude Himalayan valley perched near the Line of Control, the heavily militarised boundary separating Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. About 80 miles (125km) from Srinagar, the valley remains cut off each winter when snow closes Razdan pass, its main road link, which sits at roughly 3,600 metres.
It is home to the Dard-Shin people, an Indigenous community who speak Shina and have a culture that is distinct from Kashmiri, with community links across the border in Gilgit-Baltistan, administered by Pakistan.
Potatoes account for about 45% of Gurez’s cultivated area, according to a 2019 study by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research’s National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (ICAR-NBPGR), a government body that studies and conserves India’s crop diversity. Yet the genetic diversity of the valley’s potatoes has not been systematically documented.
Dr Sheikh M Sultan, a senior scientist based at ICAR-NBPGR’s Srinagar station, surveyed the valley and later struggled to find some of the varieties he had once encountered. “When I first visited, I saw many varieties,” he says. “Later, I could hardly locate even one sample of some. The loss of genetic diversity is tremendous.”
Sultan says migration, improved roads and changing lifestyles have contributed to the decline. As traditional farming disappears, so does knowledge about selecting, cultivating and preserving local varieties.
“When people stop producing their own seeds and start relying entirely on commercial varieties, the loss can be irreparable,” he says.
He warns that research institutions often prioritise introduced varieties over indigenous crops whose characteristics remain poorly understood. “Our indigenous varieties may possess valuable characteristics, including tolerance to cold and resistance to certain pests and diseases,” he says.
“These are resources we should be studying and improving, rather than neglecting.”
Climate breakdown is adding to the pressures on farmers across the Himalayas. People in Gurez report drier springs, reduced snowfall and water shortages, which they say have affected potato production.
Abdul Jabbar Mapnoo, 70, a farmer in Chorwan, remembers winters when deep snow covered the valley. “Every house used to have two or three khraw, each holding about five quintals – 500kg – of potatoes,” he says. “The springs are drying up, and there is less snow in winter. Potato production has fallen. I remember winters when six feet of snow would cover the valley in January or February.”
As farming becomes more difficult and markets easier to access, households have less incentive to grow their own potatoes. Varieties adapted to local conditions over generations could disappear from cultivation before researchers establish what makes them distinctive.
Dr Parveen Kumar, a scientist at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir, says locally adapted varieties should not be overlooked. “Climate change is a reality, and farmers need to be aware of adaptation strategies,” he says.
Pressure on farmland poses another risk. In Gurez, where cultivable land is scarce, the Kishanganga hydroelectric project has affected land in the valley through acquisition and submergence. Among the areas affected is Badwan, a village known for its potatoes.
One potential route for preserving the varieties could be through using geographical indications – a designation granted by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, and is similar to the French appellation d’origine contrôlée. It can be used on goods that have a specific origin and possess qualities or a reputation linked to this – which can help increase the market value and give them greater recognition. This, and the globally important agricultural heritage systems programme have helped areas such as the saffron-growing landscape of Pampore in Kashmir.
However, recognition alone will not preserve the varieties. They must be identified and documented before they disappear from cultivation, along with farmers’ knowledge of how to select, store and replant them.
In Chorwan, Begum unloads the last sack of potatoes into the pit and covers it, ready for another winter. Some will feed her family; the rest will be replanted in spring. Knowing which potatoes to eat and which to save as seed relies on knowledge passed down through generations.
If these varieties are not documented while they are still being cultivated, Kashmir may lose a living agricultural treasure trove before scientists can fully understand what it contains.

A purported video of former Western Command chief Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.) is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows him expressing concerns over India’s military preparedness and alleging that China has advanced 25 km into Arunachal Pradesh, an advance that Indian forces have been unable to contain. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.) expressing concern over China’s 25 km advance into Arunachal Pradesh.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. The original footage is from Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd. )’s media interaction at Chandimandir, Panchkula, on 30 March 2026, ahead of his retirement. He discusses Operation Sindoor, Operation Rahat and Western Command initiatives, but makes no remarks about China advancing 25 km into Arunachal Pradesh. The Indian Army’s fact-checking wing also confirmed the manipulation, while AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya, indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.) made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating it.
We noticed that the viral video carries a watermark from the news agency ANI. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 30 March 2026, featuring the same footage of Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.), in the same attire and speaking against an identical background. However, his remarks in the original video are entirely different. He was speaking ahead of his retirement and discussed the successful thwarting of Pakistan’s objectives during Operation Sindoor, the procurement of new equipment, including drones and counter-drone systems, and various welfare initiatives undertaken by the Western Command for its personnel. He also highlighted the Command’s role in Operation Rahat during the floods that struck the region the previous year. The original footage contains no remarks about China advancing 25 km into Arunachal Pradesh or concerns over Indian aircraft losses, as claimed in the viral video.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, suggesting that fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear that Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.) was expressing concern over China’s alleged 25 km advance into Arunachal Pradesh.
The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also debunked the claim in an X post, stating that the video was digitally manipulated and falsely attributed remarks to former Western Command chief Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.). It clarified that the original footage was from his media interaction at Chandimandir, Panchkula, on 30 March 2026, on the eve of his retirement. The Army confirmed that he discussed Operation Sindoor, Operation Rahat, operational preparedness, and other Western Command initiatives, but made no statement about Arunachal Pradesh becoming India’s next major military flashpoint.
To sum up, this viral video of Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.) expressing concern over China’s advance into Arunachal Pradesh is AI-manipulated.

The Kapoor family is famously known for its love of food and celebrations, with Raj Kapoor is particularly remembered for hosting grand gatherings and throwing some of the biggest parties for his Bollywood peers. The family continues to uphold this tradition, especially during Christmas every year. Recently, speaking to The Curly Tales, Neetu Kapoor recalled how her in-laws loved entertaining guests and were very particular about their Diwali traditions. She also shared a heartwarming anecdote about her mother-in-law, Krishna Raj Kapoor, tearing up an envelope full of money after her late husband, Rishi Kapoor, missed the family’s Diwali celebrations.
Recalling her early days in the Kapoor household, Neetu said that the table would always be full of food whenever the family hosted a celebration. She said her late father-in-law “loved to see his family eat” and this was “his way of feeling happy.”
She then recalled the family’s Diwali traditions and how everyone would gather at Raj Kapoor and Krishna Raj Kapoor’s home in Chembur after performing puja at their respective homes.
“Mom used to have these envelopes ready for everyone,” she said suggesting that the enveloped would be full of cash. However, one Diwali, things did not go as planned because Rishi was caught up with work. Recalling the incident, Neetu said, “Next day, we went to meet her and she took out the envelope, took out the money, and she tore the envelope.”
Neetu recalled her mother-in-law’s reaction and shared, “She said, ‘You don’t deserve it. I missed you yesterday’. It’s just that she had so much love. She just commanded love, she didn’t demand it.” Neetu also revealed that she has carried forward the family tradition and is now the one handing out envelopes to her children, Ranbir and Riddhima, during Diwali celebrations.

In the same interview, Neetu also described her mother-in-law as a “big joker” and recalled how she would often make her laugh with her witty observations, even in the most unexpected situations. She recalled how when they once visited someone’s prayer meet where everyone was in mourning but her mother-in-law noticed someone’s “weird outfit.” “She came to me with a straight face and said, ‘Make this for me,’ and I couldn’t stop laughing. I said, ‘Mom, someone’s prayer meet is happening,'” she recalled. She also shared that both her children, Ranbir and Riddhima Kapoor, adored their grandmother.
Speaking to SCREEN in 2024, Neetu’s daughter, Riddhima Kapoor Sahni also recalled some of her fondest childhood memories with her grandparents. She shared: “One of mine and Ranbir’s best childhood memories is spending our weekends with both our grandparents at the Chembur house. Every weekend, both my brother and I used to go there, and even take our friends for sleepovers sometimes. They used to be overjoyed to have us and all the other kids.”
Recalling her grandfather’s love for cooking, Riddhima added: “He used to cook on his own. My grandfather used to prepare our favourite dishes. I loved the macaroni and cheese; it was our staple. It was in his style, unka hi tadka tha. There was a secret ingredient, I am sure. They used to make it with so much love. I can literally taste the flavour even today. It was yummy.”
After Krishna Raj Kapoor’s death in 2018, Neetu Kapoor took to Instagram to share an emotional note remembering her mother-in-law. She wrote: “She was such a huge influence in my life. Admired her elegance with generosity, warmth! She will always stay in my heart.” Neetu and Rishi were in the US at the time for his cancer treatment.
Raj Kapoor passed away in 1988 at the age of 63, while his wife, Krishna Raj Kapoor, died in 2018 at the age of 87.

The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.
The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.
“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”
Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.
Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories
- UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.
- Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.
- US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.
- Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
- Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.
In depth: Everything we know (or don’t) about the Nvidia affair
Last month, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, the former executive of a Singapore-based computing company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips they produce, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. The US government had already been investigating whether Megaspeed could be flouting US restrictions and smuggling chips into China – allegations that both Nvidia and Megaspeed deny.
US intelligence officials, who had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, eventually concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been passing on information to Beijing. The intelligence behind this assessment is classified, so we don’t know exactly what they found – or which intelligence body was conducting the surveillance. Nvidia said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected”, but on Sunday, Huang admitted in a letter to his employees that he had been having an affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” he said, adding that he was “deeply sorry”.
Nvidia’s valuation is inextricably linked to Huang. By yesterday, $430bn (5.5%) had been wiped off its share price, and in the early hours of this morning, that figure ballooned to about $600bn following reports that Nvidia’s board was deciding whether to oust Huang (you can follow the latest on that here). The company has appointed outside counsel to review the pair’s relationship and says it has no reason to believe that secrets or national security were compromised.
The most interesting aspects of this story are the questions we can’t (yet) answer. Did Nvidia’s board know that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang was a spy? What evidence led US intelligence to conclude she was spying for China? What information could she have passed to Beijing? And …
Who is Alice Huang?
Reporters and sleuths on Chinese social media have been trying to get to the bottom of who the Megaspeed chief really is. On Tuesday, the Financial Times published an interesting report (£) about Alice Huang’s backstory. She was born in the rural area of Hunan, worked as a journalist at China’s state broadcaster, then at HSBC and the investment bank Citic Securities. In 2015, she joined an investment management company Hexi.
There, she met financier Kang Wei. The two became romantically involved, and together they reinvented themselves as AI entrepreneurs. In 2023, Huang and her business partners acquired Megaspeed, a Singaporean subsidiary of a Chinese gaming company, which she and Wei aimed to turn into a datacentre business. According to the FT’s report, the two pitched investors on their ability to secure access to Nvidia chips.
Nobody knows exactly when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, when their relationship became romantic, or what information she might have passed to Beijing while it was going on. The earliest picture of them together is at an after-party following a tech trade show in Taipei, taken in 2024. As Aisha Down and Dan Milmo pointed out earlier this week, Jensen Huang is close to Donald Trump, so it’s possible that Alice Huang could have gained glimpses into US AI policy as it was being formed, into Trump’s thinking on AI, or into Nvidia’s company strategy. But without seeing the evidence, all this is speculation.
What does this reveal about Chinese espionage?
The US has been historically cautious about allowing AI chips to end up in Chinese hands. In 2022, Joe Biden’s administration introduced the Chips and Science Act, which restricted the sale of US chips in China, banning the export of most Nvidia chips. “The Chinese have a very strong pedigree for industrial espionage and copying other nations’ technologies,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute, tells me. “They’ve been doing this for decades. And now it’s no longer engines they’re interested in, but AI.”
Both the US and China have an interest in gathering intelligence about each other’s AI firms. What’s more remarkable is the possibility that the Chinese spy agency, the MSS, could have recruited Alice Huang as a “honeytrap” to ensnare Jensen Huang – a method fraught with risk, which seems more reminiscent of 1970s spy fiction than contemporary counterintelligence (China, for its part, has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy).
“The facts clearly aren’t established, but it seems more likely that if Alice Huang was working for Beijing, the MSS would have recruited her after they became aware of her relationship with Huang, not before,” Nigel Inkster, the former director of operations and intelligence for the British Secret Intelligence Service, tells me.
China has built a large intelligence gathering operation: the MSS is now bigger than the CIA, and various national security laws mean that Chinese nationals can be required to provide assistance to the Chinese state. “You have a lot of people who can be co-opted into intelligence gathering, all of whom can be tasked with different requirements,” Inkster says. “Business delegations travelling abroad can be tasked with gathering information. So can visiting academics.”
“The big question, to my mind, is whether the Chinese intelligence agencies have actually been willing to deliver unwelcome information to the party leadership,” Inkster adds.
What approach has the US taken?
Jensen Huang is the most influential figure in the US AI industry outside major labs such as Anthropic, and has cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump. He’s successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen regulations on AI and roll back restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China (last year, Trump controversially approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips directly to China in exchange for the federal government taking a 25% cut). Huang was present at the White House twice last month: once for a state dinner with Xi Jinping, and again for a meeting of tech and AI executives.
Huang’s close relationship with Trump could help explain why the president has so far played down concerns about Chinese espionage, appearing remarkably ambivalent about the recent allegations. The president was reportedly briefed last year about US intelligence conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, and in spring this year, his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, supervised the drafting of a classified memo warning that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy. In May, Trump issued a last-minute invitation to Jensen Huang to board Air Force One in Alaska and join a delegation of executives bound to China. A US government official told reporters at the New York Times that when Rubio learned that Huang would be joining the trip in Alaska, he briefed Trump on the memo.
But on Monday, Trump, who is due to meet Xi Jinping later this month, said he had not known at the time of the trip about Huang’s relationship. He said the FBI had been investigating a matter relating to Huang, and defended the Nvidia CEO, describing him as an “honourable guy” who “built a great American company”.

For decades, efforts to detect the cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours. “We asked … what if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” said study leader Rajan Gogna.
Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The study found that women experiencing these changes have elevated levels of a molecule called Tu-Stroma in their blood.
The study’s co-author Dr Esha Madan says the discovery “could transform how we approach prevention”.

While Friday's nationwide ground stop has been lifted, airports in Canada are dealing with the influx of traffic and passengers from canceled and diverted flights.
Toronto Pearson International Airport provided status updates on X throughout the day regarding its domestic and international operations. At 9:20 p.m., the airport said the ground stop was over — the FAA had lifted it around 8:30 p.m. — but flights to and from the US would still be disrupted.
Still, that doesn't mean the chaos is over — with planes and crews displaced, it could be well into the weekend before things get back on track.
Toronto Pearson said it brought in additional staff to manage the crowds and help travelers.
"We are increasing staffing across the airport to assist affected passengers," the airport said. "Our support teams are being deployed throughout the terminals, with additional resources available in the U.S. departures area. We are also working closely with airlines and have implemented a parking plan for aircraft."
Other airports, including Montreal, Calgary, and Vancouver, also implemented traffic management systems, NAV CANADA, a privately run nonprofit corporation that owns and operates Canada's civil air traffic system, said Friday evening on X.
It said during the outage that its systems were "operating normally" and that it issued the programs to "safely manage traffic volumes."
Mark Stephens, a retired Delta Air Lines pilot, told Business Insider that Canadian airports would take on US-bound international flights that need to divert.
He added that the planes on the ground at the airports will return to their gates, meaning traffic management will be imperative to handle the potential increase in volume.
As of 10 p.m. Eastern time, nearly 7,000 flights have been canceled within, to, or out of the US, according to FlightAware.com. Another 7,000 have been delayed.
Cirium, an aviation analytics company, said nearly 1,000 flights were diverted on Friday, with airports like Denver, Chicago, Los Angeles, and Cleveland taking on additional aircraft.

In French Election, Centrists Eye a Judo Star and a Central Banker
Centrists want alternatives to a matchup between the far right and far left in the 2027 presidential election. Teddy Riner, the judo champion, is in, while Christine Lagarde is less likely.
When Teddy Riner, a judo champion and one of France’s most popular athletes, announced this week that he would run for president, it was less a game changer than a welcome diversion. For all of his appeal, Mr. Riner, 37, is unlikely to win the race to replace President Emmanuel Macron next spring.
Yet his quixotic candidacy reveals a hard truth about France’s presidential campaign. Five months before voters go to the polls, many are eager, even desperate, for a fresh face to upend a race that looks increasingly as if it’s on a glide path to the election of France’s first far-right government since World War II.
The main far-right candidate, Marine Le Pen, has held a commanding lead over all her rivals for months — a lead that has only been reinforced by weeks of protests, marred by violence, that have shaken France. The most prominent center-right candidate, Édouard Philippe, has faded in the polls as the unrest has sharpened the appeal of far-right calls for law and order and left-wing calls for social justice.
Another beneficiary of the upheaval is a far-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who now appears to be the likeliest candidate to advance into a second round against Ms. Le Pen in France’s two-round system. As things currently stand, French voters would be confronted with a choice between two poles of the political spectrum.
Centrist voters are “afraid of being confronted with a duel between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon,” said Jean-Daniel Lévy, deputy director of Toluna France, a polling firm. These voters, he said, are an “orphan electorate,” lacking an inspiring candidate, and are “still looking for someone.”
Raphaël LLorca, an analyst at the Jean-Jaurès Foundation, a left-leaning research group in Paris, said the search for a white knight showed “the panic of the centrist bloc.” He added, “It is clear that the election is slipping away from them.”

WASHINGTON — Two senators are introducing a bill Friday to rein in conflicts of interest on an influential federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services.
The bill, from Sens. Angus King (I-Maine) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), follows reports that a number of members picked by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. could profit from the decisions they make on the panel, known as the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. It would codify standards for membership on the panel and for avoiding conflicts of interest.
The bill comes after STAT reported that members of the panel hold stock in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and that two of them own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care. The New York Times reported on the financial investments as well. Federal officials granted all members blanket waivers, allowing them to remain on the panel, though they could still be required to recuse themselves from particular matters. The panel has not met in more than a year.

The Keralam government will take steps to implement ‘Family Sustainability Mapping’ across the State to identify, at an early stage, children living in high-risk environments, Minister for Women and Child Development Bindhu Krishna has said.
Speaking at a press conference to announce the Ujjwala Balyam Awards on Wednesday (November 11, 2026), she said a decision regarding the mapping was reached during a meeting convened following the death of a two-year-old child in Alappuzha recently due to suspected malnutrition.
The circumstances of families and children will be assessed with the cooperation of schools, Anganwadis, local self-government institutions, District Child Protection Units, healthcare workers and the police. Children facing risks such as malnutrition, neglect, domestic abuse, child labour, begging, school dropouts, substance abuse-related issues or various forms of exploitation will be identified and necessary protection and rehabilitation will be ensured.
“Child protection efforts should not be limited to intervening only after abuse or exploitation has already occurred. The government’s objective is to proactively identify high risk situations and ensure timely protection for children. Coordinated action among various departments and institutions will be strengthened to prevent issues such as sexual abuse, physical and mental abuse, neglect, child labour, child begging, human trafficking and online exploitation,” she said.
Activities will be jointly coordinated by departments including the Department of Women and Child Development, the Health Department, the Police, and the Local Self Government Department. This will enable the strengthening of existing child protection systems as well as the proactive identification of risks and the implementation of preventive measures. The Minister stated that the active participation of society is essential to ensure a safe childhood and equal opportunities for every child and to create an environment in which they can grow up with self confidence.
Ms .Krishna said that a total of 52 children from 14 districts have been chosen for the Ujjwala Balyam Awards for showcasing exemplary talent in arts, sports, literature, science, social work, environmental protection, information technology, agriculture, waste management, humanitarian activities, crafts, sculpture and acts involving extraordinary courage.
The winners were selected by a committee chaired by the District Collector in each district. The award consists of a cash prize of ₹25,000, a citation and a plaque. The awards will be presented at the State-level Children’s Day celebration to be held in Thiruvananthapuram on November 14.
The award recipients are children who have demonstrated excellence in various fields, including social work, environmental protection, information technology, agriculture, waste management, humanitarian activities, crafts, sculpture, and acts involving extraordinary courage.
