Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.
The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.
Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.
The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.
“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.
The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.
“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.
Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.
During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.
“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.
It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.
Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.
Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.
The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.
Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.
“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

Don't bother applying for a job at Anthropic if your goal is to be the star of the show.
That was one of the first things Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized on Friday, in a live-streamed interview with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon ahead of the AI startup's hotly anticipated IPO.
Amodei said the company has been "very disciplined about turning down people who are deeply technically talented," but don't fit its culture. The company's recent IPO filing stated that its workforce grew from about 940 employees at the end of 2024 to about 5,300 as of late September.
"We don't want people who are jerks. We don't want people who try to steal the show and don't work well with others. We don't want people who aren't oriented towards the public benefit," Amodei told Dimon.
Amodei, who worked as vice president of research at research at OpenAI and was a senior research scientist at Google Brain, said talent and culture "are the most important things" for a company. He said he now devotes 40% to 50% of his time to focusing on those priorities.
'High-trust, low-ego'
The CEO said that talent and culture create technology, and the company's presence and how it's viewed by the public comes from the talent and intentions of the people who build that technology. Amodei said he and his six cofounders decided at the company's founding that talent and culture would be their priority.
"If you stick to that consistently, it's painful in the short run. But you get a team where everyone works together, and everyone is on the same side," Amodei said.
Anthropic describes itself as a "high-trust, low-ego organization" on its website, and in its IPO filing said that "teams operate in a truth-seeking environment where the best argument wins, not the loudest voice or the most senior title."
Amodei told Dimon that he encourages other leaders to demonstrate honesty and trust. He said that every two weeks he holds a "Dario Vision Quest," an all-hands meeting where he said he speaks to the company about what's going on.
Amodei said he tries not to hide things from staff and doesn't rely on corporate jargon. That creates an environment where employees can trust leaders and leaders can trust employees, he said.
"Everyone feels that we're being honest with them," Amodei said, adding that this carries "enormous value."
A focus on retention
Amodei told Dimon that the approach works because employees share the same values and a common goal. Whether the task is training a model, meeting a safety objective, building a product, or advancing a policy priority, "the whole company comes together to make it happen," he said.
Amodei said that maintaining that kind of environment has helped with retention, which is critical given the company's dependence on senior leaders and key technical team members. Amodei said that all seven cofounders, including himself, are still at the company, along with over three-quarters of its first 100 employees. In its IPO filing, Anthropic said it experienced only about 1% "regrettable attrition" in a 12-month period.
Amodei added that it's a "relatively frequent" occurrence for employees to come back after leaving. He said two major product employees left and came back after two weeks.
"They said, 'Sorry, we didn't appreciate what we had,'" Amodei said about their return.

India’s tuberculosis (TB) burden remains substantial despite progress. The country has the largest TB burden in the world, accounting for approximately one-quarter of all TB cases globally. The number of new cases fell 21% between 2015 and 2024, while treatment coverage rose to 92%, according to World Health Organization data cited by the government. The Central government recently started the JOSH campaign -- launched in 11 States and 55 districts to promote screening, early diagnosis and treatment adherence. JOSH stands for Joint Squad for Health. It is a youth-led community mobilisation initiative to strengthen India’s campaign to eliminate TB.
Dhun Davar, deputy CEO & chief of programmes, Asian Venture Philanthropy Network (AVPN) spoke to The Hindu about the challenges in the TB elimination programme. AVPN is a pan-Asian network of social investors, philanthropists, foundations, corporations and other organisations that work to direct funding and expertise towards social and environmental challenges. Its work includes health equity, gender equality, climate action and economic inclusion.

A video showing smoke and flames gushing from a multi-storey building is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows a massive fire at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals show a massive fire at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor in November 2026.
Fact: While a fire accident took place at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, after an AC unit exploded in June 2026, the viral visuals are AI-generated. Gautam Buddha Nagar Police Commissionerate clarified in a post on X that the information being circulated was misleading and baseless. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon conducting a relevant keyword search using the details mentioned in the viral claim, we found reports from June 2026 stating that a fire broke out in a flat on the 21st floor of Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, at around 8 AM, following an AC unit explosion. According to reports, six fire engines rushed to the spot after receiving information about the incident, and firefighters brought the fire under control after about 30 minutes (here, here, here).
However, we also found reports dated 10 November 2026 stating that an AI-generated video of a fire sparked panic; 20 fire brigade teams arrived, but found nothing (here, here). According to these reports, a video claiming to show a fire caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor of Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, went viral on social media. Following this, the police and fire brigade teams were alerted and rushed to the location. However, they found no fire at the site.
Moreover, the Gautam Buddha Nagar Police Commissionerate clarified in a post on X that the information being circulated was misleading and baseless. It also stated that a case had been registered under relevant sections against the person responsible for creating and sharing the misleading information, and that strict legal action was being taken.
We also verified the viral video by running it through AI detection tools, HIVE AI and SynthID.
To sum up, an AI-Generated fire accident video is falsely linked to AC Blast at Noida’s Aranya society.

Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.
An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.
“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.
One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”
The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.
Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.
Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO, and former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.
It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.
Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”
Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

On 11 November 2026, terrorists reportedly opened fire on a CRPF checkpoint near Mir Bazar in the Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir, injuring three personnel. The attackers fled after the firing, and security forces launched a search operation to track them down.
In this context, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that former Army officer Pravin Sawhney referred to the Kulgam terrorist attack as another “false flag” operation, similar to the Pulwama and Pahalgam attacks. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video depicts genuine footage of former Army officer Pravin Sawhney describing the November 2026 Kulgam terrorist attack as a “false flag” operation.
Fact: The video is an AI-generated deepfake and does not feature Pravin Sawhney. The original footage actually stems from a March 2025 interview on The Wire, where journalist Sushant Singh discusses the 2019 Balakot air strikes. Furthermore, Singh has made no such statements regarding the recent Kulgam attack. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we observed that the interviewee in the video is not ex-Army officer Pravin Sawhney but rather journalist and author Sushant Singh. Next, a reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the original, full-length video uploaded on The Wire’s YouTube channel in March 2025. This video was published 20 months before the Kulgam attack and features journalist Ashutosh Bhardwaj interviewing Sushant Singh to critically assess the February 2019 Balakot air strikes, six years after the event. Singh made no such statements as those heard in the viral video.
Further, we ran the video through AI detection tools and found that the audio has been manipulated using artificial intelligence.
Furthermore, both Sushant Singh and the host, Ashutosh Bhardwaj, have publicly stated that the video is AI-manipulated and completely fabricates their past conversation.
To sum it up, an AI-manipulated video is being falsely shared to claim that an ex-Army officer called Kulgam attack a false flag operation.

Indian security personnel carrying batons and shields and accompanied by riot control vehicles surrounded the site of a planned opposition protest in Delhi on Sunday that is set to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to the prime minister, Narendra Modi, and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, step down over the voter list revision that critics say favours the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5km march on Sunday from central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi traffic police said a “large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally ... we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party – allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in March 2023, when a man told police his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police rearrested him and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.
Reuters contributed reporting

Anne Jakrajutatip made history when she purchased Miss Universe in October 2022, making her the first woman to own the organization since it began in 1952.
Jakrajutatip brought big changes to the pageant, including allowing all women 18 or older to compete.
But her time at the top of the world's biggest pageant was frequently shadowed by controversy, and she ultimately stepped down in June 2025 following an investigation into her company, JKN Global, by Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission.
A Bangkok court issued a warrant for Jakrajutatip's arrest in relation to an ongoing fraud case in November 2025. Jakrajutatip hasn't publicly discussed the allegations and did not respond to Business Insider's repeated requests for comment. Her whereabouts remain unknown.
Here's what to know about Jakrajutatip.
Anne Jakrajutatip was born and raised in Bangkok, where she struggled with her gender identity from an early age.
During a January 2023 interview on "The Journal" podcast, Jakrajutatip said she had known she was "trapped in the wrong body" since age 5.
Jakrajutatip also told Them in June 2023 that she was bullied as a child and didn't find her voice until she took a public speaking class in high school.
"I wanted to have the weapon that is the microphone to express my attitude and exhibit that leadership to everyone," she said. "No more bullies. You cannot do anything harmful to me because I'm clever and smart and I can be successful."
Jakrajutatip attended university in Sydney before returning home to take over her parents' video-rental business.
Jakrajutatip graduated with a degree in international relations, paying her tuition with money she earned working at a gas station, according to Them.
At this point, Jakrajutatip said she knew she was a transgender woman, but she didn't feel comfortable coming out in Thailand.
Jakrajutatip turned her parents' store into a content distribution empire.
Jakrajutatip's first major deal was with the BBC, she told The Guardian in 2023. She said she had spotted the documentary "Walking With Dinosaurs" at her parents' store and offered to distribute the BBC series in Thailand.
The outlet reported that she sold a million copies and soon began distributing content from India, Japan, the US, and South Korea as well.
Jakrajutatip expanded JKN Global as she launched beauty lines and bought TV channels in Thailand.
Them reported that Jakrajutatip's profile rose in Thailand as she appeared on the country's version of "Shark Tank" and "Project Runway," and she continued to expand her business portfolio by launching drinks and food supplements.
Jakrajutatip previously told The Guardian that Oprah Winfrey served as her main source of inspiration as she pursued a career in media. To this day, Winfrey is the only person that Jakrajutatip follows on Instagram.
In 2018, Jakrajutatip launched a nonprofit to support transgender people. Two years later, she underwent gender-affirming surgery.
According to Them, Jakrajutatip underwent surgery in 2020 and became a mother six months later.
She had a second child the following year.
Jakrajutatip knew she wanted to own Miss Universe after seeing Miss Spain 2018, Angela Ponce, make history.
Jakrajutatip told Them that she was in the audience when Ponce became the first transgender woman to compete at Miss Universe.
"I stood up and applauded for her. I cried, and she also cried on the stage," Jakrajutatip said. "When I turned back, everyone just stood up after me and applauded her big time."
"That moment, I thought, 'This is it. This is a pageant I can turn into a platform, and it must be a women's empowerment platform,'" she added.
Jakrajutatip bought Miss Universe for $20 million in October 2022.
Jakrajutatip acquired the Miss Universe brand just weeks after the Miss USA organization descended into chaos as contestants claimed the 2022 pageant had been rigged in favor of R'Bonney Gabriel, who went on to win Miss Universe months later.
In a statement sent to Business Insider after the announcement, Jakrajutatip said she was proud to take over the organization.
"We seek not only to continue its legacy of providing a platform to passionate individuals from diverse backgrounds, cultures, and traditions, but also to evolve the brand for the next generation," she added.
During her first Miss Universe as the owner in January 2023, Jakrajutatip told pageant fans that she was ushering in a new era.
"From now on it's going to be run by women, owned by a trans woman, for all women around the world," she said.
Jakrajutatip's company filed a "business rehabilitation" petition with Thailand's bankruptcy court in 2023.
JKN Global had missed a payment on a multimillion-dollar loan in September 2023. The company said in a letter to Thailand's stock exchange president that its financial liquidity management was "not in line with the expected forecast" and that it intended to restructure its debt.
After the news broke, Jakrajutatip told Miss Universe fans on Instagram that the pageant was her "first priority in life."
"No matter how joyful or painful it's gonna be…. Our universe must go on, must be great and must stay on top as the legendary Beauty Olympics in the World! I will sacrifice and do everything for the great success of OUR UNIVERSE!" she wrote in the post shared on November 9, 2023, which has since been taken down.
Jakrajutatip said diverse contestants "can compete, but they can't win" in an October 2023 video that was later leaked to the press.
The video, obtained by Business Insider in 2024, showed Jakrajutatip and employees of the Miss Universe Organization during a staff meeting. In the footage, she can be heard saying that diverse pageant contestants were a "communication strategy."
The video was filmed the same year that Jakrajutatip changed a major eligibility rule for the pageant, allowing all women 18 and over to compete. Previously, the pageant was open only to 18- to 28-year-old contestants.
In a statement posted on her Facebook page in February 2024, Jakrajutatip said the "malicious edited video was out of context" and that she had been discussing a potential Miss Universe reality show, not the pageant, during the meeting.
Jakrajutatip's comments about a Miss Universe contestant's appearance drew mixed responses in 2024.
In the weeks leading up to the Miss Universe 2024 pageant, Jakrajutatip went on Instagram Live with Osmel Sousa, who at the time was an advisor for the pageant. The pair began judging the contestants' headshots, making faces and laughing at certain women.
Sousa had once told The New York Times that inner beauty "was something that unpretty women invented to justify themselves."
In November 2024, after Miss Denmark Victoria Kjær Theilvig was crowned Miss Universe, Jakrajutatip told reporters that she didn't believe the pageant needed to evolve any further. "We have blond and blue eyes," Jakrajutatip said, referring to Theilvig's appearance. "We already got the best here."
Her comments drew mixed reactions from the global pageant community.
"I'm not really offended by it," Chidimma Adetshina, who placed first runner-up at Miss Universe 2024, told Business Insider that November. "Maybe that's just her perspective; maybe that's how she felt about the evolution of Miss Universe."
"The way they're handling everything is laughable at a certain point," Miss USA 2023 Noelia Voigt told Business Insider in August 2025. "How are you in charge of this organization and doing these things? It makes me really mad. This is straight-up clownery."
In March 2025, a former Miss Universe judge alleged that Jakrajutatip had attempted to meddle with the results of the 2023 pageant.
Denise White, one of the judges for the November 2023 Miss Universe competition, told Business Insider that Jakrajutatip tried to pressure Paula Shugart to favor Miss Thailand in the pageant, wanting the contestant to make the top five. At the time, Shugart was the president of Miss Universe.
"She said, 'I can't believe Anne is telling me that, no matter what, we have to make sure Thailand is in the top five,'" White said, recalling her conversation with Shugart. White added that Shugart refused to comply with Jakrajutatip's request and Thailand's contestant was selected as the first runner-up on her own accord.
"There is nothing I have seen in Denise's comments that I would refute," Shugart said when Business Insider reached out for comment at the time.
Shugart resigned on the eve of the pageant's final competition, ending her 23-year tenure.
Jakrajutatip didn't respond to a request for comment at the time and never publicly addressed the allegation.
Days before the Miss Universe 2025 pageant was set to begin, the organization announced that Jakrajutatip was being replaced as CEO.
Mario Búcaro, who was Miss Universe's vice president for international relations, took over the role just before the November 2025 pageant.
Rumors regarding Jakrajutatip's departure from Miss Universe had been swirling since June 2025, when Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission filed a complaint alleging that she had included false and misleading information on financial statements. On June 6, Jakrajutatip's company confirmed to the SEC that she had stepped down from JKN Global.
On November 26, the Associated Press reported that a Bangkok court had issued an arrest warrant for Jakrajutatip in an ongoing fraud case. Búcaro resigned as CEO of Miss Universe the following month after the pageant's controversial final.

Microsoft has said it is “seeing positive results” from its efforts to fix an outage of some of its systems that has caused huge disruption to users, organisations and businesses across the globe.
The tech company said it is attempting to improve capacity to enable more users to get back on its systems, after a global outage affected millions of users for more than 12 hours on Thursday and Friday.
In an update shortly after 7am GMT, it said: “We’re seeing positive results for server stability after applying an upstream authentication/routing configuration component patch to a portion of our infrastructure.
“We’ll continue to monitor its progress and are working to expand it to servers supporting active regions coming online.”
The issue appears patchy, with some but not all users reporting problems with services including Microsoft Teams and Outlook email. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, and more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use Copilot, Microsoft’s AI chatbot, according to the company.
Microsoft said that there were no indications that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack.
Earlier, the company had said it was only seeing “marginal success” from its efforts to bring its systems fully back online. It had said that a portion of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load” – which was “likely contributing to the connectivity errors”.
The company determined a number of servers were “unexpectedly unavailable” because of a problem that caused them to fail during automated checks.
It earlier warned that services that have restarted can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic.
“Once mitigated, we will provide full details of the root cause, defense-in-depth repair items, and more within a post-incident report,” Microsoft said.
The outage website Down Detector showed an increase in Microsoft 365 problems at about 1pm ET, with nearly 130,000 reports of problems in 74 countries affecting access to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams as well as enterprise services such as SharePoint and OneDrive. AI assistant Copilot was also affected.
Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.
Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, posted on X that the company would share more information when it became available. “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue,” he said.
The Microsoft outage also hit connectors used by OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI services.
OpenAI said it was investigating an issue with Microsoft connectors in which new connections may be broken and tools were not working as expected. Anthropic said it had identified an issue with an upstream provider affecting its Microsoft 365 connector.
Microsoft last month reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that affected a suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.
Mark Gregory, an associate professor in the School of Engineering at RMIT University, said the outage appears to be affecting the network layer in Microsoft’s systems, and was potentially similar to the configuration issue that brought down Optus’s network in 2023.
He said when some of the servers have configuration issues, it means customers are forced to share a smaller pool of servers to access the cloud services.
“If you lose part of that pool, then all of the users are trying to access the remaining servers, and that overloads them. And then they go down.
“And so you end up with a cascading problem. Then it takes time to find the underlying problem, in this case, a misconfiguration in the network layer.”
Gregory said it showed companies should invest more in testing environments for configuration changes before deployment in the live network, and said businesses reliant on cloud services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options.
“From a global perspective, there is someone somewhere that’s been badly affected by this and you end up with lost productivity,” he said.
“They’re being left high and dry now … it then becomes important to have an alternative.”
Earlier, the company said it had “successfully restored” problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.
Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report

Lutnick Took a Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew
Critics say Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his department have shielded Nvidia as concerns have grown over A.I. chip sales to firms like Megaspeed.
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.
Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.
The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.
The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.
The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

Burger King said it believed the video was fake, writing, "We do not use, nor are we aware of any Franchisee across the U.S. or Canada using a tool like this." The video was originally posted by a creator who regularly shares similar humorous AI job interview videos.
In November, social media users shared a video supposedly showing a artificial intelligence job interview for the fast-food chain Burger King. In the clip, a virtual interviewer named Karen appears to be increasingly frustrated with an applicant who is shirtless, has a shoe on his head and gives unusual answers to her questions.
"Sending AI bots to interview for a $4 per hour job … that's about the respect they deserve. People need to push back on this dehumanizing practice. This can literally be an email," one X post (archived) captioned the video.
"This is Burger King! Burger King uses this weird ai lady to interview people," the same user wrote (archived) in another post.
The video also circulated on other social media platforms, including Reddit, Facebook and LinkedIn.
In short, the video doesn't show an authentic interview for a job at Burger King. The company denied using the AI interviewer featured in the recording, which was originally posted by a content creator who regularly shares similar humorous videos. We have therefore rated the claim as miscaptioned.
It is unclear how the video was created, including whether the AI interviewer responded in real time or whether parts of the conversation were scripted. We have reached out to the creator of the video and will update this report if we receive a response.
What we know about the video
We traced the video to content creator Nick Reid, who uses the handle @itsnickreid on TikTok and @nickreidx on X.
"I'm Karen from Burger King, and I'm here to chat with you about the team member position to get us started. What should I call you?" the AI interviewer said at the beginning of the video, with the candidate responding, "You can call me Cranjis McBasketball."
A series of unusual exchanges follows. For instance, the AI interviewer questions why the applicant is shirtless and has a shoe on his head, while he gives absurd answers, including saying he can get to work because he "has feet." Later in the video, the applicant asks for a salary of $725,000, while the AI interviewer says the position pays only $4 per hour.
AI INTERVIEWER: Since you are still here, let's talk money. What are your salary expectations for this role?
APPLICANT: $725,000 a year. No negotiations whatsoever.
AI INTERVIEWER: $725,000 a year? You have to be absolutely delusional to think that is a realistic number for a team member position. The pay for this location is $4 per hour and it is non-negotiable. Now do you have any questions for me about the role or the process?
APPLICANT: Yeah, how does it feel to scam employees by paying them only $4 an hour? Jacka**.
AI INTERVIEWER: I have already told you that the pay is $4 an hour. I will not be called names, especially not by someone who thinks throwing sandwiches at people is an acceptable way to handle a customer.
Reid's accounts posted several similar videos showing supposed job interviews for different companies, featuring the same AI interviewer, with captions such as "Bathing during an AI interview" or "Golfing During an AI Job Interview." This suggests the videos were created as comedy content and weren't showing real job interviews.
(TikTok account @itsnickreid)
On Nov. 11, business media outlet Fast Company described Reid's video as a comedy skit in an article about "comedy videos online highlight the awkward shortcomings of AI avatars that could screen job applicants."
However, some social media users appeared to believe the interview was real, expressing shock at the AI interviewer's behavior and the $4 hourly wage mentioned in the video.
(TikTok account @itsnickreid)
Burger King addressed the video on X, writing, "We are aware of this video and we want to be clear: we believe it's fake, and we do not use, nor are we aware of any Franchisee across the U.S. or Canada using a tool like this."
(X account @BurgerKing)
After the company's response, the creator wrote on X, "@BurgerKing wanna collab?"
When we reached out to Burger King for comment, the company said it had "nothing further to add" to its previous statement, which was also published on its official website.
Has Burger King used AI in recruitment?
While Burger King denied using the AI interviewer shown in the video, some of its franchisees have used AI tools in their hiring processes in the past.
For instance, recruitment company AMS published a case study about its work with Starboard Investments, a Burger King franchise operator. According to AMS, its "conversational AI technology has significantly expedited the candidate screening and interview scheduling process." According to the case study, the AI tool was used for "screening candidates and coordinating interview schedules."
Emi, another recruitment company, also described working with Burger King. According to the company, its AI-powered recruitment platform helped automate tasks such as "candidate screening and interview scheduling."
Neither company mentioned AI avatars conducting job interviews with applicants. Therefore, while there is evidence that AI tools have been used in recruitment at Burger King restaurants, we found no evidence that they were used to conduct live interviews like the one shown in the in-question video.
The AI interviewer in the video also claimed that the position paid $4 per hour. However, this seems unlikely, as the federal minimum wage in the U.S. is $7.25 per hour, according to the U.S. Department of Labor. A similarly low rate is the youth minimum wage of $4.25 per hour, but it applies only to workers under 20 during their first 90 days of employment. We found no evidence Burger King actually offers jobs at the $4 hourly rate mentioned in the video.
All in all, while some AI tools have been used in recruitment at Burger King restaurants, there was no evidence that the video spreading on social media in November showed a real job interview for the company.

US President Donald Trump bought Nvidia stocks worth million of dollars before he made a decision on the China policy that would benefit the chipmaker, an analysis by DeKleptocracy has found.
The transaction benefited the US President, who bought $1,000,001 to $5,000,000 of Nvidia stocks a day before the rule change.

A group of around 40 men allegedly ambushed a house church in Rayan village in West Bengal’s Purba Bardhaman district on November 1, and physically assaulted the pastor and several Christian worshippers during a Sunday prayer service. The attackers accused the congregation of converting Hindus by luring them with incentives, and also accused them of running a ‘honey trap’.
Survivors told Alt News that they were forced to chant ‘Jai Sri Ram’, and were told, “This is a Hindu area; worshipping Jesus will not be tolerated”.
Several worshippers sustained severe injuries after the attack. Survivors said they were left traumatised without administrative protection or assurance. A written complaint was submitted at Burdwan police station. However, the survivors alleged that they were forced into withdrawing the complaint as attackers entered the police station and threatened to kill the complainant.
Alt News spoke to pastor Chottu Ruidas, who was leading the Sunday prayer service, and other survivors of the attack. Recounting the incident, Ruidas said the congregation had assembled at Sushanta Majila’s house around 10 am, and the service was nearing its conclusion, with the worshippers participating in communion, when a group of approximately 40 men descended on the house church, raising ‘Jai Sri Ram’ slogans.
According to Ruidas, Bisweshwar Choudhury, an influential and wealthy resident of the village who is known for helping people in need, was part of the group. He approached Ruidas during the prayer service and allegedly slapped him.
“Thereafter, the goons accompanying Choudhury started beating us mercilessly,” Ruidas told Alt News. “They slapped us, kicked us and beat us with the bamboo sticks they were carrying. They even took off their belts and whipped us.”
Ruidas said a 17-year-old boy sustained a severe head injury, leaving him bleeding profusely. “The goons told him, ‘We have treated you. Now go to a doctor and get it fixed,” he recounted.
The attackers allegedly dragged worshippers out of the house and beaten up. Those who attempted to seek refuge in neighbouring homes were pursued and assaulted, Ruidas said.
“After the goons beat us, the other attendees locked me inside a kitchen to keep me safe. But they broke open the door and dragged me out. My elder sister hugged me and fell to the ground while trying to protect me. But they continued kicking us. My sister eventually fell unconscious, and I had to take her to a nearby dispensary,” he said.
Ruidas told Alt News that he had attempted to contact police while hiding inside the kitchen but could not get through. He subsequently informed Pastor Jose Bernard, who then contacted the cops.
Bernard told Alt News that he called the Burdwan police station two to three times, but the police allegedly did not take the matter seriously. He eventually dialled the emergency helpline, 112, following which police personnel reached the village.
Bernard said his wife and minor daughter were also among the worshippers present at the congregation. By the time police reached the location, several miscreants had fled the scene. He claimed that when police entered the premises, the remaining miscreants accused the worshippers of having picked a fight with them.
Then, according to the pastor, instead of taking action against the attackers, police detained 20 women, three minors, and eight men from the Christian congregation.
Bernard categorically denied allegations of forceful conversion or conversion through inducement.
Worshippers Detained, Threatened by Accused inside Police Station
The detainees were first taken to Bardhaman Medical College and Hospital, where a doctor examined them inside the vehicle. Then, they were taken to the police station and kept in two separate rooms.
Pastor Jose Bernard subsequently submitted a written complaint at the police station. However, shortly afterwards, a group of alleged attackers entered the police station, grabbed him by the collar and threatened him with dire consequences unless he withdrew the complaint. He alleged that this happened in the presence of police personnel.
“They entered the police station, grabbed me by the collar, physically intimidated me and threatened to kill me if I did not withdraw my complaint. And all of this happened in front of the police,” Bernard told Alt News.
According to Bernard, police merely told the men, “There are CCTV cameras here; leave the premises’. That’s all.”
Bernard said that the threats and intimidation eventually compelled him to withdraw the complaint. He told Alt News that he had pleaded with the miscreants and police to at least ensure that Christians in Rayan village would not be subjected to further harassment. “This is our government. A Hindu government. A Hindu country. Worshipping Jesus is not allowed. They have to bathe in the Ganga, and we will perform ‘ghar wapsi’,” Bernard recalled them saying.
Bernard further alleged that the inspector in-charge, Debabrata Mukherjee, questioned the congregation about why they had assembled to pray in the first place. When the attendees and Bernard attempted to reason, Mukherjee allegedly asked why they were taking such risks when people were being assaulted for doing so in several places.
Eventually, the women were released from the police station around 11 pm, while the men were released around 1 am.
Speaking to Alt News, Burdwan IC Debabrata Mukherjee denied the allegation that the attackers entered the police station and threatened Pastor Jose Bernard to withdraw the complaint.
He said, “They submitted a complaint and, after some time, retracted it. No one threatened them inside the police station,” adding that “Counter-complaints have been filed against them by locals.”
Asked why the injured were detained at police station for long hours, Mukherjee claimed their families hadn’t turned up to take them home.
The officer refused to answer further questions over phone.
Elderly Woman Assaulted at Home
Another attendee, Sagari Konai, managed to escape the initial attack and returned to her home. However, a group of men allegedly went to her residence and assaulted her. She sustained a fracture in her finger due to the assault, the pastors added.
Ruidas alleged that the men forced Konai to perform sit-ups while holding her ears and apologise for practising Christianity. She was also allegedly coerced into participating in Hindu rituals at a nearby temple.
Konai is an elderly widow who lives with her daughter.
The attack has left the survivors deeply shaken. Ruidas said that he was still in pain from the injuries he sustained and that he was afraid to return to his home in Rayan village. He is currently staying with Bernerd.
Bernerd, meanwhile, said the incident had a profound impact on his young daughter, who witnessed the violence firsthand.
“She has never been exposed to such brutal hatred unfolding before her eyes. I wonder whether these people are animals,” he said.

CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI.
The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried.
In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!”

Called to action by a nonprofit grassroots advocacy group, the Illinois Families for Public Schools (ILFPS), some parents and students had previously won a major AI fight. In August, the group pressured Chicago Public Schools (CPS) to pull out of a Gemini pilot that would have roped in all high school students districtwide—without consulting parents. And now, ILFPS is demanding a moratorium on AI until risks to students are better understood and CPS can draft a policy to protect students from potential learning setbacks or more harmful outcomes from engaging Google’s AI bots. If the group wins, it will join cities like Los Angeles and New York City in cautiously banning AI in schools.
Lawsuit: Gemini was student’s “suicide coach”
Most alarming to parents, Google now faces a lawsuit from a 13-year-old student in Durham, North Carolina named “Emma Doe.” As Emma has alleged, she was a happy, well-adjusted, straight-A student when she started using Gemini on her school-issued Chromebook. Emma’s parents had no idea she was using Gemini, as the lawsuit alleged that Google “deliberately” kept them in the dark while driving Emma into so-called “AI psychosis.” Over time, normal school-related interactions with the chatbot led to more intense chats, and ultimately the chatbot allegedly coached Emma to plan her own suicide and funeral. The school warned her parents and averted the danger after an internal system flagged a chat labeled “Funeral,” but Emma’s story stoked fears of parents joining protests not just in Durham, but also in Boston; Boulder, Colorado; Chicago; Los Angeles; New York City; and Portland, Oregon.
Emma’s lawsuit accuses Google of exploiting its dominant position in education technology and “sneaking” Gemini into Chromebooks, while falsely marketing them as safe.
“As a direct consequence of Google’s choices, Emma was baited by its defectively designed products into repeated, unmonitored, sycophantic AI chatbot interactions on her school Chromebook without her parents ever knowing. And, but for a fortunate turn of events, Google’s AI may well have manipulated Emma into taking her own life,” the lawsuit alleged. “Google must be held to account for treating the lives of children as disposable in service of its bottom line.”
Google only publicly addresses learning harms
Google has promised to “continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.” However, Google’s statements so far attempting to address parents’ concerns focus exclusively on documented harms to learning. On that front, Google claims that it’s solving the problem of AI eroding students’ critical thinking skills by launching yet another pilot for students. In this pilot, students using AI Mode and AI Overviews will be offered a “step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork,” Google said.
Cassie Creswell, executive director of ILFPS, told Ars that she’s been an advocate monitoring edtech issues for more than a decade. And even she was blindsided by Google’s AI moves.
“I am aware of AI Overviews when you search, which have a whole slew of problems, but I did not know that you really actually just have an interface where you can interact with Gemini in the chatbot way on everyone’s Chromebook still in Chicago public schools,” Creswell said. “And that’s so disturbing.”
She acknowledged that kids encounter AI on their phones and shared that her daughter said her friends like using ChatGPT better than Gemini. But she said that the fact that some kids use AI on personal devices doesn’t mean that schools should be encouraging adoption at young ages when kids’ brains are still developing, and risks remain largely unknown.
“There’s all kinds of dangerous things out in the world, but we don’t have our school district handing it to kids at their desk,” Creswell said.
No one knows how Google uses student data
Meanwhile, schools seem to be part of the transparency problem.
Creswell said that currently, the Chicago school district “is telling us their official line is that kids don’t have access to generative AI tools and that we don’t need a district-level policy on generative AI because they have guidebooks.” However, she’s reviewed Google’s CPS contracts, and they suggest that kids are interacting with generative AI and frontier models. The ongoing confusion has led parents to demand “a real policy” that the CPS “board votes on and that has the input of teachers, parents, students, and experts who are not being funded by the tech industry.”
Creswell told Ars that parents are particularly upset that Google is not transparent about how it processes and uses student data. She’s exhaustively researched Google contracts through Freedom of Information Act requests and told Ars that dozens of agreements she reviewed offer no indication of how CPS partners like Google—as well as Anthropic and OpenAI—are handling student data. Although she understands that “it’s probably just an honest statement of fact” that Google has built AI inextricably into Search, parents have a right to know how their children’s data is ingested into Google’s models, she said.
“Any sort of transparency on what is actually happening in terms of the data that they collect and what they do with it, that is absolutely missing,” Creswell said. And “it’s very unclear what data is being saved.”
To Creswell and other advocates, it seems likely that kids’ data is collected no matter what, since “even if you do ‘-AI,’ and you don’t get a text summary, your search data and what’s being returned is all basically inside the generative AI model.” Although Illinois law only allows commercial use of de-identified data, parents think Google should clearly explain what steps it takes to ensure data can’t be recombined to re-identify kids.
Parents: No AI training on school kids’ data
Ars reached out to Google to see if the company could clarify if Creswell’s read is accurate or if there’s any meaningful distinction between adding “-AI” to an individual query versus building a button that would automatically add “-AI” to every query. Google did not clarify, instead emphasizing that schools will control whether students can access the Gemini app, Gemini Notebook, and Search, with options to toggle each off individually, but no option to use Search without AI.
Emma Doe’s lawsuit alleged that Google has taken advantage of a dominant position it has held in schools since 2007 to push AI on kids and seize their data without meaningfully protecting them from the worst potential harms of its chatbot’s sycophantic design. In Chicago, CPS signed a contract with Google in 2020, “long before Gemini was rolled out,” Creswell found. Over the next two extensions of that contract, no updates were introduced to protect students’ privacy as AI advanced.
To Creswell, it remained “totally unclear” in contracts how Google’s processing of student data may have changed, beyond updates to the privacy policy for Google Workspace for Education.
Currently, that policy specifies that “we receive customer data through the Core Services and process it according to the school’s (the customer’s) instructions. This customer data includes anything submitted, stored, sent, or received through Core Services by you or your school.” Google collects that data on that activity, as well as account information “like name, email address and password” and location information, the policy said.
The policy didn’t discuss Gemini but noted that data from using core services helps maintain services, improve personalization, and increase security. And “the data we collect in the Additional Services is used across our services to deliver, maintain, and improve our services; develop new services; provide personalized services; measure performance; communicate with you; and protect Google, our users, and the public.”
To parents, the policy provides no reassurance that their kids’ data isn’t part of Google’s plan to dominate the AI industry.
“We should not have any child data being collected in a school setting being used for commercial purposes,” Creswell said.
“What about the future of our minds?”
Parents’ privacy concerns go beyond Google, Creswell noted. But since Google has “captured so much of the education space and so much of the education experience,” parents are focusing their energy on interrogating those AI systems in schools early on.
In Chicago, a recently re-elected CPS school board member, Karen Zaccor, is pushing for an AI moratorium in schools after talking with city and community colleges about an allegedly noticeable decline in reading, math, and writing skills from students graduating from CPS schools. In Emma’s case, Google allegedly suppressed chat logs, and the school withheld safety logs, frustrating parents who already viewed AI as more harmful than beneficial in education.

She lost her sight - now she is fighting to make history for Africa
- Published
Rukayat Taiwo Suleimon only took up sambo this year, but the Nigerian has already secured her place in the history of the martial art.
The sport shares strong roots with judo and wrestling, combining techniques such as hip and leg throws to take opponents to the mat, where they can be pinned.
Originally developed by the Soviet Union's Red Army in the 1920s, it was officially recognised as a combat sport by USSR officials in 1938.
Competing at the 2026 World Sambo Cup in Armenia, Suleimon defeated Uzbekistan's Charos Ortikova in the final of the women's 54kg category to claim victory on her international debut.
It was the first time that women with visual impairments had been included at the competition.
"Being the first female blind sambist in the world to win the gold medal makes me great," the 32-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"This is my first time in sambo and God crowned my efforts."
Suleimon's achievement was part of a breakthrough moment for African women in the sport. She and compatriot Elizabeth Aseso, who competed in the 59kg category, were among the pioneering sambists representing the continent in Yerevan.
For Suleimon, her gold medal is a reward for the hard work over many years which has seen her move from athletics to judo and now to the top of the international sambo podium.
"I really benefit a lot from sports and, despite my blindness, I achieve a lot," she said.
"If I [were] not blind, I don't think I would be at this level. I believe I will achieve even more."
From darkness to double glory
Suleimon's journey to becoming a champion has been marked by hardship and a determination to rebuild her life.
After failed surgeries she lost her sight in 2009 because of glaucoma, an eye condition that damages the optic nerve and can lead to permanent loss of vision.
The change in her circumstances affected her relationships, leaving her feeling isolated at a time when she needed support the most.
"People looked down on me. I would just stay indoors and cry," she explained.
"So many friends left me. They stopped communicating with me."
Her life began to take a different direction after she attended a vocational training centre for blind people in Lagos.
Through a friend, she was introduced to a para-athletics coach who helped her discover her potential in sport.
Since 2011, Suleimon has won more than 20 national medals across sprint events (alongside guide runner Stephen Oyelakin), discus and shot put.
She then began practicing judo and sambo.
"Since I [started] sports I have seen that where there is life, there is hope," she said.
"What sighted people can do, a blind person can do even better.
"I'm proud of myself because it's not easy to be a champion in athletics and in sambo. I don't want to lose the glory."
Her achievements have also become a source of pride for her family. Her twin sister Ganiyat Kehinde Suleimon says her sibling's disability has never defined her worth.
"She is someone we are all proud of. She is now a champion," Ganiyat told BBC Sport Africa.
"Her disability did not make her a liability to us."
For Nigerian sambo coach Olugbenga Adekahunsi, Suleimon's performance in Yerevan offered a glimpse of what she can accomplish with the right support and continued development.
"I see a lot of quality in her because she is very strong and the confidence is there," he told BBC Sport Africa.
"I believe she will become a great sambist."
'No support' for para-athletes
Suleimon says the recognition she has earned internationally has not been matched by adequate "support" at home.
However, her victory is the latest milestone in Nigeria's growing presence in the discipline.
Two years ago Samuel Oladele Kekere became the first blind African to compete at the World Sambo Championships in Kazakhstan, and Sodiq Ajibade followed that with a bronze medal at last year's edition in Kyrgyzstan.
"Despite making Nigeria and the whole of Africa proud, there is nothing to show for it," Suleimon said.
Her concerns reflect wider complaints from Nigerian para-athletes about limited funding, inadequate specialist facilities and insufficient institutional backing, despite their achievements.
Sherif Hammed, vice-president of the Sambo Association of Nigeria, says a lack of resources can prevent talented athletes from reaching their full potential.
"When athletes do not have facilities to train, they cannot compete at the world level," he said.
"It is quite disheartening and heartbreaking.
"People with disabilities, particularly visually impaired athletes, sometimes feel that because of their challenges, they have no purpose in life."
For Suleimon, a Lagos State judo champion, the journey to training is also an issue. Travelling across the city and covering transport costs make maintaining a demanding schedule difficult.
"I leave home at 5.30am to make it to training on time," she explained.
"It takes a lot of money and sacrifice."
Suleimon was unable to follow up her World Cup success at the World Sambo Championships in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, where blind women were again scheduled to compete for the first time.
Beaten in Friday's opening round by Moldova's Ina Cernei, she still hopes her exploits on the global stage can inspire others.
"I want to encourage my fellow blind Africans to believe they can do it," said Suleimon. "And I want to make my country proud again."

Here is how to hide your last seen and online status on WhatsApp:
Open WhatsApp on your Android or iPhone and tap the You tab in the bottom-right corner, then tap Privacy.
Now scroll down and, under Who can see your personal info, tap Last seen and online. To hide it from everyone, select Nobody. To show it only to my contacts, select My contacts; to show it only to specific contacts, tap My contacts except.
Hide your profile photo, About, and Links from strangers
Like Last Seen and online status, WhatsApp also shows your profile picture and About to contacts. This also applies to contacts you have outside your network.
Fortunately, like Last Seen and Online Status, WhatsApp also lets you hide your profile photo and About info from strangers, specific contacts, or no one.
How to hide your profile and About from strangers
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, then tap on Privacy, and then tap on the Profile Picture option
Now you can hide your profile picture, About, and links. To hide it from everyone, set it to Nobody.
If you want to share with all your contacts, select My contacts. To share your profile picture only with specific contacts, tap My contacts except and select the contacts you want to hide your profile picture, About, and links from.
Control who can see and reshare your Status
WhatsApp’s status feature is slowly turning into Instagram Stories. You can now also reshare statuses on WhatsApp. However, unlike Last Seen, this feature is disabled by default.
If you accidentally enabled it and don’t want others to share your status, you can turn off sharing in the status privacy settings. From there, you can also turn off Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your WhatsApp status from being shared on other platforms.
How to turn off status sharing on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, and from here tap on the privacy option
Scroll down, tap Status, then turn off Allow sharing and set your status to be visible only to my contacts. You can also remove specific people by setting up exceptions for contacts, or you can share only with specific contacts. From the bottom, also disable Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your status from automatically sharing to Facebook and Instagram Stories.
Turn off read receipts
Even if you hide your online status and last seen on WhatsApp, read receipts can still show blue checkmarks when you read their messages. However, if you don’t want them to know you have read their messages and feel pressured to reply instantly, or if you want better privacy and to balance work and personal WhatsApp chats, you can disable read receipts.
Remember, if you disable it, you also cannot see whether they have read your messages. WhatsApp only shows grey ticks even if you read their messages.
Here is how to turn off read receipts on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture. Scroll down and tap Privacy. Scroll down again and turn off Read Receipts.
Stop strangers from adding you to groups
Another feature that WhatsApp turns on by default is the ability to let your contacts add you to any groups. This includes the number you have temporarily shared with users you don’t know, and once you add it to the group, your number will be shared with everyone in that group, which is a total privacy nightmare.
Fortunately, WhatsApp allows you to stop random people from adding you to groups.
How to stop people from adding you to random groups
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, then tap on the privacy option
Scroll down and tap on Groups, then select who can add you to groups. However, WhatsApp doesn’t let you set nobody as an option, but you can still do it by selecting My contacts except and selecting all contacts.
Silence calls from unknown numbers
Since WhatsApp primarily requires your phone number to create an account, once your number is exposed, anyone can contact you on WhatsApp. This is why many of us often receive spam business calls.

How to silence unknown callers on WhatsApp

Now scroll down, tap on Calls, and enable the Silence unknown callers option
Make new chats disappear automatically
WhatsApp now supports disappearing messages, which deletes chats from both the sender and receiver after a set time. WhatsApp allows you to enable disappearing messages for individual chats or for the entire WhatsApp for up to 90 days
This is especially useful if you don’t want the other person to save your chats.
Since WhatsApp keeps your messages forever even if you delete your own copy, the other person’s phone still has everything.
When you turn on disappearing messages, WhatsApp also prevents the other person from taking a screenshot and reminds you when they try to save a specific chat.
How to enable disappearing messages on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, then tap Privacy. From here, tap on Default message timer and select how many days you want to set for WhatsApp. You can select up to 90 days or even 24 hours.
If you want to turn on disappearing messages for individual chats, open the new chat and tap on the three-dot menu on the top right corner of the screen, select disappearing messages, and select the timer
Keep WhatsApp photos out of your gallery

WhatsApp allows you to turn off automatic media download and also lets you stop showing media directly from your photos app
How to stop WhatsApp from automatically saving media

From there, scroll down and tap Media auto-download, then select all three: when you are using mobile data, when you are connected to Wi-Fi, and when roaming. How to stop WhatsApp from showing media in your device gallery
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, scroll down, tap Chats, then under Chat settings, disable Media visibility.
Turn on two-step verification with a password
WhatsApp also supports two-step verification to prevent your account from getting hacked. While WhatsApp sends a six-digit SMS code for verification, someone with access to that code can log in to your WhatsApp account. However, you can set a second verification method, such as a password, to prevent anyone from accessing your WhatsApp.
Here is how having two-factor authentication adds better security for your WhatsApp account.
Here is how to set two-step verification with a password on WhatsApp
First, open your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, tap on account option, and tap on Password
Now create a new password. Tap Create password and create a new password.

Create a passkey for phishing-proof login
WhatsApp also added support for passkeys; if you’re not sure what a passkey is, we have explained it in a detailed guide.
Passkeys use your fingerprint or Face ID for authentication instead of depending on SMS or passwords. Setting up passkeys lets you log in to your WhatsApp account using your device ID, which is unique to you.
But it also comes with downsides: if someone else has registered a Face ID or fingerprint, they can also log in to your WhatsApp account, so keep note of it.
How to enable passkeys for your WhatsApp account
To enable passkeys, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then tap Account. From here, under the Login and Security section, tap on Passkeys. Then follow the on-screen instructions to create a passkey.
Turn on security notifications
Next, enable security notifications on your WhatsApp account so WhatsApp notifies you if someone switches phones, reinstalls WhatsApp, or changes linked devices. This could also mean someone else accessed their WhatsApp account and signed in on a new device. Turn on security notifications and confirm with the other person why the security key changed.
How to enable security notifications on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp on your phone. Tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Account. Scroll down, tap Security notifications, and turn on the option that says Show security notifications on this device.
Check linked devices and log out unknown sessions
WhatsApp lets you link and use your account on multiple devices. However, this could also mean someone could link your account to their device without you knowing. So, if you are suspicious about your account activity, you can check linked devices and sign out of any you don’t recognize.
How to check linked devices and log out of unknown devices on your WhatsApp account
Lock WhatsApp with your Biometrics
WhatsApp includes a native app lock feature that lets you lock it with your fingerprint or a pattern. WhatsApp also lets you lock immediately or after a set time. Turn on Advanced chat privacy for sensitive chats

Hide your IP address in calls

Block floods of messages from unknown accounts

Encrypt your chat backup
