A little-known law could upend the dairy industry
California grants animals a right to exercise. Will the state finally enforce it?
Deep-blue, regulation-happy California is not usually imagined as factory farm country. But the state leads the US in agricultural output, and it is, by a wide margin, America’s top producer of dairy, one of the most brutal sectors in our food system. And it turns out that one of the most foundational, most disturbing practices found in modern dairy farming may already be illegal under a California animal cruelty law — but state officials have shown little inclination to look into it.
At any given time, 9 million to 10 million dairy cows populate farms across the US, and California is home to 1.7 million of them, the vast majority of whom are raised on mega dairies. Because cows, like other mammals, must give birth to produce milk, dairy farming is organized around continuous cycles of pregnancy, birth, and lactation. Dairy cows typically give birth around once a year; their calves are then promptly taken from them. Depending on their sex, the calves will eventually join a milking herd or be raised for beef.
But whatever their ultimate market destination, the overwhelming majority of baby cows born in the dairy industry, in California and nationwide, spend their first few months of life housed alone, in individual crates or enclosures. Many of them look like this:
Earlier this year, I wrote at length about that practice. These wooden crates provide each calf about 13 square feet of living space, less than one-tenth the size of a typical parking spot. “We’re talking roughly the size of a coffin,” Vanessa Shakib, a lawyer and co-founder of the Los Angeles-area nonprofit Advancing Law for Animals, told me. Confining calves in this manner is not dissimilar to the use of gestation crates in the pork industry — tiny metal enclosures where pigs barely have room to move. Gestation crates have sparked intense national controversy that’s reached the halls of Congress and the US Supreme Court. But the extreme confinement of dairy calves has not received anywhere close to as much legal and political scrutiny.
In California, there’s an obvious legal problem with calf crates. The state has a plain-English law, Section 597t of its criminal code, that mandates that confined animals be provided an “adequate exercise area.” Though it doesn’t define what constitutes such an area, Shakib and other farm animal advocates argue that it strains credulity to believe the minuscule, barren crates provide one. The practice “is squarely at odds with the plain meaning of the words,” Shakib said.
But California has never enforced that law against calf crates in the state’s powerful dairy industry, where millions of newborn calves have been kept in extreme confinement (nor, apparently, has the law been enforced against any factory farm). It’s a prime example of agricultural exceptionalism — the doctrine running through American legal and political culture, as Vox’s Kenny Torrella has written, that effectively absolves agribusiness from having to play by the same rules as everyone else.
Shakib and her organization are now hoping to change that.
They’re leading a lawsuit against Hettinga Dairy, a Southern California farm that has kept thousands of calves in individual crates, alleging that it’s violating Section 597t. If the case succeeds, it could create a blueprint for similar challenges statewide, and even spark a broader reckoning within America’s dairy industry.
The case that could transform how dairy calves are treated
Advancing Law for Animals just filed suit on behalf of the Caru Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, a California animal protection nonprofit seeking a court ruling that the calf crates violate state law. The case names Hettinga Dairy and related defendants in connection with a San Jacinto, California, facility that specializes in raising calves. The most recent available records from California’s State Water Resources Control Board report the farm’s animal population as 4,200 calves.
Such facilities, often known as “calf ranches” or “calf nurseries,” have become increasingly central to the US dairy business — as we wrote earlier this year, they “raise calves on dairy farms’ behalf during the fragile infant stage in which they’re too young to bring in any revenue.”
Caru SPCA (which is formerly known as the Animal Legal Defense Fund Cruelty Prevention Unit) flew drone cameras over the Hettinga facility earlier this year to document the calf housing there, filming the small wooden crates that are common in California and the Southwest, typically providing less than 15 square feet of space per calf. Many dairy farms and calf ranches use a different, plastic hutch design that provides more space, but the smaller wooden hutches remain widespread.
Calves typically spend about two months in these hutches before being moved into larger group pens; the lawsuit alleges that Hettinga keeps them in crates for around nine weeks.
“Calves are trapped for months, even in summer heat, unable to stretch their limbs or move freely,” the lawsuit alleges. Under 597t, “animals have a statutory right to minimal movement, and Defendants systematically violate that right daily, creating immense and ongoing suffering.”
That San Jacinto farm is part of a broader network of dairy farms and calf-raising facilities linked to the Hettingas, a prominent dairy family whose farms collectively confine thousands of calves and cows across California, according to state public records. Most consumers have never heard of Hettinga, nor of the hundreds of other industrial dairies and calf-raising farms across California that operate largely out of public view. But the Hettingas also have a presence on grocery store shelves: According to the brand’s website, the family also owns Sarah Farms, a mass-market milk label in the Southwestern US.
Vox emailed a list of questions about the allegations in the lawsuit to multiple contacts associated with Hettinga businesses. An employee at GH Processing, a Hettinga family-associated dairy plant in Arizona, confirmed receiving the email and said she would pass it on to colleagues in California. No one responded to Vox’s questions by publication time.
A representative from the California water board told Vox that the 2024 annual report for the San Jacinto calf facility identified Hein and Ellen Hettinga as the farm’s operators. But state regulators have not received the 2025 report, which was due in January 2026, and could not verify the facility’s current ownership. Hein Hettinga, who built the family’s dairy empire, died in 2023; Ellen, his wife, is one of the defendants named in the lawsuit.
Dairy industry trade groups often defend calf crates, arguing that they allow farmers to provide each animal with individualized care and reduce their exposure to pathogens. Whether that’s true is contested — some industry veterinarians endorse that view, while others maintain that it’s based on a narrow view of calves’ well-being and that properly managed social housing need not harm their physical health. Even within the industry, there’s growing acknowledgement that isolation is harmful to calves, and that it would be better for dairy farms to transition to a different system.
A 2023 assessment of calf welfare from the European Food Safety Authority — the EU agency that provides scientific guidance on animal welfare — found “no locomotor play behavior possible” for calves given a space allowance of about 16 square feet each. A calf in such confinement “is expected to spend most of its time lying down because no other activities can be performed,” the review states. To fully express natural behaviors like galloping, jumping, and kicking, it recommends that calves housed alone be allotted 318 square feet each, and calves housed in groups be allotted 215 square feet each, though it notes that even smaller increases in space could meaningfully improve their welfare.
Guidelines from Calf Care and Quality Assurance, a US industry-created animal care program, state that “individually housed calves have a harder time coping with changes in housing and diet and may have cognitive and developmental disadvantages, including poor learning skills and deficient social skills.” Temple Grandin, the famed livestock scientist at Colorado State University, has written that “calves should be raised with other calves, not in isolation.” They are, after all, intensely social herd animals.
Regardless of the industry’s opinion on the practice, though, 597t makes no exception for livestock industry standard practices, the way some states’ animal cruelty laws do. “It doesn’t matter whether this defendant or whether the dairy industry believes solitary confinement of baby animals serves a useful purpose,” Shakib said. “California law here is crystal clear — it requires an adequate exercise area. Industry custom or convenience does not erase that requirement.”
California’s animal cruelty double standard
The ubiquitous confinement of dairy calves in tiny crates remains poorly understood by the general public, and even, to some extent, within the animal protection movement. That is because, for many years, animal advocates focused their campaigning against extreme confinement in the dairy industry on veal, the notorious specialty meat made from male dairy calves.
Those efforts helped bring about California’s Proposition 12, a landmark law passed in 2018 that bans certain forms of extreme confinement, including tiny crates that used to be the norm in veal production. Any veal raised or sold in California must now come from calves allotted at least 43 square feet of living space each. But the overwhelming share of California’s dairy calves are not raised for veal and thus get no protection under Prop 12, even as many members of the public may assume the problem of extreme confinement of calves has been solved.
In the last few years, however, a small wave of animal advocates have been drawing attention to the continued plight of dairy calves. The animal rights group Direct Action Everywhere (DxE) over the last year has documented and mapped calf confinement across California, including at Grimmius Cattle Company, the largest calf raiser in the state and the subject of Vox’s earlier reporting. This fall, DxE investigator Lewis Bernier obtained footage showing calves from a dairy farm that the group said supplies to Land O’Lakes being transported to Grimmius, where the newborn animals are raised in the same standard, approximately 13-square-foot wooden hutches. Land O’Lakes did not respond to requests for comment.
The crates aren’t the only problem
Beyond extreme confinement in crates, DxE’s investigations have surfaced allegations of overt abuse of calves — including animals being kicked, punched, and pulled by their ears and tails — at calf ranches and dairy farms throughout California.
Drone footage taken earlier this year at a dairy farm that DxE linked to Leprino Foods — a major cheese supplier that reportedly sells to Domino’s, Papa John’s, and Pizza Hut, among others — shows calves being kicked, pushed, pulled by their ears, and thrown to the ground. In one clip, a calf appears to be kicked in the face. One of DxE’s investigators followed a milk truck from that farm to a Leprino plant, the group said. Leprino Foods did not respond to requests for comment.
DxE has also captured drone footage of calf and dairy facilities that California records list as operated by members of the Hettinga family, separate from the one that is being sued by Advancing Law for Animals. At one of the calf ranches, in San Bernardino County, Robert Drummond, a member of DxE’s Los Angeles chapter, filmed handlers who appear to be whipping frightened calves and pulling them by their tails. Hitting calves and pulling them this way are both considered “unacceptable” handling practices by the industry’s own calf-raising guidelines. DxE reported those findings to the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department, which did not provide comment for this story.
An annual report filed with the California water board identifies Gerben Hettinga as the operator of that farm, a representative from the agency told Vox. Vox attempted to reach Hettinga using the email addresses and phone number listed for him in state records but received no response.
Advancing Law for Animals’ lawsuit is not the first time animal advocates have accused California’s dairy industry of violating 597t. “There’s a long history of animal activists and organizations trying unsuccessfully to enforce this law,” Will Lowrey, founder and legal counsel at animal advocacy legal nonprofit Animal Partisan, told me in an email. His organization has also sought enforcement of 597t in the dairy industry.
DxE has sent criminal complaints about calf crates, citing 597t, to eight law enforcement agencies throughout California; the group says that none of them have taken enforcement action. In March, the sheriff’s office of Tulare County, in the heart of the Central Valley’s dairy industry, rejected one of these complaints and stated in its reply to DxE that calf confinement did not violate the law because “the facilities reviewed do not raise calves for veal production.” But 597t doesn’t exclusively apply to veal; it applies to all confined animals. The sheriff’s office may have confused it with Prop 12. The office did not respond to a request for comment.
DxE has also met with California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office about calf confinement, and office staff asked the group questions about its investigative findings, DxE director of communications Cassie King told me. Responding to Vox’s request for comment about whether 13-square-foot crates are permissible under 597t, the attorney general’s press office said, “we cannot provide a comment at this time.” DxE plans to rally outside Bonta’s office in Sacramento this week calling for enforcement of that law against Grimmius Cattle Company. The group submitted a packet of documents to the attorney general, including a statement from more than a dozen veterinarians about the animal welfare harms of small calf crates.
“The California dairy industry seems inclined to act like [597t] doesn’t exist and no law enforcement officer, prosecutor, or judge that I have come across seems inclined to enforce the law as written,” Lowrey wrote to me. “It’s hard to imagine that this is for any other reason than deference to the state agriculture industry.”
The law enforcement officials that have rejected these complaints haven’t explained how calf crates could satisfy 597t’s requirement for an adequate exercise area; they largely sidestep the question altogether. For non-livestock animals, meanwhile, California has enforced the law more readily. A state appeals court recently upheld 597t convictions against two people who had continuously kept German shepherds in kennels measuring 48 to 50 square feet. For hundreds of thousands of calves kept in cages one-quarter of that size, though, the protections offered by California’s animal cruelty laws have proven illusory.
Police and prosecutors have broad discretion to decline to pursue criminal complaints, but a lawsuit like Caru SPCA’s may be harder to brush aside. The question will now be addressed by a judge, and California’s dairy industry could finally face an on-the-merits ruling on whether these crates are legal. “At some point, I believe a judge will find that the law says what it says and will decide that a California dairy keeping calves in hutches [is] in violation of Penal Code 597t,” Lowrey wrote. “It’s just a matter of time and maybe—hopefully—Caru v. Hettinga is that case.”
It’s understandable that state officials may hesitate to enforce a law that could upend a linchpin of the dairy industry, whose products are consumed by nearly every American and woven into virtually every corner of our food system. But animal agriculture has a long history of warning that animal welfare regulations will devastate its business, only to adapt when regulation takes effect.
And although California has earned its reputation for overly burdensome regulation in other domains, giving newborn calves enough room to move hardly seems like an unreasonable imposition (especially considering that dairy farming makes up only a tiny share of the state’s massive economy). Freeing them from this form of solitary confinement would amount to one of the most consequential animal welfare advances in California’s history. And it need not require passing any new laws — the state merely needs to hold the dairy industry to a standard already in place.

Indian teenage batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi scripted history on Saturday, November 14, by becoming the youngest captain in men's T20 cricket history. At just 15 years and 232 days, Sooryavanshi took charge of the Bihar cricket team in their opening fixture of the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy (SMAT) 2026-27 against Saurashtra at the Holkar Stadium in Indore.
The left-handed batter achieved the remarkable milestone while leading Bihar against a Saurashtra side captained by experienced pacer Jaydev Unadkat. Sooryavanshi won the toss and elected to bat first, marking the beginning of his first official assignment as captain of Bihar's senior men's team.
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi Creates MASSIVE World Record At 15
The Bihar Cricket Association had announced a 17-member squad ahead of the tournament, appointing Sooryavanshi as captain for the opening two matches. Suraj Kashyap was named his deputy.
Interestingly, this is not Sooryavanshi's first experience with leadership responsibilities. Earlier this year, the teenager was appointed vice-captain of East Zone for the 2026-27 Duleep Trophy, where he served as deputy to Ishan Kishan. He also briefly took over the captaincy during the competition when Kishan had to leave the field due to an injury.
Meanwhile, his stint as Bihar captain could be brief, as he is likely to join the India A squad for the Rising Stars Asia Cup in Qatar, scheduled to begin on November 19. Nevertheless, becoming the youngest captain in men's T20 cricket history adds another extraordinary achievement to the teenager's growing list of records.

For several hours on Friday, one of the world's busiest aviation networks came to a near standstill. Airports across the United States witnessed mounting delays, grounded departures and diverted aircraft after a communications failure forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to halt flight operations nationwide. Thousands of passengers were left stranded as airlines struggled to manage the disruption.
The FAA imposed the nationwide ground stop on November 13 after communications problems affected air traffic control centres across the country. Although aircraft already in the air were allowed to continue towards their destinations, departures remained suspended for more than four hours.
The shutdown, the second nationwide aviation stoppage of its kind since the September 11, 2001, attacks, affected an estimated 1.5 million passengers. More than 10,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, while hundreds were diverted.
The FAA lifted the restrictions at 8:15 pm ET. However, the disruption continued as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crew. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned that similar incidents could happen again unless the country's ageing aviation infrastructure was overhauled.
Here is how the disruption unfolded, what triggered the shutdown and how authorities responded and why the impact could continue beyond Friday.
How it unfolded: From communication failure to nationwide ground stop
The disruption began at around 3:36pm ET on Friday, when the FAA experienced telecommunications problems at air traffic control facilities and Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) centres across the country.
The outage affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, including the 22 regional facilities responsible for guiding aircraft travelling between airports. Citing safety concerns, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop to prevent further departures.
The agency described the situation as a telecommunications outage and said the restrictions were imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.
At the time, more than 3,500 aircraft were airborne across the United States. Flights already in the air were allowed to continue towards their destinations, with pilots and air traffic controllers following established procedures to ensure safe landings.
Providing a timeline of the disruption in a post on X, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the number of aircraft in US airspace had fallen to fewer than 400 by 8 pm ET as planes landed safely.
Duffy clarified that the FAA had not completely lost its radar or telecommunications capabilities during the outage. Exceptions were also made for critical medical evacuation flights, life-saving cargo operations and law enforcement aircraft to continue operating.
International flights were handled on a case-by-case basis, while airlines adjusted their schedules to manage the disruption.
The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop at 8:15 pm ET after the affected systems began recovering. However, the resumption of departures did not immediately restore normal operations, as airlines continued to deal with delays, cancellations and aircraft displaced from their scheduled routes.
What triggered the disruption 
Transportation secretary Sean Duffy attributed the disruption to ageing communications equipment that became overloaded with data and began transmitting inconsistent information to air traffic controllers.
Speaking at a White House briefing, Duffy said the system experienced intermittent radar and communication failures, prompting the FAA to shut it down.
"We have old, old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines," Duffy said.
He described the failure as a breakdown of legacy equipment that had remained in use for decades.
"What went down was old, right? It was the old legacy equipment. It failed," he said.
"And listen, it's going to continue to fail."
The communications network is used by air traffic controllers to coordinate aircraft movements and maintain contact with pilots. When such systems become unreliable, authorities may restrict departures to prevent additional aircraft from entering an already disrupted airspace system.
What happens to planes already in the air?
When the FAA orders a nationwide ground stop, aircraft already airborne are not automatically instructed to make emergency landings. The restriction primarily applies to departures, while flights in the air continue to be managed by air traffic controllers using available communication and surveillance systems.
During the November 13 disruption, more than 3,500 aircraft were airborne when the FAA imposed the restrictions, according to US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Pilots and air traffic controllers followed established procedures to land the aircraft safely. Duffy said the number of planes in US airspace had fallen to fewer than 400 by 8 pm ET. He also clarified that the FAA had not completely lost its radar or telecommunications capabilities.
However, the situation becomes more complicated if an aircraft loses two-way radio communication with air traffic controllers. The FAA's Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM), under Section 6-4-1, lays down procedures for such situations, referring pilots to 14 CFR Section 91.185, which governs instrument flight rules (IFR) operations during communication failures.
Under these rules, pilots encountering a communication failure in visual meteorological conditions (VMC) are required to continue flying under visual flight rules (VFR) and land as soon as practicable. This does not necessarily mean landing at the nearest airport. The FAA clarifies that pilots can use their judgement and are not required to land at an unsuitable airport or abandon a destination when landing there remains practicable.
If the failure occurs under instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), pilots must follow specific route and altitude procedures. They are required to follow the last route assigned by air traffic control, the route specified in their radar-vector clearance or, if neither is available, the route filed in their flight plan. They must maintain the highest applicable altitude among their last assigned altitude, the minimum IFR altitude and any altitude previously advised by controllers.
Pilots also use a dedicated transponder code, 7600, to indicate a radio communication failure. According to the FAA's air traffic control manual, controllers then attempt to re-establish contact through alternative means, including emergency frequencies and other available communication channels.
If an aircraft cannot safely reach its intended destination because of congestion or operational restrictions, it may be diverted to another airport. The objective is to maintain the safe movement of aircraft already airborne while preventing additional traffic from entering an overloaded system.
How many flights and passengers were affected?
The disruption affected airports across the United States, leaving passengers facing widespread cancellations, delays and diversions. An estimated 1.5 million passengers were affected, according to aviation analytics company Cirium, as reported by CNN.
More than 10,000 flights were delayed or cancelled across the country. According to FlightAware data reported by ABC News at 6:04 pm ET, 1,913 flights had been cancelled and 10,494 delayed.
At least 827 flights had been diverted by 7:05 pm ET on Friday, according to Cirium. Of these, 670 aircraft were sent back to their original departure airports, while 157 were redirected to other airports. More than 3,500 aircraft were initially airborne when the FAA imposed the nationwide ground stop, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
The disruption also put pressure on airport infrastructure. Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport reportedly ran out of space to accommodate additional diverted aircraft and stopped accepting them.
Major airlines, including JetBlue, United Airlines and American Airlines, warned passengers of continuing disruptions and advised them to check their flight status before travelling. JetBlue cancelled its remaining domestic flights for Friday, with exceptions for certain Europe-bound services from New York's JFK and Boston. The airline also warned that further cancellations could affect Saturday operations.
President Trump 'fully engaged' in response
US President Donald Trump remained "fully engaged" in addressing the nationwide aviation disruption, Duffy said during the White House briefing.
The transportation secretary said he had spoken to Trump following the communications failure and that the administration was monitoring the situation.
The president's involvement came as the shutdown affected airports across the country, stranded passengers and forced airlines to cancel or divert flights.
Meanwhile, homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that the incident involved a deliberate attack or posed a national security threat.
"There was no indication as of yet this was a nefarious attack against us," he said.
Authorities were continuing to investigate the cause of the communications failure, including whether it had any connection with the FAA's rollout of a new artificial intelligence-supported system known as SMART.
However, officials said there was no indication that the system was responsible. ASI, the company that designed SMART, also denied any connection.
In a statement, the company said, "the current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."
Microsoft separately said it had no indication that the FAA disruption was related to its services outage reported earlier in the week.
Duffy pushes $50 billion aviation overhaul, warns of more disruptions
Even as the FAA restored flight departures, Duffy warned that similar disruptions could occur again unless the United States replaced its ageing air traffic control infrastructure.
He urged Congress to approve $50 billion in emergency funding to overhaul the system, including outdated hardware, telecommunications equipment and control towers.
"This is an emergency. I want Congress to give us emergency funding," Duffy said. "This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion."
He said the Trump administration had already secured $12.5 billion for modernisation but argued that additional funding was necessary to complete the overhaul.
“You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can’t wait for that,” Duffy said in response to a question from CNN's Kristen Holmes about why the FAA was not prepared for such a failure.
Holmes asked why the agency had not anticipated a catastrophic failure of this nature.
“Well, I can’t anticipate every catastrophic failure that’ll happen with a TDM network, with an analog network,” he replied.
Asked whether the same incident could happen again, Duffy said he could not predict the circumstances of another outage.
“Is this exact thing going to happen again? I don’t, I don’t know that this exact scenario will happen,” he said.
The transportation secretary also pointed to previous communication failures involving the country's aviation infrastructure, including incidents in New York and Newark.
“We had this happen in New York when we had global leaders were flying in for the UN. We had a similar issue. We had an issue in Newark. It happened twice,” Duffy said. “How many times does this have to happen before Congress gives the money to fix it?”
Why the US air traffic control system faces modernisation challenges
The latest disruption has renewed scrutiny of the technology used by US air traffic controllers, much of which relies on legacy infrastructure that the government has been attempting to replace.
The modernisation programme includes replacing ageing copper wires with fibre-optic connections, upgrading communication systems and installing new equipment at air traffic control facilities.
In April, the FAA awarded a nearly $5 billion contract to Rohde & Schwarz USA to replace up to 462 outdated voice communication switches.
More than 40 new switches have since been installed, according to FLYING magazine. Federal officials have also reported replacing roughly half of the ageing copper wiring used to transmit radar and communications data with modern connections.
Duffy argued that the newer equipment installed under the Trump administration had not experienced the same failures as the older infrastructure. He said replacing the entire system would be more effective than continuing with temporary repairs.
The issue, he said, should be treated as a national priority rather than a political dispute.
"This is not one of those issues," he said. "This is an American issue."
What happens next?
With the nationwide ground stop lifted, the immediate priority for airlines and airports is to restore normal operations and manage the backlog of disrupted journeys.
However, the return to normal schedules could take time. Aircraft and crew displaced by cancellations and diversions need to be repositioned, while airlines must accommodate passengers whose journeys were interrupted.
The FAA and other agencies are continuing to examine the communications failure. The investigation is expected to establish the precise technical cause and whether additional vulnerabilities exist in the country's air traffic control network.
For passengers, disruptions could continue through the weekend as airlines work to restore schedules.
Meanwhile, Duffy's demand for $50 billion in emergency funding has put the modernisation of the US air traffic control system back in focus, with the transportation secretary warning that further failures remain possible without a comprehensive overhaul.

Japan's unlikely leader who turned down the All Blacks

Warner Dearns didn't want to go to Japan. Now, he doesn't want to leave.
A decade ago, Dearns' father Grant got a job as a strength and conditioning coach with top-flight Japanese side NEC Green Rockets, taking the family from New Zealand's North Island to a satellite city outside Tokyo.
For Dearns, like most 14-year-olds, swapping class-mates, countries, continents and cultures didn't appeal.
"I said I didn't want to go," says the second row, who will co-captain Japan against England at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.
"My sister and I wanted to stay with our grandma and grandad [in New Zealand]."
But, reluctantly, they made the trip, with Dearns' mother Tanya, a former New Zealand netballer, giving up her own coaching job to help the family settle in Japan.
"The first year or two took a bit to adapt to, it is a very different culture from New Zealand, and the language barrier didn't help much either," remembers Dearns.
"At high school there was no-one else who spoke English. I was the kid who stood out, the only one with blond curly hair, so it was lots of fun."
There were other reasons that Dearns stood out.
Even as a teenager, he stood 6ft 8in tall and weighed more than 19 stone (120.6kg).
In New Zealand, Deans had been more interested in basketball than rugby. But at Kashiwa Senior High School – one of Japan's strongest rugby-playing schools – they moulded him into a monster prospect.
To supplement his size and galloping, long-legged sprint, Dearns' school coaches introduced gymnastics into his training schedule, having him hurdle team-mates and perform flips, to improve his agility around the pitch.
Away from school, he would hit the gym at his dad's employers, working out alongside the likes of former England full-back Alex Goode.
Given that super-charged rugby education, Dearns progressed fast.

Having qualified on residency grounds, he made his Japan debut In November 2021 at just 19.
By France 2023, he was a regular, featuring in all four of the team's matches at the Rugby World Cup.
This past season, he has been a revelation.
He has spent the year back in New Zealand at the Hurricanes on a season's sabbatical, where his bottomless energy, soft hands and line-out prowess helped the Wellington side to their first Super Rugby title in a decade.
Playing alongside All Blacks Jordie Barrett, Ruben Love, Cam Roigard and Peter Lakai, broadened Dearns' horizons once more.
"It was awesome, I got to sit back and see how the boys prepare," Dearns added.
"The All Blacks guys especially lead the way and are part of the leadership group, I got to enjoy playing footy and watch how they do things."
The possibility of Dearns having a more permanent view was raised.
Various figures in New Zealand rugby's scene wondered whether Dearns would be amenable to returning to his homeland, waiting out a three-year Test stand-down requirement and then transferring his allegiance to the All Blacks.
Dearns, now 24, declined.
"It was nothing official, it was all sort of hearsay," he says of the possibility of switching sides.
"I had a couple of people coming up to me asking me if I would ever think about it. It was never an option for me."
Dearns is indebted to Japan for the country's role in his development. But Japan is also now home.
Dearns, who now speaks the language fluently and whose son was born in the country, was moved to tears during his adopted nation's anthem at the last World Cup.
His passion shows in the way he plays too.
On his last visit to Twickenham, back in 2022, Dearns set up a try with a break and offload to scrum-half Naoto Saito. In the teams' most recent meeting, in Tokyo in 2024, he assisted another two, one via a brilliant one-handed grab-and-go in midfield.
On both occasions however, Japan ended up on the wrong end of heavy scorelines.
If they are to shock Twickenham, Dearns will need to marshall an extraordinary forward effort, as well as produce showreel moments.
"It is always a set-piece battle and England do a very good job of scrum and line-out, they are obviously very physical," he says.
Dearns has come a long way. But victory on Saturday would be his biggest step yet.

The news earlier this week of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s exit from DC shook the town like Suicide Squad‘s Starro stomping down Melrose Avenue. Now it’s up to incoming former Marvel executive and Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves producer Jeremy Latcham to sort through the groundwork that was laid before by the duo.
You can check out the list of lingering and active DC projects below.
Note, Latcham starts the job December 1, and we understand that no mandates have been given to him by Skydance co-CEO David Ellison in regards to what’s prioritized among those projects in development.
Gunn and Safran’s “Gods and Monsters” vision, which was first unveiled in January 2023, was realized at 40%, with movies Superman and Supergirl made along with TV series Lanterns and Creature Commandos. Having seen the ills in the Marvel Cinematic Universe owing to its overindulgence in the Disney+ era with features being fast-tracked and storylines between series and movies mish-moshed, Gunn was adamant about not rushing projects through development — or worse, going into production on a movie that was missing a third act. If a project wasn’t ready, it wasn’t ready, which is why we saw some of the early pitches promised — i.e., Paradise Lost and Booster Gold series, and the antihero team The Authority feature — ultimately stall.
Watch on Deadline
James Mangold was circling Swamp Thing at one point a few years ago, but the five-time Oscar-nominated filmmaker is currently making his Paramount+ series Copland a priority. Not to mention he’s also working on a motocross heist screenplay that reteams him with his A Complete Unknown star Timothée Chalamet for the film studio.
Another thing Gunn and Safran wanted to correct in Warners’ DC-verse were the dueling TV and film mythologies for superheroes. Quite often a superhero’s storyline on TV was different on the big screen, or worse, competed against each other. Case in point: the CW series of Flash ended in May 2023, three weeks before the Ezra Miller-fronted movie hit theaters and bombed with $271.4 million worldwide off a $200M production cost before P&A (the star’s tabloid headlines at the time didn’t help the movie either). The Gunn and Safran DC universe would see their characters having direct lines through live-action film and TV. Above all, Gunn’s m.o. was to bring zhuzh to a franchise that had grown stale after Christopher Nolan’s Dark Knight series.
It will be interesting to see whether Latcham remains as strict as Gunn and Safran were on development.
In the run-up to the Paramount-Warner Bros merger, Gunn and Safran didn’t greenlight any live-action feature films beyond what was currently in production, so only The Batman Part II, Man of Tomorrow and The Dynamic Duo. Gunn has teased he’s got a screenplay he’s penning in the DC-verse post-Man of Tomorrow, but that greenlight will be up to Team Latcham (he worked with Gunn during Guardians of the Galaxy).
A bulk of what Gunn and Safran leave behind to DC’s new owners are animated TV series. Given the nature of animation production, many of these projects are already in the works even though many don’t have a streaming or network home, or even a renewal.
The new Warner Bros under Skydance co-CEOs Ellison and Ynon Kreiz remains strictly about keeping everything in the black. In a recent earnings call, the two were vocal about the bleeding that was going on in the YTD Warner Bros feature slate. There’s no room for box office kryptonite ala this past summer’s blunder Supergirl (production cost $186M, global box office $126.4M), arguably the only big miss during the Gunn and Safran administration (versus the previous Walter Hamada-run era that yielded The Flash, Shazam: Fury of the Gods and Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom).
Above all, the new Paramount administration, which declined comment for this story, is conscious about not repeating history, meaning cancelling a near-completed project to the greater upset of the town (remember how David Zaslav swatted Batgirl in August 2022? That was all before Gunn and Safran arrived on the scene).
Below is the list of projects remaining at DC.
Dated or In the Pipeline
Man of Tomorrow (dir. James Gunn) – The Superman sequel starring David Corenswet, Rachel Brosnahan and Nicholas Hoult is in post-production and set for release on July 9, 2027. Buzz is that Lanterns segues into this Superman. Gunn took to Threads to respond to rumors that Skydance is making edits to the film. “No one from Skydance has even seen the movie – the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. The Batman Part II (dir. Matt Reeves). After Reeves stepped away for personal reasons, Steven Soderbergh is finishing the sequel to 2022’s $772M-grossing Robert Pattinson movie in London for a February 18, 2028 theatrical release.
Dynamic Duo (dir Arthur Mintz) – The origin story of the Robins is a co-production with Warner Bros Pictures Animation, 6th and Idaho and New Orleans animation studio Swaybox. The latter is known for their “momo animation,” which is a cross between CGI animation, stop-motion practical elements and live-action real-time performance. Pic will hit theaters on September 22, 2028.
TV
Bat-Fam – Season 1 premiered in November 2025, with the second half of the season still to air on the Prime Video series showrun by Mike Roth. Batman, Alfred and young Damian Wayne — having taken on the mantle of “Little Batman” — welcome a few new residents to Wayne Manor. Joining the family dinner table is Alicia Pennyworth, Alfred’s free-spirited grandniece; Claire, a recently reformed Super-Villain; Ra’s al Ghul, Damian’s adoring “Pap Pap” who also happens to be Batman’s longtime nemesis; and Man-Bat, who takes up residence in the belfry. Batman Caped Crusader – The Prime Video series has clocked two seasons and is awaiting renewal. Executive producers/showrunners are James Tucker and Geoffrey Thorne. EPs are Bruce Timm, James Abrams and Matt Reeves.
Batman: Knightfall – The home entertainment animated feature from director Jeff Wamester and producer Jim Krieg. Part 1 was released in August, Part 2 is happening in December and Part 3 is coming in 2027. This movie event brings to life one of the most iconic sagas in Batman comics history.

The earliest example of the footage appeared on a Dearborn news agency’s social media account on June 28, 2026, months before the midterm elections. The video shows Shiite Muslims observing the holy day of Ashura.
On Nov. 3, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, resulting in numerous claims focusing on his religious identity. Footage spread online claiming to show Muslims in Dearborn, Michigan, demanding the implementation of Sharia, or Islamic law, in the United States.
The footage appeared on Facebook and X with captions calling it "an invasion" by Muslims. One post stated: "Thousands of Shia Muslims marched in Dearborn demanding Sharia in Michigan and rejecting American law. Now that they have a Muslim senator, they will become more emboldened than ever."
The footage in question was not taken after the Nov. 3 elections. A local Dearborn news agency shared it on Instagram on June 28 with a caption saying that it showed Shiite Muslims observing the holy day of Ashura, which has nothing to do with implementing Sharia. As such, we rate this claim miscaptioned.
Details indicated that the footage was not shot in November, including the facts that all the people marching are wearing T-shirts and the leaves on the trees are green. In November, Dearborn is cold and leaves have changed color and fallen.
Using Google's reverse image search tool, we found what appeared to be the original source of the footage. On June 28, the Instagram and TikTok account for local news organization dearborn.org, which focuses on immigrant Arab and Muslim news, posted the same footage in a reel (archived) with the caption, "From the Annual Ashura march in Dearborn."
A local newspaper, the Detroit Free Press, also covered the same march, posting photographs of the same men in black shirts, green vests and black-and-red vests.
As we have previously reported, Ashura is a holy day for Shiite Muslims. The reel shows a group of men participating in a religious ritual during Muharram, the first month of the Muslim calendar. The month is an important mourning period for Shiite Muslims in particular as it marks the anniversary of the seventh-century Battle of Karbala (in present-day Iraq) and the martyrdom of the Prophet Muhammad's grandson Imam Hussein.
It is common practice for Shiite Muslims to observe the period by wearing black, crying and beating their chests, particularly on Ashura, the 10th day of Muharram.
Similar footage of another procession went viral after Zohran Mamdani, who is a Shiite Muslim, became the Democratic nominee for New York City mayor in 2025. The footage spread with miscaptioned text claiming that the procession was taking place in New York City because of Mamdani, when it was actually from Azerbaijan.
For more reporting on El-Sayed, we have previously covered the claim that he would force Michigan students to learn Arabic numerals (they already do), the true claim that he called Michigan "the capital of Arab America" and a false rumor that he said it was acceptable for young girls to see male genitals in their locker rooms because "they are going to see them on the internet anyway."

Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?
- Published
Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?
If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.
A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.
Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?
Someone, somewhere, knows something.
The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.
Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.
"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.
"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."
His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.
They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.
"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.
"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."
Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.
The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.
Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.
What happened next, though, was not part of the script.
While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.
The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.
Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.
Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.
Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.
In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.
Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.
It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.
"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.
He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.
"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.
"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."
By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.
But there were plenty of theories.
Theory: it was not a real diamond
Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.
"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.
"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.
"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."
Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.
"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.
"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.
"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."
Theory: someone pocketed it
"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.
"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].
"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.
"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."
There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.
Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up.
"What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find.
"Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car.
"There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones.
"Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."
Theory: Klien crashed on purpose
Sidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.
And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose.
"For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.
Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to.
"Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell.
"He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond.
"No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."
While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond.
His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers.
"When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there.
"It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."
In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue.
"No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell.
"I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."
Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."
Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1.
"You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.
Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.

England boxer missed Worlds over sex-test mix-up
- Published
A teenage English boxer says he was left "broken" after he was banned from competing at the Under-19 World Championships because his team forgot to organise a sex verification test to prove he is male.
George Francis, 18, was due to fight in the 60kg category in Budva, Montenegro last month.
But he says that he was informed he was ineligible only hours before the draw because of an "administrative oversight" by governing body England Boxing.
"They got me in a room and told me that I couldn't box because they didn't know if I was a boy or a girl, basically," Francis told BBC Sport.
"The explanation was that they couldn't provide a blood sample for me in time. Everyone else was able to provide a blood sample, but they just forgot me.
"Somehow I wasn't on the system. Apparently, there were no qualified doctors in Budva to do it. It's crazy."
A multiple schoolboy and junior national champion, Francis said he had been training "non-stop" for the "dream" of representing England in his first World Championships.
"It was the worst news I've ever had in my life," said the Essex-based fighter, whose plight was first reported by the Times newspaper.
"I wouldn't wish it on anyone, to be honest. I was just broken. They were speaking to me and I couldn't even really hear. I was devastated. I couldn't really talk. I literally couldn't feel anything. There was a hole left there."
World Boxing introduced mandatory genetic sex testing for female competitors aged 18 and above last year to ensure "the safety of all participants and provide a level playing field", with national federations responsible for ensuring samples were processed.
The move followed a major controversy in the women's boxing competition at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, where fighters Imane Khelif and Lin Yu-ting both won golds, despite being disqualified from the previous year's World Championships for allegedly failing sex eligibility tests conducted by the then governing body, the International Boxing Association.
In January however, World Boxing extended the rules to include male boxers.
"I can't put into words how it just doesn't make sense," said Francis, who has now missed out on the chance of trying to qualify for the Olympics, and is planing to turn professional.
"I feel like there's nothing really left for me as an amateur.
"I turned 18 four days before flying, so it must have been that they hadn't checked their system in time to get me tested. Going forward, there should be someone there making sure it doesn't happen because I don't want any of these mistakes happening to anybody else."
While Francis' father has been contacted by Boxing England since the episode, his son claims the governing body is yet to contact him directly.
"I haven't had one phone call or message from them. I've just been forgotten about. I don't know how that's been allowed," he said.
In a statement, England Boxing said it "acknowledges that an administrative oversight occurred, once the issue became apparent, we worked closely with the competition organisers to explore all appropriate options in accordance with World Boxing's rules and regulations.
"We maintained open communication with George and his family throughout, despite this, a resolution was not possible.
"George remained a valued member of the England team, including representing the squad as flag bearer.
"England Boxing has no greater priority than the health and wellbeing of athletes on its performance pathway and are committed to learning from this experience and strengthening our processes to prevent a recurrence."
World Boxing has been approached for comment.
In 2025, a dozen female fighters across five nations were barred from the World Championships in Liverpool because deadlines for their sex tests were missed.

How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man Utd
- Published
When Mauricio Pochettino was asked the three Premier League managers he would have loved to have played for, he was unequivocal.
"Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson," replied Pochettino, who is set to be the next manager of Manchester United.
In 2023, the Argentine - then at Chelsea, and dressed in full Blues training gear - was being interviewed by Sky Sports. Still he felt a need to express his adoration for Ferguson.
Six years prior to that interview, while managing Tottenham, he had shared lunch with the legendary former United manager.
"When I was young, when I started my career as a manager, he was always my inspiration, my reference," Pochettino said.
"And when you can share two hours with a person who was the greatest manager in the history of football, you can only enjoy."
Hiring United managers has been complicated since Ferguson's departure in 2013, and one of the most prominent complications has been a back-and-forth around the club's DNA.
For some, winning by any means necessary should take precedence, while others believe the style of play and cultural heritage of United's most successful period is vital to the club's identity.
In recent years, United's managerial merry-go-round has alternated between European coaches with their own fixed styles of play, and former players from the Ferguson era.
But between his tactics of choice and his adoration for the former United boss, Pochettino may be uniquely placed to bridge the gap between both camps.
- Pochettino a decade in Man Utd's making - but Carrick deserves better 
  - Published1 day ago
Michael Carrick's United produced a series of good results to finish last season with a run unmatched by any other team in the league. They looked great, but it was a greatness built on attacking in a transition-heavy manner.
Under Carrick, in games they had less than 50% of the ball, they only lost once. In those 13 games, they boasted a win-rate of 62%. This dropped to 36% in games they had the majority of possession.
This style of play suited their direct attackers and protected their defenders.
At the same time, Casemiro's set-piece prowess provided United a reliable way to break the deadlock against deep defences - something they have struggled with this season.
With United a goal up, opponents stepped forward, giving Carrick's men more space. They could play to their strengths again, attacking quickly. It worked.
But teams at the top are reluctant to play in this way. Carrick's vision for United was a side that played slick football, with short passes in build-up intuitively, referencing Paris St-Germain's midfield three as a source of inspiration.
Building up in this manner, to entice and escape from pressure, before looking to find the forwards quickly, was the plan Carrick was working towards.
This didn't come to fruition and trying to take United from a successful counter-attacking side to one that could reliably beat teams while keeping the ball was the same hurdle that undid Ole Gunnar Solskjar and Erik ten Hag.
Pochettino gives United an interesting solution to this problem.
In his own words, he has described his sides as needing "to be protagonists, always press high, work hard and be dynamic". He refers to himself as a "disciple" of the legendary Argentina boss Marcelo Bielsa, who he played for.
If you wanted an immediate comparison in the Premier League to a coach who resembles Pochettino's ideas in possession, it would be worth looking at Liverpool's Andoni Iraola, who similarly cites Bielsa as his reference.
These are coaches who, while taking the initiative, encourage vertical football. For as different as the clubs are, both the fans of United and Liverpool have enjoyed success when their teams have played high-octane football.
This summer's World Cup was a strong showcase of Pochettino's style of play and his recent tactical adaptation.
Rather than a fixed, positional style of play - akin to the work of somebody like Manchester City's Enzo Maresca - Pochettino's USA had only certain players being tasked with holding their position.
This approach posed problems for teams who defended in a zonal manner - defending specific areas rather than individual players.
The US midfielders being able to move freely meant they could step into areas of the pitch between the zones that were being defended, which resulted in their players often being unmarked with time and space on the ball.
By playing in close proximity to each other in the middle of the pitch, the US found another benefit.
Small-space passing combinations helped draw the opposing team up towards the ball and combined with clever off-ball movement to stretch the pitch, allowed the US to find their striker with few defenders around him.
Pochettino's men looked to thread through-balls in behind and early after enticing the opposition's press and the speedy Folarin Balogun was able to turn those chances into goals.
1 of 2
This combination of a fluid midfield, small-space passing and direct through-balls doesn't sound dissimilar to what Carrick was trying to move towards implementing this season.
And although that may worry United fans, the similarity in principles will benefit the players.
"My philosophy is to give a freer style with a good organisation," were Pochettino's words in 2014.
Although philosophically similar, that latter part - a clearer organisation to his freer style - is likely to be what Carrick was unable to reliably offer his players.
For fans of top sides, fast-paced, vertical football tends to be accepted when it comes from a place of being proactive - think Ferguson's United or Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool - wanting to keep the ball, but not passing it for passing's sake.
Fast-paced, vertical football tends to be frowned upon when it comes from a place of conceding possession and defending your own goal for long periods of the match.
The first half of Carrick's stint did appear proactive, while his 4-2-4 press worked well. Leaving four players high was a risk that allowed them to win the ball back and score quickly, but as teams figured this out, United failed to adapt.
There also appeared to be a drop in the team's fitness the longer United went from the departure of ex-boss Ruben Amorim, who left United well conditioned, albeit on the back of a schedule without European football.
Hiring Pochettino will immediately begin the process of turning United into a well-drilled side, capable of applying intense pressure, likely in a co-ordinated manner.
Pochettino enjoyed relative success with Spurs, built on this intensity and co-ordination, that differentiated him from the rest of the league.
With that unique selling point more common now than a decade ago, how he builds on it will dictate how his tenure unfolds.
But watching Brighton this season, he can be assured that an approach founded on intensity off the ball can work in the Premier League in 2026, with Fabian Hurzeler's men second in the league, with the fourth highest average possession, 10 games in.
Pochettino, from a footballing point of view, feels extremely aligned to the values of Ferguson's United, and as a result will implement numerous similarities to the things Carrick wanted, but ultimately failed, to deliver.
His wealth of experience make him a more proven entity than the departing United manager and if he can get his team fit and pressing high, in typically Pochettino fashion, they should see an upturn in form.
Expanding on his managerial approach, while managing Spurs he explained how "the most important thing [was] to create a good shape for players to be comfortable and to show their real qualities".
Rather than relying on pre-defined pattern, he looks to empower individuals to solve attacking problems. Taking this approach means recruitment of top talent matters more than ever.
"He [gave] me the confidence and licence to go where I wanted on the pitch, where I [could] use my strengths," said Cole Palmer, who enjoyed his most productive Premier League season under Pochettino at Chelsea.
United have good attackers but they will need to take the same initiative Palmer did, if platformed to their strengths - something Pochettino does well.
If they don't, and if Pochettino is to stumble, it will likely be in United's inability to break down stubborn defences when asked to dominate the ball - in what would feel like Groundhog Day, again.

Inclusion in OBC reservation list cannot be treated as permanent, automatically justified: Madras HC
A Madras high court bench said on November 12 that the Tamil Nadu government must “demonstrate the constitutional validity of a community's inclusion”.
The Madras high court has held that a community's inclusion in the Other Backward Classes (OBC) list cannot be treated as permanent or automatically justified “merely because it has enjoyed reservation benefits for decades.”
A bench of Justices GR Swaminathan and MD Sumathi said on November 12 that the Tamil Nadu government must “demonstrate the constitutional validity of a community's inclusion” or “continued retention” in the list whenever someone challenges its classification.
Finding a prima facie case for examining the constitutional validity of reservation benefits extended to several Christian communities and converts in Tamil Nadu, the bench said the challenged classifications “raised serious doubts” over the absence of objective data establishing social and educational backwardness and the alleged disregard of recommendations made by expert commissions.
“There is nothing axiomatic or eternal about one’s OBC status. A clear case has to be made out for inclusion or retention in the OBC list. Merely because some entities have enjoyed the privilege of reservation for a few decades, would that necessarily mean that the original inclusion was constitutionally justified? We answer in the negative,” the high court said.
“As and when a challenge is mounted, the Government is obliged to demonstrate to the Court’s satisfaction that inclusion or retention of the concerned entity in the OBC list is constitutionally warranted or justified,” it said.
The court made the observations while admitting a petition by G Kodeeswaran, a member of the Kallar community, challenging the constitutional validity of provisions in the Tamil Nadu Government Servants (Conditions of Service) Act, 2016, which grant Backward Class (BC) and Most Backward Class (MBC) status to several Christian communities and converts.
HC questions basis
The court questioned the constitutional basis for granting OBC reservation benefits to Christian communities and converts in Tamil Nadu, observing that in such cases, “even a Brahmin could claim such benefits by converting to Christianity and joining the Church of South India (CSI).”
It added that if such a possibility were true, it required a “serious re-examination” of the State's reservation framework.
“The petitioner's counsel startled us by asserting that if a Brahmin gets converted and joins the CSI denomination, he can enjoy OBC status as per the present statutory framework. If this assertion is true, then a serious re-think is certainly vindicated,” HC said.
The case
The petitioner, who has applied for the Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission's (TNPSC) Combined Civil Services Examination IV (Group IV Services), argued that the inclusion of these communities dilutes the reservation pool meant for genuinely backward classes.
He said that the State never established their social and educational backwardness through empirical data, as required by Article 16(4) of the Constitution.
The Court, however, reiterated that historical inclusion in the OBC list does not make a community's reservation status permanent or immune from judicial scrutiny.
The petitioner’s counsel, advocate K Suresh, relied on reports of two State Backwards Classes Commissions to question the inclusion. He pointed out that the first commission, headed by AN Sattanathan, declined to examine the claims of Christian communities for inclusion. The second commission, headed by JA Ambashankar, expressly found Christian converts from Backward Classes ineligible for inclusion in its 1985 report.
Despite these findings, the petitioner argued that the State extended reservation benefits to converts from Hindu Backwards Class communities through a government order in February 1986.
The petition also questioned the differential treatment of converts from Scheduled Castes and MBCs. While Scheduled Caste members who convert to Christianity fall under the Backwards Class category, converts from certain MBC communities retain their MBC status.
The petitioner further relied on an October 2026 ruling of the Supreme Court in The Secretary to Government vs Sameer Ahamed case to argue that conversion alone cannot sustain a claim to reservation benefits tied to membership in a particular Hindu social order.
The court said that the petition raised serious constitutional questions and thus admitted the petition and issued notice to the State government and the Tamil Nadu Backwards Classes Commission, asking them to respond within eight weeks.

Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won World Cup
- Published
Sharks and ladders played their part in England's Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup success.
As they chased success in Australia, they had a ladder in team meetings to help them visualise their route to the trophy - spray painting a rung gold with each victory.
And they spent time comparing themselves to lifeguards and sharks.
It was all part of coach Tom Coyd's masterplan, which boiled down to one thing - taking an aggressive approach.
It worked. On Friday, they beat France 50-38 in the World Cup final in Wollongong, to defend the trophy they won in Manchester four years ago.
Not that Coyd ever used the word 'defend'. He has steered clear of that term since England lifted the trophy in November 2022. For four years, he has wanted his team to have a more attacking mindset in the pursuit of back-to-back world titles.
His team were positive from the off at this tournament, amassing 386 points across the group stage and semi-finals while conceding just 68.
And his approach ultimately ensured that England became the first nation to win the Wheelchair World Cup three times.
"I think your reality is the story that you tell yourself," Coyd said. "And the narrative that we felt might be upon us coming in was that we are here to defend and we are here to retain.
"We found that framing to be defensive, to be a bit passive - and knowing that we've been world number one since November 2022, we wanted to come in with an attacking mindset and with a hunter's mindset.
"If we had not spent the last four years talking about defending the World Cup, we weren't going to spend the last three weeks [at this tournament] talking about it either.
"We wanted to prime the group to be forward thinking, to attack the attack when we didn't have the ball - and when we did have the ball, to be a shark smelling blood in the water."
Across the World Cup finals of 2013, 2017 and 2022, the game's two powerhouse nations had been separated by a total of only 10 points - two in the first match, and four in the following two.
However, on the western coast of Australia - around 70 miles south of where England won the inaugural competition in Sydney back in 2008 - Coyd's group of players served up an exceptional display.
Having initially forged ahead, England then fought back from a 22-10 deficit before powering to victory against Cyril Torres' uncompromising French side.
"I think the way they executed tonight was just outstanding," Coyd added.
"I don't think France have moved backwards. If anything, they looked hungrier than I've ever seen them.
"But the rate of which these 10 lads have moved on just blew my mind. I'm so proud of them."
