As flights across the U.S. came to a halt Friday amid a rare nationwide ground stop, President Donald Trump was in a meeting with actor Jon Voight to talk about jumpstarting support for a federal film incentive.
Voight and his team, Steven Paul and Scott Karol, were at the White House to urge the president to push for the film incentive during the lame duck session of Congress.
“It was exciting to watch,” Karol told Variety, saying the president was getting updates on the flight situation and also the capsized boat in New Orleans. “He’s concerned with different things because he’s the president. He gave us attention while taking care of two emergencies.”
Voight made an impassioned speech in support of the Hollywood tax incentive bill, which would provide a 20%-30% rebate on domestic labor costs for films and TV shows.
“He was telling (Trump) he has a helpful heart and he feels this can get done,” Paul said. Voight “was great. He was crying by the end of the meeting. It was an Academy Award-winning speech.”
While Voight was still in the room, the president sent out a Truth Social post reaffirming his support for the federal incentive and urging Congress to pass it.
“Meetings are being set up, routinely, with the Leaders of both Parties in order to, GET THIS DONE!” Trump wrote. “It is a very Bipartisan undertaking, especially in that so much of the money being lost to other countries is coming out of the Blue States. Hopefully Republicans and Democrats will get together and finalize this already very actively negotiated Legislation.”
He also noted that he was working with Sen. Adam Schiff — “believe it or not.” Karol said the team had met with Schiff earlier in the day, and Schiff told them to tell Trump: “This is Tim Scott’s bill and I’m there to help.”
Schiff responded to Trump’s post on X, saying that the bill should not wait until the Democrats take over in January.
“President Trump and I agree: it’s time for Congress to pass a federal film incentive,” Schiff wrote.
Rep. Laura Friedman, a Democratic co-author, also responded, saying “there’s no excuse to wait.”
“A national film and TV incentive means jobs in California, Georgia, New York, New Jersey and every state across the country,” she wrote. “Let’s get it done.”
Karol said that the challenge is finding a legislative vehicle, in which to include the incentive bill. He said that momentum has not slowed since the Republicans’ defeat in last week’s midterm elections.
“There’s good energy on both sides,” he said. “There’s no indication from either side of the aisle that this is something that is not as important as it was before the election.”
Earlier on Friday, Politico published an article saying “Hollywood’s tax credit push runs into a post-midterm wall.” The story quoted Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., as saying chances were “pretty low” of passing any tax bill during the lame duck session.
Supporters of the incentive hope that Trump’s post will encourage lawmakers to make it a priority. Voight has served as Trump’s ambassador to Hollywood, and has met with the president several times to encourage him to back the tax credit. Those meetings paid off in August, when the president first endorsed the measure, leading to the introduction of the bill on a bipartisan basis in September.
Trump’s comment on the film incentive preceded any public statement on the nationwide ground stop. Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of Homeland Security, did address the public after the ground stop was called, telling the nation, “This isn’t another 9/11. This is a telecommunication outage.”
Read Trump’s Truth Social post below:
“I am working with Senator Tim Scott and, believe it or not, Senator Adam Schiff, and, additionally, Senators John Cornyn, Raphael Warnock, Steve Daines, Bernie Moreno, Tim Sheehy, Alex Padilla, Mark Warner, Thom Tillis, Chris Coons, Katie Britt, and Dick Durbin, together with Representatives Jason Smith, Nathaniel Moran, Brian Jack, Linda Sanchez, and many others, both Republican and Democrat, on the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act. The support and popularity of doing this, and bringing Entertainment back to the United States of America, has been unbelievable! Hollywood, and so many other places, have been virtually ’emptied out’ by the Tax Incentives, and much more, given by other Countries. Everyone feels strongly about the Motion Picture and Television Industry — and so do I, and we all want to save it. It was MADE IN AMERICA, and must STAY IN AMERICA. The Entertainment Industry has largely moved to Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and other countries, but the actors, producers, and all others involved want to come back home! Importantly, hundreds of thousands of Blue Collar Workers will be positively affected, BIG TIME, by the passage of this Bill. The amount of money spent on these Tax Incentives will be made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury’s coffers. Meetings are being set up, routinely, with the Leaders of both Parties in order to, GET THIS DONE! It is a very Bipartisan undertaking, especially in that so much of the money being lost to other countries is coming out of the Blue States. Hopefully Republicans and Democrats will get together and finalize this already very actively negotiated Legislation. It can be done quickly, accurately, efficiently and, importantly, will benefit all of America. MAKE OUR ENTERTAINMENT INDUSTRY GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP”

So, you think you’re an Elder Scrolls superfan? You say you’ve been there since The Elder Scrolls Arena on MS-DOS and have logged hundreds of hours in The Elder Scrolls Online? You say you’ve bought all of the roughly 5,000 re-releases and remasters of Skyrim that have been made available in the last 15 years?
Tell me, then: What do you think of The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey?
What’s that? You’ve never played Shadowkey? You weren’t there day one back in 2004, Nokia N-Gage in hand, ready to experience the game’s 176 x 208 resolution mobile hack-and-slash RPG combat for yourself? And you call yourself a real Elder Scrolls fan?
Well, don’t worry. Now you can fill in this crucial gap in your history without even having to track down functional, decades-old N-Gage hardware. That’s thanks to Shadowkey: Reforged, a free fan-made PC port that pairs updated art with the original game files and scripts for an upscaled, 4K experience that runs natively on PC, no N-Gage or emulator needed.
A few decades of upgrades
Moving from a pre-iPhone mobile game to a modern PC obviously comes with major graphical upgrades, powered by a completely rewritten PC graphics engine. What was once a cramped portrait orientation on the N-Gage has now been expanded for a 16:9 monitor standard that displays at up to 120 fps (though the game’s logic still matches the original game’s 25 fps). In addition to newly retextured character and environmental models, the new port also sports small touches like bloom lighting, rippling water, and an upgraded interface with sharper text rendering than was possible on an ancient mobile phone.

Adarsh Kumar, from Bihar, has won the Diana Award for advancing education and career opportunities for students across India. The award, presented to people in the 9-25 age group, was among the honours received by 49 Indians on this year's Roll of Honour. Established in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales, the award is considered the "highest accolade" a young person can achieve for social action or humanitarian efforts. Kumar, who faced financial hardships from a very young age, always wanted to help students access better career and learning opportunities. Financial difficulties did not even allow him to take coaching for the IIT entrance examination. It was then that he realised that students like him lacked proper guidance and mentoring. He wanted to make a positive impact on society by helping those in need. Kumar was only 16 when he started Skillzo, an educational platform aimed at providing mentorship, entrepreneurship training and career guidance to students across India. According to a November 9 announcement by Georgetown University in Qatar, where Kumar is currently pursuing his studies, Skillzo has helped more than 25,000 students access educational resources, mentorship and career opportunities. He has been honoured for his efforts to make mentorship, entrepreneurship training and career guidance accessible to students across India. At the age of 14, Kumar left Champaran for Kota with just ₹1,000 and dreams of pursuing engineering. However, financial constraints became a hurdle, preventing him from enrolling at a coaching institute. Kumar turned to public libraries, Wi-Fi facilities and the internet to continue learning. At the age of 13, Kumar also co-founded Mission Badlao, a community initiative focused on addressing issues related to education, healthcare and the environment. He went on to launch Skillzo in 2023, with the aim of making mentorship and career opportunities more accessible to students from underserved communities. However, building an organisation at such a young age was not without challenges. One of his biggest hurdles was convincing people to trust his abilities and take his ideas seriously. "How can I convince, being 16 years old or 17 years old, someone to believe in me?" Kumar told Georgetown University. Reflecting on how he dealt with setbacks, he said, “Those are the challenges. But you do work, you keep failing, you fail fast.” Founded by Kumar at the age of 16, Skillzo is an education and mentorship platform designed to help high-school students access learning and career opportunities. It offers students various programmes, workshops, mentorship sessions and a community where they can interact with and learn from their peers. The platform particularly aims to reach students who live outside major educational centres. The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) has begun a detailed audit to examine the reasons for higher urea consumption and assess the efficiency of the fertilizer subsidy system, according to two government officials.
The national auditor has identified 169 districts across 15 states where urea consumption is significantly above the respective state averages and the national average of 180 kilogramme per hectare.
Uttar Pradesh accounted for the highest number of the 169 districts, at 37, followed by Tamil Nadu and Bihar with 16 each. Gujarat and Punjab had 14 districts each.
The audit comes amid the Centre’s rising burden of urea imports and concerns about the diversion of subsidized fertilizer. The Centre disbursed ₹2.17 trillion in fertilizer subsidies in fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), up from ₹1.77 trillion in FY25, according to the ministry of chemicals and fertilizers’ reply to the Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2026.
Urea subsidy alone accounted for ₹1.42 trillion of the FY26 disbursement, including ₹47,956 crore for imported urea, up from ₹21,000 crore in FY25.
Even in the current fiscal year, fertilizer subsidy expenditure is expected to exceed the budgeted allocation of ₹1.71 trillion, as the government has recently approved ₹62,370 crore in subsidies for phosphatic and potassic (P&K) fertilizers for the rabi 2026-27 season, against ₹37,952 crore in the previous rabi season.
“The audit findings would help the government plug leakages in the fertilizer subsidy system and curb the diversion of subsidized agricultural urea to non-agricultural industries,” said the first of the two officials cited above.
Since agricultural urea is subsidized without quantity caps linked to farm size or farmers’ income, there have been concerns about its diversion for industrial use. Technical-grade urea is used as a raw material in several industries, including resin and glue manufacturing, plywood fabrication, crockery production, cattle feed and commercial explosives, this official said.
“The audit is being done to identify gaps in demand assessment, distribution monitoring and end-use tracking, enabling better targeting of subsidies and ensuring that fertilizer meant for farmers reaches its intended beneficiaries,” the official added.
Punjab recorded urea consumption of 375.63kg per hectare in 2022-23, followed by Haryana at 323.96kg, Delhi at 281.45kg, Uttar Pradesh at 253.54kg and Bihar at 216.24kg, according to a Lok Sabha reply by the ministry of agriculture and farmers welfare, consumption was also above 180kg per hectare in Telangana (206.56kg) and Andhra Pradesh (197.45kg).
Mint's queries emailed to the CAG spokesperson remained unanswered.
Two-phase audit
The audit began in mid-2026 and will cover two financial years, FY27 and FY28. It will examine fertilizer demand assessment, supply planning, distribution, subsidy payments and the effectiveness of measures to promote balanced fertilizer use, they said.
It is likely to be completed around mid-2028, while the first phase of the audit is likely to be submitted by the winter session of Parliament in 2027.
“The first phase of the audit, covering 2026-27, will include an all-India performance audit of the fertilizer subsidy framework, focusing on the scientific basis of demand assessment, supply planning, prevention of diversion and distribution monitoring. It will also examine initiatives to rationalize urea consumption and encourage sustainable fertilizer use,” said the second official. Both the officials spoke on condition of anonymity.
The audit will also examine the cross-border diversion of urea, particularly in districts located along India's international borders. These include districts in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Punjab and Gujarat, among other states.
“The audit will also assess whether existing fertilizer-use practices and subsidy policies are aligned with environmental sustainability, including efforts to promote balanced nutrient application and reduce excessive dependence on urea,” the second officials added.
Production and management
The CAG will also conduct an information technology audit of the Integrated Fertilizer Management System (iFMS), said the second official. iFMS is the government's digital platform that tracks fertilizer production, imports, movement, stocks, retail sales through point-of-sale devices and subsidy releases to companies.
The audit will examine data integrity, system controls, transparency and accountability. The audit will also assess whether existing fertilizer-use practices and subsidy policies are aligned with environmental sustainability, including efforts to promote balanced nutrient application and reduce excessive dependence on urea.
Another area of scrutiny will be domestic urea production and energy efficiency. The CAG has selected 13 of the country's 36 urea plants for detailed examination, focusing on production costs, subsidy calculations, energy consumption and the financial and environmental impact of manufacturing.
The audit will also examine the country's efforts to achieve self-sufficiency in urea production. Although six plants established under the New Investment Policy, 2012, have been commissioned, domestic output remains below consumption.
India's urea production declined to approximately 29.33 million tonnes in FY26 from 30.70 million tonnes in FY25, while consumption increased to 39.66 million tonnes from 38.79 million tonnes. Imports consequently rose to 10.35 million tonnes in FY26 from 5.6 million tonnes a year ago, according to the ministry of chemicals and fertilizers' reply to the Lok Sabha on 24 July 2026.
In FY28, the audit will examine urea import planning and procurement, transportation arrangements and freight subsidies, as well as implementation of the Fertilizer Control Order, 1985, which governs fertilizer quality, standards, licensing and enforcement.

Nothing OS 5 brings a bunch of useful upgrades, from on-phone widget creation and new lockscreen clocks to split Quick Settings, Dual-View Video, easier iPhone sharing, the Glyph app, translucent themes, smarter QR scanning, and the new Geist font.
Nothing has updated all of its eligible devices to the latest version of its operating system, Nothing OS 5. It runs on top of Android 17, and in typical Nothing tradition, is clean and uncluttered. And while it might seem broadly similar to its predecessor, there are a number of interesting new features – some important, some seemingly trivial – beneath that familiar surface. So if you have a Nothing phone and it has received the Nothing OS 5 update (there is a list of supported devices with rollout timelines here: https://in.nothing.tech/nothing-os), here are eleven things you must try out.
Table of Contents
Appy fizz: Now build snazzy widgets right on your phone, no coding experience required
One of the biggest innovations of the Nothing ecosystem was the introduction of Essential apps that let users, even with no coding knowledge, make widgets. In the past, you had to access Essential Apps on a computer to be able to make these widgets. Now you can do so right on your phone. And it is as easy as easy peasy apple squeezie. Mind you, you still need to sign up for Essential Apps and be part of a waiting list before you can get into design mode. No download is needed – the Essential Apps app comes to your Nothing phone when you update the phone to Nothing OS 5.g
Get a gooey or an info-loaded lockscreen clock!
On to the really serious stuff now. Perhaps the most noticeable visual change in NothingOS is the addition of two lockscreen clock widgets – Gooey and Micrographics. The Gooey clock has a bold and fluid look, with numbers looking a little melted. It is very eye-catching and, well, different. Those who want a truckload of information on their lockscreen and who opt for Micrographics get details like day, date, weather, temperature, upcoming appointments, and, of course, the time, all in rows that give it a very business ticker feel. This is how you clock into this feature:
- Long-press on the lock screen of your phone. This will show a Customize lock screen text bubble. Tap on it, and then tap on the fingerprint scanner to get into the Lock screen edit zone.
- Tap the clock widget space, which shows the time, and you will see Clock face options.
- Gooey is the second option, and right next to it is Micrographics. Choose the one you want, and also tweak its color as per your wish.
- Tap on Done, and hey, it’s, well…done.
Our own preference is the Micrographics widget, which is incredibly handy. We hope they add email and other notifications to it as well.
Split those notifications and quick settings
In the past – as on many phones – swiping down on a Nothing phone showed one new notifications, and swiping further down gave one access to Quick Settings (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Brightness, Torch, et al.). Well, you can split them into two separate zones if you wish. Once done, swiping from one side of the top will give you access to Quick Settings, while swiping from the other will show notifications. To do this segregation, just follow these steps:
- Open Settings and go to Notifications
- Go to the Notifications and Quick Settings Option
- You will see two options: Separate and Combined (classic).
- Select Separate, and now Notifications and Quick Settings will occupy different parts of the top panel.
Find out how long you have been away from your phone
One of the coolest new widgets on Nothing OS 5 is the Away Time widget, which lets you know how long you have kept away from your phone, and shows it in a simple, clean widget that can be placed on your home screen or your lock screen. It is a nice way to know about the “me time” you have given yourself away from your phone. Getting it is as easy as pressing on any place on the lock screen or Home Screen, and then selecting the Away Time widget option. We suggest going for the larger (4 x 2) one because it just looks so much better, especially with that zen-like blue background.
Keep what matters on the Home Screen – use Collector
Another widget (yes, Nothing seems to really like them widgets) that is very handy is Collector. You just open it and place images of what you want to keep seeing or consider important in it, and it automatically cuts out what it sees as important and keeps it handy on the home screen. It has a wonderful fridge sticker vibe, and keeps what matters close at hand. Just long-press on the home screen and select it from the widget collection!
Glyph Interface? There’s an app for that – finally!
The Glyph Interface has been one of the most eye-catching features of Nothing’s phones. This is basically a collection of LEDs on the back of the phones that light up in different patterns, showing notifications and battery levels, letting you know who is calling, controlling volume, setting timers, and doing more, all on the back of the phone. There was a catch, though. The Glyph UI had to be controlled from the settings of the phone, which seemed to be a rather roundabout way of doing things. This has now been fixed with the Glyph app, which gives one direct access to the Glyph Interface, letting one tweak it without having to get into the Settings. No downloads needed – the Glyph app appears on your Nothing phone the moment you update it to Nothing OS 5.
Lights, camera action…with both front and back cameras
Nothing OS 5 gives you the option to shoot videos using the rear as well as the front camera simultaneously. One can choose from having the footage one below the other, or having the selfie camera in an inset and the main camera in the larger part of the display. To access the option:
- Launch the Camera app
- Scroll across to More and choose Dual-View Video
It would have been nice to be able to take some stills with this feature, but as of now, it is limited to video.
There’s a glassy, classy “translucent” theme
Yep, your Nothing phone is now on the glass UI bandwagon. Mind you, this option is not turned on by default. You will need to follow these steps:
- Go to Settings, and then choose Customization
- Choose Theme & Style, and then choose Translucent. You can opt to have a dark theme in this if you wish.
- Honestly, it is not exactly eye-popping as of now. The translucence seems mainly to be around the widgets, and the app icons are not translucent. But it is a good starting point.
Scan that QR code, even if it wobbles
This is a pretty minor and yet handy change in Nothing OS 5. While camera icons have all been polished, a tiny yet useful tweak is in scanning QR codes, especially when using the scanner in crowded places or in slightly wobbly situations (think of paying in a moving vehicle). Now, when you use the camera to scan a QR code, the link it leads to remains on the screen, even if your hand moves and the QR code goes off or the code itself wobbles a little. So scanning codes is a whole lot easier, and you don’t have to bother about lining up the camera with the QR code all the time.
Send images to THAT friend with the iPhone easily (no app needed)
With Nothing OS 5, sending images to iPhones is pretty easy. Here’s how you do it:
- Ask your friend to switch on AirDrop on their iPhone and allow everyone to send images to it.
- Select the images you want to send on your Nothing phone.
- Select the Quick Share option, and then select the Use QR Code option.
- Scan the QR code with the iPhone’s camera. The images will be transferred.
Get the new font, Geist
Nothing’s marketing communications look very distinct because they use a font called Geist. Well, with NothingOS 5, you can now use Geist as the default font on their Nothing phones. This is how one does it:
- Head off to Settings again, and this time go to Display.
- Choose Font & Display Size.
- Once there, you can choose Geist as your default font.
- Once again, the difference is not going to jump out at you, but will become apparent as you use the phone.

Jensen Huang has reportedly resigned as the chief executive officer (CEO) of chipmaker NVIDIA. This brings the curtains down on Huang’s 33-year old tenure as the head of NVIDIA, the company he cofounded in 1993.
According to Reuters, the company’s board said that Huang had stepped down as president, CEO and board member with immediate effect.
This follows revelations that he had two extramarital affairs, one of which involved a woman accused of spying for China.
Meanwhile, chief financial officer (CFO) Colette Kress will take over as the interim CEO of the company. She will retain her role as the head of finance. The board will now reportedly consider both internal and external candidates to appoint a new successor to Huang.

Why Apple's HomeView relies so heavily on your iPhone
It all comes down to convenience and personalization without sacrificing privacy.
"There's no product in the world better designed to be your intelligent personal hub than iPhone."
That's the statement newly minted Apple CEO John Ternus made during his opening remarks at his first iPhone event this year. It should be no surprise then, that the device holding so much of your data would play a vital role with a separate "intelligent personal hub" that stays inside your home.
This week marks the arrival of the HomeView, Apple's long-rumored smart display that was announced last month. As I explained in detail in my review, it's basically a combination of several gadgets in one. It's both a visual interface and a smart speaker that is always listening for your Siri queries. It's a smart home hub for a range of connected devices. It's a sous chef in the kitchen, and it's a FaceTime station when you need to catch up with friends and family. Heck, it's even a digital photo frame.
The HomeView doesn't run apps though. It performs all those functions, and more, by mirroring the apps that you have on your iPhone or iPad. Instead of allowing you to download software from the App Store, the HomeView's system works like CarPlay does in your car. It shows you the compatible apps you've already installed on your phone or tablet, as well as Apple's core suite, including Calendar, Messages, Reminders and Weather.
This is just one of the reasons an iPhone (or iPad) needs to be close by for the HomeView to work.
"When we design home products, we always keep three things in mind," Cecilia Dantas, a member of Apple's Home product marketing team, told me. "They have to be intelligent, personal and private."
Since Siri AI needs all those apps to be able to provide the very personal context that makes its answers more intelligent and conversational, Apple needed a way to grant it that access that didn't compromise your privacy. Having your iPhone be the only container for that information and requiring it to be around for your data to be accessible helps keep it safe from prying eyes when you're away.
As a more general home hub, the HomeView has to work for every member of your household so they can turn lights off or see who's at the door. But it shouldn't be showing them every text message you get from your parents or revealing your calendar invites and inadvertently ruining surprises. This privacy is why, in addition to the built-in face and voice recognition, the HomeView relies so heavily on an iPhone or iPad.
"Everything that feels natural on a phone is now available in a subtle, glanceable device that gives you what you need in the moment," VP of hardware engineering Matthew Costello said. "It recognizes you and shows you your information, but when you step away, it's gone."
Costello further explained that the HomeView offers the best combination of personal information with the convenience of a dedicated communal device. Since the iPhone is a user's hub for their personal content — and really, their life — it only made sense to "extend and link that intelligence" into products like the HomeView.
If the HomeView doesn't recognize a user, it will only allow them to perform basic tasks. And even if you are a recognized user, you'll need to have your recently unlocked iPhone or iPad nearby for the smart display to show things like your Messages or Calendar.
"Personal information only surfaces once you've been recognized by your face, and [if] your paired iPhone is present and recently unlocked," Costello noted. "We thought building on the contextual information and the intelligence, but also the privacy, was super critical and also very unique."
By tying what shows up for you on the HomeView to your phone, your data is displayed while you're interacting with the device and disappears with you when you do. As Costello explained, it's not "posted on or housed on the device in any way."
The heavy reliance on an iPhone or an iPad has additional benefits. Like you can on a HomePod, the HomeView allows you to hand off music, FaceTime calls and more. One of the device's best features is recipe integration in Safari that makes cooking easier. It's also powered by the hand off action, so you need that other Apple device to kickstart the process. But Dantas explained that Apple doesn't see reliance on your phone or tablet as a hindrance.
"It's not just dependency, it's also part of this ecosystem," she said. The HomeView's similarity to your phone doesn't just enable familiar apps, but also a familiar method of interaction.
Speaking of interaction, there's a reason why there aren't any buttons on the HomeView. Apple intentionally built it like this. I found it odd, considering the device is a bit of a hybrid of an iPad (touchscreen), an Apple Watch (square shape) and a HomePod (speaker), two of which have physical buttons. But Costello said touch input was always meant to be secondary.
"We always envisioned it as something that was voice first, then touch second," he explained. "As we [designed] the product, that's how we thought about it, so that eliminated buttons and physical controls."
For Dantas, one of the main challenges during the product development phase was restraint. The process of bringing a new product and new software to life was obviously a tall task, but the engineering team also had to determine which parts of Apple's existing devices and services to include and which ones to leave behind.
"We've had home products for a while, and we built on that foundation," she said. "I think it was really, really challenging to go through and decide what do we bring and what do we not bring [to the HomeView]. That was very intentional to deliver this experience that's powerful and that's simple."

Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.
The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.
According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years.
The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort.
In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.
A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022.
This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.
Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.”
Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking.
Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.
The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said.
The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR).
It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.

It was July of 2024, and Jensen Huang was punchy.
I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential company? Yes, of course. I began preparing.
What ensued was, in a word, bizarre. During the first prep call for the conference, the type of call-in which PR handlers typically try to coax specific questions out of journalists to prevent an ambush, a youngish, vaguely familiar woman took the lead. This was Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter. She was clearly intelligent, commanding respect. She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides.
Slides? Tee up Jensen? What kind of “interview” was this?
I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube.) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat.
As a longtime journalist I’m used to occasional adversarial interactions; I really don’t lose sleep over them. This was just a CEO being a CEO. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Not just wanted to; he assumed he would. And to a large extent he did. Until this week.
Narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoof steps of competitors. A parent who brought his kids into the corporate fold. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the company logo on his arm.
Huang built the highest-valued publicly traded company in history. That part’s not just fairy tale. It’s true. Now, it’s starting to read more like a Greek tragedy.
Back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt:
Jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He said he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories.
WIRED: It seems like an important part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively.
Yes. Strategy setting is storytelling. Culture building is storytelling.
You’ve said many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck.
That’s right. It was really about telling the story.
Of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China.
Another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once said the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more quickly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the company’s allocation of chips.
This is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter. As one former employee put it, Huang can’t simultaneously have had knowledge of every element of Nvidia’s business and then potentially feign ignorance about where the chips may have fallen, both figuratively and literally. His apparent lapses in judgment have now led him to resign from the very company he coaxed into existence and have shattered the mythos of its ever-prescient founder.
It’s certainly not the narrative ending Huang would have chosen, were he still in control.

(Bloomberg) -- When Seema Reddy, 51, moved to the Upper West Side 24 years ago, the fresh-out-of-college art history graduate did what many broke 20-somethings do: She joined a roommate in a railroad apartment best described as a “hovel.”
“I could afford it, but it was awful,” she said, recalling the apartment was burgled while she lived there. Still, she liked the neighborhood and the location was convenient to her first job at Sotheby's Auction House.
In 2002, the median Manhattan rent for a one-bedroom hovered around $2,500, though Reddy paid $1,800 for her portion. Last month, Manhattan’s median rent hit a record $5,000. Across New York City, the rental vacancy rate is just 1.4%, according to the city’s new Fair Housing Growth Strategy report. Five percent is the target vacancy rate, which the city has never reached, according to the report.
Reddy is now married and raising her child on the Upper West Side, in a three-bed townhouse, where the average rent is over $7,500 for a unit that size. Since buying with her husband in 2014, Reddy thinks the UWS is the best neighborhood in the city with easy access to Central Park, museums and arts institutions like Lincoln Center, where she later worked. But she questions whether a recent college graduate can move there today.
The Housing Preservation Department studied what it would take to make housing more affordable, and in a report released Oct. 9 estimated the city needs 700,000 additional homes over the next decade to alleviate its shortage. The proposal, required under a 2023 law, complements Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s $22 billion plan to build or preserve 200,000 affordable homes within a decade.
It also poses an early test of whether Mamdani can deliver on his central campaign promise: make New York more affordable. On Nov. 3, NYC voters passed all of Mamdani’s five ballot proposals intended to fast-track housing, along with expanding outdoor dining and bike lanes, the Associated Press reported. Two of the measures will expedite review for projects on city-owned land and streamline the permitting process. To work, however, the housing plan still has several obstacles to clear, from outdated regulation and classic NIMBY-ism to perhaps the biggest: encouraging capital to enter its dicey market.
Step 1: Make Growth Proportionate
NYC employment hit a record high this year, yet housing production increasingly lags behind job and population growth. That’s squeezing tenants and pushing higher-income apartment-hunters into lower-cost neighborhoods, displacing longtime residents. A wealthier customer base can reshape everything in a neighborhood from rent to the cost of a morning bagel to late-night takeout.
“If you’re looking for an apartment right now, you are radicalized by how few options there are out there and how expensive everything is,” said Annemarie Gray, executive director of the pro-housing group Open New York. “New York City really risks losing its identity as a place that is open and accepting and provides opportunities for people if we don’t turn that around.”
The city’s strategy articulated in its report is to evenly spread housing growth by setting targets for community districts that are partly based on historical housing production and affordability. That means asking some of New York’s lowest-growth neighborhoods to build substantially more.
On the UWS, the report calls for more than 10,700 additional homes over the long term — one of the highest marks in the report — including nearly 3,900 affordable, deeply affordable or supportive units. New units built or preserved since Jan. 1 count toward the total when they receive a certificate of occupancy, while demolished or consolidated units can reduce a district’s total.
Housing Preservation and Development Deputy Commissioner Michael Sandler said the nonbinding strategy is a “shared framework” whose targets will require rezonings, infrastructure investments and other policy changes.
“This is the first step, not the last step,” he said.
The disparity among neighborhoods is stark. From 2010 through 2025, Manhattan’s Chelsea, Hell’s Kitchen and Hudson Yards district added nearly 21,000 units, compared with about 5,800 on the UWS and 1,900 on the Upper East Side, according to a Department of Buildings report. The figures are net units, subtracting demolitions and consolidations from new and renovated buildings.
The shortage is decades in the making. From 2003-2007, drastic rezoning boosted density in previously industrial areas like Williamsburg and Long Island City, while other changes limited growth in established neighborhoods like the UES and UWS to preserve character.
Meanwhile, Manhattan has lost over 100,000 units over the last 70 years as townhouses are combined into mega-mansions and smaller apartments are consolidated into larger homes. Reddy, who leads the local Community Board 7’s land-use committee, worries this is bringing in more ultra-wealthy residents who are less rooted in the local economy and community.
Step 2: Make Room
Sheldon Fine has watched the Upper West Side transform since 1971 from the same West 103rd Street building. When he moved there for his wife, his friends questioned why he would move to such a dangerous block. Fine, a “Bronx boy,” laughed it off. Now, historic demand has made it so there are no bad neighborhoods in New York, according to one developer.
When he moved in, Fine’s two-bedroom cost $215 a month — roughly $1,774 today. More than five decades later, he’s paying $2,225 for the same rent-stabilized apartment.
Fine has spent 41 years on Community Board 7 and runs the West Side Federation for Senior and Supportive Housing, which houses older and vulnerable New Yorkers. Walking the neighborhood with him means regularly stopping to greet someone he knows.
“We’ve had multiple people come to us and say, ‘I grew up here, but I can’t afford to come back,’” Fine said.
He advocates for more affordable housing, but he doubts the UWS has room for almost 11,000 additional homes. That question came to a head when HPD presented the strategy to a Community Board 7 meeting on Sept. 14.
Board members pointed to scarce vacant land, landmark districts and high development costs. One member, Minna Elias, said the lofty, public goal sets the UWS up for failure.
While the question of how the city could set housing targets before determining where the units could go drew the most public feedback according to HPD, the department said those decisions are outside the scope of the report.
“We were not looking at this stage at where there are buildable sites,” said Sarit Platkin, HPD’s executive director of neighborhood planning and equity initiatives. Site-level feasibility would come later, she said.
Not everyone on the board considered the target itself unrealistic. Banker Tibita Kaneene noted District 7 has grown by only about 0.28% annually and said the report’s target of roughly 1.5% yearly growth could be achieved through modest rezonings and policies the board has already endorsed.
“I don’t think that’s ridiculous,” Kaneene said. “I think it’s completely feasible.”
Community Board 7 members also asked what incentives would be available to encourage developers to build in one of the country’s most expensive real estate markets. HPD deferred questions about implementation.
Step 3: Make the Numbers Work
Even if the city creates more places to build, the housing still needs to meet developers’ profitability requirements.
Brooklyn’s Gowanus neighborhood offers a test case. Its 2021 rezoning unlocked thousands of units on formerly industrial land. Charney Companies is working with Tavros Capital Partners to build 1,100 apartments at 175 Third Street, including almost 300 affordable units.
The project was approved under the city’s now-expired rental property-tax incentive. Rosie Tilley, Charney’s head of development, said the same project wouldn’t happen under today’s laws because new affordability and labor requirements add costs that anticipated rents can’t support.
Tax abatements and faster, predictable regulatory approvals are critical to encourage new projects, especially at a time of high borrowing and construction costs, said TJ Edwards, chief production officer of real estate finance at Walker & Dunlop. Lenders must ensure future income can cover debt refinancing if operating costs outpace restricted rents.
“We can’t regulate ourselves to a solution,” Edwards said. “You need equity, debt and policymakers all on the same page working in accord with one another.”
New York may be nearing the limits of property-tax exemptions and traditional affordable-housing subsidies, said Moses Gates, vice president at the Regional Plan Association. With recent zoning reforms already expanding building capacity, policymakers should lower construction costs for developers by addressing outdated building regulations, he said.
Meanwhile, HPD is looking to streamline permitting, interagency coordination and the affordable-housing lottery through its SPEED initiative, which the city says could shorten some publicly sponsored projects by as much as two years.
Gates said these changes need time to work, but reaching 700,000 homes will require getting nearly every piece right at once.
“It’s like you’re running this race and there’s these six to eight hurdles,” he said. “You have to be able to clear all of them consistently.” And even then, “You need to hit a couple of lucky breaks.”
Step 4: Win Over Neighborhoods
Community Board 7 has proposed its own ways to accommodate more housing through “The Manhattan Plan,” including building above city-owned sites like schools, libraries, police precincts and firehouses, increasing density on major streets, expanding Mandatory Inclusionary Housing and reviving Single Room Occupancy units — dormitory-style housing with shared kitchens and bathrooms largely barred in the city.
One of the neighborhood’s last vacant parcels of land, the former ABC campus on 80 West 67th Street, is being redeveloped by Extell Development into what will be the tallest tower on the UWS. The project requires no rezoning, special permits or Community Board 7 approval, and therefore no affordable housing.
Reddy said this project is an example of the importance of community involvement. Extell founder Gary Barnett worked with Community Board 7 to include affordable units to maintain goodwill, even though they weren’t required. Still, board members said they would have liked the city’s help to push for more.
A 171-unit project on West 96th Street also benefitted from local engagement. Fetner Properties CEO Hal Fetner voluntarily engaged neighbors on designs, noise and construction schedules.
“We don’t like to fight,” Fetner said. “Any project I’ve ever done, I’ve actually worked — whether I was obligated to or not — I worked with the community.”
Completed in 2024, it was among the first substantial new rental projects in the neighborhood in more than a decade. While the 96th Street site was previously vacant due to environmental contamination concerns, Fetner said political resistance has prevented housing elsewhere.
“There’s a reason why no one’s built there right now,” Fetner said of some low-growth neighborhoods. “You’ve got city council members saying: ‘I don’t want you here.’”
Step 5: Make Building Easier
Vishaan Chakrabarti, founder of Practice for Architecture and Urbanism, said numerical targets alone are “never gonna win over the hearts and minds of New Yorkers.”
Chakrabarti said it’s possible to add almost 11,000 new homes to the UWS without sacrificing its historic character, but he said officials should emphasize the positives housing can provide for neighborhoods. At its meeting, Community Board 7 members voiced concerns about already crowded schools and public transit, as well as sewer capacity.
The city also has to make it easier to build smaller, mid-rise projects, Chakrabarti said, rather than relying on skinny supertall high-rises.
“We’ve gotta talk about both quality and quantity,” Chakrabarti said. “Having a conversation just about quantity is a losing battle.”
The city’s complicated regulatory system disproportionately benefits large developers with lawyers, lobbyists and consultants capable of navigating it, he said. To succeed, New York has to make it simpler for smaller builders to take on projects.
For Charney Companies’ Tilley, reaching the targets ultimately comes down to whether the city creates the conditions necessary for those homes to be built.
“I love their focus on locating and investing in affordable housing in certain locations which have not realized it,” Tilley said. “But it’s a shame that all of that could come to naught if there’s not the structure to make that happen.”

Doctors tell the BBC about the targeting of Sudanese hospitals by paramilitary fighters
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing".
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The health minister of the group's civilian-affiliated government, Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, dismissed the allegations as propaganda.
The BBC's Africa correspondent Barbara Plett Usher speaks to two doctors who support the claims of systemic targeting of hospitals.

Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you
What would it mean to become Miss Ghana 1986? Fame, fortune, perhaps rubbing elbows with '80s superstar Bobby Brown? For a group of six teenage girls at the Aburi Girls Boarding School, the answer is: everything.
The battle for the crown is at the heart of School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, written by Tony Award-nominated playwright Jocelyn Bioh. The play is ending a Broadway run this week and celebrating with livestream broadcasts on The League of Live Stream Theater's website for a fee (but is free for high schoolers).
School Girls is set at a boarding school in Ghana in 1986. It follows Paulina, the school's queen bee and her crew, whom she frequently belittles and bullies over their looks.
"So, do you want to be fat-fat? Or fit? And popular." Paulina asks Nana, harassing her over eating porridge instead of an apple at lunch.
Ahead of a visit from a pageant recruiter to the school, Paulina's plans to win Miss Ghana go awry after a new transfer student arrives: Ericka from … Ohio!
Ericka exposes Paulina's toxic behavior and shows her up during a performance of Whitney Houston's Greatest Love of All. Ericka, being lighter-skinned than Paulina, sparks a clash between the school's headmistress and the pageant director over beauty and who would have the best chance of winning the Miss Global Universe pageant.
Paulina becomes the victim of circumstances that she cannot control.
School Girls explores the themes of girlhood and impossible societal beauty standards with humor and humanity.
Although its title references the Tina Fey-penned 2004 film, Mean Girls, famous for its pink-hued portrayal of the toxic side of high school girls, Bioh says she wasn't actively thinking about the movie when writing School Girls.
After completing the play and needing to settle on a subtitle, Bioh found herself reflecting on the themes: "I'm like we're dealing with things and ideas and feelings and emotions." She said that her friend, actress Danai Gurira, described it as feral teenage girls. "I'm like, that archetype is incredibly universal."
A perspective on colorism
Beyond the talk about tiaras, '80s fashion and praise for Judy Bloom, School Girls tackles the issue of colorism head-on.
Bioh says she knew it was a topic she always wanted to write about after her own long journey to own her beauty as a dark-skinned woman. "I just wanted to write something that felt like it could maybe shorten the journey for somebody else who maybe felt the same way I did. Especially as a young, impressionable girl."
While School Girls approaches the topic from the perspective of Ghanaian women and girls, Bioh says the play's message has resonated with people from different backgrounds, underscoring that colorism is a global issue.
"'Cause who has decided that this one standard of beauty is the standard of beauty for everybody? I think that's a problem," Bioh explains. "I don't have a solution other than to, you know, create a play that people can feel entertained by or perhaps be impacted by, and hopefully shift their implicit bias as they move through the world."
The cast of School Girls displays a vast array of talent: Denée Benton (Paulina), Lucia Aremu (Ama), Nia Otchere-Sarfo (Gifty), Jordan Rice (Mercy), Erin Morton (Nana) and Jasmine Amy Rogers (Ericka), just to name a few. While it is an all-Black female cast, the diversity of physical appearance is clear.
"The audience, even if they are not young Black girls who went to school in Ghana, they still see facets of themselves in these girls. I think that's where the heart and beauty of it lies." Bioh says.
Audience reaction
School Girls is now on Broadway nearly 10 years after its Off-Broadway premiere. She says it's been a moving experience to see how the show's message continues to stay with audiences long after they leave the theater.
"I had a DM from Jenna Fischer of all people, who went to see the play a few days ago, and literally messaged me again today to say she's still thinking about the play," she says. "You know, how cool that someone who I just absolutely adore and also think is, like, a comedic genius, but who likely has never had any sort of experience with colorism, is still thinking about what the play is saying and how much it moved her.
For those who get to experience School Girls, Bioh hopes you have a good time and walk away with a deep sense of empathy not only for the young girls but for the adult women too.
"I ask people to shift their ideas about things," Bioh says. "If you can just move it just a little teeny bit, then I guess, you know, I've done my job."

‘Vehicle overloaded, running at 100 km/h, crossed into wrong lane’: Survivors of deadly bus-truck collision in Assam
The truck's dashcam footage, which has emerged following the accident, has captured the final moments before the collision.
The passengers who survived the deadly bus-truck collision in Assam's Golaghat on Friday claimed that the bus was overcrowded and travelling at a very high speed when the driver lost control and swerved into the wrong lane. The truck driver also alleged that the bus entered his lane, leading to the crash.
“The bus had too many passengers. Around 50 per cent of them were standing, and even the cabin space, which was supposed to be free, was filled with passengers,” said 30-year-old Moksudul Islam, one of the survivors of Friday's deadly road accident near Kaziranga, Assam, alleging that the vehicle was carrying nearly twice its seating capacity when it collided with a goods-carrying truck.
At least 25 people were killed and several were critically injured after a passenger vehicle carrying around 35 people, including school students, collided head-on with a truck in Assam’s Golaghat district on Friday afternoon, police said earlier.
