Can the Carney government end homelessness? (Not on its own)
This isn't the first time a government has embraced an ambitious goal around the issue
Mark Carney is not the first prime minister to embrace an ambitious commitment about homelessness. He is not even the first prime minister to do so in the last 10 years.
In 2017, Justin Trudeau's government released its national housing strategy. As part of a broader plan for housing, the Trudeau government set a goal of reducing "chronic" homelessness by half over the subsequent decade — at the time, an estimated 25,000 people were said to be chronically homeless.
Three years later, in a speech from the throne, the Trudeau government went further, stating that it was now focused on "entirely eliminating chronic homelessness in Canada."
However worthy the goal, and whatever efforts the Trudeau government put toward achieving that goal, it was not met. A progress report released by the federal government last December acknowledged that there had been a 34 per cent increase in chronic homelessness among shelter users between 2016 and 2024.
Carney has committed himself to a more ambitious target — putting Canada on a path to end all homelessness within 10 years.
- Audio Can Canada end homelessness in the next 10 years?
- 'Absolutely' possible: Vancouver, Victoria mayors back Ottawa's bid
- Montreal mayor endorses PM's plan to end homelessness
"There's no simple answer. This is a hard problem," Carney said in Winnipeg last week. "And hard problems demand the humility to learn from previous well-intentioned efforts that have fallen short. And it demands the resolve to build on what's succeeded."
Homelessness is hardly a new problem, but it was in the wake of the pandemic that homelessness came to the fore as a visible and salient concern in communities across Canada — exemplified by the issue of encampments in public places.
A national homelessness enumeration in 2025 found that more than 65,000 people were homeless on a given night in Canada, a 59 per cent increase over five years. The share of unhoused people living in unsheltered locations, including encampments, had also increased from 23 per cent to 27 per cent.
The underlying factors that might have contributed to the current situation are numerous and thorny: a longstanding lack of government funding for new social housing, an insufficient supply of rental housing, the disruption of the pandemic, the post-pandemic spike in inflation and the increasing cost of living, the opioid epidemic.
"It was on a rapid but slow burn from 1995 and then it hit 2018, 2019 and the housing crisis, pandemic, affordability crisis, toxic drug supply — all came together to create the problem we're seeing today," said Tim Richter, president and CEO of the Canadian Alliance to End Homelessness.
In the face of a problem that was driven by overlapping crises and challenges, the Trudeau government's actions obviously weren't enough to solve the problem.
Nick Falvo, a researcher and consultant who focuses on homelessness, said the national housing strategy lacked an emphasis on supportive housing — "deeply subsidized housing with a lot of social work support."
Richter says the Trudeau-era plan failed to create enough deeply affordable housing of the sort that people on income-support programs could afford.
Carney's homelessness agenda
The Carney plan maintains two pieces of the Trudeau strategy.
As laid out in this month's budget, the Carney government plans to renew funding for the Canada Housing Benefit, a rent supplement for low-income Canadians. Both the Canadian Alliance to End Homelessness and Falvo have argued that an expanded and better-targeted CHB could do even more to reduce homelessness. The Carney government is also maintaining a program — Reaching Home — that provides direct funding to communities to support efforts to reduce homelessness.
On top of that the government is adding three capital funds: $10 billion for supportive and transitional housing, $5 billion for "integrated supports" projects and $2 billion for new health-care infrastructure. The government is also directing new funding to Build Canada Homes in hopes of boosting the construction of non-market housing.
More broadly, the Carney government is talking about a "renewed partnership" with the provinces, one in which the federal government would provide funding for capital (i.e. building things), while the provinces would fund operations and services.
"The Carney government's announcement is different in a couple of ways. One is they've set themselves a much bigger target," Richter said. "But they've also led with a major capital infusion.… And this conversation with the provinces. So their first steps are different than the Trudeau steps, which I think is important from a first-step point of view."
The challenge that Falvo sees is operational funding — the ongoing expenses that provincial governments will have to be willing to cover.
"I would say [the Carney government's plan] was a very impressive down payment. It showed great leadership," Falvo said. "I'll be very interested to see what happens with the provinces."
The federal government has at least already found one province that was eager for a renewed partnership. In Manitoba, the Carney government committed $800 million toward the construction of 2,000 supportive and transitional homes and $200 million toward a new centre for mental health and addictions. The province will provide funding for the operation of both and cover half of the cost of constructing the centre.
'Canadians want to do something'
In Winnipeg, Carney acknowledged that governments have spent "decades" trying to address homelessness. But, he said, "too often those efforts have been inadequately resourced, poorly co-ordinated and not sustained."
Richter co-authored a proposal earlier this year for a new national accord on housing, which would align all levels of government on solving the larger crisis of housing availability and affordability. On homelessness, Richter says the conversation between federal and provincial governments should focus not just on dollars, but on approaches, priorities and desired outcomes.
Absolutely eliminating the phenomenon of homelessness is unrealistic, Richter says. But he and the CAEH talk about achieving "functional zero," whereby a community is able to house more people than will become homeless in a given month — a situation in which homelessness is rare, brief and not recurring.
If it was somewhat surprising to see the Carney government — a government that has seemed resolutely focused on large macroeconomic issues — use its second budget to make such a headline-grabbing commitment to reduce homelessness, it's perhaps not a surprise that governments are feeling some pressure to do something.
"My theory is that his government started to realize that voters were growing quite unhappy with visible manifestations of poverty, homelessness and social disorder," Falvo said.
A survey commissioned by the CAEH earlier this year found that 66 per cent of Canadians encountered homelessness at least once per week, 39 per cent considered it a "very" or "extremely" serious problem and 60 per cent believe the problem has gotten worse in their community in the last few years.
(Earlier this year, Carney also told the Globe and Mail that he was reading Encampment by Maggie Helwig, which won this year's Shaughnessy Cohen Prize for political writing.)
But if the problem has become very visible, governments could also think not only about the long term, but also about what they can do to show visible progress in the near term, Richter suggests.
"If you look at the polling, it says like Canadians want to do something. They want to do the right thing," he said. "They feel compassion. They understand a lot of it is housing. It's also mental health and addiction. But they want to see a difference."
If the years since the last ambitious goal to reduce homelessness have unfortunately seen the problem get worse, that has perhaps at least created an even greater impetus for governments to finally solve the problem.

In early November, an image spread online claiming to show U.S. President Donald Trump posing for a photograph with comedian Russell Brand, social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate, mixed martial artist Conor McGregor, former boxer Mike Tyson and former football player Lawrence Taylor.
The alleged photograph showed (archived) Trump with his thumbs up, surrounded by a group of men convicted or accused of committing sexual offenses. An X post listed the names of the men at the alleged gathering:
Every MAGAt in this picture has been accused, indicted, convicted of, or found civilly liable for sex crimes. Three are currently in jail.
Andrew Tate @Cobratate - Indicted/Charged with multiple counts or rape and human trafficking
Russell Brand @rustyrockets - Convicted of Rape
Donald Trump @DonaldTrump - Civilly Liable / A federal Judge stated he raped E. Jean Caroll
Mike Tyson @MikeTyson - Convicted of Rape
Conor McGregor @TheNotoriousMMA - Civilly liable for Sexual Assault
Lawrence Taylor @LT_56 - Registered Sex Offender. Arrest for sex with a minor.
Tristan Tate @TateTheTalisman - Indicted/Charged with multiple counts or rape and human trafficking
(X user @MAGAts_Exposed)
The above image is fake and was created by artificial intelligence. There is no authentic photograph from a reputable media outlet showing these men together, let alone any evidence or reporting that they had all met even without cameras present. Google Gemini detected a watermark showing that the image was created or edited using Google AI.
Snopes ran the image through Google Gemini's SynthID check, a tool that scans for watermarks embedded by artificial intelligence software. That scan detected a SynthID watermark and concluded, "this image was generated or edited with Google AI, and a SynthID watermark was detected."
To confirm whether an image contains a SynthID watermark, readers can upload a photo to Google Gemini and ask, "Does this image have a SynthID watermark?" We should note, the absence of a SynthID watermark doesn't automatically mean an image is authentic, as it could have been created using other AI tools.
There are numerous signs that the image is AI-generated, namely that all the men's faces are blurred and it is of very poor quality. A video camera behind Brand is flashing light toward the photographer, creating an unnatural glow.
Using Google's reverse image search tool, we also found no reputable media outlets reporting on such an image. If such a photograph was real, it would be more widely disseminated.
The individuals in the above image have cultivated both distant and close ties to the Trump administration. The Tate brothers, who have been charged with rape and trafficking, among other criminal offenses, are connected to Trump allies, with Andrew participating in a Twitter Spaces livestream with Donald Trump Jr. As of this writing the Tates are being held at a Miami detention center without bail. Tyson, convicted of rape, has made public appearances with Trump.
Brand, who was convicted of rape and sexual assault, has appeared at numerous high-profile events led by Trump allies, including a Turning Point USA event and a Make America Healthy Again event. In November he was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison. McGregor, who was found liable of sexual assault in a civil case, has visited Trump at the White House and praised the president. In 2025, Taylor, a registered sex offender, was appointed a member of Trump's Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition.
Snopes has covered numerous fake images of Trump, including one of Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein on a private jet, and another one of them on a boat.

The Motorola Signature 27 is a beast
It’s got a monstrous tandem OLED display, a huge 7,000mAh battery, fancy cameras and a massive $1,600 price tag.
The Motorola Signature 27 is slated to be the first phone on sale in the US to feature Qualcomm's next top-tier processor — the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. That alone would make the handset notable. But when you factor in a ton of other high-end hardware including a gorgeous tandem OLED display, a massive silicon-carbon battery and triple rear cameras with a dedicated action sensor, the Signature 27 becomes a powerhouse of a phone.
In some respects, it feels like Motorola's design process was simply to take every fancy component it could get its hands on and shove it in the Signature 27. The phone features a big 6.8-inch Extreme AMOLED Duo display, which is based on the same tandem OLED tech Apple used in the new ProLED MacBook Pro. Unsurprisingly, it looks awesome. Colors are super saturated and it has a ridiculous peak brightness of 12,000 nits, though I couldn't fully test that during my evening demo session. To put that number into context, the peak brightness of the Galaxy S26 Ultra is merely 2,600 nits, and that panel is still super easy to view outdoors. And then over the top of the display, Moto went with Corning's latest Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3.
Around back, the Signature 27's rear cameras are based around a 50-megapixel Sony LYTIA L910 sensor for its main camera. There's also a 50MP ultra-wide camera and a high-res 200MP telephoto camera with a 3x optical zoom. Now, those three alone would be a pretty formidable kit, and when I got a chance to take a telephoto picture of the NYC skyline at sunset, I was rather impressed at how sharp and detailed the final image looked. This is coming from someone who has often lamented Moto's inability to keep up with Apple, Samsung and Google on previous releases. When I used the main camera to take a shot at dusk, I was really pleased with the 27's low-light sensitivity and dynamic range.
The 27's photo kit doesn't stop there. There's actually a fourth EVS sensor — which the company claims is a first in a smartphone — designed to detect pixel-level changes in light to help the phone snap extremely sharp action pics. Sadly, I didn't get to test this feature out in-depth, but it could be a really powerful solution for capturing sports without needing to lug a proper camera around. It could also be a great tool for all the parents who can't get their kids to sit still for a photo.
Meanwhile, on the inside, in addition to a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip, the phone also features 12GB of memory and 512GB of base storage. And if that's not enough, Moto has included a nifty RAM boost that effectively doubles the memory to 24GB to improve things like multitasking. Furthermore, to help deliver strong sustained performance, the 27 features a large 3D vapor chamber (8,384mm²) with what Moto claims is diamond-infused thermal gel to pull heat away from its processor.
Perhaps the best upgrade on the Signature for power users is the move to a huge 7,000 mAh silicon-carbon battery, which dwarfs pretty much anything else on sale in the US right now. Naturally, its charging speeds are pretty rapid too, with up to 90 watts wired or 50 watts wirelessly. The caveat is that you'll need to rely on one of Motorola's proprietary TurboPower adapters. Sadly, the 27 doesn't have built-in magnets either, so if you want support for magnetic accessories, you'll need a case.
Really, every component on the phone is high-end in some way. That's even true of its audio, which is composed of speakers tuned by Bang & Olufsen. I must admit, I'm pretty fond of the phone's general design as well. In addition to your standard lock button and volume rocker, there's a dedicated AI button that can also be customized to open an app of your choosing. The olive green model sports a nifty finish that reminds me of a mix between cloth and leather, while the coal smoke variant features a "tactical weave" reminiscent of ballistic nylon. Even its dust and water resistance is top-notch thanks to an IP69 rating that's good enough for submersion of up to five feet for up to 30 minutes.
However, the design trait I like the most is the way the back of the phone subtly rises to meet all those rear cameras, resulting in a sloping rear panel that leaves all of its lenses basically flush against the back of the phone. There's no big protrusion or bump for stuff to get caught on. That said, with four lenses in back plus a dedicated flash, the Signature 27 is quickly beginning to look like one of those Light L16 cameras from nearly a decade ago. At this point, I have to wonder if it might be easier, and better looking, to go with a more visor-like approach similar to what Google did on the Pixel 6.
Over the past few years, there has been demand for a proper Motorola flagship phone that can truly rival the fancy handsets from Samsung, Apple and Google. With the Signature 27, it really feels like the company took that message to heart. This phone has practically everything you could ask for in a super premium handset, and then some. The downside is that all of this comes with a similarly super premium price tag of $1,600. But if you want an absolute monster of a phone and don't want to wait for next year when more devices get their own Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip, keep an eye out when pre-orders go live on November 19.

The Federal Aviation Administration issued a halt on all U.S. flights on Friday at around 1 p.m. PT and didn’t lift the order until approximately four hours later. With the American Film Market, the Governors Awards and numerous FYC panels scheduled over the next several days, the stoppage left many Hollywood insiders grounded on one of the busiest travel weekends of the year.
AFM was hit hard by the standstill, and several events were canceled as dealmakers were preparing for their final days at the major sales function. Ryan Werner, president of global cinema at Neon, told Variety he was unsure if he could make it to AFM on Saturday for the studio’s party. He mentioned “our flights” when referring to travel plans, likely meaning several members of the Neon team were shut down on the way to Los Angeles.
One agency source told Variety that when the FAA shut down travel, their department broke out in a panic to see if anyone could still make their scheduled appearances at Saturday’s Governors Awards, which take place at the Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood.
“Once the news happened, everyone jumped on the phone to see if anyone is going to be able to make it to L.A. for the Governors Awards,” they said. “One agent has a client traveling through Europe with no idea how he will get back for his next things in the U.S., so they might have to hang out in Canada to at least be close.”
TMZ reported that “Baywatch” star Brooks Nader’s private jet was stopped in New York just before taking off for Louisiana. The outlet also shared a video of “Bachelorette” star Kaitlyn Bristowe stuck in an airport. Flava Flav and Morgan Fairchild both took to social media to share that their travel plans were affected. Variety also confirmed that the Sharpe Family Singers and actor Isaac Robinson Smith were all left stuck at the airport.
News of the flight stoppage broke around 1 p.m. PT. At the time, the FAA said the pause was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin later appeared on Fox News and clarified that it was a “telecommunications outage” that caused the backup and that there was no indication of a “nefarious attack” against the United States.
The FAA announced around 6 p.m. PT that the nationwide ground stoppage was canceled.

India's real estate industry is worth an estimated $650 Bn. Yet, for a sector of this scale, the way properties are built, bought, sold and managed remains surprisingly dependent on traditional processes. From fragmented broker networks and manual verification to lengthy property transactions and construction inefficiencies, large parts of the real estate value chain have yet to experience the technological transformation seen in sectors such as banking, commerce and mobility. For startups, this presents an enormous opportunity. But building real estate technology comes with a unique set of challenges. Selling to traditional developers, converting pilots into enterprise contracts, navigating regulatory complexities and building scalable business models require far more than a promising product. It is this gap between building a solution and scaling a business that Inc42 and publicly listed workspace company DevX are looking to address with the launch of RE:FRAME, a four-week accelerator for India's emerging PropTech startups. Designed for founders who have already demonstrated early market traction, RE:FRAME will bring together 10 promising PropTech startups for hands-on learning, mentorship, industry connections, enterprise exposure and investor access. The programme will culminate in a curated Demo Day, where five shortlisted startups will pitch for potential investment from a ₹15 Cr pool (subject to investment evaluation and terms). Applications for the inaugural cohort are now open and will close on 20 December 2026. “We started DevX as an accelerator in 2017, so supporting founders is in our DNA. RE:FRAME brings us back to that root, now with the depth of a listed real estate operator behind it. We're looking for founders who want to rethink how India builds, leases, manages and invests in property. We'll give them more than desks: we'll put real customers, mentors and capital in the room," said Umesh Uttamchandani, cofounder and MD, DevX. India's PropTech Opportunity Is Growing, So Are Its Challenges India's real estate industry is undergoing a significant shift. According to a FICCI–KPMG report, India's real estate market was valued at approximately $650 Bn in 2025 and is projected to reach $5.8 Tn by 2047. Technology is becoming an increasingly important part of this transformation. While the first generation of PropTech businesses largely focussed on bringing property discovery and transactions online, the opportunity is now expanding across the real estate lifecycle. Startups are developing solutions for construction automation, developer sales, property management, smart buildings, financing, energy efficiency, land records and AI-powered analytics. Investor interest has followed. According to Inc42 Datalabs, India’s proptech sector raised around $834 Mn across 42 funding rounds in 2025. Infra.Market ($254 Mn) and WeWork India ($210 Mn) alone accounted for more than 50% of the total capital raised. The sector has also witnessed a wave of public listings, with companies such as DevX, Smartworks, IndiQube, WeWork India and ArisInfra making their stock market debuts in 2025. But for emerging founders, raising capital is only one part of the challenge. Unlike consumer internet businesses, PropTech startups often operate in an ecosystem characterised by long enterprise sales cycles, multiple stakeholders, legacy business practices and complex regulatory requirements. A startup may have a working product and paying customers but still struggle to expand beyond a handful of developers, convert pilots into recurring contracts or establish a repeatable go-to-market strategy. The questions become increasingly difficult as these businesses grow. How do founders build trust with traditional real estate enterprises? What does it take to scale distribution across developers and property markets? How can AI and technology improve operating efficiency without compromising unit economics? And how should startups position themselves for institutional capital? Solving these challenges requires more than capital. It requires access to the right industry networks, operators, expertise and opportunities to test business models at scale. This is the opportunity RE:FRAME aims to address. Introducing RE:FRAME: A PropTech Accelerator Built For Scale RE:FRAME brings together Inc42's experience working with India's startup, investor and founder ecosystem and DevX's expertise in developing and operating managed workspaces. The partnership aims to combine startup acceleration with a deeper understanding of the real estate industry's operational challenges, enterprise requirements and commercial opportunities. The accelerator is designed for founders who have moved beyond the idea stage, built working products and demonstrated early customer demand, but now face the more complex task of scaling their businesses. Rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach to startup acceleration, the four-week programme will focus on the challenges specific to PropTech businesses — from enterprise sales, go-to-market strategy and unit economics to product development, AI adoption and fundraising. “India's PropTech opportunity extends far beyond digitising property transactions. The next wave of startups will fundamentally change how real estate is built, financed, managed and experienced. But building a promising product is only the first step. The real challenge is turning innovation into adoption and sustainable businesses. With RE, we want to help founders bridge that gap and build companies that can shape the future of India's real estate industry,” said Vaibhav Vardhan, Founder and CEO of Inc42. For the first cohort, 10 startups will be selected, with applications assessed on market traction, the strength of the problem being solved, market opportunity, founding team and potential to scale. Who Can Apply For RE:FRAME? The programme is open to startups operating across the real estate value chain, including property discovery and brokerage, construction technology, developer sales and marketing, property management, rental and tenant experience, commercial real estate, real estate financing, smart buildings, sustainability, AI and real estate data analytics. Inside The Four Weeks Of RE The inaugural cohort will begin its programme journey in February 2027, and will follow a hybrid format, combining virtual learning with an intensive physical bootcamp in Delhi NCR. Starting with three weeks of learning, the final week will bring the selected founders together for a six-day physical bootcamp and a demo day in Delhi NCR. The curriculum will address four interconnected aspects of scaling a PropTech business: Go-To-Market & Enterprise Sales: Building repeatable sales processes, improving customer acquisition and navigating complex enterprise relationships. Business Models & Unit Economics: Strengthening monetisation, pricing, financial discipline and the operating foundations required for sustainable growth. Product, Technology & AI: Building differentiated products, identifying practical AI applications and developing technology roadmaps that support scale. Fundraising & Investment Readiness: Sharpening investment narratives, understanding fundraising strategies and preparing for investor discussions. Through the programme, founders will have opportunities to learn from experienced PropTech entrepreneurs, technology leaders, real estate operators, investors and specialists familiar with the commercial and regulatory complexities of the industry. Demo Day: The ₹15 Cr Investment Opportunity RE:FRAME will culminate in a curated Demo Day in March 2027, where the top five startups from the inaugural cohort will pitch their businesses to venture capital investors, angel investors, HNIs and industry leaders. The shortlisted startups will have an opportunity to secure funding from a ₹15 Cr investment pool, subject to investment evaluation and mutually agreed terms. If you're building technology to transform how India's real estate is developed, bought, sold or managed, and have the traction and ambition to scale, RE could be your next big leap. Applications for Cohort 01 close on 20 December 2026.

Eight sentenced to jail over Nurmagomedov-Dvalishvili brawl
- Published
Eight people have received prison sentences for their part in a mass brawl involving MMA fighters Usman Nurmagomedov and Merab Dvalishvili at a hotel in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday.
A video of the incident appeared to show Russian Nurmagomedov slapping former UFC bantamweight champion Dvalishvili after approaching the Georgian from behind.
Fighting then broke out between the two and members of their teams, with Abu Dhabi police later confirming the incident led to 10 arrests being made.
According to a social media post by Abu Dhabi's judicial department, all 10 defendants have been convicted for their part in the brawl.
A report by Abu Dhabi news outlet the National, external went into more detail, adding that six of the defendants were sentenced to six months in prison, fined £62,000 each and ordered to be deported after completing their sentences.
It added they have been convicted for "disturbing public security, causing panic and endangering lives".
Two others were given the same punishment, but for "violating privacy by using information technology to film and publish footage of the brawl".
The remaining two defendants were fined £10,200 each for "disturbing public security and assaulting others".
None of the defendants have yet been named, but Real American Freestyle (RAF) co-founder Chad Bronstein says Dvalishvili has been released from custody.
"I'm pleased to share that Merab Dvalishvili is back with us in Abu Dhabi," Bronstein said in a statement.
"We would like to express our sincere appreciation to the relevant authorities in Abu Dhabi for their professionalism and support.
"We remain focused on moving forward and are pleased to have Merab back with us."
BBC Sport has asked Abu Dhabi's judicial department for confirmation.
Dvalishvili, 35, is scheduled to compete at the RAF event in the United Arab Emirates on Saturday against Brazilian Marlon Moraes.
Dvalishvili released a video after the incident calling Nurmagomedov, 28, and his team "snakes" as he received treatment on his bloodied face.
Nurmagomedov is in Abu Dhabi to support his brother Umar, who was set to compete against American Urijah Faber at Saturday's event.
However, Umar has been replaced in the bout by Dvalishvili's team-mate Saba Lazishvili, who was also involved in the mass brawl but appears to have been released from custody.
Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili's teams had a previous altercation at a RAF event in July, which UFC champion Islam Makhachev - a close friend and training partner of the Nurmagomedovs - suggested led to Wednesday's brawl.
Nurmagomedov is the PFL lightweight champion but is out of contract after winning his last bout with the organisation in July.
He has been heavily linked with a switch to the UFC but on Friday the promotion's president Dana White said he had not spoken to the Russian.
White then called the altercation "ridiculous" and "stupid", and referred to the participants as "a bunch of idiots".

Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.
The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.
A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.
Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

A few hours of exposure to firecracker smoke can be enough to trigger coughing, wheezing or breathlessness, particularly in people living with asthma or other respiratory conditions. The effects, however, are not limited to those with an existing diagnosis. High concentrations of particulate matter and gases can irritate the airways in anyone.
The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a numerical measure that converts the levels of different air pollutants into a single figure to indicate how polluted the air is and the likely health effects. Europe Agrees on a Team to Represent It in Talks With Russia
After coveting a seat in the Ukraine war discussions, Europe is poised to get one. The continent wants to fill it with a six-member team.
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. They learned this week that they would get one, and simply needed to decide which official should sit in that chair.
Instead, they decided on six.
European Union leaders concluded in Dublin on Friday that they will tap a group of major nations — Britain, France, Germany, Poland, and Italy — along with a representative from the E.U’s leadership arms, the European Council and European Commission.
In some ways, the choice of a crowd plays into jibes Americans have made about the continent’s indecisiveness: “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said earlier this week.
Europe’s failure to pick one negotiator leaves open the possibility that its fragmentation will diminish its influence. Even so, Europeans have underscored that they are a democracy of many nations, though, and that many voices must be represented.
“We decide on who represents us, and that is what we have done today,” said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission.
“We need to work as a team,” António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, said at a news conference on Friday, noting that America itself has two envoys.

French-speaking nations hold a summit in Cambodia but an African conflict threatens a rift
France's President Emmanuel Macron and other leaders are attending a biennial meeting of French-speaking countries and territories in Cambodia
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — Emmanuel Macron is set to attend a biennial meeting of French-speaking territories beginning Saturday in Cambodia, where the French president contending with public unrest at home will face international political challenges as an African conflict hangs over the proceedings.
The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie is holding the three-day meeting through Monday in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh. Macron is expected to engage in bilateral discussions and join the summit meeting of the loose confederation of 90 member states and governments comprising 53 full members, five associate members and 32 observers where French is spoken.
Cambodia will take over the summit's chairmanship from Macron, who served as chair in 2024 when France was the host nation.
Before departing for Malaysia on Monday, Macron is scheduled to visit the Angkor World Heritage Site near the city of Siem Reap, where he and King Norodom Sihamoni will mark the completion of a French-supported restoration of the West Mebon temple.
The French leader's trip comes at a time of widespread domestic protests. France’s Interior Ministry said more than 600,000 people took to the streets earlier this month in a demonstration to demand higher wages and support the country’s student protest movement, which has resulted in thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire.
The summit's sticky diplomacy for Macron and other leaders will take place when participants decide on Monday who will serve for the next four years as the group’s leader and chief executive in the role of secretary-general.
The choices include candidates from two bitterly feuding African members, Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, who is seeking reelection to a third four-year term, and the Democratic Republic of Congo's Juliana Lumumba, the 71-year-old daughter of the country’s martyred independence hero, Patrice Lumumba.
Congo, the United States and experts from the United Nations accuse Rwanda of backing the M23, one of about 100 armed groups that have been vying for a foothold in mineral-rich eastern Congo, along the border with Rwanda. Rwanda’s government consistently denies backing armed groups in Congo.
Congo has threatened to leave the OIF if Mushikiwabo is reelected. With a population exceeding 110 million people, over 40 million more than France, Congo is the most populous nation where French is the official language and its withdrawal would mark a significant blow to the Francophonie organization.
Two other candidates, from Romania and Mauritania, are poised to serve as compromise picks.
France is influential in the decision as the largest contributor to the OIF 2026 budget of €71.7 million ($79 million).
The outcome also could be delicate because the challenge comes on the heels of the withdrawals of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso from the OIF announced in March 2025, following their membership suspensions over military coups.
Mali said the suspensions infringed on sovereignty, but the withdrawals also came in the context of Francophone African countries in recent decades shedding French political, military and cultural influence that they regarded as overbearing.
The summit's slogan, “Reinvest in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability,” is seen as a reflection of Cambodia’s recovery from years of war and unrest in the last quarter of the 20th century.
About 20 government leaders, including Canada’s Mark Carney, Vietnam’s To Lam, Rwanda’s Paul Kagame and the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Félix Tshisekedi, are expected to attend the summit and likely will meet with Cambodia's king as well as Prime Minister Hun Manet.
Most of the summit’s agenda is uncontroversial. Documents set to be approved concern political commitment to peaceful coexistence, social, cultural and economic cooperation, resolution of crisis situations and peace-building, and the protection of cultural heritage and the promotion of cultural diversity.
Host Cambodia, which has an opportunity to showcase tourism potential and business opportunities, is holding side events highlighting commercial partnerships, cultural exchanges, science and technology.
Local political activists see the meeting as an occasion to press for more democratic freedoms in a de facto one-party state. U.N. Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews issued a statement pleading with summit delegates to uphold OIF values and pressure the Cambodian government for the release of detained rights activists.
“No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions,” he said.
Cambodia can lay claim to helping birth the OIF, as its late king and mercurial independence leader, Norodom Sihanouk, was one of four founders in 1970 of the Agency for Cultural and Technical Cooperation. Sihanouk was overthrown and his immediate successors did not join, as Cambodia subsequently endured civil war and the brutal rule of the communist Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1979. Cambodia joined the Francophonie as an observer in 1991 and became a full member in 1993.

Noelia Voigt spent seven years working to become Miss USA.
She won first runner-up three times at state pageants before making it to the national stage, where she took the crown in 2023.
That made it even more shocking when Voigt became the first Miss USA in the pageant's history to relinquish her title, giving up the crown just months before her reign was set to end in 2024.
This is her story.
Noelia Voigt began watching pageants at an early age, but her mother didn't allow her to compete as a child.
Voigt was born and raised in Sarasota, Florida. Her mother, Jackeline Voigt, is from Venezuela, and her father, Jack Voigt, is an American former Major League Baseball player. He played for the Baltimore Orioles, Oakland A's, Texas Rangers, and Milwaukee Brewers during his 14-year career, according to his website.
After winning Miss USA in September 2023, Voigt told Business Insider that she grew up watching pageants with her mother.
"My mom is from Venezuela, and over there, pageants are their Super Bowl and Olympics — it's a huge deal," Voigt said. "So I had always wanted to do pageants from a really young age."
Voigt said she began asking to compete in pageants before she was 10, but her mother was "really protective" and made her wait.
"Depending on the pageant that you're entering at that age, it can be potentially damaging to a young girl if they don't end up winning," Voigt said. "Then they have this negative association with it, and they think that it has something to do with them."
"My mom didn't want that for me," she added. "So she waited until I was old enough to understand that, if I didn't win, it's not a reflection of me or who I am."
Voigt won her first pageant when she was 16 years old.
Voigt was named Miss Sarasota Teen USA in 2017. She went on to compete at Miss Florida Teen USA that year and placed first runner-up.
Although she found early success in the world of pageants, Voigt said her friends made fun of her newfound passion.
"I was really hurt and confused as to why people I thought were my friends were making fun of me for doing something that I was really excited about and that I was doing good things with," Voigt told Business Insider. "At first, it really did sting. But it was clear to me that it was an attempt to steal the joy I had from this accomplishment."
Voigt made anti-bullying part of her platform and authored a children's book on the topic called "Maddie the BRAVE."
Voigt credited pageants with helping her get out of an abusive relationship in high school.
Voigt told Business Insider that competing in pageants was an eye-opening experience as she navigated an abusive relationship during her teenage years.
"When you're in pageants, you're surrounded by women who are really uplifting of one another," she said. "They all have a really good sense of self-respect, and they know their worth, and a lot of times if you find yourself in an abusive relationship, that might be something that is lacking."
"Once I broke into the pageant world and started to get involved in a lot of community service, I started to realize that anybody that was toxic in my life was simply holding me back," she added. "Pageants absolutely helped me realize my worth."
Voigt moved to Alabama for school and continued to compete in pageants.
Voigt competed in Miss Alabama 2022 and Miss Alabama 2023, placing first runner-up in both competitions.
"A lot of people ask me if it hurt that I kept getting first runner-up, and I just told them the honest truth — that I was really proud of myself for getting that placement," Voigt told Business Insider after her win. "I always felt very honored that the judges still felt I could do the job if something happened and I needed to step in."
"Every year that I hadn't won the pageant, it gave me another year of opportunity to do good things for my community, so I really wouldn't have traded it for anything," she added.
Voigt moved to Salt Lake City in April 2023 and won Miss Utah 2023 three months later.
By winning Miss Utah, Voigt had finally accomplished her dream of making it to the Miss USA stage.
"It could have been very easy for me, all those times getting first runner-up, to just say, 'I can't do this anymore, I'm so frustrated,'" Voigt told Business Insider. "But instead, every time I got first runner-up, it was more fuel to the fire for me to keep on going."
Voigt was crowned Miss USA on September 29, 2023.
Voigt became the first Venezuelan-American to win Miss USA after she was crowned at the Grand Sierra Resort and Casino in Reno, Nevada. She was also the first Miss Utah to win the title since 1960.
"This is something I've worked toward for a really long time," Voigt told Business Insider. "It's been a journey of perseverance and not giving up."
Voigt went on to compete at Miss Universe 2023 in El Salvador, where she placed in the top 20.
On May 6, 2024, Voigt announced she was stepping down as Miss USA.
Voigt said she was relinquishing the Miss USA crown to focus on her mental health, but a cryptic message was hidden inside her Instagram statement. It read "I AM SILENCED." Two days later, Miss Teen USA 2023 UmaSofia Srivastava resigned as well.
The pageant queens said they couldn't speak publicly about their experience due to strict nondisclosure agreements they had signed under the leadership of Laylah Rose, who became the CEO of Miss USA in August 2023. Jackeline Voigt and Barbara Srivastava, the pageant queens' mothers, told Business Insider their daughters had endured "eight months of torture and abuse" from Rose.
"The woman who was supposed to be all about empowering and bringing women together and pushing them to speak for their causes and charities, she did quite the opposite," Barbara Srivastava said during the May 2024 interview.
In her official Miss USA resignation letter, Voigt detailed the "detrimental mental and emotional toll" of her time as Miss USA and said she had to be prescribed two anti-anxiety medications.
"I've never ever in my life been on anti-anxiety medication," Voigt told Business Insider during an exclusive August 2025 interview. "It wasn't something that came out of nowhere. I felt like I had to put on a facade to represent the organization because I had this title, but I didn't agree with what was going on."
Rose has denied the allegations.
In October 2025, Miss Universe sued Laylah Rose. Voigt said she felt "vindicated" by the lawsuit.
The owner of Miss Universe, which oversees Miss USA and Miss Teen USA, referenced Voigt's official Miss USA resignation letter in its lawsuit against Rose's company, VVV Global Ent. It noted an incident in which Voigt said she was sexually harassed during an official Miss USA appearance when she was left alone with a man in a car. The complaint from JKN Universe said VVV had failed to provide a chaperone or travel companion at times, despite the "contractual obligation to do so."
The lawsuit also alleges that Rose failed to prepare Voigt for the Miss Universe 2023 competition, including providing a national costume and the necessary fees to attend the global pageant. Jackeline Voigt told Business Insider in May 2024 that the family had to pay $20,000 out of pocket to help Voigt with the competition.
Rose filed a counterclaim against JKN that same month, and the case remains ongoing. Voigt told Business Insider in October 2025 that she hopes the Miss Universe Organization will eventually release her from her NDA.
"That's the best way for them to rectify the situation, and I hope they're open to it," she said. "It's my life and my story. This shackle on me, it would feel nice to have it lifted."
Rose has not responded to requests for comment. Lawyers for the Miss Universe Organization previously declined to comment on the complaint.
Voigt has returned to the Miss USA organization since Thom Brodeur replaced Rose in September 2025.
Voigt most recently served as a co-host for the Miss Teen USA 2026 pageant in August. She is also currently attending nursing school.
"It makes me emotional to remember the girl that I was when I first started because I was so shy," Voigt told Business Insider in August 2025 as she reflected on her pageant career.
"I'm so grateful for my whole journey," she added. "And that we're coming at this full-circle moment and getting to close our chapters with grace."

Memorial opens honoring victims of the 2015 Charleston church massacre
Eleven years after a white gunman killed nine Black parishioners inside the South’s oldest African Methodist Episcopal Church, a long planned memorial is opening to honor their lives

It took Alana Grant years to find the strength to set foot in the basement of Mother Emanuel AME Church in Charleston, where her grandfather, the Rev. Daniel Lee Simmons, attended his final Bible study.
Her fears have been replaced by gratitude and hope now that there is a completed memorial in a courtyard by the front door for the “Emanuel Nine,” the Black churchgoers killed by an avowed white supremacist in 2015.
The memorial provides a public space where “people can go and remember really what happened here,” Alana Grant said as she and her husband, state Rep. Hamilton Grant, got their first look.
On Saturday, the long-planned memorial at the South's oldest African Methodist Episcopal Church opens to the public.
Emphasizing remembrance and reflection, the marble memorial is anchored by a Fountain of Grace, symbolizing God's eternal love and mercy. Water flows from a shallow basin etched with the names of the six women and three men slain. Two Fellowship Benches with curved backs, sheltering anyone seated, flank the fountain. There is also a Cross of Hope, signifying redemption in the wake of suffering. A garden honoring the five survivors will come next.
The Rev. Eric Manning, co-chair of the Mother Emanuel Memorial Foundation board, hopes it will mean something to everyone.
“I was actually standing out there the other day,” said Manning, who took over after pastor and state Sen. Clementa Pinckney was among those killed. “Just for a moment, a peace came over me.”
How the memorial is helping victims' families
Grant sees the memorial as a place to inspire conversations with her three small children about their great-grandfather. Because the facts of the shooting have been so public, she doesn't want them to hear more from someone else.
“I spent a lot of time thinking about it and praying about it,” she said. “I do want them to go so that they can kind of see what even brought me to South Carolina.”
Former North Carolina state senator and Charlotte City Councilman Malcolm Graham, whose sister Cynthia Graham Hurd died huddled under a desk in the fellowship hall, attended the 2023 groundbreaking. He has anticipated visiting the memorial to reflect on “all the good times Cindy and I had as kids growing up, and being at the church and going to Sunday school.”
A library, scholarship and other awards now carry the name of the accomplished librarian. Now she'll live on in the memorial, too.
“She said before she died that I was the most famous person in the family,” Graham said. “She is the most famous person in our family and I still look up to her.”
As for the survivors to be honored with a garden, Grant says their living with memories of the shooting is “nothing short of heroism.”
“There are not a lot of spaces where you get to see the survivors. We as Black people have survived so much,” Grant said.
A church memorial that can be something for everyone
When a committee sought an architect in 2017, they heard from designers all over the world, said John Darby, another memorial foundation co-chair who runs a Charleston real estate development firm. The final candidates were not asked to submit design proposals, but instead give written responses to deep questions on topics like forgiveness.
That unconventional request was very prescient, said Michael Arad, an architect on the 9/11 Memorial whose design was ultimately chosen. He wrote about his admiration for the victims' families who offered forgiveness to the shooter.
A white, Jewish New Yorker who had never visited South Carolina, Arad did a deep-dive into the community for more than a year after he was selected. Having lengthy conversations with members of the congregation and researching the church's 200-year history was essential, he said, and while the 9/11 memorial was a bigger endeavor, this design wasn't any less complex.
“My job as a designer was to allow people who visit the site to see and hear what was here all along,” he said. “We understand who we are as Americans through stories like this, through our response.”
Arad said he embraces emotionally weighted projects as “a tremendous privilege” and he “could not imagine turning down a project like this.”
The foundation has raised around $25 million over the last decade for the memorial, garden and other costs, much of it from foundations, endowments and corporations, Darby said.
“It was one of those things that people wanted to be a part of,” Darby said. “We don't want it to be an expense to the church.”
Memorial stirs hope to learn from hate and tragedy
Established in 1818, Mother Emanuel was built by free and enslaved people. In the 20th century, the church became a place of resistance where the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and other civil rights figures spoke.
The Emanuel Nine's families applauded in 2015 when Gov. Nikki Haley removed the Confederate battle flag from state buildings. But with Republicans stirring an angry backlash against diversity and equity efforts, Graham said “racism, hatred and discrimination continue to be this country's Achilles' heel.”
Alana Grant has tried over the years to gather support for a hate crimes statute, and her husband is among the lawmakers who pushed legislation named for Pinckney that would add enhanced penalties for hate crimes to South Carolina's criminal code. It failed to pass, even though a senator was among the Emanuel Nine.
She sees this memorial as an opportunity to raise “generational awareness” so younger people will campaign against hate. Tourists still come to the church daily out of curiosity or sympathy, and could leave the memorial feeling inspired.
“We want more than your thoughts and prayers. We want your advocacy,” she said.

Tearful Pochettino on 'difficult' decision to leave USA for Man Utd

Mauricio Pochettino says the decision to leave his role as boss of the USA national team to become Manchester United head coach was "one of the most difficult" of his career.
The Argentine was announced as Michael Carrick's successor at Old Trafford on Friday, with sources telling BBC Sport he has signed a two-and-a-half-year contract.
United paid a release clause in the region of £7.4m to extract Pochettino from his USA contract, with a further payment being made for his backroom staff.
Pochettino only signed a new four-year deal with the USA in the summer, but will depart for Manchester after leading the national team in matches against Haiti on 14 and 18 November.
The 54-year-old broke down in tears during his first news conference after his move to United was confirmed, and thanked the US Soccer Federation for its support.
"It's difficult to talk now," he said. "I'm a very emotional guy. It's a very sad decision.
"But we are professionals and we are trying to make our dreams come true."
Asked why he signed a new deal with the national side only to accept United's offer, Pochettino said the chance to manage at Old Trafford was too good to reject.
"I never said I wanted to go back but they know there aren't too many opportunities that happen in your career like Manchester United," he said. "When it arrives, it's difficult to turn down."
Carrick was sacked on Thursday after United's worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years, which has left them languishing in 18th place in the Premier League.
Pochettino will inherit a side that have won just once in 10 league matches this season and sit just one point above bottom-placed Sunderland.
His first match in charge will be an away match against Liverpool on 22 November.

A decade in the making
Pochettino's arrival at Old Trafford marks the end of a decade-long courtship.
Thriving during an 18-month stint at Southampton, he led the Saints to eighth place during his only full season on the south coast.
Tottenham moved quickly to appoint one of the most promising young coaches in Europe in 2014, and it was in north London that his reputation rocketed.
The club had finished in the top four just twice in the 22 years before his appointment, but Pochettino led them there four times in his five full seasons.
It was two years into his time in the capital that United first considered a move for Pochettino.
The Argentine dined with legendary former United boss Sir Alex Ferguson in Mayfair, London just weeks before Louis van Gaal was sacked as Red Devils boss.
The club ultimately decided to appoint Jose Mourinho, and Pochettino was again overlooked when the Portuguese departed in 2018, with Ole Gunnar Solskjaer impressing so much in an interim role that he was given the job more permanently.
In 2022, it was between Pochettino and Erik ten Hag for the United job but the board opted for the Dutchman, who had led Ajax to the semi-finals of the Champions League in 2019, when they were beaten by Pochettino's Tottenham.
Pochettino was interviewed by United again in 2024 following his exit from Chelsea, but the board opted instead to hire Ruben Amorim from Sporting to replace Ten Hag.

In November, right around Veteran's Day, posts online claimed to show former U.S. President Bill Clinton personally helping a homeless veteran outside The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in 1997.
According to the tale, Clinton offered the man, Marcus Williams, his coat, before asking him questions about his service. He then supposedly ordered a Secret Service agent to get Williams food, and personally contacted the Department of Veterans Affairs to help Williams get back on his feet.
The posts began:
"On a freezing December night in 1997, President Bill Clinton was leaving a holiday concert at the Kennedy Center when he noticed a homeless veteran sitting near the entrance. The man wore a thin jacket and was shivering in the cold. In his hands, he held a piece of cardboard with a simple message written on it: "Marine. Desert Storm. Hungry." What happened next caught the attention of people in the presidential motorcade. Clinton stopped, took off his own coat, placed it around the veteran's shoulders, and sat beside him on the icy concrete.
The veteran, 42 year old Marcus Williams, later told reporters that the President never questioned how he had ended up on the street or lectured him about his choices. Instead, Clinton asked about his military service, the battles he had experienced, and whether anyone had ever properly thanked him for what he had done. According to Secret Service agent Larry Cockell, who later wrote about the encounter, Clinton stayed with Marcus for nearly 25 minutes despite the freezing temperatures. When Marcus admitted that he had not eaten in two days, Clinton sent an agent to a nearby restaurant to get him food. He refused to leave until Marcus had finished his meal.
The posts were accompanied by images supposedly showing the two meeting as well as Williams holding a cardboard sign reading "Marine. Desert Storm. Hungry." Snopes readers contacted us to ask whether the story and images were real or fake.
We first uploaded the images into Google Lens to perform a reverse image search. Next, we used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo with phrases such as "Bill Clinton Marcus Williams Homeless Veteran" to see whether any reputable news outlets had documented the events. If the scene had occurred and the images were real, we would find evidence in newspapers and media archives like Getty Images. That was not the case. We did not locate any examples of credible outlets publishing the images, nor reporting on the alleged meeting.
We found that neither the story nor the images were real, and that they were generated using artificial intelligence tools. Therefore, we've labeled the claim false.
We uploaded the images accompanying the story into several tools that screen visual media for signs of AI: Sightengine, Hive Moderation, and Google's integrated SynthID detector. The first two found a high likelihood that the images were AI-generated, and the SynthID detector found the invisible watermark indicating Google's AI tools generated the images. We also ran the story through the AI text detection tool Pangram, which also determined that all of the text was written using a large language model such as ChatGPT.
Let us note here: These types of AI detection tools are fallible. Snopes cautions people against using them for definitive answers on media's authenticity without supporting evidence.
Detecting that the image was fake without using those tools was more difficult, given it was grayscale and grainy, but not impossible. We noticed that the writing on the cardboard sign looked too perfect, the cardboard itself looked unusually bright and the supposedly parallel sidewalk cracks didn't form straight lines or meet at a single vanishing point.
Our searches also uncovered a January article written by the fact-checking organization Lead Stories debunking the exact same story, though featuring a real archival image of Clinton instead of an AI-generated one. That fact-check also noted some factual errors in the text, most prominently that one of Clinton's Secret Service agents wrote about the encounter in a memoir. (No such memoir existed.) Because the exact claim was also previously been fact-checked almost a year ago, we concluded that users posting the claim in October and November were doing so in an attempt to make money.
The fictional story is an example of glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental." These types of low-quality posts often use standard or template language, making small tweaks in an attempt to game the social media algorithms. They rely on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories and hope to generate a profit from advertising revenue if the posts go viral.
Snopes previously explained the ongoing trend of politically motivated, AI-generated slop content similar to the claim debunked in this article.

Microsoft says the Microsoft 365 outage that disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot for more than 24 hours is now fixed. In its final status update on the incident, the company said, “We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service.” The disruption hit users in at least 74 countries and left businesses, governments, hospitals and airlines falling back on phone lines, paper records and, in some offices, fax machines.
The trouble began on November 12, when users in the Americas reported they could not open their Exchange Online mailboxes. Microsoft first acknowledged the issue at 5:54 pm GMT (11:24 pm IST). Just 13 minutes later, it warned that users in any region could be affected. The company has since said it is “deeply sorry” for the disruption and maintains the incident was not caused by a cyberattack or AI.
Microsoft blames an earlier network upgrade for the Outlook outage
According to a Microsoft spokesperson, the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.” The company called it “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents.”
That explanation came after a long night of trial and error. 
Microsoft’s first updates on X blamed “elevated load” across several regions. Hours later, it said traffic had not gone up at all. A number of servers had become unexpectedly unavailable after failing automated health checks, and their workload landed on the servers still running, straining those too.
Engineers eventually traced part of the problem to a core process on the affected servers that handles secure connections. It was getting overwhelmed, and the servers stopped processing requests. At one stage, Microsoft admitted its actions “have not provided the anticipated relief.”
Why Outlook and Teams took almost a full day to recover
The hardest part was keeping servers up once they were back. Microsoft said servers it returned to service could stop responding again once they started receiving traffic. Its engineers worked on several fronts at once. They limited the types of traffic hitting affected infrastructure, rolled some servers back to an earlier configuration, patched an authentication and routing component and added virtual machines for extra capacity.
Email made the job slower. Mail servers outside Microsoft keep retrying messages they could not deliver, so restored servers faced a backlog of queued mail the moment they came online. To make sure messages sent during the outage were not lost, Microsoft extended its email timeout window to 48 hours.
“Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration,” the company said.
Asia Pacific was among the first regions to stabilise on November 13, followed by Europe and North America. By the afternoon of November 13 (GMT), Microsoft said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Teams chats and meetings had largely come back earlier, though calendar features that rely on Exchange Online stayed patchy for longer. Outlook.com, OneDrive, OneNote and Microsoft To Do, used on personal accounts, were hit as well.
Airlines, hospitals and courts in at least 74 countries felt the Microsoft outage
Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services. That reach showed in who got hit.
In India, the outage hit email support at IndiGo and Akasa Air. Air India rerouted its emails to keep receiving customer messages, and its flights ran as usual. At one large Indian brokerage, a backup covered for Outlook, but client calls on Teams were harder to manage.
In the UK, NHS staff switched to paper records, pharmacies warned of prescription delays and a judge in Manchester sent jurors home. In Colorado, a sheriff’s office had to ask people to post bond in person, since online payments relied on Outlook email notifications. Some companies in Japan went back to fax. Even OpenAI and Anthropic ran into problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors, while electric truck maker Workhorse Group pushed its quarterly results to November 16.
Investors were far calmer. Microsoft shares traded largely flat on November 13, even as the outage stretched into a second day.
For users, a few loose ends may remain. Emails held in queues carry the time they were delivered rather than sent, so a message stamped November 13 may well have been written on the night of November 12.
Microsoft has promised a full post-incident report once its review is complete. That report should spell out how a capacity upgrade knocked servers offline across regions for more than a day, and what the company is changing so the next network update does not do the same.

The story so far: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has cautioned students, parents, and the public against taking admission in medical colleges and institutions without first verifying their statutory recognition and regulatory approval. In an advisory dated November 5, 2026, published on its website on November 6, the medical regulator said it had come across instances of institutions purportedly offering medical and allied health courses without obtaining the requisite permission from competent authorities.
The advisory warns that misleading advertisements, websites, social media promotions, unauthorised admission offers and false representations by institutions or agents could leave students and their families vulnerable to fraud. It asks prospective students to verify the authenticity of the institution, the course being offered, the approved intake and the permission granted for the relevant academic year.

The Telangana State Women’s Commission (TGSCW) has initiated an inquiry into an alleged illegal oocyte donation racket in Hyderabad, issuing notices to eight Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) centres and egg banks over suspected irregularities in their donor records and procurement practices.
The Commission examined representatives of the eight institutions on Friday, November 13, after directing their managements to appear before it. However, TGSCW Chairperson Nerella Sharada expressed dissatisfaction after some centres sent staff members and other representatives instead of senior management, despite being specifically instructed to attend in person. The inquiry was subsequently adjourned after the institutions assured the Commission that their management would appear at the next hearing.
During Friday’s proceedings, the Commission scrutinised reports, records and details of egg donors submitted by the ART centres and egg banks. “Several irregularities and suspicious elements have emerged from the records examined so far,” said Ms. Sharada.
She also questioned claims made by the institutions that nearly 90% of their egg donors came from other States and donated their eggs voluntarily without receiving any remuneration or financial compensation. She said the claims raised several questions and warranted further investigation.
Health Department’s investigation
Commissioner of Health and Family Welfare, Sangeetha Satyanarayana, also attended the inquiry, during which Ms. Sharada sought details about the progress of the department’s investigation into the alleged illegal egg procurement practices. The discussions also covered shortcomings in the existing Assisted Reproductive Technology Act and its implementation, particularly the challenges in regulating and monitoring ART centres and egg banks.
Ms. Sharada said she would soon meet Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha and Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy to inform them of the findings and discuss corrective measures, including possible legislative amendments to strengthen regulation of the sector.
More ART centres likely to come under scanner
Ms. Sharada further said that the Commission has also received information indicating the possible involvement of several other ART centres and egg banks in the alleged racket. It plans to issue notices to their management and summon them for questioning as part of the ongoing inquiry.
“The Commission will not tolerate illegal practices that compromise women’s health, dignity and rights. We will continue the investigation in coordination with the concerned government departments to identify those responsible and ensure appropriate legal action,” she added.

Border Crossings Have Plummeted. Stephen Miller Isn’t Satisfied.
Mexico has cooperated to significantly slow the flow of migrants. The new White House chief of staff insists it is not enough.
Since President Trump resumed office, the number of illegal crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border has dropped to the lowest point in decades.
For one of Mr. Trump’s top policy advisers, that is not enough.
In conversations with both American and Mexican officials over the last several months, Stephen Miller has insisted that illegal border crossings must be reduced, according to officials in both countries familiar with the private conversations but not authorized to discuss them.
Mr. Miller’s goal, they said, is zero crossings. Mexican officials have said that, with a nearly 2,000-mile border, that is simply not possible.
In his new role as chief of staff, Mr. Miller is expected to continue driving that agenda.
One of the main forums for Mr. Miller’s demands has been his near daily calls with the U.S. ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, some of the officials said. On calls with staff, Mr. Miller, previously the deputy chief of staff, frequently rails about the number of border crossings, despite their low figures, the officials said.
That has been especially true in recent months, they said, as border crossings increased slightly, to the highest point in Mr. Trump’s second term.

On 11 November 2026, terrorists opened fire on a CRPF checkpoint near Mir Bazar in Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir, injuring three personnel. The attackers fled after the firing, and security forces launched a search operation to track them down (here, here, and here).
Amid the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel, a video is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows defence expert Wing Commander (Wg Cdr) Praful Bakshi (Retd) alleging that the attack was a false flag operation orchestrated to divert public attention from mounting political pressure on the Narendra Modi government, including Congress protests demanding the Chief Election Commissioner’s resignation and the Arunachal Pradesh controversy. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) stating that the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel was a false flag operation.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) did not describe the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel as a false flag operation. In the original ANI video, he discussed the security situation in Kulgam, the presence of terrorist sleeper cells, and the need for better intelligence coordination and proactive security measures. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also confirmed on 12 November 2026 that the viral video was digitally altered and falsely attributed remarks to him. AI detection tools, Hive and Hiya, also indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating it.
We noticed the viral video carries an ANI watermark. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 11 November 2026, featuring the same footage of Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd), wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background. However, in the original video, he does not describe the Kulgam attack as a false flag operation or link it to the political developments mentioned in the viral clip. Instead, he expresses concern over the incident, noting that Kulgam has witnessed several such attacks in the past. He emphasises the need for a more proactive security approach, better intelligence coordination, and improved intelligence gathering in areas where terrorists operate and maintain sleeper cells. He also highlights the need to investigate how these groups receive logistical support, including accommodation, ammunition, and water.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, suggesting fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear that Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) was describing the Kulgam attack as a false-flag operation.
The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also debunked the claim in an X post dated 12 November 2026, stating that the video was digitally manipulated and falsely attributed remarks to Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd). It clarified that he did not make any such comments in the original video and had instead spoken about terrorist organisations and the need for offensive action and better coordination to prevent such attacks.
To sum up, this video of Wg Cdr Praful Bakshi (Retd) alleging that the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel was a false flag operation is digitally manipulated.

Mexican Prosecutor Who Helped C.I.A. Secretly Operate in His State Flees to the U.S.
The prosecutor, who faces arrest in Mexico after allowing C.I.A. officers into Chihuahua state, is under the protection of the U.S. government, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.
A Mexican former prosecutor facing arrest after allowing Central Intelligence Agency officers to operate in his state has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.
The former prosecutor, Guillermo Zuany Portillo, shepherded C.I.A. officers for more than six months beginning last year as they trained forces in his state, Chihuahua, joined those forces on counter-cartel missions and provided expertise during ground operations, a New York Times investigation revealed this week.
Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, had repeatedly said she did not want U.S. forces taking part in operations on the ground in Mexico, calling it a breach of sovereignty. Under the Trump administration, meanwhile, the C.I.A. sought to expand its activity in the country, and saw Mr. Zuany as a partner to help it do so quietly.
The C.I.A.’s cover in Chihuahua was blown when a car crash in April resulted in the deaths of two C.I.A. officers, leading to a national scandal and Mr. Zuany’s resignation. While an investigation determined the crash an accident, the Mexican authorities recently issued a warrant for Mr. Zuany’s arrest on charges related to his involvement with the agency.
Ms. Sheinbaum expressed fury at the C.I.A.’s presence during raids in Chihuahua and denied knowledge of the agency’s activities. On Wednesday, she said in a regular morning news conference that investigations into matter must continue.
“It’s worth finding out who this person is and how he worked with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said of Mr. Zuany.
