Happy World Kindness Day! Check out our kind photos of kindness to humans — and cats
Editor's note: Today, November 13, is World Kindness Day!
Kind-minded organizations from various countries came up with the idea and announced it on November 13, 1998. (And the date stuck.) The goal is kinda obvious — do something kind!
It doesn't matter if it's a modest action. One of the founding groups is the Small Kindness Movement of Japan. And no kind deed is too small to acknowledge. One year, the Japanese movement gave an award to a cabbie who pulled over to clear trash bags off the road lest they cause an accident. According to a report in the Christian Science Monitor, the cab driver humbly said it was "no big deal."
So on Friday, November 13, 2026, try a little kindness. To inspire you, we've talked to folks whose lives were changed by kindness — and asked the photojournalists of The Everyday Projects, a global network, to submit pictures that capture a kind moment. Animal lovers will be happy to see photos of kindness toward animals as well as an image of a support donkey — a reminder that animals can be kind to us humans, too.
Let's start with a simple yet profound story about a snack.
Back in 2004, Maymunah Yusuf Kadiri, a neuro-psychiatrist and mental health advocate in Nigeria, was a young doctor working in the emergency room at the Lagos State University Teaching hospital. One night sticks in her mind. It was chaos. There were accident victims everywhere. She recalls the blood, the cries and her own exhaustion.
"I hadn't eaten for over 12 hours, and my hands were shaking," says Kadiri, who was 28 at the time. "Then an elderly cleaner, one of those invisible heroes in hospitals, walked up to me with a small nylon bag." Inside was a biscuit and a sachet of water.
"Doctor," she said, "you need small strength to save people."
"It sounds simple, but I'll never forget it. That biscuit tasted like hope. Her kindness reminded me that healing isn't only about medicine, it's about humanity," says Kadiri. "As a psychiatrist, I've seen it over and over: People don't just heal in hospitals, they heal in human connections."
And while one isolated act of kindness may seem random, it can lead to much more.
Huguette Diakabana remembers when she had to drop out of school at age 10 — until a mysterious donor came to her rescue. Her family was planning to emigrate to the U.S. from Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of Congo) and couldn't afford school fees. They figured she'd make up the year later. She had a different idea: "I put on my previous year's uniform and sat outside under the street window of my would-be classroom." One day, the director invited her inside. Diakabana realized someone must have paid her school fees, but who?
Returning to the school years later, Diakabana discovered it was a school guard. She wanted to repay him. "He told me to help others when I could, so I launched a scholarship program," says Diakabana, who now lives in Switzerland and is co-founder of The Luminous Agency, which focuses on digital literacy.
Dr. Junaid Nabi, a physician-scientist who conducts research in health care technology at the RAND School in Washington, D.C. and is a senior fellow at the Aspen Institute, says he's come to realize that kindness isn't actually a trickle in the ocean. An act of kindness is more like dropping a stone that creates expanding ripples, he says.
"There are studies that illustrate how kindness spreads through social networks in measurable ways. When we are kind to someone, they don't just feel better — they become 25% more likely to help others."
One such investigation described how kindness can be contagious. It was sparked by reports of an outbreak of kindness on a cold December morning in 2012. A stranger picked up the tab for the coffee order of the next customer in the drive-through line at a Tim Hortons coffeehouse in Winnipeg, Canada. And that customer picked up the tab of the person behind him. In the end, 226 customers passed on this act of kindness.
The study authors, citing other examples of "pay it forward" kindness at fast food restaurants and their own experiments encouraging subjects to help others, write: "Why, in the absence of external sanctions and opportunities for reciprocation, do people help strangers? One possible explanation is that helping is driven by receiving or observing help. In other words, generosity towards strangers may be socially contagious."
Don't talk yourself out of it
It might sound contradictory, but researchers studying the psychology of altruism, kindness and giving have uncovered this curious paradox: Sometimes, people can be kind-hearted, have a genuine desire to help someone, but in spite of that, not give at all.
Marta Serra-Garcia, a professor of economics and strategy at the Rady School of Management in the University of California, San Diego, is one of the authors of the study Give Enough or Not at all.
"There's a growing body of work in economics and psychology trying to understand altruism. Altruism is a result of a feeling of empathy and the emotion of feeling warm and well when you help others. We know people are altruistic, but we're trying to understand when, why and how," she says.
The study, published in the September Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, revealed that people may prefer to give nothing rather than donate an amount they consider too small — even when those on the receiving end would welcome whatever they can get.
"It seems like an odd thing," Serra-Garcia says in an interview over a video call with NPR. "You're generous, but because you want to do the right thing, you might end up not giving at all, out of concern that your gift would be viewed as inappropriate or might even offend the other person."
In one experiment in the study, givers tended to overestimate the minimum amount recipients would consider acceptable.
"We tend to think there are givers and non-givers," says Serra-Garcia. "The people who give are the generous and kind ones, the non-givers are just not generous." But the study indicates otherwise.
"That perception of appropriateness makes them think, "I'd rather not give at all, although I'm a generous person," says Serra-Garcia.
Nature or nurture?
And where does kindness come from? Are you born with it? Or can you learn to be compassionate and empathetic?
Jeff R. Temple, a professor and psychologist with UTHealth Houston, says kindness is a central thread running through his studies on healthy relationships among adolescents and young adults.
"In our intervention work — including with the Fourth R program and other school-based curricula — we teach adolescents to practice perspective-taking, to express care even during disagreement and recognize the impact of their words and actions. These are essentially the behavioral expressions of kindness."
Such kids are less likely to bully others because they know what healthy relationships are like, he says.
A ripple effect
And let's not forget that kindness can change not only the life of the recipient of the kind deed but of the kind person, says Nabi, who offers this anecdote.
In the 2013 Savar building collapse in Bangladesh, more than 1,000 garment workers died and thousands were injured. Nabi arrived at the disaster site as a Red Cross volunteer, expecting to gain experience in trauma care. Instead, he says, the experience changed his psyche, teaching him about the nature of true kindness.
"In the midst of chaos, with bodies awaiting identification, kindness came down to being present during others' darkest moments," says Nabi. "I performed CPR on workers I knew wouldn't survive and when I couldn't save someone, I stayed by their side, holding their hand."
"Before Savar, I was mechanistic, rushing through clinical work like tasks," he recalls. "The image of workers who had embraced each other as concrete crushed them — that final act of human kindness in the face of death — shattered my callousness completely."
When he returned to the hospital, he listened to patients differently, giving them more of his time. He also urges doctors to volunteer for humanitarian causes to practice compassion.
"Kindness, I learned, is about showing up completely for another person's suffering," Navi reflects, "and letting that experience fundamentally change who you are."
So if you began reading this story with the thought that World Kindness Day is … a gimmick … it is a gimmick imbued with heart and hope.
It's a good reminder to practice kindness more, Dr. Kadiri says. "And here's the beautiful part: When someone receives kindness, they don't just feel better, they become better." They may be inspired to perform their own act of kindness. And that, she says, makes the world a kinder, better place too.
Your turn: Readers! Have you ever had a life-changing moment because of an act of kindness. Share your story with us by emailing globalhealth@npr.org. We'll consider all submissions for a follow-up story. Be sure to tell us how to contact you if we are interested in featuring your anecdote.
Special thanks to the photojournalists of The Everyday Projects, who shared their beautiful images of kind moments for this story.
Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, Southern India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times, The British Medical Journal, the BBC, The Guardian and other outlets. You can find her on X @kamal_t

In a Facebook video from a Sydney anti-immigration rally on Sunday, as a man dressed like a medieval knight watches on, One Nation’s lead upper house candidate, Stuart Bonds, launches into a speech against “mass” migration.
“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” he says.
“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we [are] going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”
In an apparent allusion to the “great replacement theory”, a far-right conspiracy theory that white westerners are being actively “replaced” by minority ethnic immigrants, he continued: “That’s the socialist plan, is to destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation.”
The comments sparked a wave of criticism, but the party has shown no signs of taking Bonds off the ticket for the 2027 New South Wales state election. One Nation did, however, dump one candidate this week: the Victorian branch disendorsed a lower-house candidate over an old social media post describing Hitler as the “GOAT”, an acronym for greatest of all time.
The rally was not a one-off. On a podcast released on Monday with the rally’s organiser, the Australian Lobby Group, Bonds appeared to double down on the remarks. He did not challenge host Scott Challen’s assertion that Labor governments were building “ethnic voting blocks with Middle Eastern and subcontinent people … to stack the numbers to entrench power for themselves”, instead responding: “Mate, and that’s why we’re going to get rid of all of the multicultural grants, right?”
On Wednesday, in an interview with ABC Upper Hunter, Bonds responded to questions about his comments by citing Australian Bureau of Statistics data that shows the proportion of Australians born overseas has trended upward since the end of the second world war, from 10% in 1945 to 32% in 2025. He did not mention that the proportion of Australians born overseas was at its highest – 32.4% – in 1891, the first year of available data.
Bonds said with the Australian birthrate beneath the 2.1 required to replace the population, “I would just like to know what people assume is going to happen.”
“Where are these people going to come from?” he said.
NSW Labor pounced on the rally comments immediately, with the state’s premier, Chris Minns, calling them “frankly outrageous and racist”. The government passed motions in both houses censuring Bonds, not yet a member.
The Coalition followed four days later. On Wednesday afternoon, the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said Bonds’ language was “clearly divisive”.
But she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement with One Nation after the March state election.
“We will not form a coalition with One Nation, [but] we’ll work with anyone post-election if we’re in a minority government,” she told reporters.
The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the party to go into a Coalition with One Nation. And with the Coalition consistently polling behind One Nation, that makes Bonds not a fringe candidate, but a potentially influential figure.
One Nation could ‘clean the deck’ in regions
The ABC’s former election analyst, Antony Green, said the remarks played straight into Labor’s hands.
“This will certainly be something the Labor party uses in all those multi-ethnic seats in Sydney,” he said – seats like those on the rural fringes of Sydney, which One Nation said it plans to target.
Indeed the deputy premier, Prue Car, who has Indian heritage and whose electorate of Londonderry is one of the seats in question, gave an impassioned critique of Bonds’ comments in question time on Tuesday.
“Who’s he [Bonds] talking about when he talks about this?” she said. “I tell you who he’s talking about – he’s talking about families like mine, and families that I represent.”
Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a director of polling group Redbridge, said that while the comments likely won’t play well in Sydney seats – including alienating moderate Liberal voters worried about the party going into Coalition with One Nation – “you might be able to get away with it in certain parts of NSW”.
And Bonds, a former coalminer, has made his base in the Hunter.
Samaras said One Nation could “clean the deck” in the regions, including Labor-held seats in the Hunter, and “pretty much anything else the Coalition hasn’t got bolted down to the ground”.
The NSW One Nation leader, Mike Newman, who in September said he “made a mistake” when he told a Sydney rally he wanted to stop abortions, did not respond directly when asked if he agreed with Bonds’ comments or if he would rein in his first-placed upper house candidate.
“What I will say is that what Stuart Bonds is a patriotic Aussie. He’s a coalminer. He has very, very strong views,” he said on Tuesday.
Newman, who previously rejected claims that One Nation was racist, said on Tuesday: “What we want to do is … protect Australian values, and that is the fundamental thing that Stuart Bonds is pushing for. It’s about assimilation.”
The NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, whose parents immigrated to Australia from India in the 1970s, told the ABC that Bonds’ comments were not grounded in reality.
“I think he’s saying that there is a deliberate conspiracy to use migrants to replace the way he puts it, native-born Australians for political reasons,” Mookhey said.
The quota for election to the upper house is 4.5%, making Bonds all but guaranteed to be elected, with One Nation polling in the high 20s and low 30s in recent months.
Green expects the party to pick up four or five seats in the upper house; so far it has only named three candidates: Newman, Bonds and Jeff Bacon, a firearms manufacturer who is second on the upper house ticket.
But unlike Victoria, NSW has optional preferential voting, which means when that state goes to the polls in March, lower house preference flows aren’t guaranteed.
But Bonds has downplayed whether he may have jeopardised a future preference deal with the Coalition.
“If the Coalition have a problem with facts, the same as the Labor party, then maybe it will,” he told the ABC.
“But I’m not here to impress the Coalition.”

New York—Chaos erupted at airports across the United States after a communications failure triggered a rare nationwide grounding of departing flights, stranding thousands of passengers and throwing travel plans into disarray.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered the extraordinary shutdown on Friday, citing a telecommunications outage affecting regional air traffic control centres across the country. The restrictions were lifted after a few hours, allowing flight operations to gradually resume.
It was only the second nationwide grounding of US flights since the September 11, 2001 attacks, underscoring the seriousness of the disruption.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the shutdown was a precautionary measure and that there was no immediate evidence of a deliberate attack.
“This isn’t another 9/11,” Mullin told reporters, adding that investigators had found no indication of a “nefarious attack”.
“It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he said, assuring the public that passengers and their loved ones were safe.
But the reassurance did little to ease the frustration of travellers caught in the unprecedented disruption.
600 FLIGHTS DIVERTED
The scale of the disruption was substantial. According to aviation analytics company Cirium, at least 600 flights had been diverted by Friday evening.
Of these, 496 were redirected to their original departure airports, while another 104 were sent to alternative airports.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to depart US airports after 4 pm Eastern time, raising fears of widespread cancellations and knock-on delays.
Chicago O’Hare, Denver International, Dallas-Fort Worth and Ronald Reagan Washington National airports were among those receiving diverted aircraft.
Although the nationwide grounding was lifted, airlines warned that disruption could continue as aircraft and flight crews were repositioned.
PASSENGERS LEFT IN LIMBO
At New York’s John F Kennedy International Airport, Riley Alexis Holmes saw her plans to reach Oregon for her brother’s musical closing night collapse after her flight was cancelled following nearly two hours of delay.
“I called my mom and cried, and I’m just sitting here waiting for information,” she said.
At Chicago O’Hare, passengers stared at departure screens displaying widespread delays, desperately calling relatives and debating whether to book hotel rooms or find alternative transport.
Amber McQuilkin, a 27-year-old software engineer from Seattle, feared missing a trip to New York for the League of Legends world finals. Her friends had already reached the destination.
“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” she said, adding that she had even considered abandoning her flight and driving instead.
Another traveller, Austin Curtis, and his wife were left stranded during a layover in Chicago while travelling to Denver for a friend’s baby shower. They had boarded their connecting flight when passengers were instructed to disembark.
With their two young children being looked after at home, the couple faced the prospect of spending the weekend in Chicago.
OUTDATED TECHNOLOGY UNDER SCRUTINY
The FAA attributed the shutdown to communications problems affecting all 22 regional air traffic control centres responsible for directing aircraft between airports.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the agency was investigating the failure, including whether it had any connection to the nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system designed to help identify problems and reroute aircraft.
Officials said the AI system operates from a location near Washington and provides recommendations to air traffic control centres.
The incident has nevertheless renewed scrutiny of America’s ageing aviation infrastructure.
The government has been undertaking a major overhaul of air traffic control technology after Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Old copper wiring is being replaced with fibre-optic lines, while outdated radio systems are gradually being upgraded.
However, officials say the modernisation remains incomplete, with another $30 billion potentially required to finish the work.
Aviation safety expert and former United Airlines pilot Steve Arroyo said Friday’s disruption resembled a communications failure that affected hundreds of flights across the northeastern United States in September, but on a vastly larger scale.
Without reliable communication between aircraft and controllers, he said, grounding flights was the safest option.
Friday’s shutdown was different from the restrictions imposed after September 11, when aircraft were ordered to land immediately. This time, planes were not instructed to make emergency landings.
In an extraordinary contrast, SpaceX managed to launch its Starship rocket from Texas on Friday despite the nationwide aviation disruption.
For millions of American travellers, however, the immediate concern was far less spectacular: getting home, reaching their destinations or finding out when their flights would finally take off.
While officials ruled out an immediate security threat, the episode exposed the vulnerability of a modern aviation network still dependent on ageing communications infrastructure.

Violent attacks on critics of China in Taiwan raise concern over transnational repression
Comedian Huang Yi-hao was involved in a car accident in September, but it turned out to be a deliberate attack
TAIPEI, Taiwan -- In September, comedian Huang Yi-hao was involved in a car accident, something that could happen to anyone. But one thing stood out: the men in the other car were unusually polite, and even offered to cover his medical bills and the damage to his car.
Huang later received a call from Taiwanese police telling him it wasn't an ordinary accident.
Taipei prosecutors in October charged five men for deliberately attempting to injure Huang in a case that has drawn attention across Taiwan. Authorities say it is part of a growing trend where operatives paid by China harass or attack people on the self-ruled island who are seen as critical of the government in Beijing.
“In the beginning, it was verbal harassment, then it morphed to pouring paint and property damage ... to the level of causing a fake car accident," Chiu Shao-Chou, the commissioner of Taiwan's Criminal investigation Bureau, said. "There's a trend of increasing severity, and that's something we have to take seriously.”
Taiwan is a democratic island claimed by Beijing, which hasn't ruled out using force to annex it. Taiwanese authorities have long worried about Chinese infiltration attempts, including spy plots targeting senior military officials and the president's bodyguards, disinformation schemes during elections or the use of cultural exchanges as a way to spread Communist Party ideology.
China's tactics to harass, spy on or even harm dissidents abroad have come to light in recent years. In 2023, authorities in New York made arrests in connection with secret police stations set up on behalf of the Chinese government to surveil Chinese dissidents.
Huang said the car attack might have been linked to his performance at the end of last year, in which he criticized Chinese President Xi Jinping and compared him to Winnie the Pooh. Huang is a comedian trained in the xiangsheng tradition, a form of Chinese comedic dialogue that relies heavily on wordplay and rhymes.
Prosecutors say the five men accepted about 450,000 New Taiwan dollars ($13,900) from someone from China who went by the alias “K” and wanted them to injure Huang seriously enough that he could no longer perform.
Huang said he had stopped collaborating with other comedians and believes his criticism of Xi is the reason. He said he knows of other comedians who had performances canceled in China and Taiwan because they had collaborated with him. He has no plans of taking his shows to China.
His solo shows, however, have sold out since the attack.
“The Communist Party is very childish. Your country’s leader was criticized by a comedian and as a result, you give such an aggressive response?” Huang said.
Hong Kong gangsters have been accused of plotting to assault Japanese political commentator Akio Yaita in what Taiwanese prosecutors called another instance of “transnational repression."
According to an October statement from prosecutors, five Hong Kong triad members, paid by a fellow gangster, entered Taiwan in early July and inspected the area around the hotel where Yaita was expected to give a speech. But before the attack, two withdrew, and the pair, alongside another member, left Taiwan, the statement said.
One of the men was offered 100,000 Hong Kong dollars ($12,750) to assault Yaita, the prosecutors said. He punched the commentator in the face and was later arrested, while another, who acted as a lookout, fled Taiwan.
Yaita, a former reporter in Beijing who now leads a think tank in Taiwan, believes the assault was linked to his remarks, including his criticism of the Chinese government’s policies.
“By violently attacking me, they hope to silence others who criticize China, including myself,” he said, adding that he wouldn't change his views.
The man who was arrested pleaded guilty on Tuesday and will be sentenced later, Taiwan's Central News Agency reported.
Matt Brazil, a fellow at The Jamestown Foundation in Washington, D.C., said the recent attacks represented a “big step beyond" sending navy ships and warplanes around the island. He said anyone in Taiwan who speaks out against Xi and the Chinese Communist Party could be a target.
“(It) shows that Beijing may be turning toward a more militant stance in acting against its critics (in Taiwan). If successful, the party may expand such tactics elsewhere,” he said.
Taiwan's police say the threat of transnational repression isn't limited to Taiwan. They said they are in close coordination with U.S. authorities about similar cases that involve Taiwanese nationals overseas.
In October, U.S. authorities arrested a woman in Los Angeles for allegedly conducting surveillance on the son of Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te on behalf of the Chinese government.
“Taiwan is a democratic and pluralistic society, but with these types of actions which harm our national security, the investigation of this is of the highest importance,” Chiu, the police commissioner, said. He added that police treat the cases as national-level threats and coordinate with immigration authorities, the coast guard and other government agencies.
Catching the criminals before they leave Taiwan is a top priority, he said, adding that police would also investigate Taiwanese collaborators.
The island's Mainland Affairs Council, which handles relations with China, said it would seek to strengthen the Anti-Infiltration Act — a law designed to punish such acts.
In response to the attack on Yaita, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office said in July that the Hong Kong man who punched Yaita had acted out of “righteous indignation” and that it was an ordinary public security incident.

On Nov. 10, the U.S. House of Representatives voted on articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has been the face of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran that began in February.
The impeachment effort failed in a 211-204 vote, which many Democrats blamed on 11 of their fellow party members who were absent from the voting chamber.
The 11 absent Democrats were Reps. Julia Brownley, Melanie Stansbury, Brittany Pettersen, Laura Gillen, Nancy Pelosi, Haley Stevens, Marilyn Strickland, Frederica Wilson, Jonathan Jackson, Steven Horsford and J. Luis Correa.
Social media users claimed some of those 11 missed the vote because they were attending an event related to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a powerful pro-Israel lobbying group.
The event in question was reportedly hosted by Elect Democrat Women. According to the nonprofit OpenSecrets, the top donor to the Elect Democrat Women-affiliated super PAC, EDW Action Fund, was the United Democracy Project — a super PAC affiliate of AIPAC.
Drop Site News, a nonprofit investigative news outlet, reportedly obtained an RSVP list of the event showing that three of the 11 Democrats who missed the vote were present at the event: Brownley, of California, Stansbury, of New Mexico, and Pettersen, of Colorado. As of this writing, the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal how it sourced the list.
Two of the representatives, Brownley and Pettersen, reportedly acknowledged attending the Elect Democratic Women event. However, none of them had responded to our requests for comment by the time of publication. Until we hear directly from the representatives' offices or primary evidence confirming their attendance emerges, we've left this claim unrated.
On Nov. 11, USA Today reporter Zach Schermele posted that Brownley told him she "left last night's Elect Democratic Women event for the Hegseth vote with plenty of time to spare" and that "when the traffic jam made it clear she might not make it in time, she and other lawmakers started texting each other." He reported that Brownley, 74, then got out of her car and started running, missing the vote by "seconds" (archived).
According to Denver NBC affiliate KUSA, Pettersen acknowledged she attended the event, saying in a statement, "Last night, I was late to the floor and there is no excuse for that. I was at an Electing Democratic Women event."
Stansbury posted a video on Nov. 11 apologizing for her absence, saying, "I know I should've been there at that moment." She blamed rush-hour traffic on Independence Avenue for her absence. She did not mention the EDW event, though her comments were flooded with users accusing her of attending it.
Because the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal where it sourced the list, we are unable to rate this claim. We can, however, break down Drop Site News' findings and any other publicly available information.
The document Drop Site News reportedly obtained also included a "Run of Show" listing the event's schedule, which read:
Run of Show:
- 4:30 pm: Event begins.
  - Mix and mingle
- 5:00 pm: EDW Chairwoman Lois Frankel to give opening remarks.
  - Thank everyone for attending, supporting EDW, and our historic wins.
- 5:10 pm: Acknowledge all new members in attendance and have them answer questions.
- 5:30 pm: Guests resume mingling.
- 6:00 pm: Event ends.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., publicly posted the voting schedule on Nov. 10, which indicated the vote on the impeachment articles he introduced would take place at 5:30 p.m. (archived).
According to Drop Site's reporting, the event took place at Goldfinch Social, a venue in Washington, D.C., about 2 miles from the Capitol.

Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack

Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.
In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental hospital. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental hospital.
Fact: The video is clipped out of context. RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat was recounting an incident from the 1930s where a person named Ibrahim defended the RSS against an attempt to ban it. While making this argument, Ibrahim had said that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. Bhagwat was quoting Ibrahim’s statement, not remarking himself. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a Facebook post (archived) by The Economic Times, dated 09 November 2026, featuring a longer version of the same video. Upon reviewing the video, we found that Mohan Bhagwat was not making the statement himself but was quoting a person named Ibrahim. Referring to an incident from the 1930s, Bhagwat said that when the Central Provinces Assembly first attempted to ban the RSS, there were no volunteers or supporters of the RSS’s ideology to defend it. In this context, he recounted that a person named Ibrahim defended the RSS by saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. Ibrahim further stated that he knew Dr Hedgewar, that he was not insane but a good man, and therefore, the RSS could not be communal.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here, and here) covering the statement made by Mohan Bhagwat on 09 November 2026, while inaugurating the newly constructed auditorium at the renovated headquarters of Nagpur Nagarik Sahakari Bank Limited in Nagpur.
We also found a video of the event, which was livestreamed on 09 November 2026 on the Facebook account of Nagpur Nagarik Sahakari Bank Ltd. In the approximately 1-hour-and-36-minute-long video, we found the segment corresponding to the viral clip at around 1:16:00.
During this segment, Mohan Bhagwat said, “The RSS, which was formed 100 years ago, is being discussed everywhere. That’s why so many books are being published now. I held an intellectual class here in Nagpur, where I explained that when the first attempt to ban the RSS was made in the Central Provinces Assembly in the 1930s, none of the RSS volunteers came forward to defend the RSS or support its ideology.”
He further said, “There was a Mr Ibrahim who spoke in favour of the RSS. He said that the RSS should not be banned and that it was not communal. But how did he make this argument? He said that those who say India is a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. This is my opinion, and I know Dr Hedgewar. He is not insane; he is a good man, and therefore, the RSS cannot be communal. So, that was in the 1930s. Five or seven years had passed since the RSS was founded. Everyone knew about the RSS, but Dr Hedgewar knew“
We also found that Jagran reported that a book on the lives of former RSS pracharaks was released during the event. Bhagwat discussed the lives of former RSS pracharaks and recounted an incident from the 1930s in this context. This confirms that the viral clip presents Bhagwat’s statement without the necessary context. In the original video, Bhagwat was quoting a person named Ibrahim, who had said that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. The remark was made by Ibrahim, not Bhagwat.
To sum up, this video shows Mohan Bhagwat quoting Ibrahim’s remark about sending those who call India a Hindu nation to a mental asylum.

Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata has introduced a two-part plan for the country’s oldest and largest charity group: continue giving, but measure it by the results, and keep supporting Tata Sons’ investments in important national projects. Speaking at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi on Saturday, the 70-year-old Tata Trusts chairman said the charitable institutions would have two distinct but complementary roles. “One part is the direct philanthropy, which we do. So building institutions, giving grants to other NGOs, or alleviating hardships directly with beneficiaries. The second is through Tata Sons, to invest and nurture projects of national importance,” said Noel. “We are, from a trust perspective, we stand 100% behind Tata Sons’ efforts to build these projects and invest in projects of national importance,” he said, noting that this is part of the institution. “And while continuing the philanthropy work, and basically we end up with a balance between some direct philanthropy, which happens every year, and some money going towards investment in national projects.” Noel said these investments were not necessarily detached from commercial considerations. “They are projects which have a longer gestation period. They might have a little more risk than a normal project,” he said. He added that the expectation was that such ventures, once incubated, would eventually become public companies and prosper in the marketplace. Tata Group’s approach is not new. The Group's founder, Jamsetji Tata, donated half his wealth to educational charities and backed pioneering ventures that helped build India’s industrial and infrastructure capabilities in steel, hydroelectric power, textiles and truck manufacturing. “I had to see what the founders' intentions were. What did they leave? Because they were really pioneers in philanthropy, let’s say, 130 years ago,” Noel said. “They could have left their money to the salary, to their cousins. Instead, they decided, no, we leave our shares and our money to these two trusts… This is embedded in the DNA of the group. And I think this will continue,” he added. Their instructions, according to Noel, were clear: “We want you to create institutions,” “We want you to provide relief to people in need, communities in need” and “We want you to advance knowledge.” These principles, Tata said, would remain his guiding light in setting the Trusts’ priorities and future programmes. Noel said direct charity work will focus more on clear results than on how much money is spent. Reviewing current programmes after he became chairman in October 2024 helped him see the importance of measuring the real impact of efforts, Tata said. “I began to see that possibly impact was more important than expenditure,” he added. The comments echo his message in the Tata Trusts’ 2025-26 annual report, which signalled that philanthropy will now be judged by results, not cheque size. “It is no longer enough to ask how much we have contributed,” Noel wrote in his letter. “We must ask what difference that contribution has made, and whether that difference will endure.” He added a line that appeared aimed at the country’s wealthy donors: “Trying to become the biggest before becoming the best rarely ends well.” The letter sets out three changes. The Trusts will create new institutions that can last as public resources, rather than only supporting existing ones. They plan a network of 40 to 50 non-profit general hospitals, where patients who can pay help cover the cost of care for those who cannot. They are also open to partnering with other philanthropies on big projects, a notable shift for a group behind landmark institutions such as IISc, TIFR and Tata Memorial. The Trusts paid out ₹1,556 crore (about $167 million) during the year. Institutions and programmes received ₹1,353 crore, while individuals in need received ₹203 crore, mostly for cancer treatment and student scholarships. Rural livelihoods took the largest share at ₹458 crore, followed by education ( ₹270 crore), cancer care ( ₹178 crore) and long-term support to institutions ( ₹169 crore). Taken together, health is the biggest theme: cancer care, healthcare and medical grants to individuals add up to about ₹428 crore, or 27% of the total. From postcards to texts, the different ways a manager gets the sack - Pulis
- Published
When you hear about a manager parting company with a club, he has usually either been sacked or has resigned, but there are actually lots of different ways you can leave.
Over the years I spent working at every level of the game in England, from the bottom to the top, I have witnessed and been involved in many break-ups.
Some are smooth but others are far more fractious and don't happen face-to-face. I've witnessed managers being sacked over the phone or by text, or hearing they are losing their job by word of mouth.
One of the most soul-destroying times for a manager is when speculation is rife regarding not only your imminent sacking, but also about who is going to replace you.
During my career, I've known certain individuals who actually put their names forward for jobs before a manager is even sacked. Some go to the club involved through agents, some directly to the owners themselves.
Many managers are sounded out before eventually being appointed and another policy which has become popular with clubs is to drop names out to the press about possible replacements, to see the supporters' reactions to the names in the frame.
For the manager who is still in place, and whose stress levels are through the roof, it is devastating... but it is just another part of the job that you have to handle.
I've experienced that situation myself, in a scenario which went on for many months. Your confidence, not only in yourself but also in the club's hierarchy, takes another massive knock.
When it happened to me, I'd heard about the club's intentions from people in the media at quite an early stage and also worked out where the new manager would be coming from, but I had to bite my lip - myself and my staff were under contract, so we had to just carry on.
We kept pulling results out of the bag which delayed the inevitable, but eventually I knew my time was up.
Sacked on the drive up for pre-season
When they are getting treated this way, you can hardly blame managers for sometimes wanting to stick two fingers up to the people in charge.
One story comes to mind of a manager I know who was relieved of his duties by being placed on gardening leave while the club found a way to release him permanently.
During that time, and while he was still getting paid, the manager decided to go on holiday somewhere hot with his family. After watching his old team lose on TV in the sunshine, he sent a postcard to his chairman, which simply said 'wish you were here!'.
When he got home, he was sacked - but I bet he was still glad he did it!
Sadly, most managers don't get that kind of satisfaction - and often you don't even get a chance to say a proper goodbye to the players and staff you have worked closely with for many months or years.
My first spell at Stoke ended when I was driving up the motorway from my home in Bournemouth for the first day of pre-season in the summer of 2005.
I'd had a pretty good idea of what might happen since the end of the previous season but, over the next few weeks, the club's Icelandic owners did not say a word - until then.
I didn't have a problem with the decision, by the way. They were nice people and my view has always been 'if you don't want me, you don't want me'.
Anyway, I'd already been driving for four hours and, just as I got to the junction that would take me to the ground, my phone rang. It was the chairman, who told me he'd been meaning to call.
I was told I was no longer the manager, but also that I could not enter the stadium at any cost - I soon understood the urgency of the situation because it turned out the new manager had already arrived there. I had to just turn the car around, and head back home.
That kind of thing can happen to any manager, and you learn to be ready for it.
'Every manager needs to think about their cardboard box'
I always remember playing at Swansea in one of my early games in my first job with Bournemouth, and their manager Frank Burrows inviting me into his office afterwards.
Frank, who sadly passed away in 2021, was a wonderful man and also a superb old-school manager who was always happy to offer advice to younger coaches and share his experiences.
We were having a drink and I noticed he had this big empty cardboard box next to his desk. I asked him what it was for, and he said it was to hold all his belongings - from his files on players to his family photographs - that were in his office.
"All the important stuff I'd like to keep is on the top of my desk," Frank said. "And every time I lose my job, because that time always comes, I can just sweep it into the box and off I go again. That box has travelled around the football world with me."
That always stuck with me. Management is such a precarious occupation that every manager has to think about that box, even if they don't have it sitting next to their desk every day!
It was not long afterwards that I found out what it was like to be sacked for the first time.
I still had a year left on my contract with Bournemouth but the chairmanship of the club changed and, in the summer of 1994, I was out.
It was hard enough to go from doing almost everything at the club to doing nothing, not even going in for pre-season training - but, because it was my hometown club, I also had to come to terms with listening to stories of my children being teased about my exit at school.
I also had my mortgage and my family to look after and unfortunately Bournemouth were not very helpful with the money they owed me.
It's a lot to think about, when you have just been thrown out into the real world, especially when it's a world you have no experience in or any other qualifications to fall back on. I was lucky enough to get another chance in management, but not every young manager does.
Fortunately, I've not always left clubs on bad terms, either. I've already mentioned a few difficult separations, but I've had some happier endings too.
Finishing as friends
I've talked a lot in these columns about my affection for Peter Coates and his wonderful family. As well as owning Stoke City, they are a special group of people who have been unbelievably successful in their own ways, but they have never lost that human touch.
When the time came for me to part company with the club in 2013, they did so in a proper manner - Peter and John, his son and now chairman, were dead straight with me about wanting to go in a different direction, and made a difficult situation into a respectful parting of the ways.
I spent almost 10 years at Stoke over two spells but, while I was only at Middlesbrough for 18 months, it was a similar story with their owner and chairman Steve Gibson.
Steve has spent his entire life looking out for Boro but his commitment to his club goes far beyond being a lifetime supporter. He cares deeply for the people of that area and has devoted so much of his hard-earned cash towards making Boro a success.
I loved my time there because of the warmth of Steve and his family, and beyond. The area reminded me so much of south Wales, where the community was cherished and people, especially at the club, could not do enough for you.
After the last game of the 2018-19 season I was completely shot, and frustrated that we had not reached the Championship play-offs. My drive home that night was long and lonely but I felt worn out.
Once the dust had settled on that season, Steve and I met up in London. Our discussions were honest and open but my contract was up and we both agreed it was a good time for me to leave - I wanted it to end on good terms, and we certainly did that.
After dinner we had a fair few drinks and it ended up being a very, very late night. We arranged to have breakfast the following morning but I told him I have always been an early riser so, by 6am, I was up and on my way to the station to get back home.
My wife had just picked me up in Bournemouth at just after 8am when Steve rang to ask if I was down for breakfast yet - and he didn't believe me when I said no, I am back home.
I missed breakfast, but we remained good friends. Steve is a class act and I always hold Boro up as a club that deserves to be successful because of the attitude, commitment and honesty of everyone we came across.
My family still talk about how much they loved going there, and were genuinely disappointed when I left - something that doesn't apply to all my former clubs, obviously!
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

At St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, Keralam, faith and fitness go hand in hand. An open gym on the church premises is drawing parishioners of all ages to stretch, sweat and stay fit. The unusual initiative is adding a healthy new dimension to church life.
Set up in a corner of the church campus, the facility has quickly become a meeting point for fitness enthusiasts. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass. The altar boys, numbering around 60, are among its regular users. Parents also bring their young children, while senior citizens use the basic equipment to stay active.
Roots in fitness routine of vicar
The initiative has its roots in the personal fitness routine of the church’s vicar, Fr. Frederick Eluvathingal, 69. A footballer and basketball player during his student days, he has never allowed age or a demanding schedule to come in the way of exercise.
“I have been working out for the past 51 years, ever since my days at the Papal Seminary in Pune,” he says. His fitness routine continued during his higher studies in Rome and Jerusalem and his church assignments in Australia.
When he arrived at Kuriachira more than a year ago, he began looking for a suitable space to continue his regular exercises, including push-ups and pull-ups. Parallel bars were installed first, followed by a basketball hoop. The idea gradually grew into a community gym.
“I wanted to create a space where people could develop the habit of working out. We generally do not have a strong workout culture. If people can fit in some basic exercise when they come to church, they may gradually make fitness part of their lives,” he says.
The need is particularly pressing at a time when lifestyle diseases and obesity are on the rise. The initiative also seeks to draw more youngsters into church activities and channel their energy into constructive pursuits.
The parish welcomed the proposal, and a space around a well on the church premises was chosen for the facility. The limited space available in Kuriachira meant that the gym had to be modest, but the response has been encouraging.
“Within a week of starting the gym, quite a few people began coming here. If the demand grows, we will have to think about expanding the facility,” says P.R. Wilson, one of the church trustees.
For regular user John Vazhappilly, a real estate broker who lives nearby, the gym has come as a timely help. “I have been coming here every evening for the past week. After an accident and surgery, the muscles in my leg became weak. I want to strengthen them. This is a comfortable place to exercise, with fresh air and an open campus,” he says.
‘A form of spiritual service’
The church sees the initiative as more than a fitness facility. “We want to groom a healthy generation. Many people suffer from lifestyle diseases, while youngsters often turn to private fitness centres. We felt that providing basic facilities here would benefit the community. Spirituality is also about nurturing a healthy mind and body. We consider this a form of spiritual service,” says assistant vicar Fr. Jees Akkara.
For Fr. Eluvathingal, there is another purpose. “Youngsters rarely come to church or participate in its activities these days. This is also an opportunity to bring more of them into the church community,” he says.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced the ground stop on X, citing a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Duffy promised updates as more information is known and said FAA staff were troubleshooting the problem.
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. “This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights,” Mullin said. “There’s no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us.”
Mullin said the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis.
This is only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. The first, and most memorable, came during the attacks of September 11, 2001, when the FAA stopped all civilian departures nationwide and subsequently ordered all airborne aircraft to land. Commercial flights did not take off again until September 13. Flights were also grounded for less than two hours the morning of January 11, 2023, after its Notice to Air Missions system suffered an outage.
Unfortunately for travelers, based on what is known so far, this is likely to be a lengthy ground stop. Airlines have already canceled flights scheduled to leave later Friday, and American Airlines warned that disruptions are expected for the rest of the day. “This is going to take some time,” Mullin said. “Flights are accounted for, and there should be no fear to the public at all.”

FAA issues nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," which is currently under investigation, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Friday afternoon, the FAA said in a post on X that there has been a "temporary telecommunications outage."
"Out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis," the post reads.
The outage hasn't been linked to a threat or attack, said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
"There is no indication, and we had no reason to believe as of right now that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin told reporters at the White House. "There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones."
The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.
That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.
The telecommunication issue doesn't extend to the entire U.S., Mullin said. Without naming the regions in question, he stated, "there's two areas inside the United States that are still able to communicate just fine."
Mullin also said that other countries' aviation systems don't seem to be affected by the FAA outage.
The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.
"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.
Passengers stranded
The nationwide ground stop has caused chaos in airports and headaches for travelers — many of whom are already too familiar with flight delays and cancelations during the holiday season.
At Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Regina Harling said she waited hours — long past when her flight was supposed to depart — before she learned of the nationwide grounding by checking the news on her phone.
"There's still a sign right in front of me that says we're boarding in 16 minutes," she said.
Harling needed to travel last minute to San Diego for a family emergency. Stuck at the airport, she's thinking about how soon she can make it to her family, but she's not optimistic.
"I was just thinking to myself that it always feels like it's getting harder to travel than it used to be," she said.
This is a developing story.

Eight Army personnel were injured after a military truck carrying 14 jawans overturned after hitting a roadside tree in Telangana’s Rangareddy district on Friday morning, police said.
The incident happened at Allawada village in Chevella mandal, about 50 km from Hyderabad, at around 8 am.
“The military truck carrying 14 jawans from the Golconda Army camp left for Shabad at around 6.30 am, as part of an army training exercise. A trainee driver, who was driving the vehicle, lost control over the steering and hit the median. The truck later rammed into a roadside tree and overturned,” Chevella assistant commissioner of police B Kishan told reporters.
On receiving the information, the Chevella police rushed to the spot and launched rescue operations. “Eight Army personnel were injured and the others managed to escape,” the ACP said, adding that the injured jawans were taken to the Army hospital in Golconda.
He said no complaint had been received from the Army authorities so far and, hence, no case had been registered yet.
Further details regarding the circumstances leading to the accident were not available.

Two Celebrity Cases Put a Spotlight on British Courts’ Gag Orders
Russell Brand and the TV personality David Walliams both persuaded courts to suppress misconduct allegations against them. Some say the libel laws need to change.
Two recent cases have brought new attention to the ways that British laws can allow the wealthy and powerful to silence their critics.
The first was the rape and sexual assault trial of the comedian Russell Brand. Before his conviction last week, Mr. Brand had obtained an injunction prohibiting another accuser from telling almost anyone — including the police, her family and most doctors — about her claims that he assaulted her. (Mr. Brand has denied her allegations.) That injunction, first revealed by Dan Neidle, a tax lawyer and free-expression activist, apparently remains in force.
In the second instance, two British news organizations were temporarily blocked from reporting allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams, a television personality and author of children’s books, before a judge declined to make the injunction permanent. The Guardian newspaper and ITV News, a British broadcaster, published investigations last week into the allegations, which Mr. Walliams denies.
Though both men now face public scrutiny, the revelations of how they used court injunctions — essentially gag orders — to protect their reputations have provoked no shortage of public and political outrage. Judges in other cases have issued “super injunctions,” which prohibit publishing any information even about the injunction itself.
“What will the government do to prevent these abuses of process, and stop the abusive injunctions and super injunctions which stop scrutiny, accountability and the work of the free press?” Nick Timothy, the shadow justice minister, asked in Parliament on Tuesday.
The British government is now “looking at what we can do,” Alex Davies-Jones, the government minister responsible for victims of crime and violence against women and girls, said in response.

Russia Revives Demand That NATO Retrench to Secure Ukraine Deal
The hard-line position of Russian officials in closed-door negotiations about ending the war thrusts European security into the heart of the talks.
Two months before Russia invaded Ukraine in early 2022, it issued a series of far-reaching demands, including that NATO pull its troops back to positions they held in 1997, before the Western alliance expanded toward Russia’s borders.
Now, in closed-door negotiations with President Trump’s envoys this week about how to end the war in Ukraine, the Russians have revived that stance — in some cases word for word — in an effort to attain a larger victory after five years and hundreds of thousands of deaths.
Moscow’s unyielding position was laid out in a paper that Russian officials circulated this week, according to a copy obtained by The New York Times from a person involved in the talks.
The paper, whose authenticity was confirmed by another person with knowledge of the negotiations, shows that President Vladimir V. Putin has scarcely budged on his core objectives after more than 20 months of diplomacy by the Trump administration to end the conflict.
Russia’s demands that NATO pull back forces from its eastern flank in Poland and the Baltics thrust the question of European security into the heart of the negotiations over Ukraine. And they detail the objective behind Mr. Putin’s public statements. The Russian leader has continually insisted that what he calls the “root causes” of the war — Russia’s wide-ranging grievances with both NATO and Ukraine — be addressed before he stops fighting.
The document also underscores how the economic inducements that Mr. Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have offered Mr. Putin have yet to secure concessions from Moscow. Michael Mann, who is set to begin shooting the long-awaited “Heat 2” in January, is in a legal dispute with New Regency as he seeks to reclaim the copyright to his screenplay for the original film.
New Regency produced “Heat,” released in 1995. The company filed a lawsuit on Friday arguing that it still owns the copyright to the original screenplay.
Earlier this year, Mann’s lawyers sent termination notices invoking the right to reclaim the copyright. New Regency argues that the screenplay was a “work made for hire,” and is thus ineligible for copyright termination.
New Regency argues that Mann’s termination action clouds its ownership of the original “Heat,” and is seeking a declaration that the termination notices are void.
Mann’s lawyers intend to fight the lawsuit “vigorously,” his reps said in a statement.
“We will vigorously defend this action and are confident that the courts will vindicate Michael Mann’s statutory rights under the Copyright Act,” a spokesperson said. “This filing has to do with original and personal writing Michael Mann did on multiple screenplays during the 1980s and which evolved into the iconic 1995 film ‘Heat’ that Mann wrote, produced and directed. After 40 years Michael Mann is exercising the right of authors to reclaim their work and in this case Michael Mann’s original creation.”
Mann developed the characters and the story that would become “Heat” over two decades, beginning in the 1970s. According to the lawsuit, Warner Bros. acquired the rights to the “Heat” screenplay in 1994 in a deal with Mann’s loan-out company. The suit alleges that deal was explicitly a “work made for hire” agreement — not an assignment of rights — and that therefore it cannot be terminated.
Authors are allowed to terminate assignments of rights after 35 years under the Copyright Act.
According to the suit, Mann’s lawyers initially told New Regency that Mann had assigned his rights to his loan-out companies in 1988, and was thus seeking to terminate that agreement. New Regency sought a copy of that agreement, and was told it was an oral agreement, the suit states.
“The Oral Assignment on which the First Termination Notice is based supposedly derives from an oral agreement that Mann allegedly made with himself, in which Mann, like a Shakespearean actor playing multiple parts, simultaneously spoke on his own individual behalf, as well as on behalf of MMCo. and ZZY,” the lawsuit states.
Two subsequent termination notices were submitted cited other agreements, both of which New Regency claims are also invalid.
Warner Bros. was originally set to produce “Heat 2,” but backed out of the project last year. Amazon MGM Studios has since acquired the film. Both Mann and New Regency have done deals with Amazon that account for the copyright dispute, with Mann assigning any rights he may reclaim to Amazon, according to the complaint.
In other words, however the dispute comes out, “Heat 2” should be unaffected.
	“For clarification, this is unrelated to production of Heat 2 which will begin shooting on January 19,” Mann’s rep said in a statement.

- The claim that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth awarded a commendation medal to a different person than the soldier who reprimanded his group Nov. 11 at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is unfounded.
- The rumor stems from social media users comparing a blurry image of one side of the soldier's face with a sharper frame from a video showing the other side of the soldier's face. Aside from the apparent asymmetricality, no evidence has been offered that the images — which differ greatly in angle, lighting and distance — show different men.
- A Pentagon spokesperson told Snopes, "As shown in the photos, Secretary Hegseth welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."
On Nov. 11, video footage captured a U.S. Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Virginia reprimanding Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and his entourage after one of them talked and laughed out loud on the steps of the monument. The next day, Hegseth was photographed ostensibly awarding that same soldier a commendation medal in a Pentagon ceremony. 
Almost immediately, posts (archived) on X and Facebook popped up comparing images of the soldier taken at the tomb with one of Hegseth awarding him the medal in an apparent attempt to sow doubts it was the same person.
People claimed the sentinel's ears looked completely different in the two images and suggested the medal recipient was a body double. Several Snopes readers asked us if it was true Hegseth gave the medal to a doppelganger instead of the actual soldier.
(X user @JamesTate121)
The argument, as summarized in one post, went as follows:
Even though it's not the same side ears, most pairs of ears are pretty symmetrical. The details of the ear of the guy he gave the comm medal to, claiming it was the soldier who reprimanded his group, is totally different shape and physical attributes.
If it were true that most pairs of human ears are symmetrical, the argument might stand, but researchers say perfectly symmetrical facial features are the exception, not the rule. When you add to that the differences contributed by angle, lighting and distance in photographs, arguing that the appearance of asymmetricality, especially in photographs, is definitive proof that a pair of ears don't belong to the same person is bound to fail.
In the above collage, a blurry image of one side of a soldier's face is contrasted with a sharper frame from a video showing the other side of a soldier's face, and it's true they don't seem very symmetrical. Does that mean both ears can't belong to the same person? Not at all. Nor has any other evidence been offered to support the claim it isn't the same man in both photographs. The claim is therefore unfounded.
Snopes contacted the Department of Defense to confirm the identity of the soldier. A spokesperson responded, "As shown in the photos, Secretary Hegseth welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."
As Snopes has previously reported, soldiers have guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington since March 1926. The Arlington National Cemetery website states that the guards initially "discouraged visitors from climbing or stepping on the Tomb." The 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment has guarded the monument since April 6, 1948. Barbara Starr, CNN's former Pentagon correspondent, told the network (at 11:24) on Nov. 11 that sentinels correct any visitors who do not act with "respect and silence" at the tomb.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated numerous claims about Hegseth. Snopes has also covered many "body double" claims over the years.

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins race for Alaska governor, replaces a Republican
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from the small island community of Sitka, won the race for Alaska governor, according to a race call by the Associated Press. At 37, he'll be the youngest governor in state history.
Kreiss-Tomkins will replace outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a term-limited Republican who has been governor since 2018. The state's last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who left office in 2002.
Kreiss-Tomkins, known by his initials JKT, made his "high-energy, bipartisan, problem-solving approach" a centerpiece of his campaign.
He's said he plans to build an administration of Democrats, Republicans and independents and described himself at a debate as a "man of the middle." He was endorsed by three former governors — a Democrat, a Republican and an independent — along with Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski.
Alaskans have had enough of zero-sum partisan politics, he said in an interview just before voting at a precinct in Anchorage on Election Day.
"I strongly believe people just want things to work, and want people to work together," Kreiss-Tomkins said.
Loading...
The AP race call came after over a week of counting votes, including those coming in by mail and from remote parts of the state. In the ranked-choice system the state uses, he faced three Republican candidates, including one backed by President Trump. Winning requires getting a majority of the votes.
Voters were also facing a question on the ballot about whether to scrap that unique, ranked-choice system. That proposal failed, according to another AP race call, keeping the system in place.
With Kreiss-Tomkins' win and others in the midterms, Democrats will hold 30 governors' offices across the country, up from 24 now.
Kreiss-Tomkins will take office in a state where voters have loudly complained that things aren't working as they should.
Rising costs and relatively flat state funding have forced schools to close and class sizes to rise. Already-high costs for food, fuel and housing have risen sharply, and a looming shortage of easily accessible natural gas near the state's population centers is threatening to push prices higher. And Alaskans have been migrating out of the state for more than a decade.
The Republicans in the race were Trump-backed business owner Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor.
Kreiss-Tomkins is set to take office at noon Dec. 7.

In China’s Spy Operations, Romance Can Be a Long Game
Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman U.S. officials say is a Chinese spy has drawn attention to the role of intimate relationships in espionage.
At the height of the Cold War, a top official in China’s intelligence agency said that his country would never use seduction to entrap a person.
Such tactics might be for the C.I.A. or the K.G.B., the official named Kong Yuan, of the Central Investigation Department, told a group of agents in training in April 1960, but China was guided by principles. He looked at the few female comrades in the audience. “Rest assured, we will not be asking you to go run beauty traps.”
Despite that pledge, captured in a 2010 memoir by a former Chinese diplomat, China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people.
American officials say that China’s Ministry of State Security, which runs intelligence operations today, recruited a Chinese businesswoman to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia and one of the most powerful figures in the artificial intelligence boom.
It was not clear what role the woman, Alice Huang, or Huang Le, might have had with the Chinese spy agency. Ms. Huang was a top executive of a Singapore company that operates data centers in Southeast Asia using Nvidia chips and that rents their computing power to Chinese firms.
