Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”
Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.
“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.
Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.
Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.
“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.
During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.
“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”
Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.
Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.
For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?
“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”
Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.
“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.
On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.
“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.
However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.
“No woman in the city is fully free,” Sinha says.
Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”
In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.
“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.
Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.
“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”
Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.
Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.
But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

US President Donald Trump’s push to end Russia’s war against Ukraine is increasingly extending beyond a ceasefire, with Washington exploring a broader security arrangement involving Moscow and European nations. The proposed framework could address some of Russia’s long-standing demands, including limits on NATO’s expansion and its military presence in Eastern Europe, raising questions about the future of European security and the alliance’s role. According to sources cited by Axios, the Trump administration is now open to discussing security concerns that Moscow has repeatedly raised over the years. These issues were also central to Russia’s draft security proposals submitted to the US and NATO in 2021, which called for restrictions on the alliance’s eastward expansion and a rollback of parts of its military presence in Eastern Europe. The renewed discussions have raised concerns over whether Washington's efforts to negotiate an end to the war could give Russian President Vladimir Putin greater influence over Europe's security arrangements. The US proposal reportedly seeks to address two interconnected aspects of the conflict: ending the fighting in Ukraine and establishing a wider security framework between Russia and Europe. Two sources cited by Axios said Washington wants Moscow to put forward proposals that take into account Russia's security concerns while also offering assurances that would help European countries feel confident about their future security. The objective, according to the report, is to develop an arrangement that addresses Moscow's concerns without leaving European nations vulnerable to another potential Russian attack. The request was raised during two days of US-sponsored negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11. Russia has consistently opposed NATO's eastward expansion, arguing that the alliance's growing presence near its borders threatens its security. In December 2021, Moscow presented draft security agreements to Washington and NATO, demanding guarantees against further NATO enlargement and restrictions on the deployment of military forces and weapons in Eastern Europe. These demands became a major point of contention in the months leading up to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The latest US diplomatic initiative appears to bring some of these long-standing Russian concerns back to the negotiating table. However, any discussion of limiting NATO's military presence or future expansion could create tensions with European allies, particularly countries in Eastern Europe that view the alliance as a critical security guarantee against Russian aggression. According to The Washington Post, the proposed framework draws on the now-defunct NATO-Russia Council, which previously provided a platform for dialogue between Moscow and the military alliance. Such an arrangement could give Russia a formal channel to raise its security concerns and engage with European countries on wider security issues. However, the proposal could prove controversial. European officials are concerned that giving Moscow a greater role in discussions about the continent's security could allow the Kremlin to influence decisions that traditionally fall within the sovereign rights of individual European nations and NATO members. The central question is whether a broader security arrangement can address Russia's concerns without compromising NATO's independence or the security interests of its European members. Trump's special envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, are expected to meet Putin in Moscow on November 12 to discuss the proposed framework and assess progress made during the Abu Dhabi negotiations. According to Axios, Washington is also looking at involving European representatives in future rounds of discussions. The US envoys are subsequently expected to travel to Dublin to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who is in Ireland for discussions with European leaders. The latest diplomatic effort follows the first US-mediated direct negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian officials since February. Kushner described the discussions as difficult but productive, indicating that Washington wants Moscow to offer more than a list of demands. "We told the Russians, they have their desires and fears, but they have to provide different de-escalation and different proposals as well, if they want Europe to be able to receive those proposals in a good way," he said. Trump has repeatedly expressed optimism about reaching an agreement to end the war. Earlier, he said he had met Putin's envoy at the White House and suggested that a "big, beautiful agreement" could be within reach. His optimism was echoed by Kushner, who said US officials had held productive and substantive discussions with Ukrainian and NATO representatives in Brussels on November 5. However, negotiating an end to the war remains complicated by the competing security demands of Russia, Ukraine and European nations. While Moscow wants restrictions on NATO's military reach, Ukraine and its European partners are seeking lasting security guarantees to prevent another Russian offensive. New Indian mega library rocked by scandal over 'AI-generated books'
- Published
An Indian court has ordered an investigation into allegations that a public library in the southern state of Tamil Nadu bought hundreds of books suspected of being generated using AI.
The controversy began after Tamil novelist Perumal Murugan raised concerns about books containing false information and questionable authorship at a newly opened library in Coimbatore city.
The Madras High Court has ordered the state's anti-corruption agency to investigate the purchases and freeze bank accounts linked to a publisher accused of supplying the books.
The state government has blamed the previous Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party-led administration for buying the books. The DMK denies allegations.
Tamil Nadu's School Education Minister A Rajmohan has described the allegations as potentially "India's first AI scam" and said the investigation would cover purchases at other public libraries across the state.
The case has raised wider questions about the growing use of AI in publishing, where tools can generate entire books quickly and cheaply, but also produce false information and invented references.
It has also highlighted the challenges facing libraries and publishers in checking the authenticity of books as AI-generated content becomes more widespread.
The controversy centres on the Periyar Arivulagam library, built at a cost of about 3bn rupees ($34m; £26m). Named after social reformer Periyar EV Ramasamy, it was inaugurated on 16 October by Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay.
Murugan, whose novels Pyre and One Part Woman have received international recognition, raised concerns after visiting the library last month.
Writing in an online magazine, he alleged that nearly 1,800 books in its Tamil section had been supplied by a little-known publisher called Agal Vilakku Pathippagam.
He said many of the books carried unfamiliar authors' names, unusually high prices and questionable International Standard Book Numbers (ISBNs).
One book cited in the controversy, Naladiyar Vaazhvin Vazhikatti (A Guide to Life through Naladiyar), was reportedly priced at 1,445 rupees for 300 pages.
It describes Naladiyar as a Tamil poet and philosopher, although Naladiyar is a classical Tamil work consisting of 400 four-line verses on morality and ethics.
Another book reportedly attributes the ancient Tamil poem Madurai Kanchi to an incorrect author. It remains unclear whether AI was used to produce any of the disputed books.
Questions have also been raised about a book found at another public library in Madurai which names renowned economist Jean Drèze as its author.
The book, Democracy and People's Rights in the Contemporary World, names renowned economist Jean Drèze as its author and was published by Phoenix Publishing House.
Drèze did not respond to BBC Tamil's request for comment but told The Hindu newspaper earlier this week that he had not written the book, raising concerns that his name may have been used without his permission.
BBC Tamil visited a Chennai address listed by Agal Vilakku and another publisher named in the controversy, Phoenix Publishing House, but found no signs identifying either business.
A woman at the address confirmed that Agal Vilakku operated there. Its proprietor, Mohan, declined to comment, saying the matter was before the courts.
The controversy has prompted writers, academics and publishers to question how the books were selected for public libraries.
More than 160 writers, researchers, artists and publishers have signed a joint statement calling for an independent inquiry, the release of procurement records and an audit of library collections across Tamil Nadu.
They have also called for the recovery of public money if the investigation finds that funds were misused.
The group questioned how the disputed books could have passed through a selection process involving expert committees, price negotiations and several levels of review.
The state government has ordered an internal audit of public library collections.
Rajmohan said 523 books had already been removed from the historic Connemara Public Library in Chennai city after preliminary checks raised concerns about their authenticity and quality.
Disputed books have also been removed from Periyar Arivulagam, while anti-corruption officials examine procurement records and inspect other libraries, he added.
The controversy also sparked a political row in Tamil Nadu. Rajmohan accused the previous DMK government of ordering the disputed books and said the state would seek to recover public money if the investigation found wrongdoing.
The DMK has rejected the allegations as politically motivated and has called for an investigation into the purchases.
Additional reporting by Rachita Prasad

New Delhi: India and the US are in the last stretch of finalizing their highly anticipated trade deal, India's external affairs minister S Jaishankar said on Saturday.
Speaking at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit 2026, Jaishankar said there are few outstanding concerns on New Delhi’s end, and that most of the recent changes have come from the American side.
“We really have the bulk of the issues sorted out. There are the last stretch of issues. And in many cases, these concerns are not so much at our end because the changes have been more at the American end than ours. So, the hope is that we should close it out soon.”
He noted that India wants a trade deal which, apart from being mutually beneficial, gives it a comparative advantage over comparable economies.
Pointing out that India missed the "manufacturing bus" between the 1960s and 1990s, Jaishankar said the production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes are aimed at turning the country into a manufacturing hub while building capabilities in new-age technologies.
"The PLI schemes are designed to kick-start these different sectors. What have we missed out on, which we now need to catch up, and therefore, you're prepared to give incentives for industry to respond and set up businesses. So, we'll have to do the orthodox manufacturing. We have to support our small and medium enterprises. We have to become economically competitive, which means much better infrastructure and logistics. We have to improve our talent, which means more educational institutions, more skills," he said.
"But we'll also have to invest, say, in semiconductors. We'll have to invest in upgrading life sciences. We'll have to look at preparing for the AI era. All of this will have to address multiple levels in order to actually navigate those problems," he added.
He said that the vision of ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat’, or the call for ‘make in India’, or ‘innovate in India’ are the building blocks of a foreign policy.
Speaking on the emerging world order, Jaishankar said it will be multipolar—marked by sharper competition and greater national assertion, which inherently brings more instability. The external affairs minister added that India is expected to play a much stronger role and wield greater influence in this new order.
"The new order is not going to come out of the blue. It will be an evolution of the current order. And we will have a transition, and we are in that transition phase... We hope and we reasonably expect that the new order, for example, will have a much stronger role of India or much stronger influence by India… I think the general acceptance is that the new order will be more multipolar, that there will be many more centers of autonomous decision-making," he said.

Two of Japan’s biggest banks raised their profit forecasts and unveiled share buybacks, after cashing in on rising interest rates and robust loan demand that put them on course for another record year.

But economic risks are mounting as global investors grow jittery over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom and geopolitical conflicts keep energy prices elevated.

The derailment of the Kolkata-Sairang Express near Guwahati on November 11 has brought the train's braking system and mandatory safety checks under scrutiny, with a preliminary probe pointing to a malfunctioning main braking system, PTI reported.
A six-member probe team found that the brake pipe (BP) angle cock, a key component responsible for applying brakes in the coaches, was in an isolated condition in the locomotive. The preliminary findings have raised questions over whether the train crew conducted the prescribed braking tests before operating the train.
The Railway Board has since directed all zonal railways to ensure that running crews conduct braking tests after taking charge of a train. It has also ordered a safety drive from November 12 to 18 to check compliance with brake feel and brake power tests.
According to officials cited in the PTI report, a possible communication gap between station staff and the train crew may have led to the BP angle cock being isolated.
The Kolkata-Sairang Express earlier halted at Guwahati, where its electric locomotive was routinely replaced with a diesel locomotive. During this process, station staff would isolate the BP angle cock.
However, after electrification of the route was completed, the practice of changing locomotives at Guwahati was discontinued. The electric locomotive began operating the train beyond the station.
An official told PTI that the staff member responsible for isolating the angle cock was on leave when the locomotive interchange was discontinued. When he returned to duty on November 11, he reportedly followed the earlier procedure and isolated the angle cock, apparently unaware that the same electric locomotive would continue the journey.
The preliminary probe report has not established who rendered the braking system dysfunctional or whether the train crew failed to follow the required safety procedures.
The official cited by PTI said the crew may either have failed to conduct the mandatory braking tests or relied on the alternative regenerative braking system while checking the train's braking performance.
The crew may have discovered that the main braking system was not functioning only when they attempted to stop the train near the loop line, the official said. This may have contributed to the derailment.
The Railway Board's latest direction has reiterated the requirement for locomotive crews to conduct two tests -- the brake feel test and the brake power test.
During a brake feel test, the crew first brings a train to 15 kmph and applies the brakes by reducing brake pipe pressure using the main A-9 braking system. The speed should fall to around 10 kmph, allowing the crew to assess whether the brakes have been applied effectively.
For the brake power test, the locomotive pilot accelerates a passenger train to 60-70 kmph before applying the brakes. The speed should subsequently fall to 30-35 kmph. For goods trains, the prescribed test speeds are 40-50 kmph and 20-25 kmph, respectively.
The Railway Board has also specified the responsibilities of the assistant loco pilot. The assistant must monitor the tests, ensure that the locomotive pilot conducts them and remind the pilot if necessary.
In its November 11 communication to all zonal railways, the board asked them to ensure that running crews conduct braking tests after taking handover of trains, in accordance with established procedures.
It also ordered a safety drive between November 12 and 18 to verify whether locomotive crews are carrying out brake feel and brake power tests. Any discrepancies identified during the exercise must be compiled and sent to the Railway Board by November 20.

An iOS update did include a "Remote Control" feature that appeared to be enabled automatically.
The feature was introduced as part of the iOS 26 update, not iOS 27, and it does not allow users to remotely access a phone's "activity." Rather, it expands the functionality of the previously existing "Live Listen" accessibility feature. It is only functional on devices signed into the same Apple account, and it requires a user to intentionally initiate a Live Listen session on that device.
A rumor has circulated online since October that Apple released an update automatically enabling an option for outsiders to remotely access a phone's activity.
The claim spread on social media platforms such as Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived). Many of the posts offered warnings about the feature and instructions on how to turn it off, like this one (archived) from a Facebook user:
If you have an iPhone and installed the iOS 27 update, you might not know that Apple turned ON the option for someone to remotely access your activity on your phone.
In short, Apple did put out a "Remote Control" feature in an update, but not iOS 27, as posts claimed. According to their Settings app, the feature released in iOS 26, and the assertion that the feature allowed "someone to remotely access" activity on users' phones was overstated. As such, we have rated this claim as mostly false.
(Screenshot from iPhone/Snopes illustration)
We reached out to Apple for more information about the "Remote Control" feature and to ask whether the iOS 26 update automatically enabled it across all devices. We will update the story if we receive a response.
According to the Apple Support website, Live Listen allows an iPhone to "act like a microphone," allowing users to "hear a conversation in a noisy area or even hear someone speaking across the room." It was originally intended to work with hearing aids, but was expanded in iOS 12 to include AirPods or Beats earphones.
The iOS 26 "Remote Control" setting added new functionality to the feature, allowing Apple devices like iPads and Apple Watches to view and control Live Listen sessions, as long as they are nearby and signed into the same Apple Account.
For example, a student in the back of a noisy lecture hall could put their phone next to their professor at the start of class and remotely control a Live Listen session from their iPad signed into the same Apple account, allowing them to pause, resume and view a transcript of the picked-up audio without getting up from their seat.
Live Listen is situated within the "Accessibility" menu, indicating that Apple intended the feature especially for those with hearing-related difficulties.
(Screenshot from iPhone)
Remote control of a user's Live Listen session can only take place if that user intentionally started the session, and it only provides access to a transcript of audio near the user's iPhone. A bad actor who gained access to a device signed into a user's Apple account wouldn't be able to start a Live Listen session on that user's device using "Remote Control" — that user would have to be the one to start the session. Because of this, there is little risk of someone using the feature nefariously.
Based on user testimony and our own testing, the feature did appear to be automatically enabled as of the iOS 26 update. However, official Apple developer notes (archived) for the update made no mention of the terms "Remote Control" or "Live Listen."
For further reading, Snopes investigated the extent to which incognito mode protects users' data, and found it might be less than most users expected.

Pre-orders for some Apple Home Collection devices will open November 13
You can lock in orders for two LG cameras and a video doorbell.
On the same day that the Apple HomeView smart display and refreshed Apple TV 4K hit stores, pre-orders will open for some accessories in the Apple Home Collection. Apple confirmed to Engadget that you'll be able to pre-order the LG indoor camera, outdoor camera and video doorbell on November 13.
Those three devices, which Apple and LG collaborated on, will be the first Apple Home Collection accessories to ship. They're slated to arrive in December. Apple hasn't revealed exactly when other products in the lineup — including thermostats and door locks — will be available, but the company has said some will be available next month with the rest debuting in early 2027.
The indoor camera can capture 2.5K footage of what's going on in your home while you're away, giving you a way to keep an eye on your pets, for instance. It has low-light color night vision and infrared (IR) night vision support. The camera, which costs $200 and can detect people and pets, can tilt up when you're out and down when you're home — this can be managed automatically through the Home app or manually by pressing a button.
The outdoor camera can recognize faces, pets and deliveries. It too supports low-light color night vision, IR night vision and 2.5K video capture. The camera has IP65-rated protection from rain and dust and a two‑way talk function. As with the indoor camera, you'll get 10 days' worth of event video history via iCloud+. There's built-in storage too. The standard outdoor camera costs $300 and a version with a floodlight will run you $400.
As for the $250 video doorbell, that has a dual-camera design that can pick up (for instance) visitors and packages simultaneously — a 2.5K camera faces forward and a Full HD one points downward. You'll be able to view either feed separately in the Home app and chat to whoever's at your door using the two-way talk function. When someone rings the doorbell, HomeView and HomePod devices will sound a chime. You'll get notifications on other Apple devices too.
Again, there's low-light color night vision and IR night vision support, along with event video history in iCloud+ and built-in storage. The camera can detect people, pets, vehicles and packages and it has a dimmable spotlight.
Apple is making privacy a big selling point for these products, which offer end-to-end encryption (neither Apple nor LG will be able to access the data). Naturally, you can control them using your other Apple devices, such as your iPhone or HomeView, and view live video feeds.

After Democrats in Texas flipped a U.S. Senate seat, won 14 U.S. House seats and the governor's office in the 2026 midterm elections, a claim (archived) circulated that the wins happened only because the party fraudulently "found" 20 million new voters who all voted blue.
For example, an X user wrote, "There's no chance Texas found 20 million new voters who voted exclusively 100% for Democrats. It's fraud!"
The same text also circulated on Facebook (archived) and other social media platforms.
We found no proof that the Democratic Party in Texas fraudulently "found" and registered 20 million new voters to skew races in their favor in the Nov. 3 elections. The claim appeared to conflate a separate, unproven claim about the number of new voters nationwide with the number of new voters in Texas alone.
Therefore, we rate this claim false.
Texas had just over 19 million registered voters by mid-October, according to its secretary of state. Figures from that office showed the number of registered voters had risen by about 2% since the presidential election in 2024. The number of registered voters rose about 5.4% between the 2022 and 2024 elections. An additional 20 million voters would have created a 107.4% increase in registered voters since 2024 or a 113.2% increase since 2022.
The state's unofficial voter turnout figures showed that 9,850,031 people voted in person or by mail in the state's 2026 midterm elections — a little more than half of Texas' registered voters.
Given the figures from the Texas secretary of state, it wasn't possible for Democrats to have fraudulently "found" 20 million people to tip the state's elections, because fewer than half that number voted in the elections at all. A sudden doubling of the number of registered voters would have raised alarm bells with officials. This did not occur.
The origin of the "20 million" figure was unclear, but it may have come from a bar chart that claimed to show that House Democrats gained 20 million voters across the entire U.S. between 2022 and 2026. The fact-checking organization Lead Stories reported on this graph and found no credible source for its projected 2026 voter numbers.
Rather, Lead Stories pointed to the University of Florida's General Election turnout tables, which showed 123,540,000 ballots counted nationwide in the 2026 midterms by Nov. 6. The same source showed 112,030,874 ballots counted in the 2022 midterms, the most recent equivalent race. The bar chart claimed 126 million people had voted in House races in 2026, around 2.5 million more than the University of Florida's estimate.
The university's figures suggested an increase of 11,509,126 ballots counted between the 2022 and 2026 elections, around half of the 20 million figure the unsourced bar chart suggested.
It wasn't possible to determine how many more individual voters had voted for House Democrats in 2026 vs. in 2022 because state officials had not yet certified their election results at the time of this writing and when the graph circulated.
Regardless of the accuracy of the graph or claim, it was true that Democrats picked up a sizable number of votes in their House and Senate races to secure control of both chambers nationwide. Pollsters credited young voters, male voters and Hispanic voters with securing Democratic wins.
At the time of this writing, there were no credible allegations of widespread fraud.
The false claim played into election fraud theories about bad actors "finding" votes in elections. Snopes has previously reported on variations of this claim in the form of noncitizen voting (which rarely happens), duplicate ballots (which are extremely difficult to produce) and vote spikes (which are a natural part of vote counts).

For years, people have told me that Seth Rogen and I are voice twins.
Sitting across from him at the Middleburg Film Festival, deep in Virginia horse country, even Jeremy, the person recording our conversation, can confirm that the resemblance is very close. Even so, the year Rogen is having belongs entirely to him.
Coming off the historic Emmy run of “The Studio,” Rogen could have gone anywhere next. He chose to travel into the world of darkly comic relationship drama “The Invite” and the 2D animated world of Alzheimer’s disease with “Tangles,” a one-two punch nobody could have seen coming.
In “The Invite,” Olivia Wilde’s A24 dinner-party indie, Rogen plays Joe, a husband whose fraying marriage gets stress-tested over one excruciating evening with the upstairs neighbors, played by Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton. I think it’s his finest hour as an actor. On paper, it sounds like a “another Seth Rogen” role. On screen, he plays it in a way we didn’t expect and he credits Wilde for taking his and Norton’s ideas to heart.
“She could have just not used any of it,” he says. “and I just would not have been as funny in it.”
On the episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast, Rogen discusses his one-two punch of “The Invite” and “Tangles,” along with the recently announced “Darkwing Duck” revival at Disney+, the awards-season satire threaded through Season 2 of “The Studio” and how “Steve Jobs” opened a door to a part of the industry he had never been invited into. Listen below!
Among comedians, he says, going dramatic “almost feels like a bit of a cheat code” and he recalls Jonah Hill predicting “Moneyball” (2011) would bring him the most acclaim of his career for doing the least (Hill was right, getting his first Oscar nom for supporting actor).
“Tangles,” on the other hand, is a different kind of gamble. The hand-drawn, black-and-white animated feature, adapted from Sarah Leavitt’s graphic memoir about her mother’s Alzheimer’s and directed by first-time feature filmmaker Leah Nelson, comes from Rogen’s Point Grey Pictures and features his voice alongside Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Abbi Jacobson, Bryan Cranston and Samira Wiley. In a category ruled by studio franchises, it is the outlier and it took 10 years to make and the Canadian multihyphenate always had his eye on what’s most important. “When we give up on it is when it doesn’t happen,” he says.
Independent Film Company and Sapan Studio open “Tangles” in theaters this year for an awards-qualifying run, with a wider expansion in early 2027. “The Invite” is streaming on HBO Max.
The conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.
You’re having quite a year, with two very different movies in “The Invite” and “Tangles.” You’re coming off “The Studio,” and there’s been a lot of anticipation about what you’ll do next. This is quite a one-two punch. How does this moment in your career feel?
I feel very lucky. You only want to hope that you’re learning more in life, that you’re getting better at making choices and that once you’ve decided to do something, you get better at being the best part of the team you can be. It’s incredibly nice and gratifying that, over the last few years, I feel like I’ve been doing work I’m very proud of and pushing myself to do things that are hopefully different from what I’ve done in the past. But I also feel very lucky to have people who have wanted to work with me and have been willing to. And part of it is coincidence. We’ve worked on “Tangles” for 10 years. We didn’t know it was going to come out now. Luck has a lot to do with these things coming to life in a way that makes it seem like I planned it.
Starting with “The Invite,” this might be your finest hour as an actor. On paper, it sounds like a movie Seth Rogen would make. Playing Joe, did you feel you were doing something you hadn’t done before? Did you have one of those out-of-body experiences?
As we were making the movie, I felt like I was being given the opportunity, at least in a movie, to do something that was very representative of my exact comedic, tonal and dramatic taste. What was really amazing about what Olivia did was that she allowed us to affect the tone of the film with our performances. She allowed me to insert humor in moments where it wasn’t originally going to be, which changes the tone of the whole thing. She allowed Edward to give dramatic monologues in places where they weren’t originally going to be. And then she allowed me to make jokes that subverted those moments in ways that weren’t originally scripted.
To me, that was an incredibly new and gratifying feeling. We weren’t just being invited to change the dialogue or our characters throughout the performing process. Olivia was allowing us to change the tone of the film itself with our performances. You could see it happening in real time. You could see that a scene was much funnier than we thought it would be. Or we thought a scene was going to be funny, but it was actually much more intense than we all thought. We were encouraged to play with that and not be too beholden to what it was originally conceived as, but instead feel it out as we were doing it.
I have to give her credit for using my stuff in a way that turned out very well. I throw a lot of stuff out there, and she could have edited this movie in a way that left out some of what I think are the funniest moments I generated as we were making it. The film probably still would have been very good, but I just wouldn’t have been as funny in it.
So I’m very proud that it’s a performance people seem to like, and I genuinely feel it’s one of my funnier performances. I’ve done dramatic work in the past, and I think among comedians it almost feels like a bit of a cheat code. If I’m not funny, everyone leans in a little bit more. I remember Jonah Hill was making “Moneyball,” and he said, “This is going to be the thing that I get the most acclaim for. And it’s for sure the easiest thing I’ve done, because I’m just doing less than I normally do.” And I’ve done things like that. So what’s nice is that I do feel like I was creating comedy throughout this film, and people are appreciating that. It isn’t just because it’s not funny that people are appreciating it, which is something I think a lot of comedians have experienced.
It’s the Jim Carrey cheat code. He gets to do “The Truman Show” and “Eternal Sunshine,” and suddenly we’re all saying, “My God.”
Yes. There was a time when comedians really pursued that and wanted that, and I think it was a very deliberate thing comedians were doing for a while. I totally get it. It’s totally legitimate. It’s just that, to me, I’m very proud of my ability to generate comedy on camera. I’ve always been most proud of my funny work. It’s obviously an honor to get to be in Steven Spielberg movies and things like that are certainly less comedic, and the fact that those filmmakers think I can serve their work in any way is very flattering. But I’m always thinking, if I could also bring my full ability to make this comedic, that would be great. That’s exactly what Olivia really encouraged me to do. So it was very gratifying to be able to bring that.
I love that comedic actors can make that transition so seamlessly. I’m also dying for directors who are known for drama to go the other way. I want to see the Christopher Nolan version of “Superbad.” I want them to take a swing like that.
Apparently, “Digger” is that. I haven’t seen it yet. It’s harder than it looks sometimes. It does go both ways. Comedians try to do drama, and sometimes it’s ill-fitting. Dramatic actors try to do comedy, and sometimes that’s ill-fitting, too. I’m not saying that film is that. I haven’t seen it. But it’s something I’ve seen happen.
Then there’s “Tangles,” which is about as far from “The Invite” as you can get. The animated feature category at the Oscars has been dominated by studio franchises for years, and now we have this hand-drawn, black-and-white film about Alzheimer’s. I think people need to hear the answer to this: How difficult is it to make a movie like this?
Really hard [laughs]. We’ve been working on it for 10 years, and I think maybe the last three years of that were production. So it was about seven years of us internally developing it, but also trying to find financing, putting together a cast that would be appealing to financiers, doing readings and making sure the script was really, really good.
And the movie itself was made incredibly differently. Most animated movies, these big studio ones, are made, then made again, then made again. You screen them, redo the third act, screen them again and redo the first act. This movie couldn’t be made that way. It had to be written and then executed, and we could change almost nothing. It’s hand-drawn, so the process of changing things, should you want to, is incredibly labor-intensive and arduous.
People like Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Bryan Cranston, Samira Wiley and Abbi Jacobson, along with so many of the amazing cast members, were honestly really helpful in getting the movie made. So was having a good script and filmmakers who, when those actors got in the room with them, were willing to let them take ownership of the material. It’s so gratifying that the movie even exists. We’ve spent so long working on it.
During those first seven years, how many times did you think, “This isn’t happening?”
I thought it would happen. So many things take a long time to get made. I truly believe that if we give up on it, that’s when it doesn’t happen. Sometimes we don’t give up, and we will bring it into existence through sheer brute force. This felt worth it because it was good. If something is good, I believe you can find a way to make it. “Superbad” took so long to get made. And then there were things like “Pineapple Express” and “Sausage Party,” all these movies we worked on for so long before they were made. To me, 10 years is normal.
“Darkwing Duck” because I’m a child of the ’80s and ’90s. Congratulations on the Emmy for “The Muppet Show,” and obviously we have “The Studio” Season 2 coming. But nothing excites me more than this cartoon classic that Mark Hamill has a role in! Did that casting fall into your lap?
The cast is really great. We just cast a Scrooge McDuck who might be the most exciting casting I could ever imagine. I’ll tell you after. But it’s incredible. We’ve been working on it for a very long time. You get caught up in these corporate restructurings, but we’ve been working on “Darkwing Duck” for years and years. I’ve been watching the episodes, and they’re amazing. They’re coming together so well, and the animation is beautiful and really inventive.
I was actually surprised you didn’t go the movie route.
I’m glad we didn’t. The TV nature of it was very appealing to us, honestly. As nice as it is to make a hand-drawn, black-and-white animated film, it’s also nice to extract every penny Disney’s willing to put into a thing. Getting to work in both those ways is nice. But with something like “Darkwing Duck,” we felt that if we were going to do it, it had to be top, top-notch.
Are there other Disney shows from the ’80s and ’90s you’d love to bring back? I think of “TaleSpin,” “Gummi Bears” and “DuckTales.”
I always think of “Flight of the Navigator.” That was a Disney movie, I guess. I would never presume I’d do it, but that’s always been a movie I thought was cool. “Darkwing Duck,” though, I loved. And it’s very meta. It’s funny, I reread those “Calvin and Hobbes” comics recently and I realized they really formed a lot of my personality. Years ago, when we were first talking about doing “Darkwing Duck” again, I rewatched all of it and thought, this is really meta. It really breaks the fourth wall and comments on these shows I was also watching at the same time, at the same age.
If we can get “Gargoyles” back up and running …
That would be great. I did love “Gargoyles.”
Let’s talk about “The Studio” Season 2. There have been a lot of reports from the set: Madonna, the Venice Film Festival. Which real-life awards-season humiliation of yours is going to end up on the show?
You’ll see.
How much does Variety figure into the new season?
I think it comes up. I don’t want to reveal too much, but some of the stuff has made it out publicly into the world a little bit. This idea of playing the awards game as a studio is definitely a theme explored throughout the season.
Do you have a Season 2 equivalent of the Martin Scorsese moment, when viewers see who’s appearing and think, “I can’t believe they got him?” Does Christopher Nolan show up, for example?
We have several of those. Some are really unbelievable, and having to direct these people has been among the most terrifying moments of my entire life. For ourselves, we really tried to be even more ambitious. We wanted to get people we were even bigger fans of and make them even bigger parts of the episodes, if we could. We also wanted to dig deeper into our own feelings about the industry and our own internal conflicts as we go about all this.
Does the awards race feel more or less relevant to you now? Having made “The Studio,” how does it look compared with 15 years ago?
What’s interesting is that until I did the “Steve Jobs” movie, which was pretty deep into my career, I was never part of anything that was on that journey in any capacity. I’d been to TIFF and South by Southwest to premiere things. But that was the first time I went to Telluride, and then we were in the New York Film Festival. Honestly, it was like a door to a secret part of the industry that I’d never been invited into was suddenly opened. So it’s interesting, because I had a very lovely career before any of this was even on my radar.
But that being said, the fact that “The Studio” won awards got us things in the second season that we probably wouldn’t have gotten in the first season. So there is some tangible outcome to some of this stuff. I understand why people get invested in it, and I understand the lure and the draw. I’ve seen people go on this journey and get the exact outcome they were hoping for, and it ultimately gave them none of the things they hoped it would. And I’ve seen people go on the journey and not get the outcome they wanted, and they had a good time and seemed to have good perspective at the end of all of it. It is a fascinating part of our industry to me.
I think especially for smaller things, it is incredibly helpful. It could make or break people’s careers. It could make or break a film. It could change the course of people’s lives. If you’ve already made many billion-dollar movies, winning best picture is a feather in your cap. It’s not going to change the course of your life, per se. But what’s interesting is those people are at these events right next to the people whose lives it will change. To me, that is really interesting to see in real life and really cool. For some people, they’re at the point of their career where awards have very personal stakes, but there are many other people here for whom the awards have real-life stakes. Will they get to do the thing they’ve always wanted to do, or will it not happen the way they hoped?
That is really interesting and scary and cool to see play out. There are those moments where your heart is pounding and you’re like, we’re doing it. This is what we asked for: to put ourselves out there and subject ourselves to reality in terms of how our work is being perceived. It can be very gratifying and incredibly scary and stressful.
Can you tell me something about “The Studio” Season 2? Is there a oner episode again?
We actually try to do much more of that. There are more episodes in a much more condensed timeline. I think there are technically several episodes this season that have no cuts in them, basically, throughout the entire thing. They’re real-time, half-hour moments in time that the episode is chronicling.
It’s a weird time in the industry. Depending on who you ask, the future looks very grim. Others say it’s an evolution and we’re just going through some changes. One of the biggest conversations here at Middleburg was Peter Rice going to Netflix. Someone like him, who’s been such a theatrical guy, making that move feels like a signal: Theatrical’s back! How do you feel about this moment? Do you get nervous, or do you think we’re going to be OK?
It’s a mixture of everything. It is everything at once. I’m very optimistic about some things. The fact that so many people are going to theaters, compared to the last few years, is so encouraging. I think we are finally getting over that hump of the pandemic and the strikes and all that. It seems like things are returning to a time when there are a lot of good movies and people are willing to go see them, and that’s really exciting. From my own personal lens, I can go to the theater on a Tuesday night and it’s packed and it wasn’t like that for a long time. As someone who loves going to the movies, it’s really fun to see. It reminds me of when I was a kid, honestly, a little bit more. And I think other things are terrifying.
10 QUESTIONS WITH SETH ROGEN
Childhood nickname?
“Sethical.” Friends from growing up still call me that when I see them. They don’t even think about it. It just comes out.
Something you loved as a kid but can’t believe you were into when you think about it now?
I get why people like “Magic: The Gathering,” but I spent every penny I had on “Magic: The Gathering” cards. That’s the thing I look back on, and I’m like, I should have bought other stuff.
Go-to karaoke or shower song?
I don’t karaoke as a rule. If karaoke went away altogether, I’d never need to be in a room with some drunk person screaming a song ever again. The rooms are getting smaller and smaller. Now I’m three feet away from this person. It used to be the bar was higher because you were subjecting yourself to a real big room full of people. Now you’re in a little room with just your friends in it, screaming your ass off like an idiot. It’s so loud. I hate it. That said, “All for Love” by Bryan Adams. If you have two other raspy-voiced friends, it’s a really good song.
Alternate title for “The Invite?”
I was going to say “The Apartment.” I would take “The Apartment.”
Secret talent?
I’m pretty flexible. I can almost get my leg behind my head.
Favorite ice cream flavor?
I just like vanilla. I did that movie with Barbra Streisand [”The Guilt Trip”], and she was obsessed with McConnell’s ice cream, which is from Santa Barbara. Every scene we shot, she’s like, “Wouldn’t we be eating ice cream in this scene?” So yes, it’s become McConnell’s.
The one item you can’t live without?
My glasses come to mind. My shoes. Things like that.
What TV show or film in all of history do you wish you were a cast member of?
Maybe it would have been cool to be in “Ghostbusters” or something like that.
Who do you kick out?
Good question. Probably Dan Aykroyd.
Which fictional character do you most relate to or admire?
I always liked Homer Simpson. Not that I relate to or admire him, but I always just liked him.
Your favorite piece of advice, either given or received?
I was told at a very young age to write what only I could write, which meant writing things based on my own experience, things that were happening to me. A stand-up comedian named Darryl Lenox, who’s passed away, unfortunately, told me that and he was really nice to me. I was writing jokes that were observational, like, “What’s the deal with crazy glue?” Those kinds of jokes. I was doing OK. Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal will begin a two-day visit to Egypt on Sunday (November 15, 2026), focusing on ways to strengthen bilateral trade and investment ties and explore opportunities for cooperation in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, industrial development, manufacturing, infrastructure, ports and logistics, an official statement said.
Egypt's strategic geographical location offers significant opportunities for Indian businesses to strengthen their presence in the country and access markets across Africa, the Middle East and Europe.
The two sides are also expected to discuss measures to facilitate greater participation of businesses in each other's markets, strengthen institutional mechanisms, address trade-related concerns and promote investment partnerships, the commerce ministry said on Saturday (November 14).
"Opportunities for cooperation in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, industrial development, manufacturing, infrastructure, ports and logistics, and regional value chains are also expected to feature in the discussions," it added.
A high-level Indian business delegation comprising over 140 CEOs and senior industry representatives from diverse sectors are accompanying the minister to participate in the India-Egypt Joint Business Council (JBC), and Joint Trade Committee (JTC) meetings.
The seventh session of the JTC will be co-chaired by Mr. Goyal and Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade of Egypt Mohamed Farid Saleh on Sunday (November 15).
The trade committee meeting will provide an opportunity to review the progress of bilateral trade and investment relations and discuss measures to further diversify and expand the bilateral trade basket.
"Discussions are expected to cover market access issues, non-tariff barriers, trade remedies, agricultural and food products, pharmaceuticals and healthcare, engineering goods, chemicals and petrochemicals, fertilisers, textiles, MSMEs, customs cooperation, services, renewable energy, green hydrogen, transport and logistics," it said.
The JBC Meeting and Business Forum will provide platforms for direct engagement between business leaders and industry stakeholders from both countries to explore opportunities for enhancing bilateral trade and investment, fostering joint ventures, promoting technology partnerships and strengthening industrial collaboration.
During the visit, Mr. Goyal will also hold bilateral meetings with senior Egyptian Ministers to exchange views on further strengthening bilateral economic and commercial relations, particularly in the areas of trade, investment and industrial cooperation.
He will also interact with leading business representatives and hold meetings with the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), the Egyptian Junior Businessmen Association and participate in the Egypt-India Startups Forum.
Both countries have significant opportunities to expand cooperation in manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, automobiles, textiles, chemicals, engineering goods, food processing, renewable energy, logistics and emerging technologies, it added.
Bilateral merchandise trade during April-September 2026 stood at $5.04 billion, registering a growth of 64% over the corresponding period of the previous year.
India's exports to Egypt during 2025-26 amounted to U$3.87 billion, while imports from Egypt stood at $2.60 billion.
India's major exports to Egypt include meat and poultry products, petroleum products, organic chemicals, cotton and machinery, while its major imports include crude petroleum, fertilisers, cotton and mineral products.

Gurnoor Brar has been drafted into India’s Test squad for the New Zealand series, while Kuldeep Yadav has been released to play domestic cricket, with the team management opting to bolster its pace attack in conditions expected to favour seam bowling. Rishabh Pant has also joined the squad after recovering from a back injury.
Sportstar understands that the decision to bring in the lanky fast bowler was influenced by the favourable conditions expected during the Test series, which begins in Wellington on November 19. Brar impressed during the ongoing ODI series and is expected to provide India with another seam-bowling option.
The 26-year-old has been in New Zealand for well over three weeks. He initially travelled as part of Test captain Shubman Gill’s personal bowling entourage before joining the ODI squad. Having spent considerable time acclimatising to the conditions, Brar will now link up with the Test contingent but will miss the fifth and final ODI. India has decided against naming a replacement.
Pant, meanwhile, had been recovering after injuring his back during the Irani Cup in the first week of October. After proving his fitness in a two-day match simulation in Bengaluru on November 10 and 11, he received clearance and joined the Test squad in Wellington.
Kuldeep, meanwhile, will return home after spending much of the tour on the sidelines. With the left-arm wrist-spinner unlikely to feature prominently in the team’s plans for the two Tests, the team management and the selection committee felt that releasing him would allow him to get some much-needed game-time.
The limited-overs leg of the domestic season, Syed Mushtaq Ali T20, got underway on Saturday, giving Kuldeep an opportunity to return to competitive action rather than remain on the bench in New Zealand.
India’s updated 16-member Test squad will be led by Gill, with K.L. Rahul as vice-captain. Pant and Dhruv Jurel are the two wicketkeeping options, while Jasprit Bumrah, Mohammed Siraj, Prasidh Krishna, Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj and Brar form the pace contingent.

Cardiologists have called for a review of a recent order issued by the Director General of Health Services (DGHS), strictly prohibiting the sterilisation and re-use of single-use devices and disposable surgical items used in critical specialties like cardiology and cardiothoracic and vascular surgery, citing issues of patient safety
At the annual conference of the Cardiological Society of India (CSI), Kerala chapter, here on Sunday, the CSI Kerala Chapter president Asokan P.K. said the association would seek a review of the order by DGHS as the exorbitant cost of medical devices and accessories would make crucial procedures such as angioplasty unaffordable and inaccessible to many.
Prathap Kumar N., organising chairman of the conference, said the rising cost of complex angioplasty, particularly procedures requiring multiple specialised devices, had become a major concern. Reimbursement package rates under government-funded health insurance schemes were often inadequate to cover the actual cost of advanced cardiac interventions.
With an increasing proportion of the population requiring advanced cardiac interventions, making complex procedures affordable to ordinary patients was a major challenge. Permitting the regulated re-use of select interventional devices, wherever scientifically proven safe, could help reduce treatment costs and extend the benefits of modern cardiac care to a wider section of the population, Dr. Prathap Kumar pointed out
He said cardiologists had sought a review to determine whether selected catheters, guidewires and other equipment could be safely re-processed under scientifically validated protocols and re-used for patients.
“Patient safety must remain paramount. Any proposal for re-use must be supported by scientific evidence, validated sterilisation, functional testing and strict regulatory oversight,” Dr. Prathap Kumar said.
He called for wider consultation among medical specialists, infection-control experts and regulatory authorities to develop an evidence-based policy regarding the sterilisation and re-use of medical devices, balancing affordability with patient safety.
The order by the DGHS said the practice of re-using single-use devices and disposable surgical items was a serious concern from the perspective of patient safety, infection prevention and control, regulatory compliance and healthcare expenditure. It said such re-use may also expose patients to significant risks, including cross-infection, device malfunction, loss of performance and other procedure-related complications
However, it is a fact that sterilisation and re-use of medical devices, ensuring the integrity of the devices and patient safety, is a common practice in both private and public sector hospitals across the country.
The Cardiological Society of India had in 2017 brought out a consensus document, “Guidance on reuse of cardio-vascular catheters and devices in India”, which clearly endorsed re-use, but set out certain requirements which had to be met for re-use to be safe and effective.
The devices, which can be reused, should be clearly defined, a meticulous process for disinfection and sterilisation followed and its functionality ascertained before use. Also, “an appropriate consent should be obtained where necessary” and the cost saving entailed should be directly passed on to the patient, the document said.
The CSI(K) conference also featured discussions on the evolving roles of drug-coated balloons and drug-eluting stents in coronary angioplasty, leadless pacemakers, laser-assisted coronary interventions, invasive coronary function testing, newer cholesterol-lowering therapies, complex valve procedures and advances in heart failure management.

Lupus patients struggling with the debilitating disease are lining up to try experimental CAR-T therapies even after the recent deaths of four patients in clinical trials for a variety of autoimmune diseases, according to doctors who treat the life-threatening condition.
The trials remain halted and full details of the deaths — three linked to Novartis and one to Bristol Myers Squibb — have not been released.
Still, patients are willing to take the risk, compelled by accounts of people with advanced disease who were able to stop all medications and reclaim normal lives.
“I have patients that are literally waiting to get in,” said Dr. Anca Askanase, chief of rheumatology at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York, who has enrolled patients in the Bristol Myers CAR-T trials.
Systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE, the most common and severe form of lupus, causes agonising joint pain and raises the risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease. Current treatments, which range from steroids to immunosuppressants and targeted biologics, often fail to control the disease. Some 10% to 15% of people with lupus die prematurely.
Brittan Kopittke, 27, who works for the University of North Carolina helping to counsel patients considering CAR-T, was diagnosed with lupus at age 22. SLE, which affects about 300,000 people in the US, typically develops between the ages of 15 and 44.
What began as a rash on her chest rapidly progressed to crippling joint pain, mouth sores and crushing fatigue. Steroids to reduce inflammation and the antimalarial drug hydroxychloroquine to tamp down antibodies attacking her healthy cells and tissues failed.
“My mouth sores were rampant. I was struggling to eat. I was struggling to drink. I was just very, very miserable,” she said.
Despite trying a cocktail of medicines, her disease advanced, attacking her kidneys, heart and lungs.
“I had reached the end of the line with treatments,” she said.
In June 2024, Kopittke went to UNC-Chapel Hill for a trial testing CAR-T, a personalised immunotherapy successfully used to treat blood cancers. It involves removing blood cells called T cells, genetically reengineering them to attack rogue immune cells, and reinfusing them with the aim of growing new, healthy immune cells.
Kopittke developed two dangerous reactions: cytokine release syndrome, which causes systemic inflammation, and a life-threatening, high-grade neurological complication called ICANS that left her unresponsive for three days.
Now, some two years into remission, Kopittke said she does not “sugarcoat” the risks when advising patients. “But I do say that I would do this again.”
150 trials underway
Novartis, Bristol Myers, and other companies with approved CAR-T cancer therapies, such as Johnson & Johnson and Gilead, are currently testing the technology against other hard-to-treat diseases.
There are about 150 trials underway pursuing CAR-T for lupus, as well as many others for myasthenia gravis, scleroderma, myositis, multiple sclerosis and stiff-person syndrome.
“There’s billions and billions of dollars pouring into this space,” said P.J. Utz, a Stanford Medicine autoimmunity researcher.
The risks became clear when Novartis in late August said it halted eight trials of its experimental rap-cel CAR-T therapy in autoimmune and neurological disorders after three patients died from a rare but known hyperinflammatory complication called IEC-HS.
Novartis, in an emailed statement, said it is working with multiple investigators and external academic experts to understand the root cause of the deaths and will share its findings “once the analysis is completed and the results can contribute to furthering patient care.”
Bristol also paused enrollment in its CAR-T autoimmune trials, citing temporary inflammatory events in patients. On October 23, it announced the death of a multiple sclerosis patient in one of the trials but said it had identified the cause of the safety issue and hopes to resume testing in 2027.
Piecing together what happened
The revelation of deaths in the Novartis trials surprised doctors eager to try CAR-T, buoyed by the success of Georg Schett of the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg. In 2022, Schett published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine showing five lupus patients achieved remission with CAR-T. Subsequent studies showed lasting remission.
The Novartis deaths have left doctors in the dark, Schett said. The company needs to disclose what diseases the patients had, how well controlled their diseases were and what emergency treatments they received, Schett added.
Without those details, he said, doctors enrolling patients in other trials are left to speculate. “This is very sad for the community.”
Schett said he and CAR-T inventor Carl June of the University of Pennsylvania have tried to piece together what happened in the Novartis trials for an article they have submitted to NEJM.
He attributes the rare hyperinflammatory events in part to Novartis’ compressed manufacturing process, which reduces the time it takes to produce the cells from more than 10 days to fewer than two.
With this process, patients receive cells in an immature form, which Schett suggests is triggering a severe inflammatory response as cells expand in patients’ bodies. “We don’t see that in other programs,” he said.
He and others were less concerned about the more familiar side effects reported by Bristol Myers.
“We have treated high-grade inflammatory events that have been reversible with treatment,” said Kopittke’s doctor, Saira Sheikh, of the University of North Carolina, who chairs a network of nearly 70 lupus clinical trial centres.
Dr. Cuoghi Edens, a rheumatologist at the University of Chicago Medicine, which treats more than 100 paediatric lupus patients, said her hospital has had great success with a CAR-T therapy from Cabaletta Bio, which uses a more traditional manufacturing process.
Cabaletta has started testing its treatment in patients as young as 12. Edens said she walked through the informed consent process with a 15-year-old late last month.
“When the potential long-term impact of your diagnosis is death,” Edens said, “I don’t know if (treatment risks are) going to make that big of a difference to these patients.

NHRC notice to education ministry over complaint related to 'Veer Baal Diwas' events in schools
New Delhi, The NHRC has issued a notice to the education ministry over a complaint alleging that adequate awareness and educational activities concerning the Veer Baal Diwas on December 26 have not received "commensurate attention".
The complaint notes the celebrations organised across schools on November 14 Jawaharlal Nehru's birthday, which is celebrated as Children's Day.
According to the proceedings of the case, a bench of the National Human Rights Commission , presided over by its member Priyank Kanoongo, has sought a comprehensive action taken report within two weeks from the date of receipt of the notice.
The NHRC proceedings are dated November 13.
The present complaint has been lodged by Sanjeev Newar of Sewa Nyaya Utthan Foundation, bringing to the attention of the commission "concerns regarding the awareness and observance of Veer Bal Diwas, officially recognised by the government of India and observed on December 26 every year in commemoration of the supreme sacrifice of the Sahibzadas of Guru Gobind Singh Ji," it says.
The complainant has alleged that while schools across the country organise celebrations on November 14 as Children's Day, "adequate awareness and educational activities concerning Veer Bal Diwas and the extraordinary courage, sacrifice and historical significance associated with the Sahibzadas have not received commensurate attention," it says.
The complaint emphasises the importance of ensuring that children are "meaningfully sensitised" about the supreme sacrifices of the Sahibzadas, the historical circumstances in which they displayed extraordinary courage, and the values of bravery and the sacrifices made, according to the proceedings.
The commission is of the view that educational institutions play an important role in developing historical awareness, constitutional values and a sense of national heritage among children. It is, therefore, important that appropriate institutional initiatives are undertaken to familiarise students with the significance of Veer Baal Diwas and the sacrifices it commemorates, it says.
The commission is, therefore, satisfied that the issues raised in the complaint "warrant examination and intervention" under Section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, as per the proceedings.
The registry was also directed to issue notice to the secretary, department of school education and literacy in the Ministry of Education, asking it to submit an action taken report.

A post is being widely circulated on social media (here, here) claiming that Members of Parliament (MPs) in India are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. It also claims that MPs are entitled to toll tax exemptions and free train travel. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Indian MPs are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. They are also entitled to toll tax exemption and free train travel.
Fact: MPs are entitled to free train and air travel, as well as toll fees exemption. However, they are not exempt from paying GST on purchases of cars and air conditioners. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
First, according to the details of benefits available to MPs on the official Parliament website (here and here), each MP is entitled to 34 free single air journeys per year anywhere within India. They can use these tickets to travel with their spouse, relatives, or friends.
Additionally, MPs are entitled to free first-class AC or executive-class train travel anywhere in the country. Their spouse or another accompanying person can also avail of this facility. An accompanying assistant is entitled to a free AC two-tier (2-Tier) train pass.
According to the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) regulations (here and here), vehicles used by MPs are exempt from paying toll fees on national highways. MPs are also entitled to toll-exempt FASTags for two vehicles during their tenure.
However, there is no evidence to suggest that MPs are exempt from paying GST on cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase. Neither the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954, which outlines the benefits and entitlements of MPs, nor any official government notification mentions such a GST exemption.
To sum up, while MPs are entitled to certain travel benefits, they do not receive any GST exemption on the cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase.

Microsoft services are returning after an outage took down Outlook, Teams and more
Health care providers, schools and governmental bodies are among those affected.
Microsoft services that went down amid a widespread outage are gradually coming back online, the company said. An issue that impacted Microsoft 365 on Thursday afternoon took out services such as Outlook, Teams and Copilot 365, disrupting businesses and organizations around the world.
The company toiled overnight to restore service. Around 10PM ET on Thursday, it said some attempts to "improve serviceability" didn't work as hoped. By 2:45AM the following morning, though, it was "seeing positive results for service stability and increased capacity as a result of our latest traffic optimization actions."
Around 8:30AM, the company reported "continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific." In an update 45 minutes later, Microsoft said that while some people might be experiencing delayed email deliveries in Outlook or spotty connectivity, it was seeing "sustained improvements" in availability of affected services.
"We're seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure," the company said in an update at 10:39AM. "We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us."
The company later said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused you and your business." The outage was not the result of a cyberattack or AI agents causing havoc. "The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change," according to Microsoft, which has "addressed the underlying issue."
It added that it was "seeing broad recovery and stability across our services," which it restored gradually. A high level of demand meant it needed to validate system stability at each stage of the process. "While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration," it said. "We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete."
The day-long outage underscored how important it is for people and organizations to have redundancies in place. It had a widespread impact across the globe, affecting calls to emergency services, governments, the House of Representatives, court systems, schools and other organizations.
The UK's National Pharmacy Association said the email issues could cause "delays to some prescriptions." In Japan, where the majority of businesses and institutions are said to use Microsoft services, some companies seemingly went back to using fax machines on a temporary basis.
Given that the outage prevented them from doing their jobs properly, some workers in Australia and the UK used it as an excuse to clock off early on Friday and go to the pub. However, the inevitable return to normality weighed on some people's minds. "I thought it was heaven because I wasn't getting any emails at all, but this is just a Microsoft outage, so I'm actually just waiting in line at the gates of hell," the Japan Times quoted one person as saying.
Update, November 13, 2026, 1:28PM ET: Added Microsoft's apology and explanation of what caused the outage.
