Sports retail startup PlayBlue has onboarded cricketer KL Rahul as an investor and brand ambassador days ahead of launching its flagship store in Bengaluru. PlayBlue is set to open a 20,000 sq ft flagship store on 80 Feet Road in Bengaluru and launch its mobile app this Saturday (November 14). The flagship store will be spread across three retail floors, a café level and a rooftop terrace. Its product portfolio will span sports apparel, footwear, equipment, accessories, recovery products and sports nutrition, catering to both amateur and professional athletes. Beyond conventional retail, PlayBlue is positioning itself around specialised product discovery and in-store experiences. The store will offer gait analysis, treadmill-based footwear testing and cricket bat sensors to help customers assess products before making purchases. It will also provide services such as racquet stringing, cricket bat knocking and bicycle servicing. The rooftop space, called The Playground, will have a pickleball court, one-on-one futsal turf and a cricket net equipped with a bowling machine. The company also plans to host community classes, recovery sessions and sports club events at the venue. The startup aims to expand to over 100 stores across 25 Indian cities over the next five years. Founded in 2025 by former GMR Sports’ CEO Satyam Trivedi and former Cult.fit’s executive Jayam Vora, PlayBlue sells an assortment of athleisure, footwear, gear, fitness equipment, recovery products and nutrition through its retail stores and ecommerce platform. "We're building the store we wanted to walk into ourselves. Having KL Rahul on board as both an investor and our ambassador gives us a partner who knows what the right gear means to someone who plays," Vora said. The development comes months after PlayBlue secured $2.7 Mn (₹25.7 Cr) in a seed funding round in July, co-led by Centre Court Capital and MIXI Global, with participation from WEH Ventures. To note, KL Rahul has backed numerous brands in the Indian startup ecosystem, including Boldfit, Flam, XYXX and Metaman. With the Indian sports market projected to more than double to $130 Bn by FY30, investors’ interest remains lukewarm in backing startups in this space. For instance, fitness and sportswear brand Boldfit raised around ₹400 Cr (about $41.8 Mn) from Bharat Value Fund as part of its Series B funding round in October, for its nationwide retail expansion, product innovation, and manufacturing. Earlier in April, sportstech startup SportVot raised ₹32.7 Cr (about $3.8 Mn) in a fresh funding round led by IAN Alpha Fund, to expand its international presence and strengthen its AI-powered production and analytics capabilities.

The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue
In the weeks before Election Day, the Trump administration escalated its hunt for voter fraud and its pressure on election officials — especially in California — to crack down on illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens.
Now, with Election Day come and gone, election officials and civil rights attorneys are preparing for the administration to continue its search for noncitizens on state voter rolls, as well as what they see as intimidation tactics toward election officials.
"It's clear that there is this drive to try to conjure up facts that just don't exist. I don't think that's going to change," James Williams, county executive for California's Santa Clara County, told NPR. "So we fully are prepared to continue to deal with this."
In recent weeks, federal prosecutors announced criminal charges against dozens of people who are accused of voting or registering to vote without being a citizen. Yet compared to overall numbers of voters, noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. And since summer, the administration has touted what turned out to be grossly inflated numbers of noncitizens on state voter rolls.
In mid-October, federal officials alleged they had found 20,000 "likely" noncitizens on California's voter rolls. The Department of Justice sued the state to try to force election officials not to count ballots of voters whose citizenship had not been verified. A federal judge and a federal appeals court rejected the DOJ's requests, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene.
In the days leading up to Election Day, with the lawsuit pending, U.S. attorneys in California sent grand jury subpoenas to several counties, asking for records related to how local officials responded to DOJ's demands.
Though DOJ dropped its lawsuit last week, it has not rescinded these subpoenas.
"We have ongoing cases and investigations in various states surrounding voter process," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a Thursday press conference. "We are actively, and will continue to investigate election integrity cases criminally and civilly, and that wasn't expected to start or stop — no matter what the results of the election were last week."
But recent unfavorable rulings for the Trump administration have created new obstacles for future federal attempts to intervene on state voter list maintenance.
"Do I think they will still keep at this? I do, but there are just a lot of court losses that are going to be really difficult for them to maneuver around," Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at Campaign Legal Center, told NPR. "They've hit substantial roadblocks because it's a lawless program that Congress has never authorized."
Recent court orders reaffirmed that states have the authority to run their elections and called into question the credibility of the federal government's data on noncitizens.
One key ruling, which came down the night before Election Day, found that DOJ and the Department of Homeland Security lack any statutory authority to distribute lists of purported noncitizens to election officials. In that order, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., wrote that taking that action also violates the Privacy Act. The federal government could appeal.
In an earlier order in October, a different D.C.-based judge vacated the DOJ's project of requesting unredacted voter rolls from states, seeking to compare that voter data to federal databases, and instructing states to remove suspected noncitizens. The ruling found those actions were unlawful and disenfranchised eligible voters. The DOJ has appealed.
The Department of Justice declined to comment on litigation or future plans, but said in a statement, "The Department will continue to enforce federal election laws and will evaluate matters based on the facts and the law."
Looming criminal proceedings and subpoenas to election officials
Federal prosecutors have vowed to continue tracking down noncitizen voting cases, as have some local prosecutors. San Luis Obispo District Attorney Dan Dow is investigating the potential noncitizen voters federal officials flagged in his county. He has so far charged one individual.
"It has always been a crime but I've never had a noncitizen case referred to me. When we got 63 of them, we said, 'We will look at them,'" Dow told NPR. "It is our duty to uphold California law."
Loyola Law School professor Justin Levitt, who was a White House adviser on voting rights in the Biden administration, said he expects "a trickle of actual follow-through on actual cases" of noncitizens voting. "And that is also entirely consistent with everything we knew for decades — which is that this does happen, but it doesn't happen very often."
What remains to be seen is whether the Justice Department will retreat from the criminal threats federal officials have waged against local election officials, or try to escalate those further.
In letters delivered to every California county in October, DOJ officials warned: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime."
President Trump added on Truth Social: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"
In the days before Election Day, officials in Los Angeles County as well as Bay Area counties, including Santa Clara and Sonoma, received subpoenas from their local U.S. attorney's office to turn over records this month.
In Sonoma, the subpoena is for records about an individual the DOJ alleges may have voted in a past election without being a U.S. citizen, as well as records about how county officials responded to DOJ requests to segregate ballots of people on its list of possible noncitizens, according to Sonoma County Counsel Joshua Myers.
The Oct. 21 subpoena sent to Los Angeles County, which was reviewed by NPR, requests records related to how the registrar-recorder's office screens for unlawful voting by noncitizens, as well as records responding to federal correspondence, including the demand to segregate ballots.
The DOJ said it does not comment on alleged subpoenas. But the substance of the subpoenas has raised questions about whether there may be a criminal probe targeted at counties.
Williams of Santa Clara County declined to speak about the subpoenas but said criminal threats against government employees who are trying to lawfully administer elections "strikes at the heart of what it means to live in a free society."
Looking forward, Williams said he is hoping for a way to productively collaborate with the federal government again.
"We should be aligned — federal, state and local government — in facilitating every citizen exercising their right to vote. And of course, we want voter rolls that don't include noncitizens," he said. "There's no disagreement about that."
Inflated and inaccurate lists
Another hurdle for the federal government's efforts to publicize purported noncitizens on voter rolls is the inaccuracies in its tallies so far.
Trump claimed in July there were 250,000 noncitizens registered in four states, including in California. But state officials pushed back on the data, and federal officials admitted the earlier numbers were a "ceiling" of potential noncitizens. In mid-October, federal officials had sent California its list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote in the state.
The federal government has never maintained a complete list of U.S. citizens. Trump administration efforts to cobble together citizenship data from various sources have led to naturalized citizens being mistakenly flagged as noncitizens, and data experts have warned the federal government's methodology in California was likely to also lead to false matches.
The weekend before Election Day, a federal judge allowed data experts from University of California Los Angeles' Voting Rights Project to analyze the DOJ's list of 20,000 names. The analysis found 42% did not appear on California's current voter roll and that naturalized citizens were on the list.
Separately, several California counties have noted the lists from DOJ were riddled with duplicates and obvious inaccuracies.
Santa Cruz County's top election official, Tricia Webber, wrote in an email that of the 81 people DOJ had listed as suspected noncitizens registered to vote in her county, "more than half are not registered in Santa Cruz County; some names do not match any person currently registered or previously registered," and some dates of birth "were wildly inaccurate with some dates appearing well into the future like 2044."
Even DOJ attorneys acknowledged in court hearings under questioning from judges that there have been flaws with federal lists of likely noncitizens.
U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton nominee, who was presiding over the federal government's lawsuit against California, had planned to hold proceedings that would assess the accuracy of DOJ's lists. That will no longer happen since the DOJ dropped its lawsuit.
For Loyola Law School's Levitt, questions remain about whether federal officials violated the Privacy Act by using California voter roll data for this project without following required public notice procedures.
And with Democrats winning control of Congress, lawmakers could hold hearings that probe deeper into how federal officials came up with their list, said David Becker, the executive director for the Center for Election Innovation and Research.
"I think we're going to have some very serious scrutiny of the Department of Homeland Security and their methodology as they assisted the administration in its failed effort to try to demonstrate there was widespread noncitizen voting in this country," Becker said.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. Hundreds of roaming cows wreak havoc in North Macedonian town, frustrating farmers
Residents of Kriva Palanka in North Macedonia are dealing with a herd of over 1,000 roaming cattle
KRIVA PALANKA, North Macedonia -- They descend from the surrounding hills, mostly at night, chomping their way through gardens and crops to satiate their hunger.
For years, residents of Kriva Palanka, a farming town of about 19,000 people in northeastern North Macedonia, have struggled with a herd of roaming cattle that has grown to more than 1,000 animals, destroying property and threatening their livelihood.
It's not just crops. The wandering cows pose a serious risk to the town's water supply and to drivers on a road that leads to neighboring Bulgaria, residents say.
Many fault the country's bureaucratic maze for failing to enforce a 2024 Food and Veterinary Agency order to seize the herd from their three owners.
And even when authorities took legal action against one of the owners, bureaucratic failures derailed the case and allowed the owner to walk free, Kriva Palanka Mayor Sashko Mitovski said.
Mitovski said residents have had enough and are staging protests to urge authorities to take action.
He is asking the conservative government of Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski to declare a 30-day state of emergency in the municipality for authorities to resolve the bovine problem once and for all.
“The number of cattle has increased from 400 four years ago to more than 1,000 today,” Mitovski told The Associated Press.
“We convened a crisis management headquarters because we concluded that, for years, none of the responsible institutions had shown either the willingness, commitment or capacity and resources to resolve the problem.”
Pensioner Lazo Stamenkovski, 71, who lives on the town's outskirts, said the cattle have destroyed more than 150 trees in his orchard.
“They constantly destroy the produce in my garden, wander onto the highway and endanger traffic safety on the road leading to Bulgaria," Stamenkovski told the AP.
Several residents of a neighborhood on the town's outskirts said the animals were not to blame, but the system was. They said some angry residents have beaten the cows and in some cases even slaughtered them.
“The government is responsible for everything that is happening to us. Not just this government, but all previous governments as well,” Venka Nikolovska, 59, a housewife from Kriva Palanka, told the AP. “We are all suffering — both people and animals.”
Despite their frustration, residents haven’t lost their sense of humor.
One man standing on the bridge over the Kriva Reka river that runs through the town said that the cows had gorged on the flowers in his backyard.
“Next time, I’ll prepare a flower salad and invite the cows to a party,” he said.
Mitovski said the cows roam freely through 34 surrounding villages and he blamed the Food and Veterinary Agency for not enforcing its own order to seize the cattle from its three owners.
"Since 2024, the herd has been the property of the Food and Veterinary Agency. The absurdity is that the agency issued the seizure order but has failed to enforce it,” he said, adding that the municipality has no legal authority to intervene.
The mayor said some cattle died near the town's main water sources last year, potentially poisoning the supply. He again faulted the Food and Veterinary Agency for failing to take action.
A government spokesperson did not immediately respond to an AP request for comment Friday evening.
One of the cattle owners was charged and detained last year for obstructing an agency operation to seize the animals. But Mitovski said the owner was released from custody after an agency inspector testified in court that he hadn't obstructed the attempted seizure.
“What I am saying is that this is an interconnected system involving serious wrongdoing by numerous people, and it is difficult to determine where it ends,” Mitovski said.
He said a government declaration of a temporary state of emergency would provide authorities with the money and resources needed to resolve the problem permanently.
Based on current livestock market prices, the value of the herd is estimated at between 360,000 and 570,000 euros ($385,000 to $610,000).
Some residents point out that the government could put the cattle up for sale at an affordable price so people could buy them and take care of them.
That could help many in the country of 1.8 million people, at least one-third of whom live in poverty.
“North Macedonia imports meat, milk, vegetables and fruit, while 1,000 cows roam unchecked across the country and destroy the farms,” Nikolovska said. “It makes no sense.”

Whoop Humans is a social network designed for fitness enthusiasts
Members can only share data from their Whoop wearables as guarantee of authenticity.
Whoop, the company behind the popular screenless wearable trackers, has launched a social network for users who like sharing their exercise details and fitness efforts called Whoop Humans. It's a rather unusual name, so you might be wondering how the company decided on it. Well, Will Ahmed, the CEO of Whoop, described it as the "most verifiably human network ever launched." Members can share their fitness data on the social network, including their sleep, recovery, strain and activities information. In all cases, the data comes from a Whoop wearable. That's "real-world information that cannot simply be generated as a conventional text post" at a time when "traditional social networks are increasingly filled with artificial content," the company said in its announcement.
Whoop already has Teams, which connects users through groups and leaderboards. But the new social network lets users follow friends and family directly to comment and react to their posts. The company envisions a social network, wherein people can check in on each other based on their progress. The idea is for members to be able to congratulate each other when they reach their goals or to be able to remind a friend to take it easy if they see the other's "Recovery" data is low. Hard to imagine most people taking an interest in another's fitness information, but people who are very much into fitness might see value in the social network.
In addition to being able to share fitness data, members will also be able to share photos from their workouts with a feature called "Moments." They can keep those Moments private, however, and, thankfully, they can choose which workout types or achievements appear on the social network. Just because they're wearing a Whoop doesn't mean their data will automatically be shared. Members can still update their sharing preferences any time they want. Whoop Humans is now live and available through the company's app.

Microsoft Corp. said it was making progress in efforts to restore access to its flagship software and end an outage that has paralyzed government offices, traders and businesses globally.
The company said in an update posted at about 9 a.m. New York time that it was seeing improvements in service availability, “with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Still, the company warned that users of more than 20 products and services may continue to encounter errors.
That includes Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence tool, whose users experienced a second day of missed meeting invitations and unresponsive web pages on Friday. Previous disruptions have rarely lasted more than several hours.
Quick answers to key questions
Microsoft said a core process on some servers became overwhelmed, causing them to stop responding. The precise technical cause had not been established, and the company said it had no evidence of malicious activity.
Outlook, Teams and Copilot were among the affected services, along with other Microsoft 365 products and services. Users also reported problems with email, calendars, workplace applications and cloud services.
Microsoft reported improvements, including reduced email queues approaching normal levels, but warned that users of more than 20 products and services could still encounter errors. It did not provide a specific time for full restoration.
Organizations reported disrupted email and communications, and some business operations were postponed or delayed. Government offices in several countries also faced email or service-access problems.
Microsoft said there was no evidence of malicious activity behind the disruption. The company had not yet established the precise technical cause.
The company provided near hourly updates of its efforts to fix its malfunctioning systems and route user traffic away from affected servers since the issues started Thursday afternoon, occasionally pointing to signs of recovery that proved fleeting. It was unclear what caused the outage, though the company described “a core process” on some servers becoming overwhelmed, causing them to stop responding entirely. Initial efforts to identify the problem and deploy a fix were stifled by further server errors.
Microsoft said it would provide more detail after the disruption was over, adding that there was no evidence of malicious activity.
The shares fell less than 1% as the markets opened in New York on Friday.
Companies relying on Microsoft systems, including Swiss luxury group Richemont and US-based truck and bus manufacturer Workhorse Group Inc., had to postpone earnings releases this week. Richemont has since filed its report.
PVH Corp., the apparel conglomerate that owns the Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger brands, announced Thursday that it would cut about 4% of its global workforce. Some of the difficult conversations, scheduled to start in Asia on Friday morning, did not take place because of the outages, leaving employees uncertain of their future at the company, according to a person familiar with the matter, who requested anonymity to describe private matters. PVH did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The outage shows the ubiquity of Microsoft’s email, chat and corporate software and is another example of the risks of relying on a small number of providers for critical technology. While most glitches are fixed quickly, faulty updates and server troubles at one key technology provider can ripple across the global economy. A 15-hour disruption at Amazon Web Services last year hit hundreds of websites. A faulty software update from cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. in 2024 grounded flights and crashed systems around the world, causing billions of dollars in damages.
“The technology market is concentrated among a few providers that deliver most of the services, and we take those services for granted,” said Stefano Mele, a Rome-based senior lawyer at Gianni & Origoni who specializes in cybersecurity. “That concentration of hardware, software and IT services can create a problem when there are no backup services supplied by other providers, based in different parts of the world and operating under different national flags.”
Users in more than 70 countries reported problems accessing Microsoft’s products, according to Downdetector, which recorded hundreds of thousands of complaints. Cybersecurity software, file-sharing services and administrator tools, were also disrupted. The company sells those products, along with workplace staples like Word and Excel, in a bundle under the M365 brand. The package has more than 450 million commercial users, the company said last month.
In the UK, the National Health Service had to reschedule some procedures after the outage impacted communications, people familiar with the matter said. Guy’s and St. Thomas’ warned patients that email was offline, though the London hospital’s procedures were going ahead as planned. A number of local police forces also said they couldn’t take crime reports online, according to the Guardian newspaper.
Traders in Singapore, Indian brokerages and officials in Tokyo also reported issues with Microsoft services on Friday. Euronext sent a warning that its email communications were unavailable.
Japan’s finance ministry said in a statement that it had been unable to receive emails for most of the day. Without access to their email, government ministries resorted to pinning up paper notices to inform journalists about daily schedules.
Staffers at the Reserve Bank of Australia were also impacted, with Outlook down across departments at the bank, but critical operations ran normally. In New Zealand, immigration officials paused the processing of all visa applications.

Twenty years after the death of Ferenc Puskas, who led Hungary’s Magical Magyars to Olympic gold in 1952 and the World Cup final two years later, I went looking for his legacy on the streets of Budapest.
A hotel employee knew little about him. And a volunteer at the event I was covering offered much the same response. Whether this reflected limited knowledge or simply a reluctance to talk was difficult to tell. But for a man whose name adorns Hungary’s national stadium, Puskas was proving an elusive subject outside it.
At the arena, however, his presence was easier to find.
The Puskas Museum occupies the surviving tower of the old Nepstadion. It was the second floor, dressed in white and gold, that captivated me. At its centre stands a large chalice assembled from gilded trophies. Around it, individual spaces honour members of Hungary’s 1952 Olympic champion Golden Team, including Jozsef Bozsik, Gyula Lorant and Jozsef Zakarias. Their portraits give the alcoves the appearance of small chapels.
The resemblance is deliberate. The gallery evokes the idea that, under a communist regime that suppressed religious life, stadiums became places of collective devotion.
In a museum bearing Puskas’ name, his teammates have their own spaces and stories. Their presence is a reminder that Hungary’s greatest footballing achievements belonged to a generation, even if its captain came to embody them.
Puskas scored 84 goals in 85 international appearances and captained Hungary to Olympic gold and the 1954 World Cup final. Alongside the likes of Sandor Kocsis and Nandor Hidegkuti, he formed the heart of the Magical Magyars, a team that was once the most feared side in international football.
For Guamy, a visitor from London, the reverence recalled another city’s relationship with its greatest footballer.
“He is the biggest name in Hungarian football. When you see his name on the front door, it is absolutely beautiful. It is like Cruyff in Amsterdam,” he said.
Puskas had lived to receive that affection. When the old stadium was named after him in 2002, he was already living with Alzheimer’s disease. Released from hospital for the August ceremony, he was driven around the ground to receive the crowd’s greeting.
Hungary was giving a lasting place to his name while illness was taking its toll on his memory.
Beyond the tributes to its golden generation, however, the country is dealing with a less glorious footballing reality. Hungary has not appeared at a World Cup since 1986.
Ariana, our guide at the arena, made no secret of her dislike of Troy Parrott, the Republic of Ireland forward whose hat-trick here ended Hungary’s hopes of reaching the 2026 World Cup. In her view, Hungary had fallen asleep in the second half.
In that qualifier in November 2025, the home side had led 2-1 at half-time. Parrott equalised in the 80th minute, then completed his hat-trick deep into stoppage time to send Ireland into the play-offs.
But there has been progress. Three successive European Championship appearances, from 2016 to 2024, restored a regular place at a major tournament. But the World Cup remains elusive, and the burden of ending that absence has fallen on a generation led by Liverpool midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai.
The comparisons with Puskas are inevitable, even if the two belong to vastly different footballing eras.
During my visit, I met a father and son from Kyiv. They had five hours in Budapest and had chosen to spend time at the arena. The boy wanted Szoboszlai to reach Puskas’s level.
Szoboszlai, however, has been cautious about the comparison. In a 2021 interview with FIFA, he described it as a sensitive subject: Puskas was Hungary’s greatest player, while his own career was only beginning. Matching those achievements by retirement, he said, would make him immensely proud.
The two face very different challenges. Puskas belonged to a Hungary that expected to compete with the world’s best, while Szoboszlai captains a team that is trying to return to that stage after four decades.
At a nearby coffee shop, the owner’s thoughts were on the next match. Hungary will visit Georgia on Saturday before hosting Northern Ireland on Tuesday, November 17, in its final group fixture of the 2026-27 UEFA Nations League.
He recalled that the team’s previous home match had been in October. When I mentioned that Tuesday would mark 20 years since Puskas’s death, he admitted he had not known about the anniversary. But he hoped the stadium would be full and that Hungary would beat Northern Ireland to make the occasion even more special
On Tuesday, another Hungarian team will play beneath Puskas’ name. The hope is that the ground built to honour him will one day become the stage for new heroes and new memories.

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) indicated that it was considering steps to capture peak levels of particulate matter (PM), a major pollutant, that exceed the existing monitoring range, after air quality data from several government monitoring stations in Delhi went missing for hours during the pollution spike following Deepavali on Sunday.
The Hindu reported on Monday (November 9, 2026) that the data gaps had led to an artificially lower official air quality index (AQI), making air quality appear better than it actually was, according to experts.
In a statement on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) , the CPCB said PM levels were measured only up to 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³) for AQI calculations, which explained the missing data on Deepavali night, when actual concentrations exceeded this limit.
“The PM analysers deployed at the time of introduction of the NAQI (National Air Quality Index) [in 2015] were calibrated for a measurement range of 0-1,000 µg/m³. Accordingly, consistent with this, the designed system of automated data validation treats hourly readings beyond the calibrated range as outside range, and such readings are not used in the computation,” the CPCB statement read.
“During extreme episodes, which are occasional, like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of the relevant pollutant for the concerned station,” the statement added.
Deliberations under way
The CPCB said internal deliberations and consultations on processing data “beyond system design range” were under way.
The CPCB also said spikes in ambient pollutant concentrations, such as those caused by firecrackers bursting, are episodic and short-lived. “The NAQI recognises that prolonged exposure, rather than a momentary reading, is a more relevant indicator of ill effects on human health,” the statement read.
Under the AQI calculation methodology adopted by the CPCB in 2015, the overall index is based on eight parameters and is calculated only if data are available for a minimum of three pollutants, out of which one should necessarily be either PM2.5 or PM10.
“The methodology was formed in 2015 and at that time it was decided that the accuracy was good only up to 1,000 µg/m³ and both PM2.5 and PM10 were capped at it for calculation of AQI. But the equipment got better with time and Delhi’s air quality analysers and instruments were also updated, but the methodology was never updated after that,” an official told The Hindu.
“But now there are discussions of raising this cap so that peak values above 1,000 µg/m³ could be measured,” the official added.
Of the 59 air quality monitoring stations in Delhi, 46 are operated by the Delhi government’s Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), which does not calculate the AQI. The DPCC had recorded PM2.5 and PM10 levels exceeding 1,000 µg/m³ on Deepavali night, though several readings were initially missing.
The CPCB uses data from these 46 stations, along with readings from other monitoring stations, to calculate the AQI.
Air quality improves
Meanwhile, Delhi’s air quality improved to the ‘poor’ category on Tuesday (November 10, 2026), with the 24-hour average AQI recorded at 299, just below the ‘very poor’ threshold of 300.
Experts attributed the improvement to increased wind speeds and said air quality was likely to improve further over the next few days.

Indonesia's VP resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president resigned on Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.
Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.
Raka didn't comment as he left the meeting.
"There will always be political dynamics in public office, that's normal," his father, Widodo, told reporters from his hometown in Solo, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.
"We will continue to support President Prabowo's government, especially programs that serve the interests of the broader public," he said, referring to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.
The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.
Prabowo accepts Raka's resignation
Raka had offered to resign Tuesday during a meeting with Prabowo, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy. He personally delivered his resignation letter to the president on Wednesday.
Prabowo addressed the nation Thursday afternoon after holding a meeting with Raka and the parliamentary leadership at the presidential palace.
Flanked by Raka and top leaders of parliament, a grim-looking Prabowo said that he accepted Raka's resignation "with a heavy heart" and praised the vice president for showing "courage, responsibility and statesmanship" by stepping down.
"He chose to resign for the greater interest of the nation, the state and the Indonesian people," Prabowo said in a televised statement. "He has been a great help to me, from our election campaign through the past two years of government. Many of our achievements would not have been possible without his contribution."
Prabowo praised Raka's dedication and hard work, highlighting Raka's visits to 35 provinces and 149 regencies and cities to inspect 303 government projects during the past two years as examples of his commitment to public service.
"I will continue to support him, and I pray that he and his family are given strength during what is undoubtedly a difficult time," Prabowo said.
Under the Indonesian Constitution, a vice presidential vacancy doesn't trigger a new election. The office remains vacant until the People's Consultative Assembly elects a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.
Long-running allegations over candidacy lead to court disputes
The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents that Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.
A subsequent petition, submitted Wednesday to the House leadership by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties, began a parliamentary process that could have led to his impeachment.
The push for his impeachment was driven largely by long-running allegations that Raka's candidacy was enabled by a Constitutional Court ruling that critics see as a conflict of interest and evidence of weak political accountability and dynastic privilege.
Before Prabowo chose him as his running mate for the 2024 election, Raka didn't meet the age requirement of 40 for vice presidential candidates. But the court's contentious ruling in October 2023 carved an exception allowing those who served or had been elected as regional leaders to run at a younger age.
Under Indonesian election law, a presidential or vice-presidential candidate must have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education. Because Raka completed his secondary education overseas, he was required to provide documents showing that his qualifications were equivalent to an Indonesian high school diploma.
Raka was the first vice president of the country to resign before the end of a term since the fall of dictator Suharto and the start of Indonesia's democratic reforms in 1998.
Parliamentary leaders were due to convene immediately to begin the process of selecting a replacement, Speaker Ahmad Muzani said.
"We ask for the prayers and support of all Indonesians so that this democratic process can proceed smoothly and serve as a constructive new precedent in our constitutional system," Muzani told reporters.

How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles
Measles spreads incredibly fast. For the last few months, so has Dale Weiser's phone number.
Weiser is the clinical services supervisor for the Chester County Health Department in south-central Pennsylvania. Since August, she's been driving out to Amish homes to vaccinate people against measles. She says it usually starts with a phone call.
"I was at a house, like, at 4:30 in the afternoon, and I had a phone call at 8 the next morning saying, 'hey, I heard you were down the street. Can you come do that at my house?'" she says of a typical request she gets from Amish families. So far, she's administered more than 400 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in Amish homes.
The house calls are part of the state of Pennsylvania's strategy to wage war on measles by flipping the script on traditional public health messaging. Instead of advertising vaccinations loudly, health officials have launched a quiet word-of-mouth campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been particularly hard hit by the country's worst measles outbreak in 35 years. The state has confirmed six measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases so far — though the true count is likely much higher, since many people who get sick don't seek medical care.
Lower vaccination rates
Surveys suggest only about a third of Amish families in the region vaccinate their children. That's left the Amish community especially vulnerable to measles, one of the most contagious diseases.
There's no religious edict against vaccination among the Amish. It's very much seen as a family and individual choice, says Weiser. Often, she says, these decisions are driven by practical and cultural factors.
"They don't have health insurance. They're not interacting with the mainstream medical society. And measles wasn't a problem for 30 years, so there was no real risk to not being vaccinated, at least for measles," Weiser says.
But as measles cases have piled up in Pennsylvania, Weiser says many Amish families have changed their minds about getting the MMR vaccine. And when they do, she hops in her car and brings the shots to them.
"When I arrive at their home, there's usually a small child that will run from the back of the house to the barn to tell the men that there's somebody strange in the driveway, or that the nurse is here," she says.
A patient, personalized approach to outreach
Some days, Weiser will vaccinate a single family in their kitchen. Other times, she'll find dozens of people gathered to get the shot. She's also fielded a lot of questions. Some, like what's in the vaccine and potential side effects, are things anyone would ask, she says.
"But I was caught off guard when I was asked if there were tracking chips in the vaccine, and I was like, whoa. Flashback to COVID. Where did you hear that?" she recalls.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
As with the general population, vaccine misinformation has made its way to the Amish community. And when she encounters it, Weiser takes the time to explain why the rumors are false.
Chester County Public Health Director Jeanne Franklin says this kind of patient, personalized approach has helped build trust among the local Amish – who, along with conservative Mennonites, are known as the Plain community because of their simple way of life.
"That's why we said it has to be boots on the ground in the communities. It's not just because they were a Plain community, it was because we needed to be seen as caring people," Franklin says.
Instead of relying on traditional top-down, rigid public health messaging, her staff has spent a lot of time quietly visiting Amish church leaders and businesses, introducing themselves and asking community leaders if they would hand out flyers advertising vaccine clinics. "One of them said, 'Come on back with a clinic' at his restaurant. And he helped spread the word," Franklin says.
Vaccine questions and misinformation
When I stopped by the restaurant, Honey Brook Barbecue in Honey Brook, Pa., an area with a sizable Amish community, I found the manager grilling chicken in an outdoor tent. Like many Amish people NPR talked to, he spoke on the condition of anonymity in keeping with his community's tradition of not drawing attention to oneself.
The manager says 24 people showed up to get vaccinated at his restaurant back in August, all drawn by word of mouth. He says he decided to host the clinic for two reasons: to protect the general public and to protect his own community. He said he didn't want people blaming the Amish for spreading measles.
But he says other people in the Amish community who don't regularly interact with the public aren't getting vaccinated. For some, it's because of cultural reasons, but he says others are concerned about what they've heard is in the MMR vaccine.
"In my community, a lot of it has to do with what people think is in it," the manager says of the MMR vaccine. One concern he's heard repeatedly is that the vaccine contains parts of aborted fetuses.
That is a myth often repeated by anti-vaccine forces, and it is one heard in conversations with Amish people in Lancaster County, home to around 45,000 Amish people. It's also the county with a third of the state's measles cases — more than 500 confirmed cases.
At the Amish-owned Gordonville Book Store, where a buggy is parked outside, I meet a shopper named Lydia Esh. She says she, her husband and six adult children had all previously been vaccinated against measles. But none of her 13 grandchildren have gotten the shot, because their parents had heard that the MMR vaccine had changed and now contained aborted fetus parts — which is false.
There is some evidence that anti-vaccine groups have been targeting the Amish in recent years, says Steve Nolt, a professor at Elizabethtown College who has written numerous books about Amish history and culture. For example, he points to an advertisement questioning the safety of childhood vaccines published in The Pennsylvania Busy Beaver, an advertising publication with a large Amish readership.
But in conversations around Lancaster, I also find evidence that public health outreach efforts are working. One member of the Plain community, a visibly pregnant woman outside an Amish-owned hardware store, says her husband and two children recently got vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She asked NPR not to use her name, as did an Amish man working at a produce stall in an Amish market. He says he recently got vaccinated because "measles is scary."
Linda Beth Fisher, an 18-year-old Amish woman behind the counter at the Gordonville Book Store, says she is concerned that several Amish people in her area have died in the measles outbreak, but she's not sure what to believe about the MMR vaccine.
"Personally, I'm kind of leery of it. I'm not sure why," Fisher says. "I guess I've just kind of heard that they're not good, but I've also heard that they are good. So I just feel like it's two sides of the story. Would you encourage people to get it?"
"They almost always come back"
These types of concerns often surface at pop-up vaccine clinics like one recently hosted at the Christiana Fire Company in Lancaster County. The Pennsylvania Department of Health hosts these events in Lancaster three or four times a week — all advertised by word of mouth, says Dr. Jennifer Wallace. As medical director for the department's Bureau of Community Health Systems, she oversees pop-up clinics and outreach to vulnerable communities across Pennsylvania.
Wallace says when members of the Plain community come with questions, "We're here to give them that information and then let them ponder it. They can ask any questions they want to and then let them either get vaccinated if they choose or take that information home. Think about it. Talk with their bishops. Talk with their community. They almost always come back."
Wallace says many who end up coming are families with multiple children. Tables set up around the firehouse are strewn with crayons, coloring books and bubble wands to keep young ones entertained while parents fill out paperwork.
"And then you see the kids get vaccinated and you can almost see the mother's shoulders relax over time as each child gets that shot," she says. "We've had some mothers cry afterwards because they're just so relieved."
The state health department says 30 people attended the Christiana firehouse clinic, 24 of whom got vaccinated. That included a father and his three sons who arrived for their second doses.

For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.
Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.
“I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them. The work he had taken up to help his family has left him dependent on others, with no certainty about what his future will look like.
By some estimates, Panipat processes more than 1m tons of used clothing from across the world every year, making it one of the world’s largest textile recycling hubs. In the city’s 20,000 factories, employing about 300,000 people, discarded clothes are shredded into yarn and made into finished products, including home furnishings for brands such as H&M Home, Ikea, Primark, Tesco and Walmart.
But the fast-fashion industry, built on buying more and more clothes and wearing them less, carries a devastating cost for workers tackling its waste. Ramesh Chaudhary, an environmental activist who has worked in Panipat’s labour department, has been tracking reports of injuries and amputations across the city for the past five years. He estimates that at least one worker a day loses a limb, rising to as many as five on some days.
“Every day, we come across cases of workers injured inside factories, sometimes losing a hand or a leg, and sometimes even dying,” Chaudhary says. He gathers his information through a network of labour contractors who supply workers to factories across Panipat. But not all news of injuries reaches him, he says, suggesting the scale of the problem could be greater.
Between 17 and 24 August this year, the Guardian monitored reports from 11 private hospitals and two government hospitals in Panipat. In that period, six cases of textile workers with severe limb injuries were reported: two had lost an arm, another man lost both, one lost a hand, one lost a leg and the sixth their fingers.
Such injuries are common in Panipat’s factories, says Chaudhary, because machinery often lacks the necessary safety mechanisms. If a worker gets caught in a spinning machine, he says, cutting the power may not stop it immediately. By the time the machine comes to a halt, a worker may already have catastrophic injuries.
During numerous visits to spinning units and factories, the Guardian did not see anyone wearing any kind of safety gear. None of the workers interviewed reported having safety training.
India’s 1948 Factories Act places a duty on factory owners to protect workers’ health and safety. It requires serious workplace accidents to be reported to the authorities. But the effectiveness of safety oversight remains a concern, says Sandeep Sachdeva, co-founder of the Safe in India Foundation, which works to reduce industrial injuries.
“Factories are often audited by buyers, especially where quality and critical components are involved, and inspected by government industrial safety and health departments. Buyer audits tend to focus more on commercial requirements and product quality than on workplace safety or working conditions,” he says.
“Government inspections are selected through a central software system, but inspectors are now required to inform factories before visiting. Their role is now that of a facilitator-cum-inspector – a shift that undermines the effectiveness of inspections, particularly in factories with unsafe working conditions.”
For workers, losing a limb means losing their livelihood. Ramashankar Singh, who is in his fifties, from Chapra in Bihar, spent 18 years in Panipat’s factories before an accident last year led to him having a leg amputated.
It happened when a hot ball bearing fell on his foot. Ramashankar’s injury was first just wrapped in discarded cloth, before the factory owner sent him to a pharmacy.
The wound worsened as the infection spread. When Ramashankar approached his employer again, the owner agreed to arrange treatment and admitted him to a private hospital. By then, the infection had progressed so far that doctors had to amputate his leg above the knee.
“The factory owner said he would give me another job, possibly as a cook or a security guard at the factory,” Ramashankar says. “But that never happened.” The owner also said he would help him secure a government disability pension, but he has received no pension since the accident and relies on a prosthetic leg provided by a charitable organisation.
After so much of his life spent in a factory, Ramashankar says: “I have almost forgotten how to live without work. Much of my day now passes lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling fan.”
He also struggles with guilt that he has become a burden on his family.
India’s textile industry is the country’s second-largest source of employment after agriculture, directly employing more than 45 million people. An estimated 92% of its workforce is informally employed. In Panipat, more than 90% of workers are employed informally, says Ina Bahuguna, programme manager at the Estonia-based Reverse Resources, which monitors the city’s textile waste.
“Formal employment contracts and the social security benefits that accompany them, including pensions, are largely limited to workers in management, clerical roles and some specialised jobs, such as tailoring,” says Bahuguna.
Most workers on the factory floor lack these protections, leaving those who suffer serious injuries particularly vulnerable. Without formal employment or adequate social security coverage, they are left without employer-backed compensation, rehabilitation support or a source of income.
The Guardian asked several factory owners why they hired workers on a contractual or piece-rate basis rather than in permanent positions, and most cited the workers’ seasonal migration, saying some did not return to Panipat after travelling home.
For workers who sustain life-changing injuries, getting employers to pay for medical treatment can be a struggle. Indrapal Singh, who lost his arm in 2017, had worked in Panipat for 15 years, two and a half of those at the factory where he was injured. His hand was caught in a Chinese-made carding machine, which tore away the skin. He was given a painkilling injection but, as the infection worsened, his arm had to be amputated. The factory owner refused to pay his hospital bills.
Indrapal spent six years fighting his case through the courts, but says he received no compensation. The police told him that he had signed documents withdrawing his complaint, something Indrapal, who says he cannot read or write, disputes.
“I lost my arm, fought for six years, and in the end, all I got was a government pension of 5,700 rupees [£45]. The factory owner has faced no consequences, and the factory continues to operate as before,” he says.
Chaudhary says: “Workers have very little bargaining power when they are up against factory owners who are not only financially powerful but sometimes politically influential too. For many workers, taking them on in a legal fight is simply not an option.”
Arvind Kumar, the officer in charge at one of Panipat’s 12 police stations, says three workplace injury cases have been registered at his station so far this year. One involved the death of a worker. “Fewer than 1% of workplace injury cases reach the police and are formally registered,” he says.
Most cases, the officer says, are settled outside the formal legal system. Workers may receive a one-time payment towards medical bills, but then are generally left to manage the long-term consequences of their injuries on their own. The police rarely get involved.
For now, Suraj Kumar’’s family are grateful that the factory owner covered his hospital bills. They are not sure whether to register a police complaint.
“He [the owner] is like God to us. He is paying for our boy’s treatment,” says his mother, Sita.
Suraj struggles to imagine what comes next. “I thought that if I worked hard for two years, I could buy myself a motorcycle. I had so many things I wanted to do with my life. I never thought I would have to start by figuring out how to live without my arms.”

South Africa's ANC records worst-ever results in local elections
- Published
South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic".
While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 30.76% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 64.82% 20 years ago.
The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. In 2021 it won six. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.
The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second in the overall vote with 24.64%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party came third overall with 9.76%, unseating the ANC as winner in the city of Durban, while the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6.22%.
"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC," said secretary-general Fikile Mbalula on Saturday. "We knew this disaster is coming, we're staring at it. As we got into elections, the cost of living of our people was too high. The middle class have turned on the ANC in big numbers."
Entering the count centre tonight, South Africa's president and leader of the ANC Cyril Ramaphosa said: "We accept the will of the people however concerning it might be, we accept that this is how the people of South Africa in our towns, in our cities, in our metros have spoken - and this is their verdict, we accept it with humility. It is a decline that is concerning, that is how I characterise it."
It's a continuing decline for the ANC, which lost majority rule in the national elections in 2024 for the first time in its history. It then had to form a coalition government with a raft of other parties in what is now known as the GNU, or government of national unity.
While the Democratic Alliance made significant gains in the cities in these local elections, its overall vote share rose marginally from 21.83% in 2021, and was below the 26.9% it gained in 2016.
Voter turnout was 52.29%, an increase from 45.9% in 2021, when elections were held during the Covid pandemic.
"This election is delivering a devastating message to the ANC", said political analyst Susan Booysen. "It's an ANC in decline at local municipal level, at the metropolitan level, and when the results are reflected provincially and nationally, we see severe declines in ANC levels of support all around."
The reason for that decline in support is largely due to poor service delivery and infrastructure across the country, from water and power to sanitation. "These are huge problems," says Booysen, "and have really been affecting the lives of ordinary people, in the suburbs, in the townships, and in very dramatic ways."
The big picture looks even more bleak for the ANC. The party will elect a new leader next year as Cyril Ramaphosa comes to end of his term. He is due to stay on as president of the country until the next national elections in 2029, but there are few candidates lined up to succeed him in either role.
- ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline 
  - Published4 days ago
"It is sort of the end of the liberation movement era in South Africa," said political analyst William Gumede, "and the dominance of the liberation movement since the end of apartheid. So the ANC is going to be a party that by 2029 could be the second biggest rather than the biggest party. It may actually spiral into a long period of just total infighting. This is a new era for South Africa's politics and also the ANC."
The elections also saw a significant shift in voting patterns, with the DA, traditionally known as the "white party" for attracting a largely white vote, gaining more black votes. "We're moving towards a post-racial voting pattern in South Africa," added Gumede.
South Africa now faces days of local coalition building, with the three metropolitan municipalities in the province of Gauteng, the country's powerhouse, under particular scrutiny. The ANC may even find itself shut out in the cities of Johannesburg and Pretoria.
"We are now in a coalition country," said Gumede. "Essentially, what the voters are saying is, "Well, the ANC has dominated the last three decades, they didn't use their power to change the society for the good, so we don't want the dominant parties anymore, whether at national level, provincial level, or rather now at a local level. We actually want coalitions. We want people to work together."
Parties now have 14 days from the moment results were announced to negotiate coalitions.

US ground stop live updates: Passengers stranded and thousands of flights delayed as FAA order lifted
Over 9,000 flights were delayed Friday in the US

A ground stop for all planes in the U.S. was lifted Friday night after hours of chaos, with flights delayed and passengers stranded.
Around 8:30 p.m., Trump administration officials announced the order was over and said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy detailed that the nation’s aging traffic control system got “overloaded with data.”
The Federal Aviation Administration issued the stop around 4 p.m. Eastern Time, creating chaos at airports nationwide. Roughly 3,000 planes were in the air when the ground stop order was issued, Duffy said. Flights already in the air were allowed to land, but most were not allowed to leave.
Duffy warned that it would take some time to get the American aviation system back to normal after the order.
Passengers were stranded at airports waiting for information about when they might catch their flight. People found seats in the hallway and waited or checked their phones for the latest updates.
“I’m just bummed. I wanted to go home, I mean, it’s great to be here but not in the airport,” Emily Esterly told a Miami news station.
'I might cry at some point but not yet'
Though the ground stop has been lifted, the disruption for passengers was far from over.
From Boston to Seattle and New York to Los Angeles, passengers crowded departure halls and airline desks as delays and cancellations mounted and aircraft remained parked at gates.
Thousands of passengers faced being stranded overnight. Edward Kargbo, 50, from West Chester, Pennsylvania, had been scheduled to take a 9pm Ethiopian Airlines flight to Lomé, Togo.
Instead, he planned to spend the night at the airport before a rescheduled flight at 6am on Saturday.
“I have to squat the night here,” he said. “I’m stranded.”
Louise Maher, 47, was also caught up in the disruption at Newark after her British Airways flight to London was disrupted by the aviation meltdown.
“I might cry at some point but not yet,” she said.
In full: UK airports face major disruption as United States grounds all flights
UK airports face major disruption as United States grounds all flights
Delays and cancellations in UK after US travel turbulence
Travellers in the UK are facing disruption after air traffic control problems brought flights to a standstill across the US.
The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted all flights nationwide for several hours on Friday “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” following communications problems at regional air traffic control centres.
London Heathrow’s website said an 8.20am flight to Dallas Fort Worth had been cancelled, along with a 9.55am flight to Charlotte and a 10am flight to Houston.
A 10.35am British Airways flight to New York City was also cancelled, while multiple other outgoing flights on US carriers were listed as delayed.
Responding to customers on X, British Airways apologised for possible delays and cancellations.
It also recommended passengers travel to the airport as planned to arrive for the original departure time, unless informed otherwise.
A British Airways spokesperson said: “Following the air traffic control issue in the United States, our flights are operating as normal.
“Whilst this matter was entirely outside of our control, we want to thank our customers for bearing with us, and our colleagues for supporting them and helping to minimise any disruption.”
A spokesperson for Manchester Airport said there is not expected to be any “significant” delays on Saturday.
It is understood the situation is expected to have minimal impact on London Gatwick Airport.
Hertz see an increase in car rental activity
According to NBC News, Hertz car rental saw an increase in one-way rental requests from travelers impacted by the ground stop.
"Our teams are closely monitoring demand and working quickly to accommodate travelers and manage vehicle availability across our network as conditions evolve,” the company said.
JetBlue expects disruptions on Saturday
JetBlue warned that, because of the ground stop it expected disruptions to continue on Saturday.
“We expect disruptions to continue into tomorrow, including additional cancellations,” the company posted on social media Friday night.
The company said passengers could find a fee waiver online. They could also find options for rebooking their flight.

The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.
In the video, Hegseth and four others posed on the steps in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a monument in Arlington, Virginia, that marks the grave of the unidentified service members from the U.S. who died in wars since World War I.
As Hegseth's group walked up the stairs away from the monument (time code 00:41), someone could be heard talking and laughing. The U.S. Army Sentinel on guard shouted in response, "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
It was not clear who in Hegseth's group talked and laughed, though one woman who posed with Hegseth could be seen gesturing with her hands as the group walked up the stairs before the sentinel's reprimand.
Newsweek reported that the group caught talking and laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown soldier consisted of Hegseth, his wife Jennifer Hegseth, his chief of staff Ricky Buria, his Deputy Chief of Staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
A photo from reputable photo repository Getty Images showed Hegseth's wife was present at the Veterans Day commemoration at Arlington Cemetery on Nov. 11 and wore a dark brown or burgundy dress that was also visible in CNN's coverage.
Because the other three people in the group stood with their backs to the camera, Snopes could not independently verify Newsweek's claim that they were Hegseth's senior staff.
Soldiers have guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington since March 1926. The Arlington National Cemetery wrote on its website that the guards initially "discouraged visitors from climbing or stepping on the Tomb."
The 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," has guarded the monument since April 6, 1948. Barbara Starr, CNN's former Pentagon correspondent, told (time code 11:24) the network on Nov. 11 that sentinels will correct any visitors who do not act with "respect and silence" at the tomb.
The incident at Arlington comes at a time when Hegseth is facing immense pressure over the war in Iran, which has been widely understood as a reason midterm voters moved away from the Republican Party in the November midterm elections.
On Nov. 10, the day before the incident at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, Republicans in the House blocked an attempt to impeach Hegseth. That same day, U.S. President Donald Trump signaled his continued support for Hegseth on Truth Social, calling the outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, who led the push for Hegseth's impeachment, a "TOTAL LOSER."

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

The Telangana Health Department has intensified its investigation into the alleged illegal oocyte (egg) collection racket, with inspections conducted at 27 of the 44 identified Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) facilities across the State. Officials have detected 13 regulatory violations in seven hospitals and issued show-cause notices to their managements.
Health Minister C. Damodar Rajanarasimha has directed the department to conduct a comprehensive investigation into alleged illegal activities being carried out under the guise of oocyte collection and initiate stringent action against institutions and individuals found violating prescribed regulations.
Acting on the Minister’s directions, task force teams have been inspecting IVF centres across the State for the past four days. Inspections at the remaining facilities are continuing.
Aspects of investigation
The department said further action would be initiated after a detailed examination of records seized by the police and information obtained from the National ART and Surrogacy Registry. The investigation also includes examining the involvement of women identified in connection with the case, doctors, IVF centres and intermediaries allegedly facilitating the activities.
As part of the investigation, the Health department officials visited the National ART and Surrogacy Registry in New Delhi on November 6 and sought details of the data submitted by registered ART clinics and ART banks operating in Telangana.
The department has reiterated that oocyte collection must strictly comply with the provisions of the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act and Rules. All ART clinics and ART banks operating in the State are required to obtain mandatory statutory registration and adhere to the prescribed regulatory framework.
The Health Department also cautioned women against falling prey to misleading assurances and financial inducements offered by intermediaries, warning that such arrangements could expose them to unauthorised medical procedures.

New Zealand workers say they were forced to ‘defecate in distribution aisles’ after bathroom breaks tracked by AI
Employees stage protest demanding guarantees for future

Workers at New Zealand's largest retailer said they were forced to defecate in the distribution aisles due to their bathroom breaks being monitored by artificial intelligence.
More than 300 workers at The Warehouse Group's distribution centres in Auckland and Christchurch staged protests this week over fears of major redundancies and employee privacy due to AI surveillance.
The Workers First Union alleged that there have been instances of staff urinating and defecating in distribution aisles due to their breaks being tracked by AI.
These claims were rejected by the Warehouse Group, which argued that "this has never happened".
Workers told public broadcaster RNZ that they feel they're being treated second-best to robots and feared for their future.
"Do I look like a robot? No. I don't," said one worker who has been working at a distribution centre for 23 years. "We are here to protest about these things [because it should be a human doing] the job, not a robot job."
Union organiser Hayley Courtney said having managers follow people to the toilet and "telling them off for a fundamental right is absolutely ludicrous". Ms Courtney said she had been fighting the issue for eight months.
Ms Courtney said workers were not resisting technological advances to improve efficiency, but wanted assurances about their future.
She claimed the company was bringing in a "massive robot" for stock picking, while AI-powered drones have replaced some members of the physical inventory team.
"And AI is now tracking how long people spend on bathroom breaks," she told The Post.
She added that there have been accidents due to staff "trying to hold on" instead of going to the toilet.
“We’d been finding things on the floor. It did stop once I put my foot down, but there were accidents on the floor; we don’t know who it was or anything. Obviously, it’s very humiliating if you’re forced into that position, but there were multiple occasions where this occurred,” she told the newspaper.
The company denied the allegations and said they were "shocked and appalled by the union's claim that our team members are urinating and defecating on the floor at work".
Warehouse Group chief people officer, Richard Parker, told RNZ: "We use technology, which is not AI as claimed, that has been commonly used in distribution centres around the world for decades to monitor efficiency through scanning devices. It has nothing to do with bathroom use."
He claimed that no roles had been lost because of stocktaking drones. "In fact, we currently have three additional temp roles in this area.
"The drones improve stock accuracy and the customer experience, while making our distribution centres safer by removing the need for people to work at height in machinery every night," Mr Parker said.
"No employer can guarantee what roles will look like in the future, but we will always consult with our team and look to retrain and redeploy people wherever we can in line with our obligations."
The Independent has reached out to the Warehouse for comment.

Indonesia’s Vice President Resigns as a Political Alliance Unravels
Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who is stepping down amid a scandal over his academic credentials, was a symbol of the partnership that elevated President Prabowo Subianto into office.
The vice president of Indonesia submitted his resignation to Parliament on Thursday, succumbing to a scandal about his academic credentials and injecting new political uncertainty in Southeast Asia’s largest economy.
Gibran Rakabuming Raka was elected as Indonesia’s youngest vice president in 2024, in a precipitous rise. He was a symbol of the partnership between his father, the outgoing president, Joko Widodo, and the incoming leader, Prabowo Subianto, that elevated Mr. Prabowo into office.
“The relationship has clearly fractured,” said Yoes C. Kenawas, a political analyst at the Indonesian Survey Institute. With Mr. Gibran’s departure, “Prabowo is attempting to demonstrate that he has stepped out from Jokowi’s shadow,” he added, referring to the former leader by his nickname.
Initially a political outsider, Mr. Joko came to be seen as a transformative leader of Indonesia. He helped rehabilitate the image of Mr. Prabowo, a former special forces commander who was discharged from the military for his involvement in the abduction and torture of pro-democracy activists under the dictator Suharto. To many, Mr. Prabowo was a reminder of the country’s authoritarian past. But Mr. Joko endorsed Mr. Prabowo as his successor, with Mr. Gibran running on the same ticket.
The alliance between Mr. Joko and Mr. Prabowo was cast as one of political continuity. Many voters had seen Mr. Gibran’s vice presidency as a way for Mr. Joko to continue his political influence.
“From the beginning, Gibran was brought on board solely to serve as a ‘vote-getter,’ rather than as an integral part of a unified leadership team intended to strengthen the performance of the Prabowo administration,” said Titi Anggraini, a lecturer of constitutional law at University of Indonesia.
