For a woman who has been a witness to some of the most significant political moments in modern Indian history, Sonia Gandhi likes to insist her life has been far from remarkable. “Oh, I don’t know that I would say it’s an extraordinary story,” she says, shifting uncomfortably.
It’s hard to reconcile this modest characterisation with the course her life has taken over the last 79 years. Born to a working-class family in a small town in northern Italy, today she sits at the heart of Indian political power, having weathered assassinations and personal tragedy to become one of the country’s most influential figures. She held Indira Gandhi’s bloodied body after the then-prime minster, her mother-in-law, was gunned down at their home in Delhi in 1984. She then became India’s first lady when her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, took his mother’s place as prime minister. And when Rajiv, too, was killed, she threw aside her distaste for politics to step up and lead his fragmenting party. In 2004, having taken Congress to electoral victory, she famously turned down the prime minister post. She can still boast of being the longest-serving president of Congress, both when India’s oldest political party was in power and later, when it became the flailing opposition. When Gandhi stepped down in 2017, her son Rahul was appointed her successor.
Gandhi’s entrance into Indian politics began in Cambridge in the 1960s when, at 18, while she was studying at a language school, she fell in love with a bright-eyed boy at a Greek restaurant. At the time, she had no idea that Rajiv was heir to India’s most consequential political dynasty. “It was a coup de foudre,” she says. “After that, nothing else really mattered. He was, first of all, a handsome man. But I think his eyes told of the way he was – of his inner self. He was loving, he was comforting, he was caring. Everything I could have possibly dreamed of.”
Only later would she learn that Rajiv’s grandfather was Jawaharlal Nehru, Indian freedom fighter and the country’s first prime minister, and his mother was Indira Gandhi, who in 1966 became India’s first female prime minister.
Does she still recognise herself in that innocent Italian girl who was swept off her feet and transplanted to an alien land and culture? “Not really,” she says quietly. “Too much has happened, too much has changed.”
We meet at the grand white Delhi bungalow she has lived in for 36 years – a relic of British colonial rule, where peacocks roam the grounds. It was in this house in 1991 that Gandhi heard her husband had been assassinated by Sri Lankan Tamil separatist terrorists. Over the years, as she took on the mantle of Congress leader, her home became the centre of party operations.
The ghosts of Congress leaders past loom large in her study. A painting of Nehru, photographs of Rajiv, a carved stone bust and portraits of Indira line the walls, while a painting of Mahatma Gandhi, the freedom fighter who shaped the ideology of Congress, also hangs prominently. Heavy gilded tomes fill the floor-to-ceiling wooden bookshelves, and a long meeting table dominates the space, but the vibrant rugs, patterned blinds and scattered antiques suggest Gandhi’s own light touch.
In a dark blue sari and maroon blouse, her signature neat grey hair pushed back with a black headband, Gandhi looks every inch the composed Indian political matriarch as she sits on the sofa. The only hint of her heritage is softly accented English and recognisably Italian gesticulation.
She has, she confesses, been very nervous and tense about our meeting. Gandhi has not done an interview in a decade, and throughout her life in the public eye, has tried fiercely to maintain her privacy. She has only agreed to this rare meeting to discuss her forthcoming memoir, a strikingly personal account of her life, and has asked her daughter Priyanka, also a senior Congress leader, to sit in for moral support.
India’s media has often cast her as cold and aloof, yet today she seems warm, open and often a little unsure of herself. She’s anxious about how personal the book is, worried it will be eviscerated by the Indian media, but suggests that after years of “horrible and crazy things written about me”, it will be comforting for people to know “the truth”.
Gandhi has good reason to be nervous of the press. In today’s India, the mainstream media landscape has been crushed into submission by the hardline, rightwing Modi government and is largely devoted to promoting the prime minister’s agenda, while mercilessly attacking the Congress party, in particular the Gandhi family. She does not hold back on criticism of Narendra Modi – accusing him of being an “authoritarian force bent upon changing the very nature of our country” – and of his party, BJP, which she says has “systematically dismantled our democratic institutions”.
The Hindu nationalist vision of India that Modi has enacted over his 12 years in power is directly opposed to the pluralistic, secular India that was championed by successive Congress leaders and which remains enshrined in India’s constitution. It has led to well-documented oppression of the country’s minority groups, in particular its 200 million Muslims.
“More than disappointing, it’s very painful, having known a different India,” Gandhi says. “In parliament, we are not allowed to debate. In the past, there were discussions, there were meetings between the opposition and the government, there was consultation. Now the opposition counts for nothing.”
Since Modi came to power, she has had barely any interaction with him; he tends to avoid eye contact when they’re in a room together – a stark contrast to the past, when opposition leaders would often meet the government and “treat each other with cordiality”.
A “Congress-free India” is one of the openly declared goals of Modi’s BJP, resulting in highly personal attacks on Gandhi and her children, who have found themselves with numerous police cases filed against them. As we talk, Gandhi’s phone lights up with a call from her son Rahul – later, we learn a judge has just cleared him of defamation in one of these many cases, this time for criticising Modi’s home minister back in 2018. “They are very vindictive and vicious. There doesn’t seem to be a heart there,” Gandhi says.
So effective is the BJP’s crackdown on any form of dissent or criticism – what Gandhi describes as an “atmosphere of fear” – that her memoir almost didn’t see the light of day in India. Penguin Random House India were originally meant to release the book domestically, but after she sent them the manuscript she was met with a deafening silence. Gandhi says simply that Penguin were “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and that after she refused to make certain suggested edits, the publisher dropped the book, just a week before it was due to be announced. It will now be published by another imprint. In a statement, the publisher denied dropping the book, adding, “Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish Belonging because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances.”
Gandhi admits she was disappointed, though not altogether surprised, at what she sees as an attempt to censor her book. It is far from an isolated incident. In the days before we meet, Gandhi’s 26-year-old grandson, who is an artist and curator, is forced to take down dozens of his photographs depicting political protests that had been due to go on show in Delhi.
Gandhi had an early insight into the difficulties and loneliness of being a female leader in India’s deeply patriarchal society. When she arrived in India in 1968, she and Rajiv moved in with his mother, who at that time was two years into her first term as prime minister. Her husband, also a politician, had died years before.
They lived all together in another crumbling colonial Delhi bungalow, in relatively close and modest quarters. To outsiders, Indira was often seen as severe, an “iron lady”, and Gandhi admits that, to begin with, she was deeply intimidated by her formidable mother-in-law. Yet while Indira was imposing in public, she could be vulnerable in private, once confiding to Gandhi how terrified she was when she first bcame prime minister.
“In the newspapers she was portrayed as tough or harsh, but at home she was just like any other mother,” Gandhi says – although Indira’s notoriously explosive temper, frequently directed at political colleagues, would erupt through the house on occasion. Gandhi’s memoir recounts one incident where Indira lost her temper during a family dinner and threw her thali plate across the table.
Gandhi’s book documents the hostility Indira grappled with, both from political opponents and rightwing groups, but also from the old guard of her own party. “I saw her work day and night, constantly under pressure, constantly attacked,” Gandhi says. “It did affect her, like it would anyone. And of course, in that position, there is a loneliness. She had many interests and many friends, but it is a lonely kind of life.”
For several years, Gandhi says, her own life was “carefree”. She and Rajiv were madly in love, often embarrassing their children with public displays of affection that were highly unusual in Indian households at the time. “For this man, I was ready to do everything, to lose even my Italian identity,” she says. Rajiv was working as a commercial airline pilot, and as relations warmed with her mother-in-law, Gandhi set about redecorating the austere Delhi bungalow with some Italian flair, and learning how to cook Kashmiri food. After a traumatic miscarriage, she gave birth to two children, who were doted on by Indira. Even her pangs for fresh Italian ingredients, impossible to find in India in those days, eventually ebbed.
But in 1975 Indira would make the most controversial decision of her political life. Amid mounting political unrest, economic hardship and a concerted effort by the opposition to bring down the Congress government, Indira decided to impose a state of emergency on the country, in a bid to instil order. The repercussions were profound: the constitution was suspended, civil liberties and democratic freedoms abandoned, the media silenced and opponents detained en masse without trial. It lasted for almost two years, and is still seen as the darkest period of India’s democracy; it is regularly used to tarnish the Congress party today.
According to Gandhi, the family was split on the decision. Rajiv was against the move, telling his mother to wait for the next election, but her hotheaded younger son Sanjay pushed for it, arguing at one family dinner that the opposition would destroy his mother and telling her, “They must be stopped.” Sanjay’s forceful influence over his mother was a great source of public controversy at the time. Gandhi recalls that it inflamed tensions within the family, too; Rajiv attempted to confront his mother, but she refused to listen. “Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed,” Gandhi writes in her book.
Today, she says it was a mistake for Indira to call the emergency, and that she believes her mother-in-law came to feel the same. “I always feel that Mrs Gandhi was a democrat at heart,” she says. “I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her.”
In the following years, Indira would lose one election and be returned to power in another. Rajiv would also be persuaded to enter politics after the premature death of Sanjay. But by 1984, darkness came to their door again.
Months of escalating violence had stricken the north Indian state of Punjab. As separatist militants prepared to declare an independent Sikh state, Indira authorised a military operation at one of the holiest sites in Sikhism, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where the group were hiding out. The operation caused cataclysmic damage, killing Sikh pilgrims as well as militants, and led to desecration of the temple by tanks and heavy weaponry. Gandhi says that when her mother-in-law was shown images of the devastation, tears rolled down her face.
For Sikhs in India, it was a profound and painful attack on their religion, and Indira was inundated with threats. “She told us what to do in case she died – so she knew,” Gandhi says. “She was making preparations for her death. She told Rahul he must be brave and not to cry.” That summer Indira took her grandchildren on a trip to her ancestral home of Kashmir; Gandhi believes this was to “say goodbye”. Indira also defied advice to remove her Sikh bodyguards – something that turned out to be a fateful decision.
Gandhi was at home on 31 October when she heard what sounded like fireworks going off. Sprinting over to Indira’s office next door, she was confronted by her mother-in-law’s bloodied body, riddled with bullets, lying on the ground. Indira’s own Sikh bodyguards had opened fire on her in retribution for the attack on the Golden Temple.
What came next remains seared on Gandhi’s memory. After Indira was put into a car, she held her bleeding body and tried to revive her mother-in-law as they raced to the hospital. “There was blood everywhere and I realised she wasn’t replying to my questions. It seemed as if she had already gone,” she says.
Even after so many years, the story is clearly painful to recount and she speaks hesitantly, her soft voice growing even quieter. “I remember the drive from the house to the hospital was excruciating. There wasn’t much traffic, but it felt so slow. I also knew that because she wasn’t speaking, it must be over.”
Gandhi admits there are still parts of that experience she can’t bring herself to discuss. “I never talk about it. Only if I’m asked, then I struggle to.” Indira would be declared dead at the hospital. Her body was still lying there, cold, when Rajiv broke the news that he had been asked to step in as prime minister. Gandhi had begged him to stay out of politics and describes that conversation as a “knife going into my heart”.
In the aftermath of Indira’s death, she was traumatised and depressed, living “like a ghost”. Rajiv, too, had no time to grieve. Newly announced as prime minister, he immediately had to deal with deadly anti-Sikh riots that erupted after Indira’s death. He would later be accused of not doing enough to stop the bloodbath. “Rajiv never really showed his pain,” Gandhi says. “I remember seeing him in his mother’s study, on one of the chairs where she sat, with tears. But in public he felt he had to hide it.”
Fear took over their lives. The house became a fortress, with uniformed commandos stationed in the children’s bedrooms. Rahul and Priyanka were pulled out of school and no longer allowed to roam freely. She would worry if Rajiv didn’t come back from an engagement on time. He, meanwhile, would always want her by his side. “Fear was a very real thing,” she says. “My thought was always: he will be killed next.” By 1991, her premonition had come true.
A silence settles over the room as Gandhi struggles to recall how she went on living after Rajiv’s death. A Sri Lankan separatist militant had set off a suicide bomb while he was on the election trail, killing him instantly. Throughout our conversation, she still refers to Rajiv as “Papa”, as he is known to their children.
Priyanka, who sits on the sofa with us, interjects gently. She tells me how her mother would sit in the dark all day, listening to Mozart’s Requiem, engulfed by grief. “You were angry at him,” she says, speaking to her mother. “When you used to cry, you used to shout: how has he left me, why did he leave?”
Gandhi sits quietly for a moment. “After my mother-in-law was killed, we thought that, as we were always together, if something happens to one, it will happen to the other one,” she says. They had even written notes on how they wanted their funerals.
Yet when Gandhi’s sister pleaded for her to return to Italy, the thought was unfathomable. “India was my home, my children’s home,” she says. Gandhi last went back to Italy four years ago, when her mother died.
She found out later that, prior to the attack, Indian intelligence had intercepted death threats against Rajiv by the Sri Lankan separatist Tamil Tigers, angered over India’s intervention in the country’s civil war. However, these had been ignored by the newly elected government, who instead took away his top-level security. She still believes the truth of a wider conspiracy behind his death has yet to come out. The most recent commission to investigate it was shut down by the Modi government. “I don’t think we will get the truth now,” she says with a sigh.
Crucially, just as the foundation of her world was shattered, a wind of change was blowing across north India. A claim that a mosque in the city of Ayodhya was built on the ruins of an ancient Hindu temple had been gaining traction among hardline, rightwing Hindu nationalist organisations and political groups. In December 1992, supporters of the movement – including BJP figures – violently tore down the mosque.
Gandhi recalls crying as she witnessed the demolition on television. She says she knew then that they faced “a long battle for the secular nation that Mahatma Gandhi, Nehru and their colleagues had strived to build”. She accepts that failures of her own party in part contributed to the rise of the BJP and its hardline Hindutva politics. “I think we have been too complacent in many ways. There was a laissez-faire kind of an attitude,” she says. In 2024, Modi delivered on the BJP’s longstanding promise and inaugurated a vast Hindu temple in the place where the mosque had once stood.
Throughout her memoir, Gandhi is open about her distrust of politics, describing it as “menacing”, driven by “ambition, greed and hypocrisy”. But with Congress facing an existential threat and looking likely to fracture, Gandhi succumbed to mounting pressure and agreed to become its president in 1998. It was a decision, she says, driven by a sense of duty to her lost husband. Not only did she have to fight against her own ingrained shyness, she also had to take on political opponents in Hindi, her third language.
She insists she never had political ambition. Despite helping the party to win the most votes in the 2004 election, she shocked everyone by refusing to become prime minister. “It was clear in my mind I would never do it,” she says. “It was just not me.” Nonetheless, until she stepped back from the day-to-day of Congress leadership a few years ago, she had little time for herself. She would carry books to political events, history and autobiographies, to read on the way home. Music, both Indian classical and European operas, also became her solace. Having previously studied art restoration, “once in a while, I would slip away to an art exhibition”.
Today she stays out of the messy day-to-day of politics, though is still kept in the loop by her daughter and attends the occasional meeting. She finds joy in her small vegetable patch, but more than anything in spending time with her children and two grandchildren. Theirs has always been a dog-loving family (Priyanka once had seven golden retrievers) and Gandhi is devoted to her two jack russells, Noorie and Lapo, who were gifts from her son.
Nonetheless, the fortress of security that surrounds her home is a stark reminder of the restrictions still imposed on her freedom. Armed police man the barricades on the road outside, and my car is thoroughly inspected by security before I am allowed to drive through a towering metal gate and into her driveway.
While she was once credited with reviving the fortunes of Congress, over the past decade the Gandhi family have overseen its calamitous decline. Their previous government, in power till 2014, was marred by allegations of rampant corruption. (“In almost every single instance, the ministers resigned,” is Gandhi’s defence.) After taking over from his mother, Rahul lost the last three general elections to Modi, and Congress remains in power in only a few states. Meanwhile, the BJP’s Hindutva has become the country’s dominant political ideology. As the family has maintained its control, Congress has been unable to shake off allegations that it is nepotistic and run by political elites.
Why can’t Congress free itself from the Gandhi family’s leadership, I ask? She is dismissive, perhaps a nerve touched. “You would have to ask the party,” she says. Gandhi also skates over the question of nepotism, simply saying, “We all fight elections: we win them, we lose them. All of us have.” But after so many losses, can a Gandhi-led Congress still be a credible alternative to the BJP? While she is adamant they can, many in the country remain unconvinced.
It is true that we are meeting at an interesting moment, for both Modi and the bruised opposition. As gen Z youth erupted on to the streets in protest against the government over the summer – satirically calling themselves the “Cockroaches” after an online joke transformed into a serious political movement – the long-crushed space for dissent has opened up.
In recent weeks, young Indians have once again been taking to the streets against the government, despite being met with draconian state force. The question of whether they can shake the BJP’s grip on power remains to be seen; so far, the Cockroach movement has kept its distance from the opposition alliance. But “what encourages me is young people are coming out and demonstrating,” Gandhi says. “With determination, they’re calling out the government on things that are not right. I feel like this is a real shift.”
Congress, too, has become more energised than it has been for many years. Images of Rahul and Priyanka being manhandled by police as they tried to protest against the government have gone viral in recent weeks. After once pleading with her children to stay out of politics, Gandhi now says, “It’s good that they’re there. Now more than ever before.” The Gandhi family, it seems, are not done just yet.

The day may have been wet, but Chennaiites still went all out to bring in light and sparkles on Deepavali day, which fell on Sunday (November 8, 2026). While awareness about safety has increased, ophthalmologists in the city have once again called for caution and reiterated protective measures, as they have received dozens of cases of cracker-related injuries.
The Regional Institute of Ophthalmology and Government Ophthalmic Hospital received around 50 cases, with about 10 cases having to be admitted, a senior official said.

Over the Deepavali weekend, the emergency clinic at Sankara Nethralaya saw 45 cases of firecracker injuries at its main campus. Two underwent wound repair surgery, while two others were scheduled for surgery on Monday, November 9, according to T.S. Surendran, its chairman..
At Dr. Agarwals Eye Hospital, nearly 20 patients came in with cracker-related injuries, said S. Soundari, regional head, clinical services. Four cases involved children; the rest were adults, mostly in their 30s and 40s.

Doctors have reiterated caution. Dr. Soundari called for wearing protective eye gear while bursting firecrackers, supervising children properly, and importantly, not trying to touch the eye or take objects out by oneself. “Come to a doctor immediately if there is an eye injury,” she stressed. Dr. Rajan noted that bystanders often got hurt and should be careful to maintain an adequate distance..

Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban
- Published
FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has been given a 12-match suspension by the Spanish football federation's disciplinary committee after his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel during the closing stages of the second-tier match between their two respective sides on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30.
The disciplinary committee said it had to base its decision "on the facts expressly recorded in the referee's report", which stated the player "was sent off for 'violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play'.
"The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, is public knowledge."
The committee added the "nature of the conduct described and the accompanying circumstances" means that "the maximum sanction, a 12-match suspension, is justified".
Separately, the federation has decided the game between the two sides, which was abandoned seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred, will not be replayed.
"This avoids having to resume play from the precise moment at which the tragic incident occurred," it said.
The teams were drawing 2-2 at the time and that result will now stand, with a federation committee saying that was the "most respectful course of action, given the extraordinary and tragic circumstances of this case".
Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on 4 November, in which he said he was experiencing "the most difficult days" of his life and felt "enormous pain" about De Miguel's death.
On Thursday, FC Andorra manager Carles Manso said Equatorial Guinea international Owono is yet to decide whether he will return to football following the incident.
Manso said Owono is currently spending time with his family and is "completely free to make any decision" with regard to a potential return, adding: "What we have to do is support him in every way and be close to him.
"We will give him space so that he feels completely free to make any decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return.
"When he feels it is appropriate and when he feels genuinely ready to take a decision like that [he will do so]."

Google DeepMind employees in the UK have asked the government to intervene in a push to unionize the artificial intelligence lab.
On Thursday, the Communication Workers Union and Unite the Union—put forward by Google DeepMind staff as joint representatives—filed an application to the Central Arbitration Committee, a government body that resolves disputes between employers and unions.
The application, which was seen by WIRED, asks the CAC to confirm the unions have enough support from workers to trigger a unionization ballot. The company would be required by law to respect the results. If successful, roughly 1,000 staff working in product-focused roles at Google DeepMind would qualify for union membership.
The escalation follows a series of meetings between employees, the unions, and company representatives over voluntary unionization, which left staff with the impression their demands weren’t being taken seriously.
“They’ve been ignored. They feel like their problems have been minimized,” John Chadfield, national officer for technology at the CWU, tells WIRED. “Management has refused to come to the table. They sent it to the HR and labor relations people, who dealt with it as an administrative box-ticking exercise.”
Google DeepMind did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The push to unionize began in February 2025, when Google’s parent company Alphabet removed a pledge from its ethics guidelines stating that it wouldn’t use AI for purposes like weapons development.
“When I joined, we really made a big deal about the principles—the red lines. We were really looking to benefit humanity and make the world a better place,” a Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of backlash, tells WIRED. “A lot of this is about reestablishing that ethical and moral framework that we started with.”
The employees pushing for unionization object in particular to agreements between the company and the US and Israeli militaries. If they succeed in unionizing, they intend to demand that Google backs out of those contracts.
“We feel extremely concerned about the direction that this technology is going in,” says a second Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for the same reason as the first employee.
The company has previously defended its deals with government organizations.
“We are proud to be part of a broad consortium of leading AI labs and technology and cloud companies providing AI services and infrastructure in support of national security,” Jenn Crider, a Google spokeswoman, told The New York Times in April. “We remain committed to the private and public sector consensus that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without appropriate human oversight.”
In an email delivered to all UK staff on Thursday, seen by WIRED, the Google DeepMind employees involved in the unionization push appealed to their colleagues to participate in the ballot, which they expect to take place in the coming months. “We want a union, we want collective bargaining, and we want a say in how AI is developed and deployed,” they wrote.
The group also hopes it can establish a playbook that employees at other major AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic can follow in the UK.
“It’s pretty rare that there’s been an industry that exercises such dominance and power over the economy, where there’s so little opportunity for employees or regulators to have any checks and balances,” the second Google DeepMind employee says. “We want to show what can happen when employees collectively organize and articulate a shared vision for the way their technology should be used.”

A tanker collided with a river cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon, prompting an emergency effort to rescue people from the water, according to officials.
The Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage at about 12.30pm, said Kimberly Curth, the Port of New Orleans press secretary, in a statement.
The American Heritage had about 129 passengers – in addition to crew members – onboard when it was hit, according to Curth. About two hours before that, the American Heritage had docked at the port to begin passenger disembarkation, Curth said.
A statement from the office of the New Orleans mayor, Helena Moreno, on Friday afternoon said that “multiple individuals have been rescued”.
An emergency response source said that there were efforts under way – including by New Orleans firefighters – to rescue multiple people from the water.
“Public safety agencies are coordinating response efforts, with the immediate priority being the safety and rescue of those involved,” the statement from Moreno’s office said.
Officials did not immediately provide details about the circumstances of the crash. The emergency response source said it was possible the tanker had lost power before striking the American Heritage, but that had not been confirmed.
The website marinetraffic.com showed the Atlantic Asphalt’s path was uneventful as it went around the Mississippi River bend near New Orleans’ Algiers Point neighborhood. It had just made it past the Crescent City Connection bridge linking New Orleans’ central business district and the Algiers section when it began drifting to its starboard – or right – side.
Video showed it hit the side of the American Heritage, which slowly rolled toward where it was struck. One witness, Jamie Holford, told local NBC News affiliate WDSU that it took 15 minutes “from impact to where it rolled over”.
“Surreal – that’s what that was,” Holford said.
Maritime law expert Martin J Davies of New Orleans’ Tulane University told local Fox affiliate WVUE that the Atlantic Asphalt was lucky to have not hit the Crescent City Connection, which is estimated to carry about 160,000 cars daily.
“This is obviously a really bad, incident,” Davies said. “But it could also have struck the bridge, which it didn’t.”
A video from WDSU showed crew members of a tugboat working to pull people in lifejackets or holding on to flotation rings out of the river.
Video from WVUE showed the American Heritage slowly rolling on to its side with the Atlantic Asphalt nearby. One image on social media showed people climbing on the side of the cruise boat after it was struck, with chairs and tables strewn about.
People who had gotten off the American Heritage after it was struck were being brought inside the New Orleans port’s administration building.
The local Acadian Ambulance service took eight people from there to hospitals in the area to be treated for injuries, the details of which were not immediately available, agency spokesperson Caitlin Russo said.
Beside New Orleans firefighters and port and city police, the US Coast Guard and local emergency medical services personnel were at the scene conducting rescue and response operations, Curth’s statement said.
A statement from the US Coast Guard said the river “is closed to all vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96”, encompassing the area where Friday’s crash occurred. That is so to assist responders as they “assess the situation and conduct response operations”, the statement said.
A statement from American Cruise Lines on Friday said “guests and crew were evacuated” from the American Heritage but did not provide numbers. “We are deeply concerned for everyone involved,” the cruise operator’s statement added.
The American Heritage, a 300ft paddle-wheel ship, was built in 2015 and previously sailed as the Queen of the Mississippi. It has more than 80 staterooms and operates cruises on the Mississippi River, including ones which depart from New Orleans.
Officials said they would be holding a news conference at 3pm CT to provide more updates. Louisiana’s governor, Jeff Landry, on Friday afternoon said he was headed to New Orleans.

Study Hard, Get a Career, Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
From India to France, the implicit meritocratic bargain that underwrote stable societies by providing advancement to new generations is breaking down.
Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.
In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.
In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.
In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.
It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.
The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision
- Published
Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.
The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel, Atlantic Asphalt.
The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".
The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort went to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help".
"We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.
Calls about the collision came in around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans Chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port of New Orleans.
Passengers began disembarking from the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping on to its side, Mayor Moreno said.
Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help and officials shut down the Mississippi River for the search effort.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.
President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue was an "incredible job".
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the US Coast Guard also supported local rescue operations.
Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.
Ships have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what happened.
Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he saw the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision.
"It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic."
Holford added that he saw passengers and crew members "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking.
The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website.
Built in 2015, the vessel has at least four decks.

On the intervening night of November 8 and 9, over 250 PM2.5 data points from Delhi were missing on the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) website, according to an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Scientist and air quality analyst Manoj Kumar tweeted the statistics in the early hours of November 9. According to him, out of the 59 monitoring stations, as seen on the official website of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.
Missing hourly PM2.5 data raises concerns over Delhi’s air quality assessment.
Since midnight on 8 November until 5 am on 9 November, 227 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.
A key concern is that many missing readings occurred when concentrations approached the monitoring instruments’ upper measurement limit of 1,000 µg/m³. These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels. For a conservative assessment, such readings should be flagged as potentially exceeding the measurement range, with 1,000 µg/m³ considered as a lower-bound value rather than treating them as zero or excluding them without qualification.
Mundka recorded the highest number of missing hourly observations (10), followed by Dwarka Sector 8, IIT Delhi, Nehru Nagar, Pusa IITM and Uttam Nagar, with eight missing hours each.
There is also an unusual pattern at some stations. IGNOU Maidan Garhi, Cantonment Area, Siri Fort and Tikri Kalan recorded PM2.5 concentrations below 30 µg/m³ (Cleanest) during parts of this episode. Given the pollution levels elsewhere, these readings warrant verification for possible instrument or data-quality issues before being used in final averages or AQI calculations.
Reliable air-quality assessment during pollution episodes requires both complete data and transparent treatment of readings that exceed instrument measurement limits.
— Dr. Manoj Kumar (@manoj_kumar_nr) November 9, 2026
Air Quality Index, or AQI, turns air quality data for eight pollutants into one number and one name, providing an easy-to-understand picture of air quality. According to the All India AQI Dashboard, the pollutants are PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, Pb, and NH3. (Lead is not monitored at every station.)
Delhi’s average AQI on the night of Diwali was as follows, according to the CPCB.
However, between 1 am and 3 am on the Diwali night, over 30 monitoring stations were not showing any PM2.5 data. Over the course of the night, more stations failed.
A day after, as the mystery of missing data caused an outrage, the hourly air quality readings missing from the CPCB website became available on the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) website, which showed that the PM2.5 concentration went up to a staggering 3500 micrograms per cubic metre and beyond, which is around 60 times its standard value.
Below is the reading from Mundka station:
Below is the reading from JNU station:
Why does the Missing Data Matter?
India’s air quality figures come from monitoring stations run by state pollution control boards and committees, such as DPCC in Delhi. Stations send their readings to CPCB every 15 minutes. CPCB calculates each station’s AQI by finding a sub-index for every pollutant and taking the highest one. It then publishes the results on its portal, the SAMEER app and its daily bulletin.
A sub-index is the AQI score for a single pollutant on its own. Each pollutant is measured in different units and has a different “safe” range. For example, PM2.5 is in micrograms per cubic metre, and CO is in milligrams per cubic metre. So CPCB converts each pollutant’s reading to the same 0-500 scale, and that converted number is its sub-index.
If the PM2.5 has a sub-index of 75, SO2 has 63, and NO2 has 38, the station’s overall AQI is the highest of these, so here it is 75, driven by PM2.5. One bad pollutant is enough to push the AQI into a worse category, even if the others are fine.
If one looks carefully at the above screenshot from 12 midnight on November 9 from the Anand Vihar monitoring station, one would see that the 24-hour average of the PM2.5 pollutant is the 24-hour average AQI for that particular monitoring station. One would also note that the highest average sub-index determines the AQI.
Now, if PM2.5, which gives a measure of fine particulate matter in the air and is also highest during Diwali due to the bursting of firecrackers, goes missing, the average AQI reading underestimates the pollution in the air to a great extent. According to a Hindustan Times report, if one considers the released readings, Delhi’s AQI for 24 hours until 9 am on November 9 was 384 on a 500 scale against the 370 figure published by CPCB.
Why did the Data Go Missing?
According to Kumar’s post on X (shared when the missing data had not been released), Mundka recorded the highest number of missing hourly observations (10), followed by Dwarka Sector 8, IIT Delhi, Nehru Nagar, Pusa IITM and Uttam Nagar, with eight missing hours each.
Interestingly, the highest reading also came from Mundka at 3,744 µg/m³ at 2 am on November 9. JNU was at 3,023 at 4 am the same night and NSUT’s West Campus at 3,008 at 5 am. Eleven of DPCC’s stations went past 2,000 micrograms per cubic metre.
The CPCB released an official statement on November 10 addressing the data gaps, saying that particulate analysers like PM2.5 were calibrated for 0-1,000 µg/m³. Under the automated validation, hourly readings beyond that range are treated as “outside range” and left out of the computation. CPCB conceded this “may appear as a data gap” during extreme episodes like Diwali firecracker bursting. Those hours don’t count towards the 24-hour average for that station. It also stated that the methodology for processing data beyond the system’s design range is “under review”, with internal deliberations underway.
On November 11, Kumar posted on X, if the 255 missing PM2.5 data points were replaced with 1,000 µg/m³, the upper measurement limit cited by CPCB, the average showed a 49% increase, from 269 to 400 µg/m³.
Alt News spoke to Kumar, who also told us that while the DPCC continued to record data above 1000 micrograms per cubic metre, it was the CPCB, the body ultimately entrusted with calculating and releasing AQI findings, that did not register it. “DPCC had measured and displayed PM 2.5 concentration above 1000 on that day. But it was not reflected on the CPCB website.”
Explaining the process and the gaps, Kumar said, “Let’s say that the instrument’s operating range is between 0 and 1000. But if it is going above 1000, there will be some uncertainty, but uncertainty can be estimated.”
Even in his November 9 post, Kumar made the point that the readings had gone missing as the concentration readings approached 1000. “These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels. For a conservative assessment, such readings should be flagged as potentially exceeding the measurement range, with 1,000 µg/m³ considered as a lower-bound value rather than treating them as zero or excluding them without qualification,” he wrote.
Furthermore, to calculate AQI, one would need to have at least 16 hours in a day, if not all 24 hours of data. So missing out on important data points during peak pollution periods underrepresents the AQI value.
It’s also worth noting that aur quality monitoring is not cheap: A 2018 Hindustan Times report put the cost of a conventional station at up to Rs 5 crore.

The National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions (NCAHP), under the Union Ministry of Health, has proposed a comprehensive regulatory framework for the registration of allied and healthcare professionals, with pathways for skill upgradation, competency assessment, and transition to regular registration.
Also read | What new rules mean for allied health
The broad categories of allied and healthcare professions governed by the NCAHP include clinical laboratories, surgical and emergency technology, physiotherapy, nutrition, ophthalmology, occupational therapy, community and behavioural health, medical imaging, physician associates, and health informatics.
The proposed framework aims for uniformity, transparency and accountability in professional registration. Practitioners can enhance their competencies in keeping with prescribed standards, a release issued by the Ministry said.
The NCAHP has invited public and stakeholder comments on the Draft Provisional Registration of Allied and Healthcare Professionals Regulations, 2026 framed under the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act, 2021.
Key features of the proposed regulations include the establishment of a standardised mechanism for provisional registration in accordance with the NCAHP Act, 2021.
“Importantly, the proposed Regulations also provide opportunities for eligible provisionally registered professionals to undertake prescribed bridge courses for skill enhancement, supervised clinical training and minimum qualifying examinations, wherever applicable, to meet the requirements for regular registration,’’ the Healthy Ministry’s statement said.
This competency-based approach seeks to facilitate professional development and career progression, and improve the quality of allied and healthcare services.
“The proposed framework places emphasis on skill development, professional competence and regulatory accountability,’’ a senior Health Ministry official said.
By linking progression to regular registration with prescribed requirements, the regulations seek to ensure allied and healthcare professionals possess the necessary knowledge and clinical competencies to deliver quality healthcare services.
An integrated online registration system for submitting applications, verifying credentials, assess eligibility, and issue provisional registration certificates is also proposed.
Eligible professionals granted provisional registration will receive a Provisional Registration Unique Identification Number (PR UID). The digital platform will simply procedures, improve access, and promote uniform efficiency across States and Union Territories.
The key features of the proposed regulations include standardised criteria and procedures for provisional registration; online application, verification and issuance of registration certificates with unique identification numbers; provisions for validity, extension, termination and appeals relating to provisional registration; bridge courses for skill enhancement, competency assessments and qualifying exams; supervised clinical training and institutional requirements for professional skill development; and transition to regular registration in the appropriate Central or State Register.
The NCAHP has now invited comments from allied and healthcare professionals, professional associations, educational institutions, State Allied and Healthcare Councils, healthcare institutions, experts, and the general public by December 4, 2026.

Former Israeli and U.S. ambassadors, lawmakers and analysts largely agree on steps Gadi Eisenkot could take if he becomes prime minister. But they are risky.
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who has been given a chance to form Israel’s new governing coalition and replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is by no means assured of success.

A molecular signal in the blood helps identify microscopic changes that precede the development of ovarian cancer, researchers have found, in a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often discovered after it has already spread.
For decades, efforts to detect ovarian cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours, the researchers noted in their report published on Tuesday in Nature Medicine.
“We asked a fundamentally different question: What if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” study leader Rajan Gogna of the Hoag Family Cancer Institute in Newport Beach, California, said in a statement. Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes.
The precancerous lesions are known as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC). The new study found that women with this precursor condition have elevated blood levels of an RNA molecule called Tu-Stroma.
When researchers measured Tu-Stroma in blood, they detected STIC in 92.3% of affected women and correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women. In women with genetic risk factors for ovarian cancer, approximately 72% of positive results would be accurate, while negative results would be correct nearly 100% of the time, they reported. “For women at high risk, this could transform how we approach prevention,” co-author Esha Madan, also of Hoag, said in a statement.
Many such women face difficult decisions about preventive surgery to remove their fallopian tubes and ovaries. “Today, decisions about preventive surgery are largely guided by inherited risk, without knowing whether precancerous lesions are actually present,” Madan said. “Our discovery could eventually provide that missing biological information.”

Michael Mann won’t start filming Heat 2 until early next year, but things are already heating up legally between the acclaimed director and New Regency when it comes to 1995 crime classic.
After several attempts this year by the director to reclaim ownership of the original Heat screenplay under copyright termination, the Yariv Milchan-run company today took Mann to federal court to get the trio of notices declared “defective and invalid.” In the dispute, New Regency are claiming that Mann’s role in writing the Heat screenplay was that of a “work for hire,” and therefore his termination notices are DOA.
“Regency still holds the rights to the Heat Screenplay. As a result of its rights in and to the Screenplay, Regency owns the film, television, and other rights in the Heat film.”
Watch on Deadline
Hit the brakes, says Ferrari helmer Mann’s team.
“This filing has to do with original and personal writing Michael Mann did on multiple screenplays during the 1980s and which evolved into the iconic 1995 film Heat that Mann wrote, produced and directed,” a spokesman for the Robert Klieger represented past Oscar nominee said late Friday of the Al Pacino and Robert De Niro starring movie. “After 40 years Michael Mann is exercising the right of authors to reclaim their work and in this case Michael Mann’s original creation.”
Even with some contractual rights reverted to him under the WGA Basic Agreement, the CAA-repped Mann insists that a temporality forgotten 1988 oral agreement between himself and two of his loan-out companies assigned him core Heat rights as an independent author.
“We will vigorously defend this action and are confident that the courts will vindicate Michael Mann’s statutory rights under the Copyright Act,” Mann’s team says. “For clarification, this is unrelated to production of Heat 2 which will begin shooting on January 19.”
In that context, the 1991 founded New Regency is thinking of the past and the future, the company’s Kendall Brill & Kellyl awyers say. “If given effect, the Termination Notices would purport to strip Regency, beginning in 2028, of rights it has held for more than three decades, clouding Regency’s title to the Screenplay and jeopardizing its ability to develop, finance, and license works derived from it,” the 20-page complaint for declaratory relief states.
“In addition, certain provisions of the agreements that Mann and Regency each entered into with Amazon with respect to Heat 2 depend on the outcome of this litigation.”
Speaking of the much anticipated, Heat 2, the Leonardo DiCaprio, Christian Bale, Adam Driver, Stephen Graham and Jason Clarke starrer will see Mann directing the prequel flick from his own script. This particular script is based on Mann and Meg Gardiner’s No. 1 New York Times bestselling novel from 2022.

Ramayana, directed by Nitesh Tiwari, has become the 11th Indian film to cross the Rs 1,000 crore milestone at the global box office in eight days, joining hits such as Dangal, Baahubali 2, Pushpa 2 and Dhurandhar 2.
Directed by Tiwari and produced by Namit Malhotra's Prime Focus Studios in collaboration with DNEG and Yash's Monster Mind Creations, the first part released on November 5.
According to figures shared by trade website Sacnilk, the worldwide gross of Ramayana after eight days is Rs 1,033.55 crore with India contributing Rs 675.05 crore and overseas Rs 358.50 crore, respectively.
The film's release during the extended Diwali weekend, coupled with strong demand in other languages across India and a wide release overseas, helped Ramayana achieve the milestone in just eight days.
Tiwari's Dangal still tops the list with its worldwide gross of Rs 2070.00 crore, followed by Aditya Dhar's Dhurandhar 2, which stands at Rs 1813.40 crore.
Baahubali 2 with Rs 1788.00 crore, Pushpa 2 with Rs 1742.00 crore, Dhurandhar (Rs 1307.35 crore) complete the top five films.
They are followed by RRR (Rs 1230.00 crore), KGF Chapter 2 (Rs 1215.00 crore), Jawan (Rs 1160.00 crore), Pathaan (Rs 1055.00 crore), Kalki 2898 AD (Rs 1042.25 crore) complete the top ten list of highest earning movies in India.
"Ramayana", reportedly made on a budget of Rs 2,000 crore, is expected to rise in the ranking in the coming week.
The film, a retelling of Indian epic Ramayana, features Ranbir Kapoor as Lord Rama, Sai Pallavi as Sita and Yash as Ravana. The ensemble cast also includes Ravi Dubey as Lakshman, Arun Govil as King Dasharath and Lara Dutta as Kaikeyi.
The film traces the journey of Rama, from his birth and marriage to Sita to his exile from Ayodhya, and leads up to Ravana's abduction of Sita.
The first instalment concludes with Rama vowing to rescue her, setting the stage for the conflict that will unfold in the second part.
The two-part cinematic adaptation features music by Oscar-winning composers AR Rahman and Hans Zimmer, while the action choreography is led by Terry Notary and Guy Norris.
The second instalment will focus on Rama's mission to rescue Sita and will introduce Lord Hanuman, who will be played by veteran star Sunny Deol.
The second part is scheduled for release during Diwali 2028.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Money. No one is alien to this term. In fact, we get to know about money even before we understand how the world works. You want your favourite candy? You give money, you get it. Your favourite snacks? Money again! That shiny gel pen you have been eyeing? There you go. A themed backpack? You know the drill. You want a cycle like your friends have? All right, save up for a few months and… yay! You have it!
You want an iPhone because everyone seems to have one? Money? Well, that one seems a bit far-fetched at the moment.
And that is when you realise you might have to sit this one out. You want to capture high-quality pictures and videos of you and your friends doing the silliest things, but you cannot afford the phone that would let you do that just yet.
But wait. You can still be in those frames, right? You can still make silly reels with your friends, laugh at them together and be part of those memories. And that makes you happy, too.
At some point in life, you may have encountered a financial barrier, whether it was missing an outing, struggling to afford a gift, or feeling the pressure to own what everyone else has. These moments may seem small, but they can leave us with some big questions.
Materialism
In philosophy, materialism is the view that matter is the fundamental reality. In everyday life, however, the term is often used to describe an excessive attachment to material possessions and the importance we place on owning things. We have all heard someone say, “Don’t be materialistic.” But understanding what that really means is a different matter altogether.
It is one thing to hear that money cannot buy happiness or that a gift’s value goes beyond its price tag. It is quite another to experience it yourself. It is not simply about whether you can or cannot afford something. It is also about how you deal with that feeling and what you begin to value when money gets in the way.
This Children’s Day, here are some voices of children who have encountered these questions in their own lives. For some, it was about learning to manage money better. For others, it was about standing up for a friend, discovering the thought behind a handmade gift or understanding what it means to make someone feel included.
As one young contributor puts it, “Money can buy happiness in the sense that it fetches you things that you want to have but it is also true that money cannot ‘buy’ emotional attachment.” These are stories of first encounters with money, materialism and the feelings that come with them. There are no one-size-fits-all answers here, just children figuring things out as they go, one experience at a time.Let’s hear it in their own voices.
There is always a first
Dear readers,
Do you remember a first experience that made you stop and think? Perhaps it was the first time someone questioned whether your work was really yours, you felt the need to fit in, or money came in the way of a plan or friendship. This issue brings together stories of such firsts, from navigating an AI-driven world to understanding friendships and money. Read on, and see if you find a little of yourself in them. Have a first experience of your own to share? Write to school@thehindu.co.in. We would love to hear your story!
A conversation can fix it all
Sometimes, we learn the most important lessons from small incidents in our lives. I remember one such incident that made me understand the true meaning of friendship and the value of gifts.
It happened at a birthday party where I met a girl. Everyone was busy enjoying the party and showing the gifts they had brought. Most of the children had brought expensive gifts, but she had brought a simple one. I noticed that she was sitting quietly and did not seem very happy. She looked a little uncomfortable, so I decided to go and talk to her.
I asked her if something was wrong. At first, she hesitated, but then she told me that she was feeling bad because her gift was not as expensive as the others. She was worried that people might judge her because of it.
I tried to make her feel better and told her that a gift does not have to be expensive to be special. What matters is the love, care and effort behind it. I also told her that everyone has different situations and nobody should feel ashamed of what they can afford.
After our conversation, she seemed much happier. We started talking about other things and slowly became friends. With time, our friendship grew stronger, and now she does not worry about such things anymore.
This incident taught me that money should never decide the value of a friendship. We should never judge anyone by their clothes, gifts or belongings. Sometimes, a small gift given with love is much more special than an expensive one.
I believe that the best gifts are not measured by their price, but by the feelings behind them.
- Ishana Chatterjee, 13,Class 7, St. Augustine’s Day School, Shyamnagar, Kolkata
When an empty wallet means missing out on a memory
This situation had occurred just before our pre-board examinations. My friends and I had planned to go to a lovely place, and it had probably been the last chance we would have to all go out together before we started preparing for our examinations and board exams.
However, it had been nearly the end of the month, and I hadn’t had much money left. I wasn’t going to receive my next allowance until the following month, and I had always tried to be responsible with my money rather than asking my parents for extra. That month, however, I had been quite irresponsible with my spending and hadn’t really thought about saving any money.
I couldn’t ask my friends to change their plans because the following month would have been occupied with pre-boards and board exam preparation. Eventually, I had to miss the outing. I told them there had been an emergency at home because I wasn’t comfortable sharing the actual reason. They were understanding and didn’t push me, but I felt guilty about my irresponsible spending and disappointed that I couldn’t join them.
Although it might have seemed like a minor incident, it made me realise how important money actually was. I had felt awful about missing one simple outing with my friends, and that made me think about how, for some people, money influenced almost every decision they made. For me, it had been just a simple outing, but for others, it could have been an educational opportunity, a necessity, or an experience they might never get again.
- Srijani (17), Class XI, DAV School, Siliguri
When a simple gift says it all
It was December 12, 2025 — my 16th birthday.
All my closest friends were invited, and I was so excited to open my presents. One by one, I started unwrapping them.
I gasped! A MAKEUP SET! A JEWELLERY BOX! A HANDMADE CARD!
I was overwhelmed and felt so grateful.
Then came my best friend’s gift. But as soon as I removed the wrapper, there was complete silence. It was a plain black T-shirt. My other friends exchanged looks as if I had been gifted a bomb. However, the sparkle in my best friend’s eyes spoke louder than the silence. The next day, one of my friends came up to me and whispered, “Hey, Zohra, your best friend only gifted you a T-shirt and nothing else?”
I was stunned. What was she saying? Why were we shaming someone over a gift? Instead of defending my friend, I started justifying why she couldn’t gift me something better. I still regret not speaking up for her. But that hurtful comment doesn’t matter to me anymore. I wear that T-shirt with so much pride and contentment, as if it were the last T-shirt in the entire world.
Gifts aren’t a test of how much money someone has. The thought, time and care behind them are worth more than their price tag.
- Zohra Anwar (16), Class 11 Science F, Delhi Public School, Siliguri, West Bengal
What money cannot buy
Looking back at my childhood, I can see two contrasting beliefs. As a toddler, I thought money could buy happiness because it could get me the toys I wanted. As I grew older, I began to think otherwise. But today, I feel both my past selves were right.
“Money can buy happiness in the sense that it fetches you things that you want to have, but it is also true that money cannot ‘buy’ emotional attachment.”
It cannot buy a mother’s adoration, a father’s pampering, a grandparent’s worry, a friend’s care, or a cousin’s teasing. Money makes certain experiences and interactions possible, and buying a gift can be one way of expressing love. But it is not the ultimate reason for happiness, nor does having more of it guarantee a happy life.
I would tell anyone who feels pressured to spend more or keep up with friends to set boundaries. Never push yourself beyond your means just to fit in. If your friends truly value you, they will understand your circumstances. Relationships are meant to support you during difficult times, not make you struggle to keep up with expectations.
- Priyansi Gupta (15), Bhavan’s Gangabux Kanoria Vidyamandir, Kolkata, West Bengal
Handmade for the win
A common problem I have faced while growing up is materialism in friendships. When a close friend gives me an expensive, shiny gift, I instantly feel the pressure to give them something equally good, even if it is only in my head. I begin to associate love with money.
I have always loved giving small gifts to my friends and often choose to make them by hand instead.
Over the years, I have realised that nothing compares to the time, effort and thought put into creating something for someone. Whether it is a small birthday card, a personalised scrapbook or a crochet keychain, spending hours making something for another person makes it feel special.
There is something lovely about watching someone open a handmade gift and seeing their eyes light up. Not because of what it is worth, but because they can see the love and care stitched into every detail. We share a smile, knowing that this little creation is one of a kind. That brings us true happiness.
- Shree Sen (17), Class XI, Little Angels School, Siliguri, West Bengal
Making room for everyone
One incident I remember was when my friends and I planned to watch Spider-Man: Brand New Day. I was the one who had planned the outing almost two months in advance, and I was genuinely excited. But when the time came, I realised that the tickets were quite expensive and I was low on funds. I had to tell my friends that I wouldn’t be able to make it. It was disappointing, especially because I had been looking forward to it for so long.
My friends even offered to pay for my ticket, but I decided to refuse. They weren’t happy about me missing the movie, but they understood my situation and went ahead with the plan. I did feel left out, but eventually accepted that I couldn’t take part in every experience when my finances didn’t allow it.
Another incident that stands out was during our Class 12 farewell. Our group had planned to visit a café, but one of our friends was going through financial difficulties. Instead of letting her miss the outing, we decided to contribute towards her share so that she could join us.
She knew everyone had contributed and became emotional. We weren’t simply paying for her food; we were making sure she didn’t miss out on a memory we all wanted her to be part of.
These experiences taught me that money should not affect the quality of a friendship. You don’t have to attend every outing or spend beyond your means to prove that you belong. Real friends understand that everyone has different financial circumstances.
- Ayush Prasad (17), B.Com Semester 1, Goenka College of Commerce and Business Administration, Kolkata, West Bengal
When effort means more
In Class 4, I went to a friend’s birthday party and gifted her a bracelet-making set because she loved wearing bracelets. Others had brought expensive gifts, such as dresses, necklaces and toys. Seeing them, I felt sad for a while. Was my gift not good enough? But at the end of dinner, my friend announced that she loved it because it reflected her interests. I felt overjoyed!
That experience made me realise that making someone feel special matters more than how much you spend on them. I remember another time when a friend had brought less money to a carnival and planned to skip most of the rides. I offered to share my money so we could both enjoy them. He was happy and thanked me at the end of the day. We are still great friends.
Both experiences taught me that effort and consideration matter more than money in a friendship. Even today, I make it a point to include a simple letter or handmade card with my gifts. It is my way of showing how much I care.
Spandan Das (14), Class 10, Bhavans Gangabux Kanoria Vidyamandir, Kolkata, West Bengal
A basic present
I had forgotten my best friend Mervyn’s birthday. With only ₹70 left from my pocket money, I had no idea what to gift him. After school, I visited a nearby art shop and bought a few coloured papers, a lavender pen and some chocolates.
That night, I put my artistic skills to use. Using an old gift box, I made a Spider-Man frame, a chocolate bouquet and a bracelet. I also added a pencil pouch I had been saving for the next school session.
The next day, I took the box to school. I felt embarrassed handing it over, especially knowing that my friend had received some fancy gifts from his family. But when I returned to class, he whispered, “It was the greatest gift someone has ever given to me.”
He loved the frame and bracelet and was already wearing it. He had even saved some chocolates from the bouquet for me. He told me that he needed a new pencil pouch because his old one was torn, but had never mentioned it. Even today, when I visit his home, I see the Spider-Man frame on his table. It reminds me that sometimes, all a person wants is care and effort, not expensive things. Maybe money cannot buy happiness all the time.
Anant Bubna (14), Bhavan’s Gangabux Kanoria Vidyamandir (B.G.K.V), Class 10, Kolkata, West Bengal
Together, these experiences show that the value of a gift lies not in its price, but in the thought, effort and affection behind it. They remind us that friendship is not about how much we spend, but how well we understand and care for one another.

In 1924, Dutch physician and physiologist Willem Einthoven was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine “for his discovery of the mechanism of the electrocardiogram (ECG)”.
His work made it possible to record the electrical activity of the heart with greater accuracy. By developing the string galvanometer and establishing a standard method for interpreting its recordings, Einthoven helped turn electrocardiography into an important tool for studying heart function. Today, the ECG is routinely used to investigate irregular heart rhythms, detect signs of reduced blood supply to the heart muscle and identify evidence of previous heart attacks.

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi announced a series of social security measures for gig workers in Telangana, including accident insurance of ₹5 lakh, health insurance of ₹10 lakh, dedicated Wi-Fi-enabled rest zones and a mechanism to ensure that 1% of every transaction is credited towards their social security.
Addressing gig workers, Mr. Gandhi said the Congress government in Telangana was fulfilling its promise to protect workers engaged in the platform-based economy and ensure that they received their fair share of the benefits generated by their labour.
Describing the 21st century as the age of data, Mr. Gandhi pointed out that while companies such as Google, Facebook, WhatsApp, and Uber operated on data, gig workers had so far been denied access to information about their own work.
Under the proposed legislation, workers would be able to access complete details of their transactions, deliveries, working hours, and payments through their mobile phones. “The data belongs to you, the labour is yours, but you were not even allowed to see your own data,” he said.
He said the government would also establish dedicated, Wi-Fi-enabled rest zones in Hyderabad and other cities to enable delivery personnel and other gig workers to park their vehicles, rest and relax during working hours.
Announcing insurance benefits, Mr Gandhi said every gig worker would receive ₹5 lakh in accident insurance and ₹10 lakh in health insurance. A social security contribution mechanism under which 1% of every transaction, including deliveries and cab rides, would be contributed towards the workers’ future security.
The amount would be collected from companies and routed through the Gig Workers’ Board before being transferred directly to the workers’ bank accounts, he said.
Drawing a political distinction between the Congress and the BJP-RSS, Mr. Gandhi alleged that the latter wanted to turn gig workers into bonded labourers while allowing large corporate houses and platform companies to reap the benefits. In contrast, the Congress believed that workers were the foundation of the country’s economy and should be treated as partners.
“Do not be afraid. The Telangana Government, Rahul Gandhi, Revanth Reddy, and the Congress team stand with you. We want to make you partners and ensure protection for you and your families,” he said.
Revanth recalls Bharat Jodo Yatra
Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy said the Congress government had fulfilled the promise made by Rahul Gandhi to gig workers in Telangana by bringing in legislation to protect their rights and provide them with social security.
Speaking at an event in the presence of Mr. Rahul Gandhi, the Chief Minister recalled that during the Bharat Jodo Yatra from Kanyakumari to Kashmir in 2023, which covered nearly 4,000 km, Mr. Gandhi had understood the difficulties faced by people from different sections of society.
“The Gandhi family stands by its word. A promise made by Rahul Gandhi is as good as a commitment written in golden letters. For us, his word is an instruction,” the Chief Minister said.
Labour Minister Vivek Venkataswamy also spoke on the occasion. Deputy CM Bhatti Vikramarka, Ministers Ponnam Prabhakar, Komatireddy Venkata Reddy, Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy and TPCC President Mahesh Kumar Goud were present.
